# TO THE GENTLE READER.

[Large decorative initial A] That Alchemy (most courteous Reader) excels in variety, nobility, and dignity among all those arts which human reason has discovered for the use of life, no one, unless unjustly, would call into doubt: all philosophers, as if with one voice (though in diverse tongues), crying out that this art is not only true, but also that nothing after the divine law, in which is the salvation of the soul, has been granted by the highest God in this world to the human race, neither more magnificent nor more sublime; and therefore proclaiming that it is to be investigated with the utmost diligence and sought with every effort. But just as noble wine does not need a suspended ivy sign, so neither does this art need praise, whose not only undoubted truth, but also its supreme and widespread usefulness throughout the life of all men, which is especially observed in this art, as much in Medicine as in pharmaceutical art and many other sciences, especially in the transmutation of metals, is so clear and evident, that it seems by no means to desire the ornaments of speech or the light of eloquence. Lest anything

--- Page 11 ---
*PREFACE.*

What shall I say now about the most necessary (art), for the various uses of life, the working of minerals and metallic veins, and other countless advantages of this art, which I omit for the sake of brevity, since it will be enough to signify what it would be too much to elaborate on. Different people approach it with different aims. The Philosopher is driven by the love and pursuit of acquiring wisdom, rejoicing in knowledge itself, and by an elegant and copious discourse on divine miracles in nature for the glory of the omnipotent creator. This fruit is sufficiently generous and fruitful for a Philosopher, for whom also, for acquiring wealth, there are not lacking the most expeditious means, if he wished to use them, and not rather, inflamed by the love of Philosophy, had proposed to himself to devote himself to this, having voluntarily neglected other mockeries of fortune.

With such a mind, we see the wise men of the Saracens, Egyptians, Arabs, and Persians to have been, who, when they were oppressed by the cruelty of tyrants and everywhere were driven as exiles from their homes, consulted for themselves by the remedy and protection of their art, and acquired for themselves not only sufficient sustenance through the discovered metallic transmutation, but also an honorable and royal one.

For wherever gold and silver could be reached, they demonstrated by the very fact that a way was open to them also. About this true transmutation of metals, which is perfected by the Elixir alone, or the Philosopher's Stone, here our discourse is primarily, concerning which, although books by many authors exist, as this very book, called the Hermetic Museum...

--- Page 12 ---
PRÆFATIO.

named, which already came to light some years ago; nevertheless, since there is no small number of chemical authors, and a great diversity and variety of writings, so that one writes more clearly and openly than another, and one explains another, I was advised by some friends, very skilled in this art, to add to this very book, the Hermetic Museum, some things pertinent to the matter and most necessary for this art. For although, as said above, it had been composed some years ago from the writings of selected men most skilled in this art, it was not found so complete in all its parts, or so perfect in all respects, that it could sufficiently and abundantly bring the hoped-for fruit to the studies of its readers.

Therefore, to this most honorable will of my friends, which primarily aimed at the common utility of those studying this art, we gladly assented. And we took care to have this entire book, augmented by various most selected authors and adorned with many copperplate figures, transcribed for printing. Especially since we considered with ourselves that many counterfeit books, and false recipes (as they call them) of alchemists, composed by the fraud and avarice of impostors, in which not even a spark of truth shines, circulate among the investigators of natural and occult arts. By these, very many have been deceived, and are still being deceived. However, those who read this book, in which the mastery of the Stone is expressed most clearly and plainly: no error is placed, no false-

--- Page 13 ---
**PREFACE.**

...no error placed, no falsehood joined, so that by this means they may be safe from the wicked crowd of smoke-sellers, for whom deception is sweet. For here indeed all errors are elucidated and eliminated. Wherefore I offer this present book to the sons of science, so that while they are engaged with every thought and movement of mind in investigating nature's hidden operations, from it they may know and perceive the truth of things, and nature itself. In which thing alone consists the perfection of the whole most holy philosophical ART, provided they proceed by the Royal Way which nature prescribes in all operations. As for the rest, I earnestly ask the sons of art that they accept this my endeavor to do them good with a benevolent spirit, and when, by God's will and constant labor, they have arrived at the desired philosophical harbor, they exclude all unworthy ones from this art in a philosophical manner, and, mindful of love towards their needy neighbor in the fear of GOD, with vain ostentation set aside, they may sing eternal praises to the Best and Thrice Greatest, for this singular and divine gift, without abuse, in a silent and piously rejoicing bosom.

PREFACE.

[Large decorative initial N]o not wonder, kind Reader, and true seeker of natural
secrets, why in this old age of the world,
where it already has one foot in Charon's boat,
I have been led to write this little treatise,
since almost all libraries are filled with books
written on this subject, of which, however, the greater part
is filled with false and counterfeit philosophy, and recipes of the same kind.
Not for my own sake, but for your benefit, I have written
this, whatever it may be, so that by demonstrating the basis of truth, I may lead you
back from erroneous paths into the true path; in which, indeed,
your interest is not small. As far as I am concerned, I have long since known
whatever I ought to know in this business, nor do I need a multitude of books,
since within twenty-two years I have read, thoroughly read, and re-read
as many books as came into my hands; among which number,
which was indeed large, there were many both manuscript
and printed.
In this treatise of mine, I have outlined the matter with its theoretical
solution, as well as the practical part, allegorically delineated, in clear and plain

*words you will find, in such a way that you can scarcely find them among any philosopher. Moreover, I took pains to speak with philosophers, for which purpose I diligently noted both the names and all the places where they put forward this or that opinion, so that you yourself can inquire therein, weigh my allegations, and thereby sharpen your own intellect. Indeed, I could have composed this treatise with less effort, omitting these citations, and made myself known to the brothers of the Golden Cross, had there not been another plan for the sake of your convenience and benefit. Nor will it seem strange to you that I conceal my name and refuse to show myself to you in person. For I do not seek my own vain glory in this matter, nor to be magnified before the world, but I strive to benefit you. Moreover, my teachers, true philosophers indeed, did not authorize me to despise my life for the sake of haughty authority, sell it to avaricious robbers, and by the prostitution of this most secret arcana, provide an opportunity for many sins to be committed. I do not doubt that the fair reader has learned from Sendivogius that he, whenever he wished to manifest himself to magnates, always fell into danger and detriment. Experience testifies that many philosophers, carelessly neglecting themselves, were killed and plundered of their tincture by avaricious and proud robbers who made light of their own lives: reason confirms that anyone carrying around some great treasure in their hands shows a rich prey to robbers. Sendivogius had concealed his name with an anagram: So also, a short time ago, another philosopher, and a brother of the Golden Cross, whose name has long since become known to me, did so under an anagram,*

--- Page 18 ---
**PREFACE. 5**

...under an anagram, he manifested himself to you, and by his own enigma. Why then should I prostitute myself to this unclean world? In this, friend, be content, that I wished to show myself to the wise, and to demonstrate my name, as has been abundantly done, leaving the rest to God, thrice best, greatest, who, if he knows this will redound to the glory of his name and to my and your benefit, will make me known to you soon enough. Do not inquire too closely into my name. For even if perhaps you know this, or you know me myself, nevertheless you will be compelled to acquiesce in this little treatise. I have sworn to Bernard, Count of Tresnes and Neiges, to philosophers, and to equity, that I would reveal nothing further to any man than has been done here. Do not also be concerned whether I hold this precious treasure in my hands: inquire rather whether I have seen how the world was created? How the darkness of Egypt behaved itself? What is the cause of the rainbow? What appearance will bodies have, clarified by the universal resurrection? What is the most constant color? But from you, who rightly understand this little book of mine, I ask whether you have seen that great and salty sea, without any corrosion, which is enough to raise the tinctures of all things even to the highest mountains? Tell me where is sulfur from sulfur, and mercury from mercury? Or where is sulfur from mercury, and mercury from sulfur in turn? When was the idea of the most ardent love subjected to your eyes, where the male and the female tightly embrace each other, so that even in the future they can never be torn apart, but because of an inscrutable love they become one thing; If you have understood what this is that I say, and you have worked that very thing with your hands and have seen it with your eyes, I am your companion, and more certain you

      But if anyone wishes to complain about the difficulty of this art, let him be certainly persuaded that it will not be difficult in and of itself, indeed, that it is very easy for those who love God and have been deemed worthy of this knowledge by Him. # THE GOLDEN TREATISE,
### ON
# THE PHILOSOPHER'S
# STONE.

[Large decorative initial T]Both ancient and modern philosophers, dearest Reader, and most friendly seeker of true wisdom, after they had, by God's will, attained the goal of their desire, have always been accustomed to reveal themselves through their writings to their colleagues hiding here and there throughout the world: not only with this aim, that they wished to assure them that God, the Thrice Best and Greatest, had enlightened their understanding, had blessed the labors of their hands, and had revealed to them the most secret and greatest mystery of this earthly wisdom, for which benefit indeed, deserved praises, honor, and glory are due to Him; but also that they might offer an opportunity to their neighbor and to the art-loving disciple, God thus assenting, to attain this most sacred art and its knowledge. Men of this kind have existed in all nations: Egyptians, among whom Hermes Trismegistus uniquely stands out, Chaldeans, Greeks, Arabs, Italians, French, English, Dutch, Spanish, Germans, Poles, Hungarians, Hebrews, and many others. It is wonderful, however, that the aforementioned wise men, writing in different languages at different times, agree so much in their books with such harmony, that it is easy for any true philosopher to recognize that God has gladdened their minds with this blessed stone, and that they themselves have perfected this work with their own hands. But just as truth shines forth from such agreement, so from the disagreement of the pseudo-philosopher and the sophist

--- Page 22 ---
**On the Philosopher's Stone.** 9

sophists are identified. For they, ignorant of the foundation of this renowned art, and inventing whatever they please from their own brain, reveal their errors to all.
   The harmony mentioned, however, consists primarily in the knowledge of the matter, and its solution, weight, regulation of fire, and augmentation.
   As far as the matter is concerned, it is unique, having within itself all that it needs, and from which the artist prepares whatever he wishes, N I S V S namely in the SAND, as the philosopher Anastratus says in the Turba: *Nothing is more precious than the red sand of the sea, and it is the spittle of the Moon, which is joined to the light of the Sun, and congeals.* That this unique matter is required, Agadmon testifies in the same place, where he says: *Know, that unless you take this body of mine lacking spirit, you will by no means obtain what you desire, because nothing foreign enters the work, nor anything unless it is pure. Therefore, abandon all plurality. For nature is content with one thing, and he who is ignorant of it will perish.*
   In the same way, Arnold of Villanova writes in his Flower of Flowers: *Our Stone is made from one thing and with one thing.* Similarly, he speaks to the King of Naples: *Everything that is in our Stone is necessary to it, nor does it need anything foreign: since our Stone is of one nature, and one thing.* And Rosinus says: *Know that there is one unique thing, from which all things you desire are made.* And Lilium: *You have no need but of one thing, which in every stage of our work is changed into another nature.* So also Geber in his Summa says: *Our Stone is one, one medicine, to which we add nothing, nor diminish anything, we only remove superfluities.* And Scites in the Turba: *The foundation of this art is one thing, which is stronger and more sublime than all things, and is called the sharpest vinegar, which made pure gold a spirit, without which neither whiteness, nor blackness, nor redness exists. And when it is mixed with the body, it is contained, and becomes one with it, and returns it into spirit, and tinctures it with a spiritual, invariable tincture; again, from the tinctured [body] it receives a corporeal tincture, which cannot be destroyed. And if you place the body without vinegar upon the fire, it will be burned and corrupted.* But from these words of Scites, someone concluding might infer, not one, but two things, namely the body,
B and vine-

--- Page 23 ---
10                                  *The Golden Treatise,*

...and vinegar (as he calls it) is required, and that the moist must necessarily be joined with the dry, lest the dry be burned by the fire, but preserved from such combustion by the moist. Indeed, I gladly subscribe to this sound conclusion, while preserving the aforementioned philosophical opinions in their value and truth. For it is more certain than certain that there is only one matter of our blessed stone, named by the wise with many names, which ingenious Nature has long since prepared, and willed that it alone, and no other matter of our stone in the whole world, should exist. This matter is subject to the eyes of everyone; the whole world beholds it, touches it, loves it, yet does not know it. It is noble and base, precious and of little moment, and is found everywhere. Theophrastus Paracelsus, in his book *On the Tincture of Physicians*, calls it the **RED LION**, named by many, but known by few. Hermes, in the 1st chapter of his treatise, calls it *quicksilver coagulated in the innermost chambers*. In the *Turba*, it is here and there called *aes*. In the *Rosary of the Philosophers*, it is designated by the name of Salt. But, to be brief, this matter of ours has as many names as there are things in the world; hence it is less known by the foolish. I call those foolish who approach the art without prior knowledge of nature and its properties, like a donkey to the manger, not knowing for what purpose it extends its snout, as Arnold says. Hence Geber aptly states in *Summa perfectionis*: *He who in himself ignores the natural principles, he is already very far removed from this art.* And the *Rosary* says: *I advise that no one should involve himself in this art to discover anything unless he knows the true principle of nature and its regimen, which being known, he needs no more things than one, nor does he require great expenses, since there is one stone, one medicine, one vessel, one regimen, and one disposition.* Nevertheless, this single matter is so separated by the work of nature and the experience of the artist, as Theophrastus speaks, that it is transmuted into that white eagle, and the splendor of the sun no longer illuminates the spagyric with its rays: or, as Basilius Valentinus says, that from it is made a white spirit like snow, and likewise another red spirit like blood, which two spirits contain a third hidden within themselves. Hence King Aros says, not badly: *Our medicine is made from two things of one essence, namely from the uni-*

--- Page 24 ---
**Of the Philosopher's Stone.** **11**

union of fixed and non-fixed mercurial nature, spiritual and corporeal, cold and humid, hot and dry, and can by no means be made from anything else. And Richard the Englishman says: *The Stone is one, one medicine, which according to the philosophers is called REBIS, that is, from a twofold thing, namely from a body and a white or red spirit, in which many fools have erred, explaining it in various ways:*
     *Rebis is in the most correct form in the aforementioned descriptions, that is, two things: and these two things are one thing, that is, water joined to the body, by which the body is dissolved into spirit, that is, into mineral water, from which it was made from the beginning: And thus from body and spirit is made one mineral water, which is called Elixir, that is, ferment: because then water and spirit are one thing, from which is made the tincture, and the medicine for purifying all bodies. Therefore, from one thing, which is the water of the body and spirit, the medicine is perfected. And thus according to the philosophers we have the nature of sulfur and mercury above ground, from which gold and silver are made under ground.*
And Bernard, Count of Treviso and the Marches, says: *Our work is made from one root and two crude mercurial substances, taken, and drawn from the ore, pure and clean, joined by fire in friendship, as the material itself demands, continually cooked, until from two one is made, etc.*
And Basil Valentine in the book of natural and supernatural things, chapter 4, says: *In all truth, by the love of God, I will moreover reveal this to you, that the root of philosophical sulfur, which is a celestial spirit, along with the root of spiritual and hyperphysical mercury, and the principle of spiritual salt, exists in one and is found in a single matter, from which the stone, which was before me, is made, and not from many: although by all philosophers mercury by itself, sulfur by itself, and salt by itself are particularly alleged, as if mercury is found in one, sulfur in another, and salt in a third. But I tell you that these things, thus brought forth from their abundance, demonstrate in what [substances] they are copiously found, and how they can be conveniently applied and prepared in many particular ways, both for healing human bodies and for transmuting metals. But that universal thing (indeed the highest treasure of this earthly wisdom, and the principles of all three things) is a certain unique thing, and they are found and extracted simultaneously in one thing, which is able to convert all metals into one: And they are the true spirit of mercury, and the soul of sulfur, united together with spiritual salt, and enclosed under one heaven, and also dwelling in one body; and they are the dragon and the eagle, the king and the lion, spirit and body, tinging the body of gold into a true medicine, etc.*

In this way also, our prepared matter is called male and female, active and passive; just as Zimon says in the Turba: *Know that the secret of the work consists of male and female, that is, active and passive. In lead is the male, in orpiment the female. The male rejoices in the female received and is helped by her, and the female receives from the male the tinging sperm, and is colored by it.* And Diomedes says: *Join the male, the son of the red servant, to his fragrant wife, and being joined they will beget the art, to whom do not introduce anything foreign, neither powder, nor any other thing, and the conception will suffice for you, and a true son will be born.* Oh, how most precious is the nature of that red servant, without which the regimen cannot endure. Others call it quicksilver, or mercury, and sulfur or fire, just as Roger Bacon says in chapter 3 of the Mirror: *From sulfur and mercury all metals are made, and nothing adheres to them, nor is joined to them, nor transmutes them, except that which is from them. And thus by right we ought to accept mercury and sulfur as the matter of the stone.* And Menabadus: *He who joins quicksilver to the body of magnesia, and the female to the male, extracts a hidden nature, by which bodies are colored.* Lullius says in the Codicil: *The property of our mercury is that it is coagulated by its sulfur.* And in the practice of his testament he says: *Quicksilver is a supernatant and flowing humidity preserving from combustion.*

Others call it body, spirit, and soul. Thus Arnoldus says in the Flower of Flowers: *The Philosophers said that our stone is composed of body, and soul and spirit, and they spoke truly. For they compared the imperfect body to a body because it is weak. They called water spirit, and truly, because it is spirit. They called ferment soul, because it imparts life to the imperfect body, which it did not have before, and produces a better form.*

And a little above he says: *The spirit is not joined to the body except through the mediation of the soul. For the soul is the medium between the body and the spirit, itself joining them together.* And Morienus: The soul quickly enters its own body, but if you strive to join it to a foreign body, you will labor in vain. And Lilium: Soul, body, and spirit are together, and it is one thing which has all things in itself, and to which nothing is added.

--- Page 26 ---
*On the Philosopher's Stone.* 13

But to what end shall we bring forth and explain all the names by which this our material is designated? We shall rest content with those that are more frequent and nearer to our intention, and after investigating our material, where indeed it may lie hidden, and from where it ought to be brought forth, we shall consider something concerning the solution, as the chief part of the matter, and by its treatment we shall sharpen our intellect.

Therefore, regarding the consideration of our material, what it is and where it ought to be sought, it must be noted, as they say, with a white stone (i.e., carefully), that the omnipotent Creator, whose wisdom is as infinite as He Himself is, in the beginning of things, when nothing existed but Himself, created two things: namely, celestial things, and those things which are contained under the heavens. Celestial things are the heavens themselves and their inhabitants, concerning which we shall refrain from speaking or philosophizing more subtly or extensively in this place. But those things which exist under the heaven, created from the four Elements, are found to be three in number, and are commonly accustomed to be divided into three kinds. Of these, those which live and feel hold the first place, and are called animals. The second kind comprises whatever things are produced from the earth and do not feel, and are called vegetables. Finally, whatever things come forth under the earth are numbered in the third kind, and are called minerals. These three kinds of created things therefore embrace all things produced from the elements under the globe of the Moon, nor are more or fewer found than these, and in such a way by the highest God each thing in its own kind and species has been confirmed, so that it is impossible for them to leap from one kind to another. As if someone should try to make a man or a tree from a stone, or from a plant some ape or lead, or from lead should attempt to make some animal or plant. This, I say, is impossible by the ordinance of the Highest King. For if this were permitted in the nature of things, some of these, indeed all kinds, could be converted into one. But because from that all things would collapse, the Lord of lords did not wish to grant such a transmutation; indeed, what is more, He not only wished each thing to be preserved in its own kind, but also implanted in each of the creatures its own proper seed, by which it may be increased in its own species and persist in its own kind, nor can its species be changed into another's. As if someone should try to change the species of a man into that of a horse, or of an apple into that of a lettuce, a diamond, or another...

--- Page 27 ---
14 *Golden Treatise*

...or if someone wished to change another stone into gold, he would be utterly mistaken; since this is by no means permitted in the nature of sublunary things: And just as it was from the beginning, so it will be in the end, when the Almighty, who said FIAT in the beginning, will say, PEREAT. But among those things, whose material, seed, and composition of Elements are one and common, improvement and exaltation can easily be made and perfected according to the purity and perfection of their material. For example, we see a man endowed with a subtle and keen intellect raised to a higher degree of dignity than others who are not of such intellect, which derives its origin from the purity and subtlety of the spirits that are born from a rectified and well-constituted body. Thus we observe this horse far excelling another in its nobility, which is plainly visible in all species of living beings. Therefore, just as we see these things in animals, so much more may we observe them in herbs and trees. In trees, by transplantations, graftings, and other means known to gardeners; but in herbs, we are taught by daily experience how herbs and flowers of one species differ from another in their nobility, beauty, odor, and taste. Let carnations (which they call "tunic flowers") and tulips be an example to us, to say nothing of others. Good God, into how many species have these extended? Into innumerable ones, I say, which also become nobler and rarer day by day with diligent care, so much so that it is acknowledged that such fragrant and elegant flowers did not exist before. But what shall I say about metals, whose one common material is, namely, quicksilver digested and coagulated by the power of sulfur? Concerning this common material, Richard the Englishman thus begins:
*The nature of things has naturally produced all kinds of fusible substances from mercury and the substance of its sulfur, because it is characteristic of quicksilver that it coagulates from vapor, just as from the heat of white or red non-burning sulfur.*
And Arnold, part 1, ch. 2: *Quicksilver is the Element of all fusible substances; for all fusible substances, when they melt, are converted into it, and it mixes with them, because it is of their substance: although these bodies differ in their composition from quicksilver, in the way that it itself was pure or impure from unclean sulfur foreign to it.*
Rosinus

--- Page 28 ---
On the Philosopher's Stone. 15

Rosinus to Saratanta: *The matter of all metals is digested and imperfect quicksilver in the belly of the earth, with sulphurous heat cooking it, and according to the sulphurous variety, different metals are generated in the earth, since their primordial matter is one and the same, only by greater or lesser action, with moderation arriving or not arriving.* Therefore we see daily how nature itself is continuously concerned with their mortification and perfection, until they are perfected into gold, which is nature's final intention. For all metals show that nature has worked in them somewhat towards further perfection; indeed, no metal is found so diminished from perfection that it does not contain a grain of gold or silver. And indeed, with metals it is so arranged that nature, from quicksilver having its own sulfur with it, strives to produce gold very soon and is even capable of it, unless some external impediment intervenes, namely, impure, stinking, and burning sulfur, just as in many places we see pure, unadulterated, and refined gold being extracted, without the admixture of other metals. But because in mines, external sulfur is for the most part mixed with quicksilver, that (sulfur) infects this (quicksilver), and hinders it from perfection: according to the variety of that sulfur, various species of metals are also generated; just as Aristotle says in the 4th book of Meteorology: *If the quicksilver is of good substance, and the sulfur is not pure and burning, it converts the quicksilver itself into copper. Also, if the quicksilver is stony, impure, earthy, and the sulfur is not pure, iron will be made from it: tin, however, seems to have good and pure quicksilver; but bad and not well-mixed sulfur. Lead, however, has coarse and bad quicksilver, of bad and stinking taste, from which it does not coagulate well.*

However, that hindering, burning, and stinking sulfur is not the true fire that digests metals; but quicksilver contains its own proper sulfur within itself, which is sufficient for digesting itself, just as Bernard, Count of Treviso, says: *Some wrongly believe that some sulphurous matter intervenes in the procreation of metals; but on the contrary, it is clearly evident that sulfur is enclosed in mercury when nature operates.*

Of the Philosopher's Stone. 17

or after it has separated the external and bad sulfur of the other metals through digestion in the course of time, it may turn into gold, which is the end of metals, and the true intention of nature: we are certainly compelled to confess and say, that nature, both in this kind as well as in the vegetable and animal kingdom, according to the purity and subtlety of the subject, seeks and demands the improvement and perfection of its own nature.
    O friendly seeker of nature, I wished to pursue these things somewhat more at length, so that you may much more easily know the matter of our stone and be able to convert it to use. For if you wished to produce this stone of ours from animal matter, it is hindered by the fact that these two are founded in different kinds. For the stone is mineral, but you would require animal matter. *But nothing from any thing, as Richard our author says in the first chapter, can be extracted which is not in it. Therefore every species in its own species, and every genus in its own genus, and every nature in its own nature naturally strives for an increase of virtue, and brings forth fruit according to its own nature, and not in another nature contrary to itself: since every sown thing corresponds to its own seed.* And Basilius Valentinus says: *Consider and understand, my friend, that the animal soul is not to be chosen by you for this intention of yours. For flesh and blood, just as they were granted to animals by the Creator, so also are they proper to animals, from which animals are formed and born.* Therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder at those who wish to appear great artists, and nevertheless in women's menses, sperm, eggs, hair, urine, and other things of that kind, inquire into the matter of the stone, and are not afraid to fill so many books with their vain and empty recipes, so that they may also, with these foolish, futile, and useless things, deceive and mislead others less prudent. Rogerius in the third chapter of his mirror cannot sufficiently wonder at the vanities of such men, when he says: *Wherefore it is to be wondered at, that any prudent person should found his intention upon animals or vegetables, which are very remote; when minerals are found sufficiently close. Nor is it to be believed at all, that any of the philosophers placed the art*

--- Page 31 ---
18	*The Golden Treatise.*

the art in the aforementioned remote things, except by way of similitude. *For our Stone (says Basilius) does not grow from combustible things. Indeed, this Stone, and its matter, are quite safe from all violence. Therefore cease to seek it in animals; since it is not granted by nature to find it therein.*
	But if anyone persuades himself to find our Stone in vegetables, such as trees, herbs, or flowers, he, for the reasons mentioned above, will err no less than he who wishes to induce his mind to make a stone from an animal. Indeed, all herbs and trees, with all things produced from them, are burned, and leave nothing behind them but the salt itself with its earth, which salt it received from nature in the first composition of its species. Nor let anyone allow himself to be deceived, because some boast that the philosophical stone can be produced from wheat. Nor are those more to be listened to, who persuade themselves to make our Stone from wine and its parts. For when they less attain the mind of Raymond Lull, declared in his writings, they indeed demonstrate that by knowing too much they know absolutely nothing, and deceive themselves and others. Indeed, I will not deny that from these are prepared and made most excellent menstrua, without which nothing solid can be done either in medicine or in chemistry: but that the philosophers' stone can be prepared from them, or its seed extracted from them, I entirely deny, since, by the Creator of all things so commanding, it is right for everything to persist in its own kind, as has been said, and it can in no way transgress that. Hence anyone, devoted to true wisdom, can gather that our Stone can be drawn neither from vegetables nor from animals, as they are combustible; whence reason commands to conclude that it is to be sought and prepared only in incombustible things, namely the mineral kingdom. Since therefore the Stone of the wise is a certain mineral, and there are very many species of minerals, such as stones, among which are reckoned clay and various earths, salts, intermediate minerals, and metals, it is not unfittingly asked, from which of them it ought to be prepared? I answer, that it is impossible for it to be made from stones; the reason is, that in them there is no fusible and liquefiable mercury, nor can they be melted, dissolved, or reduced to their prime matter because of the abundance of external sulfur and adhering earthy property.

--- Page 32 ---
*Of the Philosopher's Stone.* 19

A prudent investigator of nature's secrets will also refrain from seeking the matter of the blessed stone in salts, alums, and similar things. For in these, he will indeed find a sharp, corroding, and corrupting spirit, but he will never obtain mercury and sulfur from them, according to the opinion of the philosophers. Moreover, from these, intermediate minerals, such as magnesia, marcasite, antimony, etc., much less can any metal ever be made: in what way then could the matter of the stone, which is the end and perfection of all metals and minerals, be extracted from them? I add that they have nothing in common or familiar with metals, but rather burn, corrode, and corrupt them: how then will they be able to serve their improvement?

Hear Richard the Englishman speaking on this matter in the tenth chapter: *Lesser minerals cannot become metals, firstly, because they are not generated from the prime matter of metals, which is quicksilver. But since their generation differs primarily from the generation of mercury in form, matter, and composition, therefore they also cannot become metals, because for one species there is one prime matter, and one seed from which it is generated. But the first part of the preceding statement is clear, because lesser minerals are not generated from mercury, as is clear from Aristotle and Avicenna. Therefore, if they were to become metals, it would be necessary for them to transform into the prime matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, therefore they will by no means be metals, and consequently, they cannot be the matter of the stone. Thus the second part of the preceding statement is sufficiently clear. Secondly; because lesser minerals cannot artificially become the principle of the art, which is mercury, therefore they also do not reach the middle and the end, which are metals and the tincture. But because lesser minerals are foreign to the nature of metals, although they participate in some mineral power, nevertheless they are of weaker virtue, and combustible. Therefore, metallic nature does not rejoice in them, but rejects them, but preserves those things which are of its own nature. Wherefore foolish are those who bring forth so many and such diverse undertakings and sophistries to deceive men, namely, disproportionate things, which neither give nature nor receive it. Thus he.*

But truly, none of the students of our wisdom, by the above-cited and similar sayings of the philosophers, speaking sometimes of salts,

But what shall we say about vitriol, which also leads many into error with its wondrous qualities, especially because some part of it turns into copper, and it even turns iron itself into copper. Concerning this, it should be briefly known that it is nothing other than the principle and material of copper, where in mines and veins of the earth, a mineral vapor, and a vaporous mercury, so to speak, encounters a certain place in which such a bitter, acidic, pungent, and coppery sulfur lay hidden in abundance, which it immediately absorbed, and in it, to become a metal, it was coagulated. But because nature, in separating the pure from the impure and segregating the combustible from the incombustible, fulfilled its office, and the quantity of the said sulfur far exceeded the quantity of mercury, the mercury, necessarily separated in such a segregation, was compelled to turn into that coppery greenness. This very thing demonstrates common sulfur as the cause of this corruption: when it is joined with copper and exposed to fire (for art accomplishes in a short space of time with strong fire what nature could not perfect with gentle heat over a long interval of time), it quickly burns the copper completely, and by a common manipulation reduces it to the nature of vitriol; and according to the quantity of sulfur, the vitriol becomes richer or poorer in color, hence it happens that one vitriol contains more copper, others less. And because coarse sulfur is also contained in iron, vitriol corrodes it with its acrimony, and seeks its mercury, not much different from its own, and with that, by the conjunction of its sulfur overcoming the mercury, it is reduced to pure copper.

Whence also the general rule of the philosophers has been established: *Our quicksilver is not the quicksilver of the common people.* And Lullius in the first chapter of *Clavicula*: *We say, that common quicksilver cannot be the quicksilver of the philosophers, by whatever artifice it may be prepared: because the common (quicksilver) cannot be held in fire, except by another corporeal quicksilver, which is hot and dry, and more digested.* But the greater part of those philosophizing, from their abundance, has spoken about the sublimation of common mercury and its other preparations, whence so many varied and marvelous methods of operation have been devised, by which the properties of this subject were more thoroughly elucidated: but the goal itself, which they sought so greatly, namely the treasure of this earthly wisdom, they have not yet been able to attain in this subject, since nature has not placed it in it. Nevertheless, in its operation, it is so marvelous that it sometimes deceives even those who consider themselves wiser. Let an example be for us, a certain familiar acquaintance, very well known to me formerly, who, having amalgamated it with gold, as they say, treated it so subtly and accurately that, even passing through all colors, it finally turned yellow; beyond which color, however, it would by no means ascend; whence that good alchemist, moved by this, supplied a higher degree of fire, plainly persuading himself that the same (substance) would now be most fixed, and that, according to the philosophers, it would no longer be possible to err in the regulation of the fire. But frustrated in his hope and persuasion, the glass burst into many particles, and the work was reduced to nothing, with the still volatile mercury carrying the gold with it into the furnace (which is to be well noted), and almost gilding it; whence afterwards much gold scraped off was reduced to its original form, or body, as they call it. In this it appeared that mercury, which is its body, had been able to dissolve gold so minutely that it turned into a tincture, even if several colors appeared, with heat acting on the moist (substance). If indeed that good man, and with him many others, had heeded the words of *Arnold* in *Flos florum*, he would certainly have proceeded less by that method.

the principle, and their origin, by decocting with sulphurous heat, they sublimated mercury by itself; afterwards they fixed it, dissolved it, and coagulated it; but coming to projection they found nothing. &c. Wherefore we cannot persuade ourselves that common quicksilver is the matter of the stone. We do not deny, however, that without its aid nothing substantial can be made, neither in philosophical nor in medical chemistry.
      Hitherto we have anxiously sought the matter of our stone in animals, in vegetables, in stones, in minor, medium, and major minerals; but we have not yet been able to find it in them; wherefore we will have to look further, whether it lies hidden in metals, and if it is in them, whether in all simultaneously, or truly in some, and in which it ought finally to be sought. Indeed it is known, and Rogerius testifies (spec. chapter 3), that all metals are generated from sulfur and quicksilver, and that nothing adheres to them, nor can be applied, or changes them, unless that which took its origin from them: *since the improvement of any thing improves the nature of that thing to which it belongs*, as Richard speaks in chapter 1.
      I will not say that the Supreme Creator wished it to be so arranged in all nature, that every thing generates and produces its like, lest a horse come from a man. *And just as brute animals cannot multiply their like by means of generation, except by the benefit of a similar nature: So the blessed stone (says Basil Valentine) you should not presume to seek from elsewhere than from its own seed, from which our stone was made from the beginning. But in order that you may find the seed, you will safely and properly consider with yourself for what purpose you intend to seek our stone, and you yourself will be able to gather that it cannot have an origin other than from the metallic root from which metals themselves were ordained by God to be made. I add that there is also great conformity between the generation of metals and of the stone. For in both, sulfur and quicksilver, which, as salt, comprehend a noble soul within themselves, are necessarily required; nor is it possible to discern any useful metallic form, until these three, taken from metallic substance, come together in one; inasmuch as nothing ought to be added to metals which did not derive its origin from them. And it is left clearly enough to us, says Draco, that no foreign thing, which did not take (its origin) from these two, sulfur and mercury,*

in his *Summa*, chapter 63, speaking of this impurity of imperfect metals and the properties of perfect mercury: *Through this true investigation, we have discovered a marvelous kind of two secrets. One, indeed, is that there is a twofold cause of corruption of any (imperfect) metal by fire; of which the first is, that the combustible sulfur enclosed within its inner substance is ignited by a strong fire, annihilates the entire substance of the bodies, turns it into smoke, and finally consumes it, notwithstanding the goodness of their mercury. The second cause is, that the external flame is augmented by them, penetrates them, resolves them into smoke, even if they are fixed. The third is, that their bodies are opened by calcination. For then the flame of the fire can penetrate them and turn them into smoke, even if they were fixed. However, when all causes of corruption coincide, bodies are necessarily corrupted and annihilated: but when they do not concur, the speed of the corruption of bodies somewhat diminishes. The second kind of this secret is the goodness, which is considered in bodies by reason of mercury. For mercury, since there is no other cause of corruption and expulsion in it, does not allow itself to be divided into parts of composition, but remains entirely in its substance in fire; whence the cause of its perfection can be known. Therefore, praised be God, blessed and most high, who created it, and bestowed upon it a substance, and upon that substance a property, which cannot be found in any natural thing, so that by any artifice, it can be introduced into that which is found to be akin in this power. For this is that which conquers fire, is not conquered by fire, but rests amicably in it and rejoices in it.* In these
words, Geber clearly demonstrates that the material of our
stone cannot be in imperfect metals: because, being inherently impure, they flee from fire when we wish to purify them; whereas our mercury, by reason of its purity, can persist in fire without any harm.
Therefore, just as imperfect metals alone are not the material of our stone, so too, when mixed together, they can even less provide it, since by their mixture they do not become purer than they were before, not to mention that a new confusion arises here, plainly contrary to our intention, which, as stated above, required a single material.

This Haly clearly testifies in chapter 6 of the book of secrets, saying: *There is one stone, to which you should mix no other thing; with this the wise operate, and from this remains that by which we heal. Nothing else is mixed with it, neither in whole nor in its parts.*
      And Morienus says: *This magistery in the beginning comes from one root, which afterwards is dispersed into many parts, and is converted into one thing.*
      If therefore imperfect metals cannot be the material of the stone, why did the philosophers command to operate in them? I respond. When the philosophers commanded to take impure bodies, by that they did not understand copper, iron, lead, tin, etc., but their own body, or their own earth; just as Arnold says in *Flos Florum*: *Mercury is joined to the earth; that is, to the imperfect body.* For even if their earth is in itself of such perfection and purity, and nature could perfect something; nevertheless, in respect to the physical stone, it is still imperfect and impure: And in this art surpasses nature, because it perfects what nature could not. But that the earth is imperfect before complete purification and regeneration, is clear from this, that at that time it is not yet able to dye and more than perfect, nor does it have more than what nature bestowed upon it; but after regeneration it can do much. But its impurity is most clearly perceived in our work; when indeed it is black, and is assimilated to lead or antimony; afterwards grey, and is called Jupiter, or tin, or magnesia, and this indeed before whiteness; but after whiteness it is called Mars and Venus, before it is brought to perfect redness. But that Basil Valentine is of the same opinion as me, and thinks very differently than he left in writing in the said book, he testifies in his treatise on the great stone, where, investigating the matter of the stone, he had said that in the sun the gift of all three perfections comes together, and from there it has the faculty of persisting in fire, and that the Moon, by reason of its fixed mercury, does not easily recede from fire and bears its test, finally breaks forth into these words. *That noble harlot Venus is clothed and adorned with an superabundant color, and the greatest part of its body is filled with a most abundant tincture, and such is the color that also dwells in the best metal, and because of its*

*its abundance verges on redness. But because its body is leprous, that fixed tincture cannot remain in it, but vanishes with its body. For when the body is corrupted by mortification, the soul also cannot remain, but is forced to yield and flee. Indeed, the dwelling is corrupted and consumed by fire, so much so that its place is unknown, nor can anyone inhabit it in the future. But in a fixed body, it willingly remains. Fixed salt attributes and leaves to strong Mars a hard, vigorous, and coarse body, from which the fortitude of its spirit is recognized, and this leader is not easily conquered. Indeed, its body is hard, which is difficult to wound.*

But if anyone should infer that that fixed sulfur of Venus, according to Basil's doctrine, when joined with the spirit of perfect mercury, can turn into a tincture: Let him know and gather that what has often been repeated before is that our matter certainly does not depend on many things; which Basil also assents to, teaching that *the universal is one thing, and is found and extracted simultaneously in one thing, and is the spirit of mercury, and the soul of sulfur, together with spiritual salt, simultaneously united and enclosed under one heaven, and dwelling in one body;* and undoubtedly, having been led back from his errors to the true path, leaving imperfect metals behind, he turned his mind to more perfect ones, considering that saying of Plato, book 4, chapter 2: *Why do you calcine and dissolve other bodies with great labor, when in these (perfect ones) you find what you seek.* But if you wish to use them, *it is necessary that you first convert them into the nature of perfect bodies.* Therefore, most friendly seeker of natural secrets, abandon all animals and vegetables, all salts, alums, vitriols, marcasites, magnesias, antimony, all imperfect and impure metals, and seek your stone with Arnold of Villanova, part 1, chapter 7: *in mercury and sun for the sun, and in mercury and moon for the moon; because the whole benefit of this art consists in these alone. For just as the principle of ignifying is fire, as Ripley asserts in Gate 1, so gold is the principle of gold-making.* If therefore you strive to make gold and silver by the philosophical art, for this purpose do not take eggs, nor blood, but gold and silver, which, naturally and prudently calcined, and not manually, a new generation

For our mastery, says Arnold Rosar., part 1, chapter 5, aids perfect bodies, and perfects the imperfect without admixture of any other thing.

You should likewise abandon all minerals; and *only* metals [are to be considered]. For although from them is the entrance, and our matter, as all philosophers assert, ought to be composed of quicksilver, and this is not found elsewhere than in metals, as attested by Geber etc., nevertheless they themselves are not our stone, while they are in metallic form. For it is impossible for one and the same matter to have two forms. By what reason can they be the stone, which has a worthy and intermediate form between metal and mercury, unless such a form is first corrupted and removed?

Wherefore also Raymond Lullius in chapter 56 of his Testament says: "And therefore a good artist takes metals as means in the work of the magisterium, and especially the sun and moon, because these two have come into a tempered co-equality, and are much purified from the substance of sulfur and quicksilver, cooked, pure, and well-digested by the ingenuity of nature: to which proportion an artist would vex himself in vain, if he wished to begin from natural principles without real means for the intention of making."

And in the Codicil: "Without these two, namely gold and silver, this art cannot be perfected, since in them is the purest substance of sulfur perfectly purified by the ingenuity of nature, to the purification of which art is weaker than nature, nor is it able to achieve it, although it may labor much in it."

From those two bodies prepared with their sulfur or arsenic, our medicine can be extracted, and without these it cannot be obtained.

And in the preface of his Clavicula he says: "I advise you, O my friends, that you should not work except with the sun and moon, reducing them to their first matter, our sulfur and quicksilver."

Therefore from those bodies, says Arnold in part 1, chapter 7, is extracted sulfur exceedingly white and red, since in them is the purest substance of sulfur highly purified by the ingenuity of nature.

Thus Nicarus in the Turba says: "I command posterity to take gold, which they wish to multiply and renew, then to divide the water into two parts, and indeed to compress the gold itself with the other. For that copper falling into that water will be called the ferment of gold."

But with what audacity does this philosopher call his water gold, when he says: "copper falling into that water will be called the ferment of gold"?

For the unravelling of this difficulty, let the diligent investigator of nature know, that the gold of the philosophers is not the gold of the common people, as Senior teaches.

However, regarding the aforementioned statement, someone could object and ask why philosophers, by their gold, sometimes understand water, sometimes earth; that they seem either to contradict themselves and be inconsistent, or to confuse everything and to have deliberately wished to mislead their disciples. I answer that all and every philosopher, where they reveal the truth itself, wrap it in hidden and allegorical words, yet they do not contradict themselves, but agree in a wondrous way, so much so that they seem to have spoken as if from one mouth: furthermore, they confuse nothing, nor do they intend to mislead a worthy imitator, but clearly and openly, yet in mystical expressions, they expose the truth to their eyes, which however they conceal from the unworthy and impious, and hide from them,

For to the benevolent inquirer of our art it has been demonstrated not once, but repeatedly, not only whence our matter is to be drawn, but also that it ought to be one, which, by the prudence of the artist, is to be dissolved into two things, namely earth and fire, or mercury and sulphur.

When therefore philosophers call their water or earth gold, they do not do badly, and it is up to them by what name they wish to call them; since they have not hesitated to indicate their stone as their gold, gold more than perfect, regenerated gold, and by many other such names. But that their meaning is understood at any first glance, that should rather be ascribed to one's own ignorance than to the envy of the philosophers.

And thus the diligent inquirer into this renowned secret will be abundantly and copiously instructed concerning the matter of our stone, namely, that it must be extracted from no vegetable, from no animal, or that which proceeds from them, from no mineral, and from no imperfect metals, but from gold and silver; and that our gold and our silver are not common and dead gold and silver, but those of the wise and living. It remains now that we bring forth some things concerning the solution, as being the hinge of the matter, and the greatest secret. Now solution occurs when we make the moist from the dry thing, the soft from the hard, and the manifest from the hidden, that is, when a hard thing is turned into water, not indeed common water (as Parmenides and Agadmon teach in the Turba, saying: *Some when they hear of the solution of bodies, think it to be the water of the clouds: But if they had read and understood our books, they would also know our water to be permanent,* ) but into the water of the philosophers, that is, into the prima materia, as Arnoldus Rosar. 1. c. 9. says: *The work of the philosophers is to dissolve the stone into its mercury, so that it may be reduced to the prima materia.* And Avicenna says: *You who wish to operate, need to labor first in the solution and sublimation of the two luminaries, which is the first step of the*

   However, dear reader, so that every reason for you to complain about me may be cut off, I will yet reveal one mystery to you through the love of GOD, and you shall know that although there is one solution, it is nevertheless distinguished according to "prior" and "posterior," as they are accustomed to speak in the schools. The first solution is that of which, as said above, Arnold speaks; namely, the reduction into the prime matter: the other is that perfect solution of body and spirit together, where the solver and that which is to be solved always remain together, and with this solution of the body, the coagulation of the spirit is likewise perfected.

M. S.

One thing it is in number, one thing it is in essence and one,
Which nature strives to change, but by the aid of art,
Into two, and twice two, as the writings will teach us,
Mercury, sulphur give nourishment to themselves.
Spirit, and soul, and body, and four elements,
The fifth which they provide is the philosophers' stone.
Take your matter without deceit: and let it be twofold,
Let it shine to be at once pure mercurial.
Choose it pure from all foreign sulphur,
And utterly destroy it with fire in the furnace.
Compose it again with equal weight. Thus I
Think you have entered the path of art, and of the mystery.
After you have dissolved, soon you will sublimate; and with that
Grind, let the love of distilling never cease.
Afterwards persist in congealing, and continue cooking,
After this begin to dye generously:
Then it is medicine for you, also supreme for metals,
To heal at will whomever you wish.

A PARABLE FOLLOWS IN WHICH
the mystery of the whole business is declared.

When once, walking in a thicket and a most elegant little wood, I considered the misery of this life, and at the same time lamented that through the lamentable fall of our first parents we had been led into this deplorable and most miserable state: thus progressing, I happened upon a byway, and came to a certain path, rough, unusual, and impassable, overgrown with many thorns, so that it could easily be conjectured that it was rarely frequented. When I had noticed this, struck with horror, I would gladly have retraced my steps, if it had been within my power; but a stronger wind followed me so that more easily de-
F cem

--- Page 55 ---
42          *The Golden Treatise*

ten steps forward than one backward. Therefore, I had to hurry, and the roughness of the path had to be disregarded. When therefore I had proceeded for some time, I advanced again into a very pleasant meadow, which was, as it were, enclosed and adorned with fruit-bearing trees in the manner of a circus, and was named 'Meadow of Felicity' by the inhabitants of the place. There I came upon a crowd of decrepit men, adorned with hoary beards, among whom one was of middle age with a long, darkish beard, whom I knew by name, but whose face I had not yet seen. These men were discussing various matters, about the goodness and wisdom of G O D, about all natural things, especially about a great and hidden mystery lurking in nature, which G O D concealed from almost the whole world, and revealed only to a few who truly pursued Him with love. For a long period of time I listened to them (for this discourse greatly pleased me), until some of them seemed to me to wander too broadly and erroneously, not indeed concerning the matter and operation, but as far as parables, similitudes, and digressions were concerned, following the fictions of Pliny, Aristotle, and others, which one had excerpted from another. Hearing these things, therefore, I could no longer contain myself, and like Saul among the prophets; I intermingled my mustard, as it is said, refuting such futile things with experience and reason. When some had heard this, they agreed with me, and tested me again and again by examining me in their faculty. But my foundations were so solidly laid that I persevered in the examination with the applause of all, and they marvelled at the solidity of my knowledge, asserting with one voice that I should be admitted into their college; which words affected me with no small joy: but they said that I could not yet be their colleague until I had thoroughly known their lion and its internal and external faculties. Therefore, they affirmed, I must strive with all diligence to subdue it for myself. Indeed, trusting well in myself, I promised them that I would leave no stone unturned in this matter. For their familiarity so affected me that I would not have abandoned them for the riches of this world. Therefore they led me to the lion, clearly explai-
                                                                                                ning

--- Page 56 ---
*On the Philosopher's Stone.* 43

...explaining clearly, how indeed at the beginning I ought to deal with it, no one wanted to explain to me. Some, to be sure, babbled everything about this business, but so confusedly and intricately that hardly one in a thousand could understand them. But as soon as I had bound it, and had protected myself from its sharp claws and horrendous teeth, they wanted nothing further to be unknown to me.

This lion was old, fierce, and large; its yellow mane hung down from its neck, and it seemed invincible, so much so that I was not a little concerned about my rashness, and I would gladly have retreated, had not my vow, and the elders standing around, awaiting what I was about to do, kept me to my purpose. Therefore, with a present and provident mind, I descended into the lion's pit, and I tried to coax it, but with its gleaming eyes it so terrified me that I could scarcely stand my ground, and it would have been all over for me. But recalling what I had heard from a certain old man, while going to the pit—that many indeed had presumed to tame the lion, but very few had brought their purpose to its end—I strengthened myself, and lest I should be a disgrace, I attempted various ingenious stratagems, which I had learned with tireless study in this art. I add that I was not unskilled in natural magic; and leaving flattery behind, I gently, artfully, and subtly seized it, so that, before it could feel it, I had extracted almost all the blood from its body, indeed from the very innermost depths of its heart's viscera, which was indeed very red, but choleric. I proceeded by cutting, and I found what I could not sufficiently marvel at: especially its bones

into a very high wall, which in its height reached beyond a hundred cubits towards the clouds, but at its very top did not exceed a foot in width; and from the beginning, where I had ascended, to the end, there was an iron railing in the middle of the wall, firmly secured by its supports. I came, I say, to this wall, and someone seemed to me to precede me not far to the right of the railing. When I had followed him for a while, I caught sight of someone following me from the other side (whether it was a man or a woman, I am still uncertain:); who, calling to me, reported that it was better to walk on that (path) than on the one by which I was proceeding, which indeed I easily believed. For the railing, which was in the middle and made the way very narrow, made walking very difficult at such a height, since I also saw some following me slip and fall. Therefore, with my hands even folded under the railing, I moved myself to the other side, and thus proceeding, I came to the end of the wall, to a very difficult and dangerous descent, where I regretted that I had abandoned my former position, especially since I could no longer creep along, nor was the possibility of retreating given to me; therefore, recalling to memory that fortune favors the bold, I attempted the utmost, and trusting in my hands and feet, I descended without any harm; and when I had proceeded a little further, no further danger was apparent to me, and what had become of the wall or the railing escaped me. When therefore I had come to that place, I found white and red roses, but the red ones exceeded the white in number, and I affixed some of them, plucked, to my cap. There were very beautiful women there, but a certain wall, which surrounded a neighboring garden, kept some young men walking in it away from them (for they would gladly have been with them, but it was not possible for them to go around the garden and seek its gate). Therefore, moved by pity towards them, I retreated by the way I had come, but by a flat path, and hurrying greatly, I soon came to some buildings, where I strove to find the dwellings of the gardeners. But I found many people there, each of whom had their own separate lodgings; rarely did two live together, who worked diligently, each performing their own tasks. But these labors

seemed to me to be known and elaborated before that time, and all their labors had become more than sufficiently known to me, especially considering thus with myself: Behold, do so many other men perform such sordid and worthless labors, which have a certain appearance, according to anyone's imagination, but no foundation in nature? And you will be forgiven. Therefore, not wishing to detain myself in these trivialities in vain, because I knew that such an art would vanish with smoke, I continued my intended journey; and when I approached the garden gate, some looked at me with a scowling face, so that I even feared they might hinder me in my purpose; but others, murmuring, said: Behold, this good man presumes to approach the garden gate, and we, who have spent so many years in these garden labors, have never been admitted into it; with what Sardonic laughter shall we pursue him if he suffers a repulse? But I, making little of these words (for the condition of that garden was better known to me than to them, even though I had never been in it), through the old entrance, repeatedly closed off, so that no opening was visible from the outside, through which a key could be inserted; I nevertheless felt a certain opening, which did not appear to common eyes, to be in the old entrance, and I concluded with myself that this place was to be opened; therefore, with my master key (which some wish to call a false key), already long ago prepared with diligent skill, I prepared myself, unlocked the bolt, and went in. When indeed I had entered through this gate, I found other gates bolted, which however I opened with easy effort. There was an entrance, such as one can see in well-appointed buildings, 6 feet wide and indeed up to 20 feet long, paneled with an excellent ceiling: Even if indeed the remaining gates were still closed, through them, however, I could look into the garden just as if they had been open. Therefore, with divine will assenting, I entered the garden, in the middle of which I found another square garden, and I measured six perches, which was surrounded by rose bushes, and excellent roses bloomed, and because rare rain fell, and solar rays penetrated it, a most pleasant rainbow appeared. When therefore, passing this small garden, I hastened to that place where I wished to help the virgins,

After this, I came into a water-mill built inside with stones, where there were no receptacles for flour, or other things required for grinding, but through the wall, drums revolved by water were seen. I asked by what means this was done. The decrepit miller replied to me that on the other side the milling work was done secretly; and at that very moment I perceive some miller entering through a small bridge, whom I immediately followed. When therefore I had crossed the small bridge, to the left of which were the drums, I stopped, and wondered at the things I saw. For in a moment the drums were above the small bridge: very black waters appeared, with white drops: the surface of the small bridge did not exceed 3 digits in width: nevertheless, firmly grasping with my hands the planks accompanying the small bridge, I did not hesitate to go back, and thus, sprinkled with no moisture, I crossed the water, and I asked the old man how many wheels he had. "Ten," he replied. That miracle, which had happened to me, was troublesome, and I would gladly have known its interpretation, but considering that I could learn nothing of these things from the miller, I departed. But if, contrary to expectation and opinion, any harm should occur, it would be severely laid to my charge. I bore this with difficulty; fear and foresight made me quite anxious. And reflecting with myself that this was a matter of great moment, and that the college of wisdom was not accustomed to lies, but always stood by its words, I was a little more timid. But since what could not be changed had to be endured, and the chamber, moreover, was enclosed in a strong tower, and fortified with other defenses and very high walls, where the whole chamber could be warmed by a gentle, yet continuous fire, I willingly girded myself for this duty. And after I had invoked the divine power, I began to warm the chamber and defend the imprisoned spouses from the cold.

But what happened? As soon as they felt even the slightest warmth, they embraced each other most lovingly, so much so that no similar embrace had ever been seen. And they remained in this ardor of their love, until the bridegroom's heart melted from the excessive heat of love, and crumbled into pieces. She, loving him no less than she was loved by him, seeing this, deplored him with unending tears, and as if buried him, flooding everything, hid him from everyone's sight. Indeed, he no longer appeared. But these complaints and tears were not long-lasting; for, refusing to live further from excessive sorrow, she willingly gave herself to death. Woe is me, with how many difficulties I was surrounded, disturbed by anxieties, and agitated by terrors, when it fell to me to behold both, entrusted to me, as if melted and dead before me. My undoubted ruin was before my eyes, and what was far more troublesome to me, I feared foreseen mockeries, scorn, and contempt more than the damage itself. In these therefore

Therefore, spending many days in anxieties, and considering how I might deal with my affairs, it finally occurred to me that Medea had restored Aeson's dead body to life, and I reasoned with myself thus: 'If Medea could accomplish this, it will not be impossible for you either.' Therefore, I began to consider how I might bring that about. Therefore, continuing the heat, I proceeded for up to forty days, there I noticed the waters being consumed day by day, and the corpses reappearing, black like charcoal (which indeed would have happened sooner, had the chamber not been too tightly sealed and hidden — which, however, I was by no means to open). For I observed that the ascending waters, approaching the clouds, gathered at the top of the chamber, and fell like rain, and nothing at all could depart, until our groom, dead with his most beloved bride, had putrefied, and from that, smelled exceedingly foul. Meanwhile, in the chamber, from the sun's rays acting upon the humidity, a most beautiful rainbow was seen, adorned with the most beautiful colors, which filled me with no small joy after so many endured sorrows, especially I rejoiced that I beheld my lovers lying before me. But just as there is no joy so solid that it is not disturbed by some adversity: so too was I saddened in this joy of mine, because I was convinced that these entrusted to me were still dead and utterly without life; but this one thing comforted me, that their most solidly sealed chamber did not release their souls and spirits, but still held them well preserved: wherefore, by cherishing them with my said heat and abundantly performing my assigned duty, I continued, plainly persuading myself that they would not return to their bodies as long as those humidities lasted (since indeed they delight in humid natures), which I also found to have happened in reality. P R E F A C E
TO THE CHRISTIAN AND WORTHY
Reader.

[Decorative initial P]Most friendly and pious Reader, especially you, sons of wisdom and doctrine; after some years ago, Almighty God, in response to my daily and most fervent prayers, opened my eyes so widely, through the illumination of His Holy Spirit (from whom we receive all wisdom, and who was sent to us by the Father through Christ), that I recognized the true Center in the Triangle of the center, the one and true matter of the noble Philosophical Stone, and held it essentially in my hands. Nevertheless, for almost five years, I was ignorant of how, namely, to profitably, correctly, and properly separate from it the blood of the red lion and the glue of the white eagle; much less how I ought to proceed in mixing those [elements] very tightly and optimally, according to the proportionate weight of nature, enclosing them, sealing them, and committing them to the arcane fire—a process which must not be done without singular reason and practiced prudence. And although I investigated with singular industry in the writings, parables, and various figures of the Philosophers, and to the manifold, wonderful, and partly expro-
*(The text ends mid-word here.)*

--- Page 69 ---
56                                     P R E F A C E.
enigmas born from their own minds, that I might toil greatly to solve them: nevertheless, I truly discovered, that all these things were mere absurdities and most vain phantasms, just as the Authors of the Philosophers themselves similarly testify: namely, that all the preparations, about which Geber, Albertus Magnus, and others of that kind, etc., and their purifications, sublimations, cementations, distillations, rectifications, circulations, putrefactions, conjunctions, solutions, ascensions, coagulations, calcinations, incinerations, mortifications, revivifications, etc. Similarly, also their tripods, Athamor, reverberatory alembics, liquefactory vessels, horse dung, ash, sand, cucurbit, Pelican-viol, retort, fixatory, etc., are mere sophistries, and seductive and useless things, just as I myself must confess that in the very truth of the matter. For noble Nature, who gladly delights in her own substance, knows nothing of this futility. Hence Theophrastus, in his 'Magical Secret concerning the Philosopher's Stone,' concerning those who seek the matter of the stone in wine, imperfect bodies, blood, Marcasites, Mercury, sulfur, urine, dung, orpiment, and in herbs, such as: Celandine, Hyssop, Ivy, etc., rightly says: 'All things are full of lies and thefts, by which they deceive men, drain their purses, consume time rashly and uselessly, and merely follow their own foolish heads, because they can achieve nothing that is required by Nature.' Come now, I ask, tell me now, who will help me in the Minerals of the earth, in the distillations of waters, etc.? Or perhaps are there also men found in these same things who renew wine, or infant urine-

--- Page 70 ---
PRÆFATIO. 75

...they urinate, from which metals are made: or do you suppose apothecaries are inside, who thus sell everything with which you can make metals: Foolishly, do you not understand that you are mistaken, and that none of those things pertain to nature? Or do you try to separate God, because you attempt metals from blood? Make therefore a man from a horse, or a cow from a mouse, which then yields good milk for you: this likewise is multiplication. But it is not done at all, and the less that can be done, the less also will you be able to make metals from the aforementioned remedies. For art is not from nature, and what nature created, art can have no operation there. If a woman has given birth to a male infant, nature then cannot form a little girl from him: and these things should also be applied to that principle. From which anyone of sound mind can easily infer how, and by what reason, namely, and in what things also, the blessed matter is to be sought and found. But let no one perhaps imagine for himself, much less let him allow himself to be persuaded by any artisan, that, although he may truly know the true matter, either through a secret revelation of God, or of those who know it, and may know it and have it in his hands, he then in the same way completely understands how to unlock it, to separate the pure from the impure to the highest degree, and to purify it. Ah, my laborer, you are greatly mistaken. The dog now for the first time lies hidden buried in musk, and both art and an educated mind are required for the task. See, for example, what you have heard from me from the beginning, namely that I myself for a full five years knew the true matter of the stone, and yet, during all that time, I was ignorant of the method of proceeding with it, until finally, after the sixth year, the key of power, through a secret revelation

--- Page 71 ---
58          PREFACE.
revelation, was entrusted by almighty God. Indeed, the ancient Patriarchs, Prophets, and Philosophers always, and at all times, kept this same key as arcane and hidden. For if, says the Monarch in the aforementioned place, they had written it down openly, so that any swineherd or peddler could understand it, that would be a great theft, no mystery at all, and great evils could arise from it, which would certainly be against the manifest will of God, etc. For these reasons, and others which I have partly alleged in the Epilogue, and lest I seem to bury the talent entrusted to me by God: therefore, in this my revived Golden Age, as much indeed as has been granted to me by Nature and God, I have wished to reveal the great mystery of the wise, such as has been seen by my own eyes, and to apply my hands to the work, which, by divine grace, was again undertaken at the right time with great power and glory. May the reader who loves piety and integrity interpret that intention of mine not in a bad, but in a good light, nor allow himself to be led into error, because sometimes contradictory things occur simultaneously: for indeed, it was not possible, nor even proper, to proceed otherwise from Theory to Practice, since to write more openly and clearly about this profession in the chemical Republic will be strictly forbidden. Relying on firm hope, that all those, looking at this little work with true faith, with the inner eyes of the mind, to which absolutely nothing is denied, will pore over it day and night, and at the same time implore God from the innermost depths of their hearts, and thus, together with me, will perceive the hidden and wonderful Philosophical fruits, according to the divine will. And in this way are and remain the true brothers of the Golden Cross, and cho-
