*Philosophical Summary.* 177

...nourishment than it would have received in a space of even a hundred years from another land.

Therefore, by this very fact, it must be understood that one should take the Mercury, which is a most highly praised tree, which simultaneously has within itself, and indeed indissolubly, the Sun and the Moon: and then it should be transferred to another land, somewhat nearer to the Sun, so that by this method it may achieve a wonderful utility, in which matter the dew abundantly suffices. For where it was planted before, there it was so agitated and weakened by wind and cold, that indeed little fruit was to be expected from it: in which place it also remained for a long time, and produced absolutely no fruits.

But truly for the Philosophers there is a garden, in which the Sun dwells incessantly, both in the morning and evening hours, by day and by night, and that with the sweetest dew, by which it is well sprinkled and moistened, whose earth produces trees and fruits that are planted from there, which also receive proper nourishment from the most pleasing pasture. This happens daily, and there they are strengthened, enlivened, and do not wither at all, at least almost more in one year than they would have done in a thousand years before, so to speak, in another place where they were troubled by cold. Let them therefore be taken, and let them be constantly nurtured day and night over a fire in an alembic. But not a charcoal fire, or one made from wood, but a clear and transparent fire shall be made, just like the Sun itself, which should never be hotter or more burning than is right, but always of the same heat: for the vapor is the dew and seed of all metals, which must not be altered. It is to be seen in growing fruits, if they abound in too much heat, without moderate dew, that they remain dry, and die on their twigs, and finally reach no perfection: But if they are sustained on the tree by heat or moderate humidity, then they become elegant and fruitful. For heat and humidity are the nourishment of all earthly things, such as animals, vegetables, and minerals. Therefore, charcoal fires and fires made from wood are by no means beneficial to them: those are violent fires, which do not nourish, as the heat of the sun usually does, which also all
                                          Z                                          things

--- Page 191 ---
178 Philosophical Summary.

...as the sun's heat usually does, which also preserves all corporeal things, because that (fire) is natural. For this purpose, true Philosophers have also chosen no other fire than the natural one, which they follow, not because the Philosopher does what nature does: For nature indeed created all things, such as vegetables, minerals, and animals, each in its own degree where it rules.

In a similar way, I will not now say that, namely, men make natural things by their art: But if nature truly perfects or operates on such things, then by human art they are made more perfect than what is done by nature. And in this way, the ancient Philosophers, to instruct all of us, labored at nothing else than naturally with the Moon, and the true mother Mercury, from which they made the Mercury of the Philosophers, which, in its operation, is much stronger than natural Mercury. For this (natural Mercury) at least performs its work on simple, perfect, and imperfect, cold or hot metals; but the Philosophical Stone serves even more than perfect and imperfect metals, so that it quickly perfects and restores them, and that without any diminution, addition, or alteration. It leaves them in the same state in which they were created by nature, yet neglects nothing.

I will not now say the same here, that Philosophers combine all those three (things) to better perfect their Mercury, as certain men ignorant of things, and unlearned Chemists do, who take common gold, silver, and Mercury, and treat them so badly until they vanish into smoke, and in that way try to perfect the Mercury of the Philosophers: yet they by no means reach that (Mercury), which is the first matter of the stone, and the true ore. But if they wish to reach it, and find something good, then they must go to the mountain of the seven, where there is no plain, and from above look down at the sixth, which they will see from afar. On the height of that mountain, he will recognize the triumphant Royal herb, which some Philosophers have called mineral, others vegetable, and which is named Saturnialis: However, let the bones be left, and a pure and clean broth be taken from it; and in this way, the more powerful part of the work can be done. And this is the right and subtle Mercury of the Philosophers, which you must take.

And first indeed it will make the white work, then also the red, if you have understood my discourse well: For both is nothing else than, as they call it, the practical work: Sun & Moon are prepared in one and the same way; from which the white and the red (work) in practice proceeds, which is so simple and easy that even a woman can accomplish it with difficulty by her distaff, or if she places eggs for incubation under a hen in winter time, and yet does not wash them. For eggs placed for incubation are not washed, but as they are, are placed under the hen: and no further labor is required in it than that these eggs be turned daily, so that the chicks may emerge better and more quickly. To which end I pray and implore the supreme creator of all things, that He would most mercifully deign to bestow His grace upon all faithful Chemists for finding such a chick, by which they may sustain themselves: just as I received that little which I have declared here from above from God the Father, who also bestowed it upon me out of love and according to His goodness. Therefore for you I have written this present little work, so that you may inquire with greater desire, and enter the right path: But that little work I have therefore included in the Summary, so that you may better comprehend the work, according to the sayings of the Philosophers, which I persuade myself you will understand more correctly in the future.

[Large ornate initial P] Since up to now, beloved friend and brother, many deceptions have been proposed to the simpler folk in the celebrated art of Chemistry by certain pseudo-chemists, whose writings, however, are nothing else than mere impostures and lies; although the aforementioned simple folk, who consider it to be great, believe these lies more than is just, and proceed further in their work, by that very fact they cast themselves into difficult labors and immense troubles: For indeed, from a sinister and evil understanding, that which has been begun can never be brought to any praiseworthy end. Therefore, you see indeed the greater part of men, who in our present time devote themselves to that excellent art of Chemistry, hunting for false chemical processes, certainly persuading themselves that they have found there the true and correct art, which nevertheless is not described without parables in books; but, on the contrary, many false R. [recipes/rules/principles] are found in abundance, which wicked false men have also devised, who themselves knew nothing of the truth: and therefore also could write nothing true about it, and both the Reader and the Writer understood equally little at the same time, namely what pertained to nature. For if the Writers had known the requirements of nature, they would never have written such shapeless confusions and R., or attempted to defend them by their false sublimation, calcination, distillation, solution, coagulation, and feigned putrefaction and Corruption: just as it is seen daily among those ignorant of these matters, who squander all their goods by their false defilement; all of which happens through pseudo-chemical books, which are accustomed to falsely teach about false regimens, by no means conforming to nature.

184                                  *Via Veritatis.*

Absolutely no connection exists between such useless and less necessary processes and true Chemical Processes; instead, they follow that revered Nature, just as she prepares it in the veins of the earth, and that without solution, coagulation, putrefaction, which nevertheless is very simple in itself. For consider and weigh with yourself, I beg you, my friend, whether so many instruments, alembics, retorts, circular and sublimatory vessels, various kinds of fires, and various materials are found in the veins of the earth, in which metals flourish and grow; and whether nature in those very, just mentioned, veins of the earth uses so many different alembics, or vessels, and so many materials, such as shoemaker's ink, salt, arsenic, Mercury, sulfur, and other ridiculous absurdities (which are here deliberately passed over without dwelling on them), just as Chemists use them, by which they utterly and shamefully lose both their time and their fortunes in a preposterous manner. Therefore, they are also not undeservedly to be called ignorant of things, since they daily exercise themselves in Chemistry, and nevertheless persist in their shameful solutions, coagulations, distillations, putrefactions, and other worthless and frivolous things, and thus rashly consume their time and fortunes, as we have said, since nature acts so simply, and likewise completes her work simply. What good, therefore, is such a foul deception of pseudochemists and most laborious work to us, all of which, nevertheless, are esteemed by true artisans as mere foolishness? Indeed, they are daily held up to ridicule by them, because they do not open their eyes better, but stubbornly persist in those sophistries, in which it is fitting for them both to dwell and finally even to utterly die, since they strive to inquire into and read nothing more than sophistical books of this kind. Therefore all their actions are sophistical, not Philosophical, and for that reason they can attain to no art or truth.
   But now I want this truly affirmed to you: as long as you have loved lies, and not the philosophical art, so long also will the truth not be revealed to you. Although I myself also persisted in sophistical regimes of this kind, and in sublimating, distilling, calcining, circu-

...I labored by circulating, nor did I spare certain substances, such as urine, shoemaker's black salt, alum, etc. In hair, wine, eggs, bones, and all kinds of herbs, too, I tormented myself with various labors, and I tried Arsenic, and Mercury with sulfur, I tested all minerals and metals, through strong waters and lyes, I worked with them, and that by dissolving and coagulating: I exercised myself in amalgamating and precipitating, and nevertheless, I gained no pleasure or joy from it: I had placed much trust in the Quintessence, but here too I found myself deceived.

Therefore, beloved brother, I most diligently warn you that, if you wish to apply yourself to inquiring into such an excellent art, you should by no means intrude yourself into the sophistical ordinary regimen of the sublimation of Sulfur and Mercury, or the solution of bodies, or the coagulation of spirits, nor should you care for their precious alembics, since they will be less suitable for the true art. As long as you have not investigated the true essence of nature, so long also, believe me, you will remain without comfort, and at last, you will discover that this art is nothing, fictitious, and false.

If therefore you desire to seek profit, for that reason you must renounce sublimation, calcination, solution, and coagulation, together with putrefaction itself, and on the contrary, you will become a disciple, to inquire into the true foundation of Philosophy: which, according to its genuine sense, will be able to show you another solution and coagulation, and likewise another regimen—the latter of which is natural, and all of which agree with nature itself. For just as that works by nature in the veins of the earth, where metals grow, so too here you must follow nature. For you see that nature uses no more than one single substance in its essence, and in the aforementioned substance you see all things hidden. But this substance needs no other labor than cooking, by which it is raised more and more, up to its highest degree. From this simple cooking and gradation, cunning sophists have devised the names of solution, coagulation, calcination, putrefaction, sublimation, and other phantasms, fashioning from the true simple essence, or cooking, an entirely different essence Aa

This they will most difficultly excuse before God, while they little considered what Christ says: LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF. They trampled the truth under their feet, and substituted lies for it, which they wonderfully adorned, and wrote huge books about it, as if the correction of metals were such a laborious and difficult work, when nevertheless only some simple cooking (coction) occurs.

For as long as you cook, so long also do you putrefy, and the substance becomes subject to putrefaction, like grain, which, cast into the earth, is preserved in the earth itself by the heat of the Sun, and by natural rain must first putrefy before anything new grows from it: That they called putrefaction and solution. So also you sublimate in Coction: Indeed, they named the correction of the substance sublimation and multiplication, so that they might better deceive the simpler folk. In a similar manner also you coagulate: For while humidity is changed into the nature of fire, so that it can resist fire, and is neither consumed nor vanishes as smoke, then they call it coagulation. In coction, the Philosophers circulate, for in it fire is united with water, lest the fire be entirely consumed, just as we see daily that water protects all things from fire, as long as water is at hand. Similarly, water in coction takes care of the fire and unites itself with the fire, so that it may become entirely pure fire, and thus it was called circulation or conjunction by the ancients.

And by this means you see, how they invented so many names concerning this simple coction, and instituted so many false regimens, to deceive men. Indeed, they imposed those various names on this unique substance for this reason, lest anyone should perceive what it truly was, by which (through divine grace) so many excellent and outstanding things might be prepared—

might be prepared. First, they call that our Mercury, by which they understood nothing else than humidity, which began little by little to unite itself with fire, and so was compared with Mercury. Moreover, that Hyle, that is, the principle of all things, was so called because all things are first generated from water and fire. If therefore you are not so deceived now, and wish to consider nature a little more deeply, then without any doubt you will easily recall to memory what that matter is from which metallic creatures are generated. Before all else, however, you must rightly understand metallic nature, why Sol, Luna, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are metals, and what their origin will be. You also undoubtedly need to know that all created things are distributed into three Kingdoms, namely vegetables, animals, and minerals, and that all things will be comprised in these three: For all herbs, all woods, and trees are called vegetables: then all living animals, or whatever is comprised of flesh and blood, is animal: finally, all metals, and stones, and other things which emit no flame from themselves are minerals, and are comprised under mineral nature.

You see therefore, my brother, that all things, divided into three different Natures, will be comprised under the same. Wherefore I exhort you again and again, as a faithful friend, not to allow yourself to be deceived when they speak of the black color, as if you must likewise have or take a black substance, or that the material itself in the work becomes black, white, and red. But they made mention of black for this reason: that the Essence, first at the very beginning, mixes itself with some glowing bodily fire, by which action a liquid is separated from the Essence, like some black smoke. And that black smoke the Ancients called the black raven, but the essence they called the raven's head. Therefore, you ought to observe this aforementioned separation carefully: for from it indeed the wise Ancients took the opportunity and occasion to inquire into the three natures, namely vegetable, animal, and mineral, and learned from it only this, that the separation of natures was nothing other than a defect of coction in nature. Then they sometimes considered the matter more deeply, how namely these essences, less cooked by nature through common fire, could be helped in a natural way, so that the essences, which are already combustible, and their liquids (which the Ancients, out of envy, named Mercury) which are separated black from the Essence, could be perfected by art, so that the Essences might remain safe and protected from combustion by the Liquid, and the liquid might not separate itself from the Essence. That the Ancients called our sulfur. For after this preparation, the Essence is no longer vegetable nor animal, but by Coction: it has become a Mineral Essence, and is therefore called sulfur: The Essence is nothing other than some elemental fire, and its liquid, which is protected from combustion, is true elemental air, so much so that, since air is naturally hot and humid, it is called Mercury by the envious. For air indeed embraces the nature of fire within itself, and again elemental fire has the nature of air within itself, so much so that, by the addition of their likes, a true conjunction ought to be made from these two. That, however, by no means pertains to Alchemy, but is entirely contrary to it: for even to this day many people attribute knowledge of true Alchemy to Bodenstein, and believe that he knew many secrets: But, as we have said, he deviated much from the mark, casting a veil over the ignorant and unlearned, as if great things lay hidden beneath that matter, which matter, however, among experts, lacks a certain foundation: But as the common proverb sounds, it is good to fence before the blind. Therefore, I also leave that aside for now, since that Bodenstein will no longer be among the living, nor will I slander him much: *For concerning the dead and absent, nothing but good.* But I want this affirmed about him, that he was a physician and a good Sophist, but he did not rightly understand the true natural art of Alchemy and the Secrets of Natures, as his writings testify: although the matter does not touch me so much that I should praise anyone excessively. They will cause me no harm or detriment: But for the sake of simpler people, who trust them and nevertheless are led into a precipice by them, I write these things, so that they may know from whom they should beware, for deception is immense, but truth is simple.

   If, therefore, truth smiles upon you, then you must set aside sophisms, along with all their labor by which you have hitherto wearied yourself, and at least consider that by which Nature operates, and how it labors towards the Essence. If you do this, then you will by no means err, but whatever you may desire, you will behold without any trouble, nor will you need much labor and expense. For by some simple coction the whole matter is accomplished, so that through this coction, the solution and coagulation of bodies occurs, and indeed, sublimation and putrefaction are thereby finished, as is to be seen in the writings of the wise. Some, however, instead of the simple and true Essence, established some other Essence, by which they deceived the entire world and afflicted many people with the greatest detriment. But whether they did this rightly and well, I leave that to God, the just judge of all. For it would indeed be much better if not so many writings were pub-

were published, by which so many men are cast into sorrow, who rely solely on the sophists' processes of this kind, which they learned in such deceitful Writings, and are thus shamefully deceived. For if so many Writings about Alchemy had not been published, nor even today would so much be written by those ignorant of Nature, there would certainly be so many thousands of men in our present time who could investigate the true Art and comprehend it by themselves: since now, for many years, scarcely one can reach the truth, because almost all lovers of Philosophy rely solely on books and sophistical labor, and think that even the Ancients achieved the art with such great labor. This, however, I publicly condemn, and I deny that the matter is so, since the true art by no means needs such trifling, which modern workers use: The ancient wise men themselves did not manage it so, although they wrote about it somewhat more extensively in their books, so that they might better deceive those ignorant of things. And in this they did not act so prudently, since even those who perhaps entered the right path could be cast into error, unless they were taught otherwise by living Teachers.

But truly indeed, since even for the living Masters themselves certain limits will be prescribed, how widely, and to whom precisely they ought to reveal this secret art; or even may, lest they wish to become Corruptors of the seal of divine mysteries, and be subject to the curse of all Philosophers: therefore it is better that, all books and human teachers now being set aside, Nature alone, or its marvelous operation, not only in the production of metals, but also in the germination of all fruits of the earth, should be considered, and its circulation, both in summer and also in winter, in spring, and in autumn, by day and by night, with heat and constant warmth, should be placed before the eyes and pondered. For if it were known to you from the very foundation, from what and in what manner Nature brings each thing to its growth, flower, fruit, and perfection: then you would also readily apply your hand to the earth's sprouts, and from the matter which nature uses in the caverns of the earth for diverse sprouts, you would also bring your intention into effect, according to your desire.

     In a similar manner also, just as from male sperm in the mother's womb, by the benefit of coction, an infant is generated, and from an egg, through the natural incubation of hens, a chick is brought forth: so also metals have some certain substance from which they are born. Not however in such a way, my brother, that you should understand, or remain in doubt, just as false charlatans have taught you, that Mercury and Sulphur will be the first material of metals: for indeed in the veins of the earth, where metals grow, neither Mercury nor sulphur are found, which they simply fabricated for some deception, which

...which they show, when nevertheless a single and true way suffices for truth. Many diverse solutions, coagulations, sublimations, calcinations, and putrefactions, which nevertheless are all of no moment, and which Nature does not use in the veins of the earth where metals grow. For revered Nature does nothing more than to cook the elementary fire, which is exalted and confirmed by its liquor, which it now changes from one Nature into another, through some constant cooking, so that, as was said before, all things have been distributed into three natures: and although these three natures are corporally distinct, namely into vegetable, animal, and mineral, nevertheless they are elementary, or, in secret, have arisen from one substance: All have a single root, from which they grow green and increase, which the Ancients, for the sake of deception, called the first matter or Hyle. But it is nothing else than the hidden elementary fire, with its liquor, which the Ancients also called the radical humor, and they did not speak unskillfully: For liquor is the root of all created things.

      But that this humidity, together with its fire, is divided into diverse Natures, this happens in no other way than solely, as has been said, through various cookings that occur in nature: For one Nature is cooked more with its elementary fire, through its humidity, than another, of which the vegetable Nature is least in cooking, because its essence is easily burned, and its liquor is also very easily separated from the elementary fire by means of common fire.

      The animal Nature is not far dissimilar in its prior cooking, since its essence is likewise easily burned: and therefore the mineral nature is supreme in cooking, because metallic liquor becomes more and better united with the elementary [fire] through cooking, than those other two natures mentioned before: For this reason also, metals resist common fire better than created things which are comprised under the vegetable and animal nature: as can be seen, that metals placed in fire do not emit such a flame as wood does, for its essence is not so [united] with its liquor, as metallic humidity with its

...its essence [is united]; [instead, the vegetable] essence is cooked, and the conjunction of the liquor with the essence, not metallic but simply vegetable, which is consumed in black smoke, came to be. But after the essence has reached coction through nature, then it no longer remained vegetable, but has now become metallic, and is now consumed by common fire in white smoke, no differently than, as you see, imperfect metals, when they are liquefied in fire, emit white smoke from themselves. Just as, therefore, vegetable essence is purified by natural coction, and is changed from black into some white smoke: In a similar way also, and indeed for the same reason, the Ancient Sages said: First you must blacken, before you whiten: then first whiten, before you redden. Reddening, however, is to be understood as making fully and perfectly, just as the Sun and Moon, both these excellent metals, rendered perfect through coction, their essence entirely united with the liquor, and at the same time all rendered pure fires, and were called rubrefactions by the Ancients.

And for that very reason, beloved friend and brother, lest the books of the Ancients, written quite corruptly, cast you into error, but simply learn to fundamentally understand metallic nature, and then you will most easily understand the sayings and phrases of the Ancients, nor, with the other Chemists, will you look around here and there, who from the opinions of the Ancients understand, or at least persuade themselves, that a substance is to be taken, which is to be putrefied and dissolved for so long, until the matter blackens: Which having been done, the same is to be washed again, calcined, and elaborated, until the blackness vanishes, and it begins to whiten, and the fire is likewise to be increased for so long a time, and it is to be calcined or labored for so long until the matter reddens, which however is entirely false, not Philosophical, but merely a sophistical labor. Thus now all the opinions of the Ancient Philosophers are held by the ignorant as sophistical in their method: which indeed the Ancients saw not unwillingly, and for that very reason wrote and spoke so obscurely, that scarcely anyone could grasp their true meaning. Indeed, all of them direct us to metals, and make frequent mention of Mercury and Sulphur, but all those things are merely for the sake of deception. It is not in any silver or gold either, but it is prepared, which can be made good, yet it cannot be made better than how it was created by God through nature. Nor can it be prepared for tincture, but that tincture must be given to it, therefore our art is not from it, nor does it proceed from it, for it is another thing. It is not in any metal, as we said before: For if it were in any metal, then deservedly it would be either in the Sun or the Moon: but since the Moon is not good, how then, I ask, will it be able to produce anything good from itself? Nor is it in Mercury, or any sulphur, or Salt, nor in any herbs, or other things of that kind, as you will later be made more certain of that matter. With these things we wish our exhortation concluded, and now we will enumerate the things themselves.

It is one stone, and no stone, nor does it have the species and nature of any stone, and yet it is a stone: It is fire, and has no species and nature of fire, and yet it is fire: It is also air, nor does it have the form and nature of any air, and yet it is air. ANOTHER UNDERSTANDING OF OUR VENERABLE
*Stone.*

The elder PHilosopher says: Our Stone is named a sacred rock, and it is divided, or signified, in four ways. First, into earth: Second, into its accretion: Third, by fire: Fourth, it is separated by the flame of fire. If therefore anyone knows how to extract its solution and salt, and its perfect coagulation, he knows the secrets of the Philosophers. Therefore, if the salt whitens and appears fatty, then it tinctures.
There are three things in the secret of the Philosophers, or in our art. First, the transmutation of the whole substance into one salt. Second, it is that three subtle, incomprehensible bodies are rendered: Third, the repetition of the entire solution of the whole substance. My son, if you know these things, then labor diligently: But if you do not understand, then withdraw your hand: for it is no more than one thing, even if hundreds of thousands of books have been written about it, because this art will become such a treasure that the entire world itself cannot compensate for it, and yet it is at least one thing, from which the art is worked. Therefore it is written secretly, although it is publicly named, and known to all men. But if it were to come into the hands of all in the world, then no one would labor, nor would it even be esteemed so highly: Nor moreover does God Himself grant that individuals should have such a great good: therefore it is also by no means fitting that it should be named or written about without being concealed. If therefore God has given that grace to anyone, let him also understand it: and truly that seems impossible to the world, but those who love it are mostly esteemed as wicked men and scoundrels: and that the most learned men themselves, such as Doctors and others, cannot find it, is because they never become intent on this thing, although they have it daily before their eyes, nevertheless they give no credit to it, because namely such great [power].

CONCERNING THE TREASURE AND THE TINCTURE.

IF therefore you shall have made such great progress in your work, and shall have obtained the red, you must further know that you possess a treasure which the whole world will not be able to pay for. But if you wish to have the tincture for the Moon (silver), then take five half-ounces of the red, and cast it upon five hundred half-ounces of well-calcined Moon (silver): Which, finally melted, all are then converted into tincture and medicine. Then take one half-ounce of it, and cast it upon five hundred half-ounces of Venus (copper), or other metals, then it is changed into true Moon (silver): but of the red, which you have labored so much for, take one part to a thousand parts of the Sun (gold), then it is converted into tincture and medicine: Add again one part of that to a thousand parts of Venus (copper) or other metals, and then it is converted into true Sun (gold). For these things, however, you do not need to buy any Sun (gold) or Moon (silver): for you complete the first addition with a Drachma, and thereby you always tinge more and more.

ANOTHER KNOWLEDGE OF OUR STONE.

My sons, know that the stone, from which our art is elaborated, must not have touched the earth of the earth, but [must be caught] before it is born. For if it has touched the earth, then it is no longer useful for our art, although in its first birth it is generated by the Sun and Moon, and will be demanded from the earth in its accretion. For it received its first birth in the earth, and yet it is broken, destroyed, and mortified, but the sun, the son, is generated by some temperate heat, through vapor, and is born anew, when it comes to the sea with the wind, they lie there, and when it comes from the sea to the earth with the wind, it quickly vanishes again. But if you wish to elaborate it, then you must walk with it, and catch it in the air, before it reaches the earth, otherwise it evaporates: but as soon as it brings itself from the sea to the earth, then be present at once, and enclose it in your glass, and work with it, as you know, so that you may rightly recognize it, when it comes with wind, rain, and thunder, then observe it carefully, for it cannot escape you. And although it is born anew daily, nevertheless it has been from the beginning of the world, but as soon as it falls to the earth, then it no longer serves our art.

So, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, it was from the beginning, when God through His divine providence willed heaven and earth to be made according to wisdom: but nothing was at hand that had any singular name, except only one matter: that was neither dry nor humid: it was not earth, not air, not fire, not light, nor even darkness, but one matter, similar to vapor or mist, so that it could neither be seen nor touched: that was called Hyle, or prime matter: For when a thing must again be made from nothing, then that nothing must be united: and one thing must be made from the one palpable matter, and from the palpable matter one body, to which a living soul is given, from which, through God's grace, it receives its own similar species. So also it must be noted that when God caused matter to be made, then it was dry and compressed with moisture. But if therefore something humid ought to have grown from it, then it was necessary for that to be separated from the dry, as fire for itself, and earth also for itself: earth also needed to be sprinkled with water, if anything humid was to grow from it: for without humidity nothing can grow. In a similar way also nothing grows in water, unless earth is present, in which it may stand. If therefore water ought to moisten the earth, then matter must be present there which floats on the water. For example, wind bestows water upon creatures: for unless it blew, or existed, then water could not help it; water also, by flooding the earth at one time, would return to the sea, where all waters have their return and influx, and from there they never return. All inhabitants of the earth, also, because of dryness and aridity, would be forced to perish and waste away. Therefore one element, without the aid of another, is able to produce no fruits, nor would any thing be present that would compel the wind, and drive it to work, for otherwise it would always be at rest: Therefore fire is at hand, which compels and drives it to work and motion.

First, it must be known, that after Almighty God, from the beginning, had placed our first progenitor Adam, together with all celestial and terrestrial bodies, in Paradise, and had forbidden him to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of Good and Evil under penalty of eternal death, that at that time, before Adam had transgressed the divine command, man had absolutely no need of anything, because he was still immortal: But as soon as he had partaken of the forbidden fruit, he immediately became needy of all things of the world, while by divine command, he was driven by an Angel from Paradise into exile, into this unclean world, and brought nothing but poverty, calamity, sickness, tribulation, anxiety, and finally also bitter and harsh death. But if he had been obedient to the divine command, then he would have lived his time, namely a thousand years, in Paradise, and then from there would have been taken up into heaven, just like all men of his kind. But because of his disobedience, he provoked God's wrath against himself, and his descendants, and indeed all creatures of the whole world, who visited him with all kinds of diseases: nevertheless, as a merciful and compassionate GOD, He again created medicine, and other most noble things of that kind, for the various defects of miserable men, out of pure grace and clemency, by which these miserable mortals could sometimes relieve themselves from diseases and drive away hunger and bodily necessity, and other calamities and distresses, just as also...

TO THE READER.
Lest you, very friendly Reader, be long detained, but that you may understand my opinion and foundation as conveniently and certainly as possible, and lest the reading perhaps become troublesome and tedious to you: therefore, observe with the utmost diligence what I have revealed and named to you from the beginning, middle, and end of this little work of mine, for this reading will indeed excite no weariness in you, but joy. Since therefore Almighty God, whose most holy name I am obliged to celebrate at all times and to render due thanks to Him through His divine grace, has granted to me these things – the mastery, understanding, and experience of that noble and true art – nevertheless, I am moved by brotherly charity and true fidelity to bring forth into light that most noble treasure, which by God's grace, with manifold expenses and troubles, I have obtained, so that by this means the opinions of slanderers may be corrected, you may be able to guard yourself from other, less necessary, expenses, and lest I also be apprehended as a false, envious, malicious, and avaricious man. Therefore, I do not wish this noble treasure and most abundant gift of God to die with me, or to be covered with rust and decay, especially such an ineffable and comforting secret, which God Himself cultivated, poured forth with His rosy blood, sprinkled in His material time, and commanded that it should not be revealed to the unskilled and foolish in these matters: wherefore also this noble medicine can not undeservedly be called the oil of mercy, and that for many reasons indeed, which your own understanding will supply to you. Therefore, it is by no means necessary that I now speak or write more about this matter; I will explain, teach, and reveal according to the proper manner, as required, so that no one who is to labor hereafter in Philosophy may err or be led astray any longer, but rather may have a certain, true, and joyful access to the operation of this art.

*INFORMATION ON THE TRUE ART.*

I make known to all lovers of this art, that Philosophers embrace truth and falsehood under one saying: namely, truth for their children and disciples; but falsehood for the stupid, those ignorant of things, and the foolish, who refer falsehood to truth, and vice versa: For Philosophers have never been caught in a lie.

And for what reason? They rightly named the things of our art and truly indicated the work, but the foolish did not understand the writing and accepted uncertain things, as for example, while workers vaporize waters

It is enough therefore that it be found by grace: But the material of our stone is compared to all those things with which artisans labor: For our stone is our salt, our Mercury, verdigris, halonitrum, sal ammoniac, Mars (iron), sulfur, and countless other things of that kind, not however dug out from wooded and open mountains with hammers and other instruments: But our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs: in our Salt-spring our Salt is found: from our earth our metal, Mercury, and sulfur are produced, and not from wooded, foreign, and open mountains; all of which artisans do not understand, nor can they believe, nor comprehend; for the Lord has obscured and stopped up their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to be done, and aimed least at the goal, nevertheless they persisted in that contrary sense, and obeyed their stubborn heads; as for instance, when they ought to distill gently, there they sublimated with a strong fire, they burned strong waters, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, and reduced them to nothing. # NOW FOLLOWS MY OWN OPINION, AND A PHILOSOPHICAL STATEMENT.

[Large decorative initial F]or a fundamental Epilogue in place of a preface, and of the book, and of the information hitherto signified by me, and before I transcend to this beginning of Philosophy, I will first declare my well-founded opinion, so that any possessor of this book may the sooner reach the multitude of philosophers written below. But if he cannot sufficiently perceive and understand this opinion of mine, then let him consult the subsequent Philosopher, where that opinion of mine, with each of the things mentioned before, is sufficiently explained.

Since therefore I know the blessed and true art, and have recognized the matter and nature, as much indeed as the Lord has granted: therefore, out of compassion, I have communicated the same to you quite clearly with this book, and I have brought it forth into light not in a chancery style, and with sesquipedalian words, but rightly and simply, in a simple manner and form. Therefore, let everyone very deliberately observe and read the sooner, and then he will well understand my opinion. But I am certain that many will kill me with insults and slanders, since the art has not yet, from the creation of the world, been so plainly manifested as I have now made it public property, which has been hidden from all the wise and "big-nosed" people of this world; and to those, I say, who have read this book of mine, it will wonderfully ring in their ears. I conclude my discourse, approaching the very beginning of my opinion.

Sons and disciples of this art, out of Christian charity and fidelity, I make known to you, how truly you can and ought now to find, understand, and know the tools and operations of our stone: Know therefore, that the Philosopher's Stone is found in its operation in our trees, even in apple trees in the air, in all creatures, animals, all growing things that have vegetability, growing and not growing. For the impulse and tempered heat of the Sun, from which that vapor arose, drives the vapor again so that it either descends or falls. But in descending, the vapor is transmuted into some humidity, it becomes sulfur and Mercury, of which some part of each remains behind, and what is volatile descends up and down; and through this multiple ascent and descent, they are finally fixed in the course of time: and are transmuted into metals, which then adhere so tightly to the earth and stones, that they must be extracted from there by strong fire fusion. And the more the mountains have coarser stones or earths, so too are the metals formed.

For if the soil is subtle, and the stones are of the same kind, then also a subtle vapor emerges from it, and subtle sulfur and Mercury are formed: which two, if pure and clean, agitated up and down by tempered heat, and fixed, then metals likewise become clean, pure, and constant. But if the mountains are mixed with coarse stones and similar earth, then also Sulfur and Mercury are hindered by this coarseness, so that they cannot reach perfect operation: Therefore also metals are transmuted in diverse ways and manners, and each indeed according to its own species: just as every tree of the field has its own proper odor, taste, and species: so also every mountain has its own peculiar ore growing within it, from those natural stones, no differently than the leaves of trees, the growth of all things usually occurs: and this according to the operation of the Planets of the sky: for the closer the mountains are to the Planets, the more metals grow in them, and derive their smoke and taste from there: But if the mountains are situated towards the Sun, and both their stones and earths become subtle, then all metals are transmuted into gold: But if they are also closer to the Moon, as if to the Moon, for its operation, then metals are converted into silver. For all metals have this property in themselves, that they are finally transmuted into Sun and Moon, through the long [operation] of the Sun

and the operation of the Moon: For the Sun is the father, and the Moon the mother of metals and all growing things. For you see that gold shines like the Sun, and silver like the Moon. Wherefore children are similar to their parents: and therefore all metallic things, in growing, are transmuted according to their species, and nevertheless still embrace the property of the Sun and Moon within themselves: for nothing more is lacking than fire, from the scarcity of which they suffer, just as you see, when the Sun retreats with the approach of winter, then the flowers of the fields die, leaves fall from the trees, all herbs wither, for the element recedes from them because of the cold, beyond which nothing can grow, and from excessive heat things and fruits of nature wither: Therefore these two, namely the Sun and Moon, must operate together and jointly, so that what the Sun heats, the Moon cools: and what the Moon cools more than is just, the Sun reheats: Wherefore fire, that is, the splendor of the Sun, sustains diverse growing things, and by that very means they become perfect, each according to its species. Imperfect metals, however, are not yet made mature, because through their accretion they will become imperfect.

Wherefore, through the singular grace of God the creator, this highest and noblest art has been invented, by the benefit of which natural fire can be prepared both in art and in nature, which is able to fix all imperfect bodies and metals in a moment, which the Sun cannot accomplish even in a thousand years. So also that same matter can cure or heal all growing things, each according to its species, if it is added to them: Indeed, the matter of our work, like our art, is joined by the four elements, and is united and coupled unanimously, so that they can never be separated: Wherefore this one thing appeases the discordant elements in all kinds of metals and growing things, and renders them harmonious: so that all their sickness flies away from them, for the sickness and inconstancy of all things comes from nowhere else than that one element commands another, and one oppresses another, whence men then fall ill, and metals are impure and inconstant, and for that reason,

       *WHAT IS THE MERCURY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS?*

**M**ercury is nothing else than water and Salt: Which two elements
have been concocted together for such a long time in natural heat, and
joins and coagulates these two: When this is done, it is then called dry water,
which is not humid, nor does it moisten, and is named Mercury,
but I speak here not of crude Mercury, but of the Mercury,
by which the stars from the firmament work one body on earth, which
is hardly comprehensible: For the Philosophers speak of the fifth element:
This is the virtue of all vegetable things, and the supreme efficacy
brings about maturity and perfection: the other and lowest Q.E. (Quinta Essentia) which
is in the earth, and has partly become corporeal in it, increases and multiplies the seed,
which it comprehends according to its species, and thus
grows from the earth: And then the supreme Fifth Essence comes to the aid of the lowest, which
removes the earth's coarseness, and renders that said seed mature:
For it dries out the bad humidities from the Fifth Essence of the earth, that is,
Mercury and the Q.E. of Heaven, that is, the Sulphur of Air: Therefore the
Philosophers say: Sulphur is the hardening of Mercury, and this is indeed truly so:
That, moreover, is husband and wife, and here on earth they generate many
children. What man does not observe that? But if perhaps
you think that I wish to conceal the truth from you, far be it, I say,
that, of which thing I now propose an example to you: You have common sulphur,
which coagulates common Mercury, just as you see it here,
and in other things: For Sulphur is poisonous, and Mercury is lethal.
How then would you extract something good, which ought to
help another, which is not well possible: for both indeed need

*DICTUM OF ABEL.*

II. Abel, son of Adam, wrote thus in his treatise: After God had created our father Adam and placed him in Paradise, He subjected all things, plants, mountains, stones, animals, which were not named, to our father Adam, so that he might be Lord of all things. From this, nature seized the opportunity that man should be the mountain of all mountains, the stone of all stones, the tree of all trees, the root of all roots, and the earth of all earths, and also be able to be so named and held for the same. For God bestowed upon him that all things are preserved in man.

III. Seth, son of Adam, describes thus: Know, children, how often and how much vinegar is cooked in the art and reduced to ashes, so much and so often it also extracts and makes a white body. If you cook it well and deprive it of its blackness, then it is transmuted into a stone, which is called a white stone for so long, until it is broken apart. Then dissolve it in well-tempered mouth-water, and know that the whole thing will become white, which redness follows, and the whole art is accomplished only through the sharpest vinegar, the power of God, and the perfection of the work.

IV. Isindrus, in his treatise, depicts thus: The air is very vast, because the air corrects a thing, if it becomes thick, or thin, hot or humid. For the thickness of the air exists from this, when the Sun sets, or turns, or rises, that is, hot or cold, and it is dryness and thinness, and it denotes winter and summer.

V. Anaxagoras writes thus: I say that the Principle of all things will be God, and His goodness. Therefore, God's gentleness also reigns under the earth, the thickness of all things, and under the earth, thickness. From creation, gentleness and sincerity represent themselves, under the earth, thickness. But gentleness is not perceived except in the body itself.

THEOPHILUS, Take white Magnesia, that is, quicksilver mixed with Luna (silver): grind it for so long until it becomes a thin water; then cook that until forty days pass, then the flower of the Sun will be made in its splendor. But you will seal the mouth of the glass well, and cook it for forty days, then you will find an elegant water, which likewise cook for so long until its blackness passes away, and constantly cook until you have brought forth its nature, and no longer any manifest contamination, but it will become pure, then it will be fragrant, cook it with its own proper regimen.
XXII. BÆLUS, I command you to take Mercury, which is the Magnet of Luna (silver), and cook it with its body for so long until it becomes soft, thin, and similar to river water: then cook it, as said before, for so long, until all humidity becomes coagulated, and then it becomes a stone.
XXIII. BASAN, Lead the tawny one to the Bath, with his wife, after the marriage, and do not make the bath too hot, lest both be deprived of their senses: therefore make the bath gentle and that for so long, until the body of the man and wife become one thing: then gather their sweat for them, sprinkle it again, and place it back into its rest: but beware lest you drive it away with too much heat. Now honor the King and his consort, and do not burn them. Why that? You do not know when you may need them, who may make the King and his consort better: Cook them for so long, until they blacken, then whiten, and redden. If you understand that, O then you are happy artisans! But if not, then that must be attributed to your ignorance: wherefore do not blame Philosophy, but your gross inexperience.
XXIV. ARISTOTLE. Know, you disciples: Philosophers sometimes call our stone earth, sometimes water. All earthly things are accomplished in regimen and labor, observe nature in labor, in humidity is water, then stone, then the earth of Philosophy, which they sow as their grain, that growing makes it high, each according to its own kind.

By which deed you have the glory and clarity of the whole world: wherefore all poverty and darkness will flee from you, for it overcomes Mercury, which is subtle, and penetrates all firm and hard bodies: thus it is compared with the world, thus I am called Hermes, having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world.

*NOW FOLLOWS THE TRUE EXPLANATION*
*of certain philosophical sayings mentioned above,*
*word for word, to all points and articles*
*of these opinions.*

So that you, kind Reader, may better understand what, and to what
the Philosophers, in their obscure and allegorical sentences, referred,
all of the above-mentioned Philosophers were true Philosophers, and knew and
practiced this art: although many more of them have existed since the time of
Adam, nevertheless not all have come into my hands:
Moreover, it is not possible for me to touch upon each one here,
and it suffices that the truth and foundation of the art be taught
and explained in these sayings, the least of which would also be sufficient.
But that I have produced so many in order, that was done for your benefit,
so that you might be more learnedly informed, might labor more securely, and might
diligently guard yourself against loss of money and useless expenses.
Therefore, out of Christian charity, I have declared and explained this true
Philosophy, according to my understanding, and as much as GOD has granted me,
and I ask any expert in the art who has labored in it, as I have,
not to despise me if I have perhaps erred in words while writing, but
to correct the errors, and that from a faithful heart, just as it has been
done by me, and let no one rashly deceive or mislead, so that the name of God may be
glorified, and the utility of the neighbor promoted: But you will not change
my sense and opinion, for I know what I have written, and that
it was divine truth.

*EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING OF ADAM.*
After almighty GOD had created our first parent
Adam, and placed him in Paradise, then there to him

268                                  *Gloria Mundi.*

...showed two things, namely, earth and water. Earth is fixed
and constant, water is fleeting and inconstant. In these two, all kinds
of things which God created are hidden, namely: in water dwells
air, and in earth, through the creation and ordination of God, as dwelling in earth are
stones, fire: and from these four elements all things arise
in heaven and earth, through the creation and ordination of God,
namely: in earth dwell fire, stones, ores, Salt, Mercury, and all
kinds of metals: In water and in air are all kinds of living, visible, and
essential things, namely: animals, birds, fish, flesh, blood, bones, wood,
trees, flowers, leaves, and other things of that kind: and to each of these things GOD
attributed to each its own virtue, efficacy, and operation,
and because all were subject to Adam, He appointed him as Lord
over them, so that he might use all those things for the sustenance
and health of his body. In these things it is clearly to be seen
how indeed each one agrees with human nature, while man
takes the power of things into himself through the ingestion of food, which
are united with man's nature, and have a kind of necessity to agree: from which
you well understand that the knowledge of all things will become hidden
in men, according to wisdom, understanding, and reason. To understand how this will happen,
then observe how it is written in Genesis chapter 1.

In the first year of the world, on the sixth day, which was the 15th day of March, GOD
created the first man Adam, from the kind of red earth, in a field
near Damascus, a man of elegant stature, according to God's image: and
when he had been created, then he stood naked before the Lord, and with
hands raised gave thanks to Him, saying: O Lord, Your hands fashioned
me: therefore be mindful of me hereafter, because You formed me, and
clothed me with flesh, and strengthened me with bones: Grant me
life and mercy.

These things having been thus said, GOD endowed Adam with great wisdom, so that, without
any teachers, from the sole efficacy of original justice, he perfectly knew
and understood the seven liberal arts, the knowledge of all animals,
plants, stones, metals, and minerals. And, what
is still more, he had a clear understanding concerning the Most Holy Trinity, and
                                                                                                     Christ

Christ's coming in the flesh. And Adam was Lord, King, & Emperor of all other creatures, which, by an Angel, by divine command, were brought to him, so that he might give each one its name, according to the will of his Creator. Thus all creatures acknowledged Adam as their Lord, so that the property & virtue of all things might be revealed to man. Since therefore our first father Adam received wisdom, together with the knowledge of all things, he therefore accurately observed nature, its origin, and its end, and especially pondered the word of God (when the Lord said to him: from where you were taken, to that you shall return): he moreover inspected the division & destruction, Generation & corruption of all things, from which indeed they derive their origin and end: inasmuch as they have their origin from dry & wet, and into dry and wet they must again be transmuted: and these things, he (Adam) knew all of them well within himself, especially the matter which is called primary. For he who knows how all things are again transmuted into their primary matter, no longer needs questioning: for from the very beginning such was the matter of all things, when God created heaven & earth, as if from dry & wet. And from such matters is made one thing, which did not exist before, namely a new earth, fire, water, air, Sun, Moon, Stars, all new at the same time.

And just as from the beginning all things were created new: so also it is with our art, which thus orders itself in every form, manner, & species, and no otherwise. Therefore it is no wonder at all that Almighty God forbade Adam, namely, that he should not conceal the forbidden things, which were preserved in two, dry, & wet, from all his sons: nevertheless Adam revealed that to his son Seth, with divine permission however. But Abel learned the art from the profound wisdom & understanding which God had granted him, through experience of nature, he knew it, and inscribed it on a beech tablet: Similarly, that same Abel was the first to invent & devise writing: he also knew of the future destruction of the world by a flood, all of which he inscribed on wooden tablets & enclosed in a stone column,

Wherefore, let everyone carefully observe this saying and its explanation, but especially let them diligently consider the divine word which God spoke with Adam, and then the whole mystery of that noble art will be revealed to them. 	*EXPLANATION OF ABEL'S SAYING.*

This saying almost explains itself, and has also been sufficiently declared in God's words and Adam's saying. However, according to my judgment and knowledge, I respond to that thus: that man has within himself all the powers of those things, just as that saying testifies to this fact, while man is considered a small world, and is also entirely compared with the world; for his bones lying hidden beneath the skin are compared with rocky mountains: for with them the body is strengthened, no differently than the earth with stones, and flesh is considered as earth, and large veins as large flowing waters, but small ones as tiny rivers which discharge themselves into the large ones. The bladder is the sea, in which both large and tiny rivers are equally gathered: Hair, with growing plants: Nails on hands and feet, and what is found both within and without in man, all according to their kind, are compared with the world. The inner parts of man also, such as: Heart, lung, liver, and other things of that kind, are similar to the metals of mountains: But these hairs are roots, which have their roots in the air, and their head in the earth, as if in flesh, in which they obtain their strength and growth: just as Philosophers also say, that the root of their minerals is in the air, and their head is in the earth. Indeed, that which ascends through distillation is volatile: in it, it has its feet in the air, and that which remains fixed below at the bottom, its head is in the earth: For the feet carry the head, and the head governs the feet. Wherefore one cannot exist without the other, if otherwise its operation
									its

--- Page 285 ---
Gloria Mundi. 271

should have its own [proper] way. * Therefore, man is compared to a kind of inverted tree: for he has his roots, namely his hair, in the air, while other trees have their hair, that is, their roots, in the earth.
In a similar way, it is also compared with our stone: for this reason, Philosophers can well affirm that it has its head in the earth and its root in the air. Likewise, you can seek a similar [example] from Euripus: for the water that flows hissing is the root of its minerals, and the liquid of the water is the head, and it is in the earth. This similarity has a twofold meaning: first, where the matter of our stone is found; second, it extends to understanding the separation and repeated conjunction of the stone. For if our stone has risen upwards in the alembic, then it has its root in the air, which, if it wishes to return to its virtue and its root, must again be reduced to its earth, and then it has its head in the earth and perfect power. And in this way, with respect to these sayings, it can be esteemed as a small world, and deservedly held as such: For that it is called the 'mountain of mountains,' from which we take our ore, is to be understood thus: inasmuch as our labor is considered a small world, provided it does not degenerate, and is created like the world. For that is the prima materia, or the origin of all things, from which all new things are individually prepared. For know that the prima materia will be made when something, buried everywhere in the earth, putrefies, just as food is cooked in man, and in putrefaction the gross separates from the subtle, just as stench from the pure, and the pure is the prima materia, which has been separated by putrefaction. If you understand these things, then you possess the true art. However, keep these things constantly with you, and do not cast pearls before swine: for that art is held as a mockery by the ignorant, but its experts rightly magnify and venerate it.

EXPLANATION OF THE SAYINGS OF SETH, SON OF ADAM.

**P**hilosopher Seth says: 'As much vinegar as is cooked and changed into ashes:' By this, he understands so much distilled water, which we call 'sperm,' if it, through prolonged coction, is converted into a body—

is converted, which he calls ashes, extracts so much blackness from the body, that you wash it for so long until it becomes white: indeed, the water, once abstracted, through continuous coction, transforms itself into a body, and all kinds are elevated in the work, which drive away stench and blackness from the earth. Know however that if there were no earth, then the spirit could by no means coagulate, for it has no other receptacle in which it could contain itself, just as it can coagulate and be bound in no other thing than in its own spirit. Wherefore the spirit purifies its own body, as the Philosopher Seth says, and makes the body white. Furthermore, that same Philosopher truly says: If you cook it well, and deprive it of its blackness, then it is converted into a stone, which is called the white coin of the stone. By this the Philosopher wishes to imply that it must be cooked well, properly, slowly, and not too hot, and then, in the course of time, it is changed into a body which remains constant in fire, and is called a stone: For, as has been said, it obtains a constant and indeed a very white color, and is called a coin: The reason for this is: He who has a coin, for which one can obtain beer and bread for oneself, he obtains whatever he desires for that price, such as health, wisdom, long life, Sun, Moon, gems, pearls, etc. Therefore it is not undeservedly called a coin, and all things which cannot be obtained for other coins, and indeed for the riches of the whole world, those things, I say, all of them, are acquired for this coin. It is also called a coin because it is minted by the Philosophers themselves: for they have impressed their own signs, or images, upon it, just as Kings and Princes arrange for their coins to be stamped. Therefore it is also called the COIN OF THE PHILOSOPHERS, for it is their own money, and their own coin, minted by them.

By this he implies: that the stone must be cooked within itself for so long until it is converted into water, that is, dissolved. This happens by itself: for the body is called Moon, as soon as it is changed into water, and the abstracted spirit

which good also can never be repaid by the entire orb of lands, and all
its Kings and Princes.

EXPLANATION OF ISINDER'S SAYING.

Oh immortal God, in what a wonderful way the Philosophers have hidden
this thing: so much so that it would have been much better if they had
ceased entirely from writing: For it has reduced many to extreme poverty,
and not a few it still daily plunges into the greatest poverty, especially
all those who labor imprudently and without any understanding, neither the
beginning, the middle, nor the end, indeed not even the subsequent
parts.

--- Page 288 ---
274		*Gloria Mundi.*

...sterior, or anterior part of these things do they know. But
the Philosophers truly and rightly write. But who would understand or
comprehend that, who is ignorant of the foundation of these things? No
mortal indeed, even if you were a Doctor of Doctors, and the Light of the
World, nevertheless you would still be entirely blind here. Therefore they wrote,
that which is as if they had not written. For they both wished so great a
good for their descendants, and at the same time also envied them: just as you will be able to
see in their secret sayings, especially those of Isindrus, while
he says: "Indeed, great is the air, because air corrects the matter, if it becomes thin or
thick, hot or cold." Hereby the Philosopher implies: While it
ascends with water, then the air is hot, for fire and air carry
our Stone as a hidden fire hidden in it, and the water, which
ascends from the earth, that in its ascent has become air, and thin, and, in its de-
scent, it lets itself down into water, and fire dwells there, and if it is
put into glass, then the earth is corrected, for it leads fire with itself into the earth:
for fire is indeed the soul, and the Moon is the spirit. Therefore air is immense,
for it transports water and fire with itself, and contributes to all
things, and then cools in itself: for things have taken water from the air.
That air then becomes thick when it is transmuted with fire into a body,
and thus air corrects the matter in its thickness: for it both expels and
brings in our Stone, and corrects it both in its ascent and its descent.
In the same way likewise, air corrects all growing things or vegetables of this world,
thence it offers its food, for it contributes water and
fire to them, by which they are sustained, just as
you yourself are an eyewitness, that it carries clouds, and reduces them into dew and rain,
in which dew or rain fire is hidden, which it conceived from the earth,
and the splendor of the Sun, in its ascent, and contributes to all things in place of food.
And although the splendors of the Sun and Moon may become immeasurably
subtle, agile, and incomprehensible: nevertheless, our
splendors of the Sun and Moon are much swifter and more subtle,
than vegetable things have taken into themselves in their growth: for the Earth
digests the splendors of the Sun and Moon, and most subtly
sustains vegetable things: and the splendors of the Sun and Moon sustain all things which still
live,

--- Page 289 ---
*Gloria Mundi.* 275

...live, nourish creatures: through concoction they conceive their splendor, from which they obtain their life. Therefore the air is exceedingly great, for it performs great works through the grace of almighty God.

Furthermore, when the Philosopher says: If the air is thick, as if the Sun strays or is changed, and there is thickness while it exalts itself: By this he means: If distilled water, which is taken for the Sun or for fire, is made into a body given into a glass, and is transmuted into one body: then the Sun falls, and lowers itself into the earth: By which act the air becomes thick, for it is conjoined with the earth; and if the Sun is again exalted, then the air becomes thin, that is, while water is extracted from the earth through an alembic, then at the same time fire tends upwards, that is, the Sun is exalted, and then the air is thin.

And furthermore, when he says: That also is hot and cold, and thickness, and thinness, or softness, by that very thing the Philosopher implies: The Sun is hot, the Moon is cold: For the earth is esteemed as the Moon, if it becomes dissolved, and water, in which there is fire, is for the Sun: and these two must be united and conjoined, so that they can no longer be separated. And if they are united in this way, then immediately also the elements are united in all metals into which they are injected, into perfect purity and health, both metallic and also carnal bodies.

When finally the Philosopher concludes, and says that thickness and thinness denote summer and winter, by this the Philosopher signifies that our art consists in thickness and thinness. These two must be conjoined with some temperate heat, yet not too hot, nor too cold, lest nature be burned, that is, winter and summer; and when these two agree, then a temperate heat arises therefrom, as in some natural bath: and such temperate heats confer the Sun and the Moon: Wherefore our Isindrus proposed this parable, which, by divine grace, has been rightly explained by me, if only you have prudently observed my mind.

EXPLANATION OF THE DICTUM OF ANAXAGORAS.

God is from the beginning of all things. That is true, for God is light, like fire: Therefore God in His Essence is compared with fire: For fire is the principle of all vegetable and visible things. Things stand the same with our art: For fire is the principle: heat impels nature to begin to operate, and in that operation, Body, Spirit, and Soul manifest themselves, that is, like earth and water: inasmuch as earth is the body, oil is the soul, water is the spirit, and this happens through divine gentleness and goodness, without which Nature indeed can accomplish absolutely nothing, just as the Philosopher himself says: The gentleness of God rules all things: and beneath the thickness of the earth, after creation, gentleness and integrity reveal themselves, beneath the thickness of the earth: Where the Philosopher implies: If earth is separated from water (in the beginning, which is called creation), and dissolved into oil and water within itself, then oil is integrity, and water is gentleness: for water bestows soul upon oil and the body, and assumes nothing more than what is imparted to it from heaven, that is, from water, and water under oil, and oil under earth are manifested. For subtle fire, with subtle waters, ascends upwards from the earth, and and is hidden in the earth, but oil is not raised from the earth through labor, but only fire, water and air, together with oil and earth, are purified through their own spirit: Therefore oil in the body is integrity, and Spirit is gentleness, and the body is constricted. And although the spirit in the first operation descends from the body (for it restores life to the body, although the oil becomes pure and always remains with the body), nevertheless it cannot be of help to itself without the spirit, but the body, as said, suffers force and distress: for by force it is dissolved and purified. And while the Philosopher says, beneath the thickness of the earth, although gentleness is not perceived except in the body, he implies: The thickness of the earth is transmuted into a thin matter, as it were into water and oil; and then gentleness is perceived in the body. For the body is so gentle or soft that it is even converted into water or oil, although previously it was entirely dry. Therefore in the earth oil is perceived—

is seen, which is richness, living, but the life of water is, that is, fire,
air, and water, as three elements, conjoined. Therefore, now, when
no more than only water, which is offered to the body to be drunk,

nevertheless, the power remains with the body, as you see,

and then all gentleness and integrity are seen in the body,
when it is transmuted into white and red.

DECLARATION OF THE OPINION
*Of Pythagoras.*

The Philosopher asks, what is that which is touched, and yet not
seen. By this the Philosopher wishes to signify: There is one thing of our
art, which is prepared by our art; and there is one thing which is touched, and
not seen. This is to be understood thus: it is felt, but not
seen, nor is its operation known: But he who knows it, and yet is
ignorant of its operation, never attains the art. For there is no
more than one thing in the entire world, by which the art is completed,
and elaborated. And this thing proceeds from a certain dark place,
where it is never seen, nor are its operations and virtues recognized by anyone,
except by the wise ones of this art alone. Similarly, also in the
matter itself a great mystery is hidden, namely air, and fire,
that is, Sun, Moon, and Stars: this is hidden in it; and yet it is
invisible, as the Philosopher says: "That which is not seen, nor known,
is only heaven." But that which is touched, and not seen,
is earth. By this the Philosopher implies: Earth is thickness, or body,
which is found at the bottom of matter, and that which has accumulated
itself in matter, that can be felt and known. And while the philosopher further says:
"That which is between heaven and earth, which is not known, this is,
in the world." By this the Philosopher signifies: The matter of our stone in
Mm 3 the world

--- Page 292 ---
278 	Glory of the World.
is found in the world, as it were in a small world, and not in wild,
rocky mountains, or on the earth, but between heaven and earth, in the air, as
if in a lesser world. And when he further says: In it are senses,
and integrity, namely: Smell, Taste, Hearing, Touch. By this
the Philosopher means to imply: In humans there is integrity, as it were, a whole
soul, and senses: For man can know, touch, feel,
and understand these three things. By this very thing, he also gives us an indication of where
our stone is to be found, namely: through sight, hearing, smell,
taste, and touch. Through sight, when the matter of the stone is thick, thin, and
clear, and can act in the ordinary way, and so that you may know
when it will become black, white, and red, etc. Through smell, a bad
odor is recognized before a good one, as when it is separated from its stench,
and transformed into the clearest and purest form. Through
taste, when it passes from its harshness and bitterness to a noble and sweet
taste. Through touch, whether the Stone will become hard, soft, mature,
or coarse, or subtle: which must be done in this art, and senses, and
intellect must be applied, so that one thing may be known before another,
namely earth, and water, black, white, and red, as by distilling,
putrefying, dissolving, coagulating, imbibing, fermenting, and
tinging. And for this reason, through the senses, one is always known before the other.

work is perfected within forty-six days.

Take the body: which I have shown you, and reduce it into thin leaves:
Implying the essential earth, which adhered to the bottom of our matter,
and became dry, which now presents itself, and yet before was not
yet seen, nor known: But now it is water and earth. This
is to demonstrate. For the earth has been manifested, and into two parts;
namely earth and water, divided. Let this earth be taken, enclosed
in glass, and placed in a warm bath, so that in that heat, or coction,
it may dissolve itself, into itself, into water: This, by the Philosopher, to reduce into thin leaves,

For our work here is called a small world, and thus it is the water of our sea. And if this water is added to the body, and cooked with it, purified, ground, imbibed, etc., then the body is purified through long cooking, and is transmuted from the blackest, most foul-smelling color into the whitest and most benevolent color, but the water added to that body, all of it coagulates into a ferment, is joined with the body, and is referred to as the constant Philosophers' Stone: now use it for the honor of God and the benefit of your neighbor.

*EXPOSITIO DICTI PARMENIDIS.*

Know that hateful and malicious Philosophers have spoken of many waters, likewise of many metals, stones, etc. And this is because they tried to deceive you. By this the Philosopher means, that they have hidden these things from us for this reason, lest all these things be revealed to all men. For those who wish to work thus, and according to this letter (although the Philosophers have written correctly and truly), they will deceive themselves, because they wish to work, and yet are destitute of the foundation or knowledge of the art: and it is not the fault of the Philosophers, but the ignorance of the workers themselves. For the Philosophers have written of stones, and there are Stones, and indeed dug out from our mountains. They write of metals, then metals are waters, but liquefied from our ore. They write of waters, then they are waters, but drawn from our spring and sea. They write of sulfur, then

--- Page 294 ---
280                                  *Gloria Mundi.*

then it is white or red sulfur, but separated from our ore. They write about Salt, then it is also Salt, but taken from our salt-works. For that is our Sun, our verdigris, halonitrum, our Alkali, Orpiment, Arsenic, our poison, our medicine, and similar things of that kind. Even if they were to name all things of the whole world, nevertheless it is our thing, and however many names they may impart to it, yet it is at least one single thing. Therefore, the Philosophers write correctly, but those who seek and yet do not find cannot understand it: they also ignore the operation of that thing: for this reason the Philosophers say: Leave the Sun, Moon, Venus, for our material: Thus the Philosopher says: In all metals and earthly things, it is not only in our material: And when the Philosopher concludes and says: All labor is of nature, and yet nature is made. He who understands this well is a blessed artisan, and let him pay due thanks to God.
