	*EXPOSITION OF ETHELIUS'S SAYING.*

He says: Cook our stone for so long, until it shines like some
flashing marble, then it becomes great, and the arcane stone:
For sulphur added to sulphur, preserving its property within itself,
where he implies: If our stone is now separated, as the moist from the dry,
then the dry is taken as the foundation for our stone, and it is black,
like a raven: It must be cooked with its water, which has been separated
from it, for so long until its blackness passes, and it becomes white,
like some bright shining marble: And then it is the arcane stone,
which, by the grace of God, in the cooking, has been transmuted into
fixed Mercury. Furthermore, that arcane stone, for the following two reasons.
One is: because it is found in a certain arcane place, of which no one
suspects, so that in such a vile thing so great a virtue, mystery, and the highest
treasure will be hidden, that no one can find it by their own reason,
without some teacher, and the instruction of some master, or a singular
gift of GOD. Therefore, the Philosopher can rightly affirm: IT IS THE
ARCANE STONE. And while he further says: Sulphur is joined to sulphur,
preserving its property within itself, there the Philosopher understands:
When the matter is separated, as it were, the spirit apart, and the body
also apart, it is nevertheless separated: And although two matters are
present there, nevertheless at least one matter exists, and again one is
transmuted into a body: Indeed, the lowest, as the body, is sulphur,
and the highest, the spirit, is also sulphur: And when the spirit
approaches the body, then one sulphur comes to the other, that is,
sulphur joined to sulphur, and that is its property: Namely,
the spirit belongs to the body, and the body belongs to the spirit: For
one cannot be without the other. Therefore these two sulphurs are
hidden in nature, both white and red, and white sulphur in the body

--- Page 297 ---
*Gloria Mundi.* 283

in the black thing, but the red is hidden under the white: And if the spirit is added to the body in order, gradually, until it has completely coagulated itself into the body, and then sulfur is added to sulfur, and it is completely perfected. No foreign thing intervenes there, and this is its property. Therefore it assumes nothing but its own spirit, for the body has preserved the soul of the body within itself, and what has been extracted from the body, that must always uniquely be restored to it. Therefore nothing is more pleasing and acceptable to it than its own soul, its own body, that is, its own nature, to which end the Philosopher says: If it is thus accumulated: namely, spirit to body, sulfur to sulfur, earth to water, and it becomes completely white, then the body will retain the spirit within itself, nor will it fly away, so that they cannot again be separated from each other. And in this way you have the earth of the Philosophers, most purely purified, into which we sow our grain, so that it may produce infinite fruit.

<center>*EXPLANATION OF THE SAYING*</center>
<center>*Of Pythagoras.*</center>

You would not undeservedly wonder, on account of the earth and the wonderful sayings of the Philosophers: for how manifoldly indeed they have described this matter, yet in this one matter they completely agree, for all their sayings refer to one thing: If only you observe correctly, you will certainly discover the truth. For where the Philosopher says: We give you a regimen concerning these matters, which will become water, dry, like the water of the Moon, which you have prepared, there the Philosopher asserts; When we wish to elaborate this art, then properly, according to our understanding, we ought to conform ourselves: in which if we err, and aim least at the target, then we can deservedly blame them as impostors: for they publicly hand down the regimen: But if you do not aim, then at least it must be ascribed to your own cunning or foolishness, while you interpret the writing otherwise than it sounds, according to your insane and restless minds. Furthermore, while the Philosopher says, that its own

its own water it drinks: by this he implies, when the dry is separated from the moist, then the extracted water of the body is true water, and the water of the Moon, which you have prepared through putrefaction and distillation. Indeed, that extracted water is taken for the husband, and the earth, as the body, for the wife. If therefore the water is now in itself, then you will uniquely transport the water from the husband to the water of the wife, so that they may then unite in marriage. This done, the body drinks its own prepared water, from time to time, and always becomes purer, yet never drinks more, until it becomes white beyond all measure: And that is then called our calx, and pour the water of our calx onto the body, and take care to dry it in natural heat: let this be done so carefully, until it colors itself, and is rendered most white, and then it is prepared for the white and imbibes its own humidity. But if you try to bring it to the red, then you will again dissolve and coagulate it, no differently than it was also done by you with the white, in every form, and not otherwise. And this, amen, amen, is truly true, simple, and right, according to the true Philosophical work.

And in this way the stone is born from the mass, and which embraces all four elements in itself, namely, from two parts, body and spirit, is naturally born: wherefore the wind carries it in its womb, for it carried the stone from earth upwards into heaven, and again carries the same from heaven to earth, and in this way the stone takes spirit from above, and from heaven, and from below from the earth, and becomes a regenerated fruit, no differently than all other fetuses generate in the mother's womb, and all creatures bring forth fruit, so also the air, or wind, brings forth our stone, truly no differently. And since Hermes further says: Its strength, or power, is whole, if it is transmuted into earth, by that very thing he means, as soon as the spirit is transmuted into the body, that then it has its strength and power: for you will notice that when the spirit is still fleeting, and not fixed, or made constant, then in a moment it operates all that it ought to operate, and if it ought to arrive there, then one must deal with it, just as a baker deals with bread: For a little of the spirit is taken, and is delivered to the body, just as a baker gives leaven to flour, and then that leaven transmutes the whole substance into leaven, and our spirit also, that is, our leaven, does the same, and transmutes the whole substance, that is, the body, into its own substance, and so it must be fermented indefinitely, until the whole mass returns into one leaven. Indeed, in this way the body ferments the spirit, so that also one body is made, and the spirit ferments the body, so that also one spirit is rendered: and while these two are transmuted into each other, in the same way all things are transmuted, in the manner they are introduced.

PREFACE.

H
aud undeservedly might all marvel, that Philosophers, in honor
of this most precious and divine art, which is called THE SECRET
OF THE PHILOSOPHERS, have invented so many hidden and allegorical sayings,
so that in this way it might by no means be revealed to the unworthy, which
nevertheless accomplishes nothing fruitful among the disciples of these secrets,
since they themselves have been intent on concealing the truth. And while the un-
wise read their writings and hear how many riches, virtues,
and efficacies our art can produce, then they perceive a pleasant and most
sweet sound in their ears, so much so that they imagine themselves
to be sitting on golden leaves, and pure chords to be affixed to the sky, from which also
a great art and desire arises, so that, soon to be Doctors themselves,
they persuade themselves, and try to perform great miracles, yet they do not
feel that they are erring, or that the Philosophers are deceiving them, much less
do they know that the wise have concealed the foundations of this art from the very beginning, and
have explained the truth, at least to their children, through parables and similitudes:
nor can it happen that a man, as long as he lives in this troubled and impure world,
can explore the meaning and opinion of all Philosophers, much less
can he read their books and writings with judgment: much more truly is it impossible
that anyone from these books and writings can draw forth a sufficient foundation and
a complete understanding, unless Almighty God, out of singular
grace and compassion, opens his understanding, so that he may recognize
the property of nature, by which he may be able to judge concerning the writings
and sayings of the Philosophers: For nature alone is it that operates all things
through art in our Magistery, and she alone, I say, gives the correct knowledge of the thing.
                                 Oo                                 knowledge

...contributes knowledge, from which we prepare our art. For thus Ba-
son says: Beware lest you mix in anything foreign, for such is its nature,
which surpasses all things. And Bondius explains this matter thus, and
calls it that water, saying that the entire business, or its
whole regulation, is done solely through the water, which comes from the stone.
And Alphidius asserts that the stone of the wise has in itself four natures,
each in its own essence and species, in a diverse and visible manner,
and that virtue and efficacy are in no other stone of the earth.
Therefore the Royal Philosopher Haly says: Do you know no other
[stone] which can be compared with the stone, which has the power of perfecting these things?
To which Morienes thus replies: "I have known no other stone," he says,
"which can be compared with the stone, nor has such great power
and operation, for in itself it visibly embraces the four elements,
therefore it is also added to the world and its creatures,
nor can any other Stone moreover be found in the whole world, which can be
compared with it in operation and nature." Wherefore if anyone
takes another thing, or even another stone, than this aforesaid stone of the Magistery,
his work is lost, just as that ancient Philosopher Arros also speaks:
"The stone," he says, "is by no means apt and suitable for our work,
until the gross earth is separated from it." Similarly Morienes also says:
"Unless you have well purified the body from its grossness,
then the spirit cannot be joined and united with it:
but as soon as it is purified from its gross nature, then the spirit
associates itself with it, and rejoices with it, for both
have been made subtle and pure from their gross nature." And Ascanius in the Turba:
"Spirits are by no means united with impure bodies: But if the
bodies have been well concocted and purified, and the spirit has joined
itself to them, then in a moment great miracles present themselves: for there
all colors that are in the world appear, and the imperfect
body is tinged with the constant color of the ferment, for the ferment
is its soul, and the spirit together with the soul are joined and coupled
with the body itself, and also immediately with the body, they are transmuted
into the color of the ferment, and from these, one thing is made." To which end they truly say

Philosophers say, though in obscure words, that a conjunction of husband and wife will occur, that is, of body and spirit, so that by this means a progeny may be born from both of them; for just as are the parents, such generally are their children: For man generates man, and from metals are generated metals, and whatever is similar also seeks its similar.
   Therefore, whoever is unskilled in the matters of this most noble art ought to imitate nature; just as it is equally necessary that he recognize the nature of the thing, for art ought to follow nature. Many artisans are found, however, who neither wish to understand nor even to pay attention, laboring without reason, and are confused in their thoughts, ignorant whether their art will be an imitator of nature or not, which they nevertheless try to correct and augment: Concerning these, that most celebrated philosopher Arnold says that they approach art, namely, like a donkey to a manger, who does not know where to extend its snout; so similarly they also are ignorant about what they are occupied with, much less the principle of nature, nor do they know how they ought to imitate it with their art. Indeed they try to perfect the works of nature, but, the work now completed, they see well what indeed they find. Therefore, true is the proverb: He who is slow to study books, he also cannot be worthy to prepare the things of art, since there will be no doubt that that divine art has the true principle of natures: For the nature of ore indeed produces true bodies in the earth, some perfect, such as gold and silver, some imperfect, namely Venus (copper), Mars (iron), Saturn (lead), and Jupiter (tin), as the course of the Planets works and influences. Therefore, whoever wishes to perfect our magistery, or desires to become a participant in that most noble art, he needs to know from what seed these bodies of metals are generated by nature in the earth, which seed we take from nature, and purify and prepare it through art, so that from it we may receive something much nobler and more excellent, so that in a short time we may be able to render impure and imperfect bodies of men and metals pure and perfect. But that seed we must extract from perfect, pure, and mature bodies, if we wish and ought to reach the desired end.

Therefore, so that every noble investigator of this art may arrive at the knowledge of nature better and more quickly: For this reason, I have appended the following treatise, concerning the principle of nature, the creation and generation of men, which the disciple and imitator of our mastery should read thoroughly, consider, and diligently turn over and over in his mind, by doing which he will then stray least from the right path.

THE FEAR OF THE LORD IS THE BEGINNING
Of Wisdom.

**A**ll wise and chosen and excellent Philosophers indeed left no stone unturned, but that they might first of all recognize God Almighty from His wonderful Creatures, as much indeed as could be done by human reason: This, however, they could achieve or explore by no other means or way, than that they considered with the utmost zeal the beginning of all natural things, from which also they most diligently recognized God. For in these natural things they truly perceived the omnipotence of the creator, and how great a virtue and operation, power and Secrets of nature He had imparted. For which reason also they diligently labored to that end, how indeed they might, with great prudence, bestow those mysteries with public light for the benefit of the human race. And so also first of all they manifested the principle of natural things, but especially the origin of the first man, and his death and destruction, saying in this manner:

After God Almighty immediately from the beginning, from a subtle liquid: or an imperceptible mist, whose appearance was neither humid, nor dry, neither cold, nor hot, but a certain subtle vapor, which also was neither luminous, nor dark, but was a confused chaos, as the Philosophers maintain, that God changed into the first matter, i.e., into water, then separated from each other, and commanded one part to become hard, i.e., earth, and this is the element of earth and water. Afterwards God divided the element of water, created air there, and from the element of earth

--- Page 307 ---
Gloria Mundi.                                     293

...of the earth, he caused fire to be made, that is, the element of fire. And therefore even today it is to be seen, that namely in these first two elements, earth and water, the two last elements will be hidden, which are fire and air: for indeed fire is in the earth, and air is preserved in water, as daily experience testifies to that more than sufficiently. And in this way God the Father also created the firmament, the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars, and placed each in its order as soon as possible. Then the eternal Creator created an animal in his own image, and formed it from some moist earth; by which it is implied, that he took the greater part from the earth (in which fire was preserved), and moistened it with water (in which air was held enclosed), and formed man from it. Therefore it is said that man was created from four elements, and will be called a small world. But after God had formed man sufficiently perfect in the aforementioned manner, and according to his own image, he then lay there like a corpse, and it is written, that God raised him up and breathed the living spirit into his nostrils, whence also the eternal God, beyond all doubt, named man Adam. In a similar manner also, Almighty God created from the four elements all elements dwelling between heaven and earth, just as also all vegetables and minerals, and commanded them to grow. And so much for the first creation, which being completed, Almighty God transferred Adam into Paradise, which he had planted with his own hands: which was adorned with so many most elegant, wonderful, and pleasing flowers, fruits, roots, herbs, leaves, and grass, in which man Adam fulfilled every desire and joy of his heart, and from it understood the omnipotence of God his creator more than sufficiently, he extolled his name with praises, celebrated, honored him, and truly saw there with his own eyes what his heart desired: for he then lacked nothing, and was made Lord of all animals, as well as of the rest of God's creatures. Therefore the eternal creator commanded his holy angels to lead all animals to Adam, so that they might acknowledge him as their Lord, and in turn Adam [assigned] to each its own peculiar

AND Almighty God granted them his paradise to be inhabited for a thousand years, whose descendants would also spend a thousand years, with all excellence and glory, in that same Paradise, and then be received with body and soul into heaven and eternal life, and this was because man at that time was formed entirely pure and chaste by the Almighty Creator, and no fragility was seen in him, nor was he subject to any fevers or diseases, and, in short, he had absolutely no blemishes in himself, but was entirely perfect, pleasing and acceptable to God his creator, who created him in his own image, and all the fruits of Paradise, so that he, together with all his descendants, might eat of them, he perpetually forbade him only the tree of knowledge,

Therefore, Almighty God chastised man with a heavy yoke, which was made of misery, calamity, tribulation, want, and disease, under which bitter death hangs: that Almighty God cast upon Adam's neck, and, together with him, cast him out of Paradise, and cursed the field, so that in the future it would not produce its fruits of its own accord, but only mere weeds.

And since Adam, by divine command, now driven by an Angel from Paradise into a horrid and uncultivated world, had to sustain himself by digging and cultivating the field, and to eat his bread in the sweat of his brow, and, moreover, had endured many calamities, with care and anxiety, Adam, bearing this impatiently, seriously considered the wrath of God, and deplored his transgressions with many tears, and becoming a suppliant to God, implored His grace and clemency, and with utmost zeal, and without any intermission, invoked His help. This done, God mitigated His paternal heart, and by remitting His wrath, became so mindful of His mercy, that He again freed man from the yoke previously imposed: The weight, however, appended to that yoke, namely temporal death, always followed him, and finally conquered and killed him.
But indeed, God not only mitigated Adam's punishment and removed the yoke of tribulation from him, but also provided means by which he could in the future protect himself against impending calamities and tribulations. Therefore, to that same Adam, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the properties of natures were revealed, so that a complete [understanding] of them—

And finally, when Adam recognized that the medicine no longer cheered him, and in his sickness, he perceived no effect or further refreshment of his life: therefore, he diligently awaited the end of his life and death, and, his life's course now finished, he abstained from the cure and implored God's grace. Having sent his son Seth (to whom he had entrusted all secrets) before Paradise, he asked that the tree of life be given to him, which, however, was then denied to him. Seth, therefore, having returned to his father, indicated to him that denial by the Angel. Adam, therefore, being sad and perceiving that his sickness would not abate, now near death, sent his son Seth again to Paradise, so that he might ask for the oil of mercy from there and bring it to him, but in the meantime, Adam piously expired. But Seth, coming to Paradise, inquired about the oil of mercy, but by divine command, he brought back olive seeds from the Angel, which, having returned home, he planted on his parent's tomb. And finally, from these aforementioned seeds, a tree grew, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, for us wretched sinful humans, suffered a bitter death. Although that oil was not given to Adam in a bodily manner, and he could not enjoy the tree of life in this temporal life, nevertheless, Almighty God blessed him from his death and irrigated him with the oil of mercy, which is as much as to say that the eternal God has now forgiven him all his sins, out of pure grace and mercy, nor will He remember them any more for eternity.

And first indeed thus: After you have perceived God in the order of creation
(His Paradise now adorned with all kinds of sprouts, herbs, roots, flowers,

until he lies with the female: so long also is the earth dead, until, if it
wishes to obtain life, water is added to it, by which the earth, or body,
again obtains its life. And this is the same thing about which that most
ancient Philosopher Hermes speaks, namely, that the dead must be brought back
to life, and the infirm made healthy.

Therefore it is necessary that you join the body and the soul, and thus the lower is converted upward, that is, the Body becomes spirit, and the spirit becomes body. This, however, is not to be understood in such a way that the spirit of its own accord converts into body, and the body of its own accord into spirit, but both must necessarily be joined, so that the spirit, like water, dissolves the body, like earth, that is, revives it, and conversely the body attracts the spirit, like water, and they unite themselves for so long until one Mass is made: that is, the earth is softened by the water, and the water is hardened by the dryness of the earth, as little boys playing in the streets testify, who, having taken dry powder, sprinkle it with water, and make a paste, or amalgam, from it: whence also the Philosophers say that our work is the play of children, in which the death of one is the life of the other: or the hardening of one softens the other, and it is nothing else than body and spirit, which two are of one and the same nature, and from one mother. To this end the Philosopher Hermes thus speaks, or rather exclaims: O nature strong, conquering, transcending, and exhilarating nature! For water is the strongest Nature, which transcends and excites the fixed nature in the body, that is, gladdens it, concerning which you will hear more later (do not be impatient). Just as therefore it was said that Adam, that is, the body without Eve, will become dead in birth, that is, without spirit: Wherefore it is to be noted from this, when water is distilled from our matter, that then the body at the bottom of the alembic will become dead and sick in its birth, because the spirit, or soul, has been subtracted from it and has gone out of it, and the body also is entirely black, poisonous, and lethal, as it is described by the Philosophers. If anyone therefore wishes to revive the body again, and to purify it from its blackness and stench, so that it may become apt and suitable for generation, then the extracted sweat (soul) must be restored to it, that is, its spirit, its Eve, so that the body may embrace the soul, and work in it, so that it may conceive. The Senior says that the highest smoke must be reduced to the lowest smoke, and the divine water is the king descending from heaven, it is the restorer of the soul to its body, which finally revives it from its death. But note well that in the body a fixed, or constant, salt will be hidden, that enclosed in it

is, no differently than masculine sperm was hidden in Adam, which the spirit, like Eve, attracts. And it becomes pregnant, because, as has been said, the sperm of the body, which is called fixed salt, is extracted from the body by its own water, which was separated from it, so that it also becomes subtle and volatile, and ascends to heaven with the spirit, and then the fixed is made volatile, or the dead is resurrected, and, as has been said, nature, having confessed, is exhilarated, and receives life from its spirit: Therefore it is also called 'living water from the man' by the Philosophers, for it is extracted from the body, as from a man: To this end, the Philosopher Lucas prescribes that it should be taken, and, according to the custom of nature, cooked. Other Philosophers call the body 'black earth' for the following reasons, because the fixed salt, like fruit, is invisibly hidden in the body: Others call it 'black raven,' in which a white dove lies hidden, and they call the water distilled from the body 'virgin's milk,' by which this white dove will be drawn out from the black raven: and by many other names is this thing called by the Philosophers, as their writings sufficiently and more than sufficiently testify, therefore it is by no means necessary that more be said about this matter.
      And in the manner recalled, the water embraces the body, and the sperm of the body, that is, the fixed salt, works in the water so that it conceives and becomes pregnant from it, for the water dissolves the body, and in distilling, it carries a particle of the fixed salt with it through the alembic, and through the repetition of distillation, the water begins to become thicker again and again. Therefore, much certainly lies in repetition or reiteration, and it is also praised by the Philosophers, who say that this labor should not cause anyone annoyance. Hermes, concerning this matter, speaks thus: 'When I saw that the water gradually began to become thicker and harder, I rejoiced, for I knew for certain that I would find what I was seeking, and obtain what I desired.' Therefore, water is to be poured onto the body and digested with it, so that the body may be dissolved, and again drawn off, so that the body may be coagulated: and in this way the body is well ground, and purified by washing: which ought to be done repeatedly, and indeed by pouring on and drawing off for so long, until all its salt, or power, and efficacy

in the form of semen, and then is transmuted into flesh and blood,

then it is moved by natural heat, so that it may grow further day by day,

infant, by the natural heat of its mother, is transmuted into flesh and blood.
Then if the matter begins to redden, then great joy is seen,

what should be done. Therefore, this mystery is hidden in nature,
and has its progress through nature.

CHAPTER I.

[Large decorative initial Q in a square frame with foliage]
Since all temporal things derive their origin, state, and essence from the earth according to the order of time, which the influences of the heavens, of the stars and planets (such as the Sun, Moon, and others), and the four qualities of the elements, both internally and externally, move without any intermission, by that very means are produced all growing, enduring, and generating things, each unique species in its own substance, just as it was created and established from the beginning of creation by the Most High, that is, by God.

Therefore no one will be able to deny that metals derive their origin from the earth, having been collected into one singular and proper matter, they flowed together from the four qualities, or properties of the four elements, with the impression of metallic forces, or spirits, and in their Universality, from the influences of the stars and planets serving that purpose: just as natural Doctors excellently describe it, especially Aristotle in Book 4 of Meteorology, when he says: that quicksilver will become the common matter of all metals.

But, it must certainly be known: In nature, the first is Matter, concerning which it has already been said, accumulated into one from the four elements, and that only according to the knowledge and properties of nature, which matter is called by Philosophers Mercury, or quicksilver: yet it is still imperfect, due to its superfluous sulphurous earthiness, which is too dreggy, muddy, and combustible: and likewise due to its superfluous wateriness, by which all things are collected into one from the four elements, through the operation of the supreme planets. And this kind of Matter, mixed from the hottest sulphurous earth and watery substance
                                        Qq 2                                 mixed

--- Page 322 ---
308           *A Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.*

mixed, so that also, for this reason, it could not unsuitably be called imperfect sulfur by philosophers.

      But since Nature always strives to reach the highest point, and to that end to which it was ordained by the Creator of all things: therefore it also never ceases, namely, to bring forth the hidden [potential] into imperfect matter, with the circulation here and there of the four qualities of all four elements until it perfects its operations: and by the accidental heat of the Sun, and natural warmth, this aforementioned matter is moved, together with its sulfurous nature, so that it rises in the passages and veins of the earth in vapor and smoke. But if now such vapor or smoke cannot break forth, but becomes enclosed: nevertheless, it often needs to penetrate some muddy and earthy fats, and impure sulfurous substances, which are in the deep veins of the earth: and however much more this Matter attracts superfluities and foreign impurities, so much more impure it becomes. And this is also the reason why it acquires so many diverse colors, which can at least be conceived, before it reaches purity and its own proper color.

      Indeed, Nature has its best operation in those regions for perfecting metals and minerals, where effective, sulfurous, and Mercurial spirits and vapors, or smokes, are enclosed together: and each quality of the four elements has its own peculiar operation and change in the aggregation of earth or matter from them, due to the external heat of the Sun, and the sulfurous earth, which operate in them. Therefore, this Matter is very often resolved and coagulated, inasmuch as it ascends either more pure or more impure, for which indeed much time, and not a few years, are required. Nor is it impossible for nature that all metals even flee, before this Matter reaches the highest point, that is, gold: And this is quite clear from the fact that several ores, or metals, are found in one mine or vein of earth: which indeed I would like you to understand thus: In the ascent of these sulfurous and Mercurial vapors, they are mixed from the preceding Matter, and united by coction: and if these sulfurous spirits are earthy, crude, and im-
                                                                                                        pure,

*Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.* 309

But if [they are] pure, the heat of the Sun or of the ore will truly become too efficacious in the matter, before it is purified from its crudity and separated; then it hardens with that crude sulphureousness and is reduced to the sulphur of nature, which pertains to metals: and if finally the quicksilver becomes hardened, then it is informed with the form of one of the metals, if this accumulation and congelation serves through the influence of some Planet, which in that congelation penetrates more than others with its property into the mixed qualities: Nature indeed first perfects its operation in the conjunction, or union of the four elements, by which from Matter, or a body arises, which then without any intermediary, is informed with the form which pertains to that mixture, according to the influence of one of the Planets. For each influence has its own peculiar operation on the qualities of the elements, from which then also its own form follows. Thus are made copper, tin, lead, iron and quicksilver: although many descriptions are found, as to how their mixture ought to be, now from impure sulphur, now from impure and weak quicksilver, for each metal its singular form and kind: nevertheless, this mixture is not unknown to Nature: wherefore I shall not describe the generation of each metal, especially of the imperfect ones in particular. But however it may happen, nature nevertheless does not cease operating on these imperfect metals, while they are still enclosed in the earth, until it apprehends the highest and best end, which has been appointed to it by God, in these metals of separating the impure from the good quicksilver, and from its pure sulphur, until it penetrates to gold.

But if such vapors are raised purely and clearly, with an internal, subtle, pure, and white earth, without the mixture of crude, earthy, and sulphurous impurities, and these vapors erupt with force, and are not well enclosed, before they have hardened into the sulphur of nature, and have had heat either in excess or in defect, then they remain quicksilver, nor does any metal come from them.

But if pure quicksilver of this kind is raised without any crude mixture in some pure ore, then into pure, white-

it is hardened into pure and white sulfur of nature, after a little heat, which pertains to silver, provided also that it is formed with the form of silver, from which gold can likewise be made more easily than from other metals, unless it is deprived of its heat, or its natural operation is not taken away from it. But if the power of greater natural heat approaches this quicksilver, before it becomes formed to its end, namely into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into pure and red sulfur of Nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver, and it remains in it perpetually, before the end is reached, to which nature tends by laboring.
      Quicksilver, of which we have just made mention, is the mother of all metals, on account of its coldness and humidity: and if it becomes pure, and separated from all superfluity, then no more crudeness can be mixed with it, so that it is again reduced back into some imperfect metal. For nature does not work backwards, nor is there matter,

*CAPVT III.*

In that preceding chapter, mention was made of some form or Medicine, by which imperfect metals can separate impurity by means of perfect Mercury, and with that form of gold or silver, be reduced into perfect metals: now the time advises that we also bring forth something about the form and Medicine to be made by art.
I find all books of the Philosophers filled with this, while they say that the Alchemical art, or their art, consists solely in gold, silver, and quicksilver, if these have been reduced to their origin, just as perhaps thousands of years ago, and before metals were made. For natural labor always proceeds, but does not recede. Therefore, various methods are also attempted, such as: dissolution in strong waters, and amalgamation of gold or quicksilver, or of silver and quicksilver, and they suppose that these have been reduced to their principle. But in the very truth of the matter, they have strayed far from the goal. For if it is immersed in water, or if someone distills water from them, or if quicksilver is sublimated from them, or if smoke is allowed to it, then the entire metal is found again, just as it was placed. Therefore, there is nothing by which this singular form is introduced into it, since the first form does not destroy nature and species in the metal in its property, as Aristotle well demonstrates, saying: that metals are not changed unless they have been reduced to their prior matter.

*CAPVT IV.*

From the aforesaid cause of the preceding chapter, it can be found that the Alchemical art does not consist in gold, silver, or quicksilver. But that

312          *Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.*
but the books and sayings of the Philosophers are not, because of their lies, to be heeded:
therefore, in the following Writing, it is to be seen how, namely, it is to be understood:
Our Art is in gold, silver, and quicksilver: But that I may pass over this here,
and speak further in the first place, and demonstrate that the art is not made
in quicksilver and other imperfect metals by producing from them the first
beginning of the Philosophers or the true and perfect Mercury, which in these
is impurely hidden and coagulated by sulfur, namely in such a way, as we said
a little before, by strong waters, and amalgamations, or in another way, by
which they can be purified on the one hand, and reduced to another splendor.
     But by no means is the first substance of origin, or of Mercury, correct;
therefore, the art is sought in metals in vain: Where you may simultaneously
observe, whether two, three, or four metals are mixed, and allowed to flow
together: nevertheless, one cannot bring aid to another, such as would serve
that origin and its perfection, inasmuch as each needs the help of the other.
And although some imperfect metal may even be added to gold, nevertheless
gold by no means abandons its constant perfection: For nothing is lacking to
it, nor does it have anything superfluous with itself, that it could communicate
something to an imperfect metal: And even if it were that imperfect metals
would assume its virtue, nevertheless it would become inconstant and faulty.
Therefore, this form and Medicine is sought in vain in metals, which would
lend its service to the perfect Mercury enclosed in metals.

*CHAPTER V.*

Furthermore, it is also read in the books of the Philosophers that quicksilver
and sulfur are the origin of all metals: Wherefore many, and almost all
Chemists, when they clearly find the name 'quicksilver,' suppose that it is
common quicksilver, which nevertheless can in no way be: For it is an imperfect
metal, and as it were, arisen from the beginning, from which other metals are
made: although few things will be written about its generation, and that for
this reason, because the name of sulfur, or

--- Page 327 ---
*Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.* 313

...or Mercury, is used by Philosophers, above the true beginning of perfect metals. And if that [philosophical Mercury] were no metal, then also among metals nothing would be found that would correspond to the influence of the Planet Mercury, just as gold to the Sun, silver to the Moon, and so each one, according to its property, to its own planet, from which it received its property. For if it were one metal [like others], for that reason also the other metals could by no means derive their origin from it, much less could their perfection be obtained through or from it, although the perfect Mercury of that [philosophical principle] abounds in it [vulgar mercury], as well as in the others. Much less will that be possible with the admixture of sulfur, which nevertheless is against the impurity and imperfection of metals due to superfluous sulfurousness: this one can easily maintain: For to whatever metal sulfur is mixed, that [metal] becomes much more impure than it was before, and perhaps in one part, or even entirely, is destroyed.

CHAPTER VI.

IN their writings, Philosophers further assert that quicksilver, or Mercury, is a spirit of metallic nature and property accumulated from the four elements through the influence of the Planets and the operation of Nature in the earth: and from it can be made gold, silver, or another of the seven metals, insofar as it is mixed in its own coction, either pure or impure, according to the property of a certain Planet, which then in that natural coction breaks through the others by its influence, as mentioned above.
Therefore, foolish Chemists say: that this spirit is quicksilver, which most men know from those things, that it mixes with all metals, and that it is soft and volatile. But even here they stray too far from the truth. For why would it therefore be no metal, since it is volatile? In a similar way, for the same reason, tin, lead, and the others would be no metals, since they also do not remain in a strong test of fire, although one is more constant than another. Or also, for the same reason, would the origin of metals
Rr

--- Page 328 ---
314	*Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.*
...would be, that it easily mixes with others: then also copper would be a more suitable beginning for them, since, however, mixed with silver or gold, it remains more constant among them than quicksilver, because it admits liquefaction and the hammer. But also for this reason, no final composition has been made, since they can be separated from each other again: much less through the mixture of quicksilver, since it allows itself to be separated from metals much more easily than any of the others. Only, however, does this union or mixture of metals occur from their origin, in which they agree. Now indeed it is manifest that often triple, or even more, metals are found mixed, as a true judgment that in their beginning they become one thing, and at least to the highest point, that is, gold, they would have been reduced by nature in their peculiar ore, unless nature had been hindered by thick, sulphurous, arsenical, and earthy impurity, which is found in metals. If metals are purified from this, they liquefy, and many stenches, dirt, and dregs are purged from them, and this more from one than from another. And if Nature in its operation had not been abbreviated by the excavation of perfect maturity, or if the working heat, metallic forces, and vapors of the aforesaid matter boiled out too prematurely through the veins of the earth: wherefore also these are forced to remain in the form which they assumed, and now no longer penetrated to the highest point, that is, gold, through Nature's operation, since they are now torn away from that operation. Therefore, let us begin where nature necessarily had to cease; let us wipe away the impurity, which Nature itself would also have done if the enclosure of mountains or of metals, and the veins of the earth, had likewise been tightly enclosed, and they could have broken through and wiped away the impure sulphureity, matured and cooked the matter or origin, according to the right division and measure according to the length of suitable time, which seemed to pertain to their operation: and then from them no other metal but gold would have been made. For Nature indeed does not cease to operate in that, while they still lie hidden beneath the earth: nothing moreover falls away from them except water, which is found superfluous in them, and impurity, for the sake of which they cannot by nature apprehend the form of gold,

grasp, unless this impurity has been properly separated: concerning which, however, we have touched upon not a few things in the second chapter.

CHAPTER VII.

Therefore, since this final union of metals, or their per-
fection in this mixture, is not to be sought, while everywhere their
origin and first Matter, by natural congelation and proper
form, is enclosed, and one cannot dissolve the other, except as much
as any thing admits, whether it becomes pure or impure,
then it desires to remain in its own species, as far as nature has embraced
it, unless it is destroyed by a superior contrary, since all metals
are of one common origin, as if born from one father and
mother, and separated only accidentally into another
form or species, but not in their first matter. And, for that very
reason, the first Matter or Origin of all of them is one thing, which,
through the operation of nature, has coalesced by flow, which always
desires the purest form, which from its own, natural condition,
it ought to have. And this is the form of gold, the highest and best,
as far as metallic nature is concerned. If therefore such a pure
form, which can be prepared by art, through nature,
is added to imperfect metals, then the impurity of the imperfect metals
is overcome. For not the impure, but the pure matter is similar to it: For
indeed, it is the first form for which this Matter was made: Therefore
like is joined with like, in incomprehensible time, they separate
the impure, as if saying: 'Have you come, what is mine, and what belongs
to me?' If anyone, however, tries to argue from this that this form
must be gold, which is commonly known: that is nothing:
although it will be the proper body of metals, from common material metals, and the form
of gold, united by nature. And it cannot extend its form to inform
the metals of other materials. For of these, there are no more
than at least their own proper matter, which it has seized, by which
it is informed, to which it is extended, and no further to the whole common
[nature].

common matter of all metals. And for this very reason, this form prepared by art is to be considered much better and more worthy than gold, inasmuch as it is more excellent, and will be able to inform that common matter of all metals into gold.

CHAPTER VIII.

FROM the natural things now enumerated in order, anyone, ignorant of the true alchemical truth, could hold the opinions and sayings of the Philosophers for fables, and lies, indeed for a certain impossibility. Therefore, as I promised you above, I will explain to you, namely, how the art will be made in quicksilver, gold, and silver. Likewise in quicksilver and sulfur, and by what method their Mercury will become a spirit. Therefore I begin with quicksilver, and truly I affirm to you, that all things which you read written about quicksilver, you ought not to understand concerning common quicksilver, which is one of the metals, but concerning that, which is the origin of all metals, and, in its own Nature, is no metal at all: It is indeed of metallic nature and property, through the influence of the Planets, reduced from the four elements into one. For if it were a metal, then perhaps it cannot be the origin of metals. The case is thus, common quicksilver is far different. Neither too hot, nor too cold, nor too humid, nor too dry, but equally tempered at the same time. And when the quicksilver is perfectly mature, and external heat approaches, which operates in it, then it flies away incombustibly and invisibly, therefore also in the very truth of the matter it is called a spirit by the Philosophers. It could also be named soul, when it becomes swift, or agile, yet essential. Moreover, it is also called body, while it is comprehensible and visible: For if external cold approaches it, then, because of that cold, it is congealed into a permanent body, and those three, Spirit, Soul, and Body, are uniquely in it, a single thing, and contain in themselves the properties of all four elements. For if externally it becomes humid and cold, then it is called water, or quicksilver: but because of its internal heat it is called air: But if externally it appears hot and dry,

--- Page 331 ---
*Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.* 317

appears hot and dry, then fire or sulfur: but because of its internal cold, it is called earth. And for this reason, mercury and sulfur are the single origin of all metals: however, it should not be understood that sulfur individually, or mercury in the same way, should be taken, which are common, and mixed into one. That is nothing. The mercury and sulfur of which the Philosophers speak, accumulated by nature mixing and expressed, first into the appearance and form of mercury, which is humid and watery: Secondly, through continuous coction, it is reduced into the appearance and form of sulfur, which is dry and fiery.

CHAPTER IX.

If, however, I wish to speak here only of the Philosophers' mercury and sulfur, which bestow power and form upon all metals, then indeed I find nothing else written by all writers, than that mercury is a heavy and muddy water, mixed with a very subtle white earth, and cooked with the strongest mixture for so long, until humidity with dryness has transformed itself into an equal natural Union, flowed together into one body, and, by means of accidental cold, the four Elementary properties, similarly tempered, have been formed and coagulated into one substance. And this is the material of all perfect Alchemists, if it is made perfect and purified by coction of suitable heat, if the superfluous viscous earthy sulfurousness is separated, along with the superfluous combustible watery nature of mercury, so that one single, clear, pure, and eternal substance is made from that dual substance, the property of sulfur and mercury, containing within itself the purest mercury and sulfur of all. In art, the operation of Nature is very similar, which is why the Philosophers have spoken rightly and truly: "Our Art," they say, "is in mercury, gold, and silver:" For their beginning is indeed similar to mercury: understand this specifically, while nature begins to elaborate in it, and transforms it into metal, which it has sublimated and purified in its natural gentle heat, found in rocks or metals through some pure Rr 3

--- Page 332 ---
**Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.**

some vapor, as has been said above. To this we now add gold and silver, and that for this reason: that nowhere do we find, nor can we otherwise have in any single thing on earth, metallic powers which have the power to excite the unique sulphur of quicksilver, by which it is coagulated, other than at least in gold and silver. For if it is made outside the earth, then it cannot have the influence and powers of gold and silver, nor can it acquire them without gold and silver: nor can it be done by any natural art, that the quicksilver of the Philosophers be prepared and brought to its end, so that it becomes constant, without gold and silver: For it is impossible for Art, that, through coction, without gold and silver, it should attain the end and goal which has been destined for it by gold and silver. For Art lacks the natural Ore, in which the natural Influences, for gold and silver, have hidden themselves in the earth. Therefore, compelled by necessity, we must take gold and silver. For in them indeed we find the proper powers of the influences serving that purpose.

It must be known however, that to this quicksilver we are first compelled to add silver, which will become volatile, and cannot tolerate great heat. Silver likewise has the power to excite the innate sulphur of that said quicksilver, by which it is coagulated into the form and Medicine for making silver; and this happens with a very gentle heat, until gold is first added to it. For gold indeed desires much greater heat: and if gold were added to it before silver, then also, according to its property, it would require heat, and the quicksilver would be changed into some red sulphur, which would not be fluid, nor useful for the art, or for the Medicine of making gold: for its radical humidity would be taken away from it; it would also be against the property of the art, if one were to try to fix the end first, that is, the red sulphur of the Philosophers with gold, before the white with silver, which ought to be made from quicksilver without any intermediary, and that whiteness must necessarily precede redness, since redness, before whiteness, will be the destruction of the whole work.

*CHAPTER X.*

**C**oncerning the Philosophers' mercury, as prescribed before, it is not *therefore* that form (of which it has been spoken) of imperfect metals. For unless gold and silver are added, then it is only in its essence and first origin, nor does it have the metallic powers, spirits, color, and hardening to bestow upon metals of gold and silver, although it has the potential to acquire that natural property: Yet it does not yet possess the same operatively, unless it is strengthened and matured in the coction itself by the addition of gold and silver. For example: The first origin of metals, both in Nature and also in art, is similar to water: And if you mix saffron with water, then one is mixed with the other, and the water acquires the color of saffron, and if this colored water, just mentioned, is mixed with some other water, then it also imparts to that water the same color which it had previously received from the saffron. If therefore the first origin, or mercury, is not tinged with gold and silver, and rendered fixed with their constant efficacy, then it will also be able to communicate no color, nor mix itself with the water, or origin, of imperfect metals. For according to its own property, it is spirit and volatile, and if it is applied to imperfect metals, then it cannot assume their origin or water, which on one part is permanent and constant; because of its sulfur, which has coagulated it. But if the origin has been made fixed with the addition of gold and silver, then it is a permanent and eternal water: which if it is mixed with imperfect metals, then it assumes their origin and water, and thus they are mixed with each other: then necessarily the combustible and impure (part), by the benefit of fire, is forced to recede from them. And the less this origin, or water, or Philosophers' mercury, gains constant and permanent power without the addition of gold and silver: so much the less also is gold and silver dissolved and led back to the first origin, of which it was spoken above in chapter 4, without the commixture of mercury, or Mercurial water, of which mention was also made above. And in this is true what Haly the Philosopher says:
                                                                                                Spirit,

--- Page 334 ---
320 *Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.*

The spirit, he says, does not coagulate—meaning quicksilver—unless the
body is first dissolved, namely gold and silver: and in this, time is
not indifferent. For then gold and silver have become spiritual and
fluid, and can be extended to the common matter of all metals,
inasmuch as the metallic forces and spirits of quicksilver are more
and more deeply coagulated and united with it: and one cannot
accomplish this without the other, as we also indicated above, in chapter 5.
And although it flows in a strong fire, nevertheless the first body,
(Note) if it cools again, is neither changed into a consistent
and spiritual essence: nor is it likewise united with that medium,
as saffron with water, if it is to impart its color to other water.
Therefore there is no true art in Alchemy, except solely in quicksilver:
and indeed, in quicksilver consists all the power of the aforesaid form:
If anyone lacks this, he must also lack the feminine virtue of gold
and silver, by which they grow in the earth.

*EPILOGUE.*

Enough and more than enough has been said about what quicksilver, or
the origin of all metals, will become, without which no metal, either
in nature or in art, can be made perfect. But it is not yet
known where it is to be sought and found. However, the Philosophers
conceal and hide it with the greatest diligence, so much so that out of
many thousands not even one is chosen by God to know the method of
seeking that Philosophical quicksilver. And although many write much
about it: nevertheless I find a singular Philosopher who says concerning
it thus: that God from the beginning created the earth flat, simple,
fertile, and very fruitful, without flint, sand, stones, valleys, and
mountains: but, through the influence of the Planets, and the operation
of Nature, the earth has now been changed into various forms, outwardly
indeed by hard stones, high mountains, and deep valleys: but inwardly
by rare things and colors, such as the ores of the seven metals or their
origins: and that with these things the earth has entirely departed from
its first form, and that this has happened for the following reasons.
								Firstly

--- Page 335 ---
*Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone.* 321

First, that the earth was created thick, great, deep, wide, and ample: therefore also through the daily operation of the sun's heat, an ebullient, fervent, and vaporous heat was produced in it, which penetrated the entire earth, even to the abyss. For the earth itself is cold, and not without internal moisture of water, and from this, the penetrating heat of the sun excited a strong smoke, or a cloudy and airy vapor, which were enclosed in all parts of the earth: in the course of time, many of these became so strong that the earth could no longer contain them within itself after they naturally sought to penetrate upwards, and finally, in those places of the earth where many of them gathered, they accumulated a part of the earth, one part here, another part in another place, and in this way they created many hillocks, hills, and deep valleys, especially in those regions where such mountains and hills were formed, there also the earth was cooked, boiled, mixed, and tempered by heat, cold, and humidity, where at the same time the best ore, or metal, is found. But where the earth becomes flat, there such smokes and vapors by no means created such mounds, especially in muddy, fatty, and viscous places: therefore, humidity from above penetrated the earth, by which it again became soft, and like masses, firmly cohered together, which at length, by the expression of the sun's heat, a long time afterwards, became more and more firm, hardened, cooked, and finally transformed into very hard stony rocks. But as for the earth that was still fertile, soft, and thin, or where small sand, or gravel, or pebbles, like coherent grapes, remained: that earth, due to excessive fatness, was too lean, and had little humidity: wherefore it also could not be sufficiently cooked together, and for this reason, it remained a less ground pulse, or a floury, insufficiently moistened mass. For no earth is converted into stones unless it is made from some fat and viscous earth, well mixed with humidity. For after the expression of water and the sun's heat, the fatness must contain the earth, otherwise it remains soft and fragile, and would again be torn apart from itself: And that which has not been made perfectly hard, that still Sf today

--- Page 336 ---
322 *Treatise on the Philosopher's Stone,*
in our time today, through the continuous operation of nature and the
heat of the sun, can be converted into hard and firm stones. Moreover, in the earth, the aforesaid fumes and vapors, which first yielded themselves, are tenaciously enclosed by the qualities of the four elements, and are cooked by nature and the influences of the Sun and other Planets, or their operations. If, furthermore, it apprehends those watery humors with some pure, subtle, and earthy substance, then the Philosopher's mercury operates. But if it is reduced to fiery and earthy hardness, then the Philosopher's sulfur operates. And, indeed, this discourse just presented shows us the way of seeking and finding mercury, or the origin of our art. And although that mercury is found abundantly in ore mines, nevertheless it is known by very few people. It is not silver, or gold, or common mercury, nor any of the other metals or sulfur, or shoemaker's ink, etc. But the Philosopher says: It is a vaporous substance from the four elements, watery, and pure. And although it is found in all metals, nevertheless in imperfect ones it is immature. Therefore, it must most certainly be sought in that ore where gold and silver can be found. And since it further says: If this mercury is reduced to its hardness, then that is the Philosopher's sulfur, and this cannot happen otherwise than through gold and silver, which it apprehends, and, at the same time, it is sublimated and coagulated, and that through its continuous natural cooking, by the heat of the Sun, and in its own Mine.

O Heavenly Father, show this mercury
only to those whom you command to
enter your way.

THE BOOK OF ALZE, WHICH IS THE NAME OF THIS LITTLE WORK, ITS BEGINNING.

[Large decorative initial S]If anyone wishes to ask about the order, which is touched upon here—namely, why the most revered Alze ought not to be placed before Medicine, but first the Moon, then the Sun, and other Planets, with certain others as follows, and in the third place the Law of Medicine—so that this doubt may be satisfied, [know that it is] in such a way that the true end will become more worthy than the beginning: and since these things make white and red, nor can red be made, unless white precedes it: And then Simon the Philosopher thus says: Know this, unless you wish to make the white stone, that you cannot make the red: And through the red the other Planets are united, and Medicine proceeds unguarded, unless this Order with white and red is observed: so that first the Moon is placed, and with the white, the Elixir is made, which is the white of the Moon [joined] to the white of Mercury, from bodies it comes to the red: Concerning which the Philosophers of this art speak, that the red lies hidden in the white, and they dare not extract it until it becomes entirely red. Thus, in the second place, it can be done with the Sun, and by the Sun Medicine is perfected, without the aid of other Planets. From which you can infer, why indeed Medicine is placed last, so that from the Father proceeds the Son, and from those two the Holy Spirit.

He therefore who now has ears to hear, let him hear, and perceive the remarkable Philosophy in the book called "Turba Philosophorum", where it is read: Know this, that no true Tincture is made, except from our bronze. Concerning which we, with the explanation of other Philosophers, intend to direct our thoughts to our bronze, and our conjunction, which is called water and Mercury: concerning which Eximenus says: that nothing fruitful is made from the elements without conjunction and governance.
Bronze.

Lucas names it white bronze/copper, and it is designated by various names by other Philosophers, and this on account of the various colors which it acquires during the work itself: and also because the envious and impious conceal it from men, and thereby they can deceive men, as Hermogenes says: And Pythagoras says: Although many names are attributed to it, yet it is nothing other than the true and unique thing, and that through the transgression of its nature. Moreover, the envious designate it by the name of all bodies, such as silver, lead, copper, etc., because it has colors, and becomes the Elixir. Similarly, Lucas also says: You do not need many things, but only one unique thing. Diamedes and Basan say: Beware, lest you bring anything foreign to the one thing: For the nature of metals is a unique thing, which surpasses and excels all other things. Thus the whole work, and its regimen, becomes nothing other than water, that is, one with this thing, which corrects the water: otherwise nothing you seek will happen: Synon says: Understand, posterity, that sulfur and bronze/copper will be made from one thing, and is changed into four. Lucas says: Cook the white bronze/copper for so long, until it generates itself. Thus the conjunction becomes perfect in all four elements: Also, that it shows, with generation, life and soul. Thus at all times it is one and only thing, and not many, or more: and the thing is made from three, namely: soul, body, and spirit, indeed, I name the infusion Vegetability: Man is from it, and this is his life after God. Thus the bronze/copper receives spirit from humidity, from which it receives its powers, and, like other things, it grows. Concerning these things the Philosophers speak: If the bronze/copper is often blinded in its cooking, then it becomes better than before: and if the bronze/copper has a body and a soul, like a man. Therefore one body does not penetrate another, but the nature of the soul, which is agile, penetrates and tinges the body. The soul, hidden in it, is called sulfur, and it is hidden in four bodies. The four bodies are named male and masculine, and they denote liquefaction without water, and water is made from our bronze/copper. Arisleus says: Observe the water which came out of it, that is, the permanent water: Take the humidity which it casts off from itself: Thus other Philosophers say: Take the water with its companions, and let it be dried with that vapor which is similar to it, and let it be coagulated in its own water.

And the male is called spirit, and the Agent, which cannot be had, except from a flowing body. TO THE MAN
Most learned among Hippocratic Physicians, most humane among the most learned, that is, truly sincere, upright, and refined by virtue, by erudition, by genuine nobility of spirit,

TO DN. JOHANN HARTMANN BEYER, D.M.,

Most excellent ordinary Physician of the renowned Imperial Republic of Frankfurt-on-Main, and most select and experienced Counselor to various Princes of Germany in administering medical matters and preserving health,
Gives, Dedicates, Devotes.

MICHAEL MAIER, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine,
Count Palatine, Knight, Exempt Imperial Palatine Count, formerly Court Physician to His Imperial Majesty.

[Large decorative initial D containing a landscape with a tree and a bird] As the dispute, most excellent sir, which the Dogmatic Physicians have with the Hermetic or those devoted to Vulcan, comes to mind, and as it was by chance my intention to publish these three most perfect authors of Hermetic Medicine—namely Basilius Valentinus, a German monk of the Benedictine order, Norton and Cremer, Englishmen—rendered into Latin from their respective vernacular languages, so that both foreigners and inhabitants might have their oracles common to them, it seemed good not only to designate them by the title of the GOLDEN TRIPOD, but also the response of the Delphic Phoebas to the Ionians, when she was consulted on a certain doubtful matter, which was given, occurs to me in this manner:
Mi

--- Page 390 ---
[ornament] (376) [ornament]
The strife of mortals and Ionians will not cease before,
Before the golden tripod, which Hephaestus cast into the sea,
You send from the city, and it comes to the house of a man,
Who knows what is, what will be, and what was.
That is,
Not sooner will this strife of the Meropes and Ionians cease,
Than you send from the city to the house of that man the golden Tripod,
Which Vulcan cast into the sea,
Who knows what things are, and what things are to come, and what things have been.
For by this reasoning I thought that the aforementioned dispute between the Dogmatic and Hermetic physicians could be ended, if I were to offer and consecrate these Authors, as VULCAN'S TRIPOD, in the manner of a gift to a most distinguished Physician among both parties; but when I sought and searched in my mind throughout all Germany for such and so great a man, concerning whom that Homeric saying, 'For a physician is a man worth many others,' could deservedly be applied, behold, I was able to find no one else more suited to this purpose than you (I give no flattery, the unanimous fame of all attesting), placed here in Frankfurt am Main, as if on a watchtower of the highest Germany, not to say Europe, towards whom, like another Hippocrates, the vows and desires of many Princes and Magnates incline. Therefore, accept, O man, as most learned of all, so also most humane, this golden Tripod, or three treatises elaborated by the Hermetic Vulcan, as a gift due to the wisest and most discerning, approaching none of the common sort, and from this, value my affection for you more than the price of the thing offered: For I have no doubt that this work, under this name, will be so very pleasing to all Dogmatic as well as Hermetic physicians, that, the dispute being laid aside, just as those Meropes and Ionians of old, they will enter into treaties of friendly concord: and if I achieve this, I shall not regret whatever labor was expended in translating these into the common language of all Europeans, that is, Latin: However that may be, you will not fail to return the affection of one who loves you, since you are always generous to all equally, especially to the learned. Farewell. Given in Frankfurt am Main;
In the month of January, in the year 1618.

Not so many riches did the Pactolus, nor the gold-bearing Hebrus
Yield such metals in its sandy shoals:
As Valentine spreads out in one book,
An INDEX, which are better than your treasures.
For indeed, he brought fruits from the Hesperian garden of the tree,
With which he well blessed the German fields.
And he led from Colchis the lamb of the golden fleece,
Which was a great work of no small labor.
These things, when he succumbed to the mortal law, he left behind:
For us, that we might enjoy Basil's work:
What you may wonder at, you have here, and what you may imitate, but unless
You seek deeply, perhaps you will be empty:
All things are one, which, though discordant in various words,
Are consonant in things, our author here presents:
Let these things suffice for you, and do not seek too many things of the work.
The instruments, it is enough, if this has become known to you.

PREFACE OF BROTHER BA-
SIL VALENTINE OF THE BE-
NEDICTINE ORDER CONCERNING
THE GREAT STONE OF THE ANCIENT
SAGES.

[Large decorative initial P]After I had suffered some human fear, I began to consider, from the simplicity of nature, the miseries of this world, and I deeply lamented with myself the sins committed by our first parents, and that there was no place for repentance on earth, but that men were daily becoming worse, and that eternal punishments, without end, inscrutably enduring, would threaten those not performing penance; Therefore I hastened, as much as I could, to withdraw myself from evil, and to bid farewell to the world, and to dedicate myself to God as a servant:

And since I had already lived for some time in my order, and I did not wish that space of time, which would remain after the completion of the task of adoration imposed upon myself, to be wasted in vain, lest my thoughts, through idleness, should provide a cause for new sins, I resolved within myself to explore nature, and through its anatomy to investigate its secrets, which, after eternal things, I found to be supreme among temporal things; and after (reading) many books in our monastery written by Philosophers long before me, who themselves, by studying and investi-
Bbb 2 [space] gating

--- Page 394 ---
380                                  PREFACE.
gated and achieved, I found, this added a more eager spirit to me, to learn those things which they themselves had known; and although this happened to me with difficulty, nevertheless, since everything is difficult at the beginning, and easier at the end, God, moreover, whom I diligently prayed to, that I might see what others had seen before me, granted it.
    In our monastery, I had a colleague whom nephritic pain from a stone tormented, so that he often lay ill; He had called many doctors to himself, but feeling no immediate help from any, he surrendered his life to God, abandoned by all human aid.
    Then I undertook the anatomy of herbs, I distilled them, extracted salt and the fifth essence; but I could find none among them all that would free that brother from its effect, although I tried very many: For they were not effective enough in their degree to cure this evil: And thus I found no vegetable that I had not touched within the space of six years.
    From this, with a sharper mental inquiry, I directed my thoughts to this matter, considering, and I began with myself also to learn and acquire with fundamental knowledge those things which the Creator had hidden in the metals and minerals of the earth; And the more I sought, the more I found: for one stream always flowed from another; And God granted me the fortune to experience many things, and that my eyes might see even those things which nature had infused into minerals and metals, so diverse that it is most difficult for the ignorant to grasp.
    Among all these things, I came across a mineral which is composed of many colors and is of the greatest efficacy in the art; from this, I extracted a spiritual essence; and with this, my sick brother in a few days to his former
                                                                                                state.

...restored to his former health. For this spirit was so strong that it was able to strengthen the spirit of my brother, who prayed for me daily for hours until he died. But he survived for a long time after he had recovered. His prayers and mine also had such power that the Creator revealed to me, and through my diligence also demonstrated, that which remains hidden from the prudent, as they call themselves.

And so, in this treatise, I wished to indicate and, as far as was permitted to me, to reveal the Stone of the Ancients, granted to us from heaven for the health and consolation of mankind in this valley of miseries, as the highest treasure of earthly things, writing, as it were, safe precepts, not for my own, but for the benefit of posterity; after I had obtained knowledge from the writings of many most experienced men, so that you too, from my doctrine, dedicated to Philosophy, which is very brief in words but extensive in meaning, may attain the rock upon which truth rests, with a temporal reward and the hope of eternity. Amen.

*Concerning*
