[Decorative initial I]N my preface, dearest friend and eager student of the art, I made a promise that I would indicate to you and others burning with the desire to learn the properties of nature, and diligently inquiring into the arts, the cornerstone and the rock, as far as it has been granted to me from above, from which our predecessors and the ancients fashioned their stone, which they had received from the Most High, to be used for the health and convenience of this earthly life. Therefore, so that I may fulfill my promises, and not long lead you astray into digressions with sophistical errors, but rather open up the fount of all benefits from its foundation, hold fast to my following words and weigh them well, if indeed you are affected by the desire to know the arts; for I cannot do much in the way of eloquence; nor is that my intention; since very little can be learned from it, but I delight in brief words, which contain the foundation of the matter.
      Know therefore, that very few attain possession of this dominion, although very many are occupied in building our stone: For the Creator willed that true knowledge and its attainment be granted not to all in common, but at least to certain ones who shun lies and embrace truth, and who, devoted to the art with groans of the heart, most diligently seek it, especially to those who love God without pretense, and therefore pray.
                                                                                                   Quo-

--- Page 397 ---
*Practica, de Lapide Sapient.* 383

Therefore I tell you in truth, if you attempt to make our great and ancient stone, you must be devoted to my doctrine, and above all things, pray to the Creator of all creation, that He may grant you His grace and blessing for this purpose. And if you sin, confess and do good, and purposefully think that you will no longer be wicked, but upright, so that your heart may be enlightened to all good. And remember, when you are raised to honor, to help the poor and needy, free them from their miseries, and restore them with your generous hand, so that you may obtain a greater blessing from the Lord, and attain a seat in heaven through the confirmation of faith.

And do not despise, my friend, nor scorn the truthful writings of those who possessed the stone before us. For after God's revelation, I derive it from them. And let that reading be multiplied and repeated very often, lest the foundation fall away, and the truth, like a lamp, be extinguished.

After this, do not forget your most diligent labor, always inquiring into the writings of authors. But do not keep a fickle mind, but a firm, fixed rock, in which all wise men unanimously agree. For a man of varied mind often does not walk the true path, and precipitates himself into errors, nor are lasting houses built by men of changeable minds.

Since also our most ancient stone does not originate from combustible things, because it itself is safe from all danger of fire, therefore cease to seek it in those things in which it is not granted by nature to exist or be found; as if it were said to be a vegetable work, which it cannot be, although a certain vegetation may be present in it.

For note, if it were so with our stone, just as with another herb, it would very easily be burned up, so that nothing would remain but a certain salt. And although those who were before me wrote many things about the vegetable stone, yet know, my friend, that this will be easily difficult for you to conceive. For since our stone vegetates and augments itself, they therefore called it a vegetable (thing).

Furthermore, know that brute animals produce no augmentation of themselves, [ornament] unless it happens in their similar nature. And therefore you do not need the true stone

--- Page 398 ---
384                                 *Fr. Basilii Valentini*

...to seek the stone or presume to make it for yourself, except from its own proper
seed, from which our stone was made from the beginning: Whence you may perceive and
understand, my friend, that you should not choose even the soul of an animal for this inquiry:
For flesh and blood, just as they were given and granted by the Creator to living
beings, pertain to living beings, from which God composed them, so that an animal was
made from them: But our stone, transmitted to me hereditarily from the most ancient
ones, came and originated from two and one thing, which hold a hidden third: This is the
purest truth and rightly said: For male and female were accepted by the ancients as one
body, not considering the external appearance, but for the sake of the love implanted
and infused into the operation of nature from the beginning, to be known as one, and
just as these two can propagate and augment their own seeds, so also the seed of the
matter, from which our stone is made, can be propagated and augmented.
      But if you are now a true lover of our art, you will magnify this discourse and
consider it wisely, lest you fall and slip with other blind Sophists into the pit prepared
by the enemy.
      But so that you may know, my friend, whence such a seed may come, ask yourself
to what end you strive to bring our stone, then it will become manifest to you that it
flows from no thing, except from a certain metallic root, whence also the metals
themselves were ordained by the Creator to be generated, which you should note how it
happens.
      In the beginning, when the spirit was carried upon the waters, and all things were
still covered by darkness, then God, omnipotent and eternal, whose beginning is without
end, and whose wisdom was from eternity, by His inscrutable counsel, created heaven
and earth, and all things contained within them, visible and invisible, however they may
be called, out of nothing; For God made all things out of nothing: But how this most
precious creation came to be, I will not philosophize about that now; let the sacred
scriptures and faith judge concerning it.
      In such a creation, the Creator implanted a peculiar seed in each nature, lest it tend
towards destruction and detriment, so that by it augmentation might occur, and that
humans and living beings, plants and metals might be preserved; nor to man

--- Page 399 ---
*Practica de Lapide Sapient.* 385

...nor is it permitted for man, and it is contrary to God's ordination, to produce new seed at his own will, but at least propagation and augmentation are granted: For the Creator himself willed to reserve the creation of seed to himself alone; otherwise it would be possible for man to act as Creator, which cannot be, and is proper to the omnipotence of the Most High.

Now know concerning this seed generated from metals in this manner: that a celestial influence, by God's nod and ordination, descends from above and mixes itself with astral properties. When now this conjunction occurs, then these two bring forth a terrestrial substance, as a third, which is the principle of our seed, of its first origin, by which it can demonstrate the ancestors of its generation. From these three arise and proceed the elements, namely water, air, and earth, which furthermore operate through subterranean fire, until they produce something perfect, which Hermes and all before me, because besides this we can find nothing from the beginning of the magistery, called the three first principles: And these were found: the intrinsic Soul, the impalpable Spirit, and the corporeal and visible essence.

When now these three cohabit together, they proceed by copulation, in the course of time, through Vulcan (fire) into a palpable substance, namely into quicksilver, sulfur, and salt. If these three, by mixture, are brought to their induration and coagulation, as nature operates in many ways, then from it a perfect body is made, as nature requires, and its seed is chosen and ordained by the Creator. You who now presume to investigate the source of our work and hope to obtain the prize of the art through eager striving, I declare to you by the eternal CREATOR, that this is the truth of all truth: That if a metallic soul, a metallic spirit, and a metallic form of body are present, then also metallic quicksilver, metallic sulfur, and metallic salt must follow from it, which necessarily can provide nothing other than a perfect metallic body.

If now you are unwilling to understand what it behooves you to understand, you will not be devoted to philosophy, or God will keep you from it.

Therefore I say briefly thus, it will not be possible for you with profit a mere
Ccc in

--- Page 400 ---
386                                     *Of Fr. Basil Valentine*

to achieve in metallic form, unless you have perfectly joined the aforesaid three principles into one. Then furthermore understand, that animals of the earth are composed of flesh and blood, just like man, and have a life-giving spirit and breath instilled in them, which they possess just like man, but they are destitute of a rational soul, with which man is endowed above other living beings. Therefore, when brutes exchange life for death, it is entirely over with them, nor does any hope concerning them remain for eternity. Man, however, if he offers his life through temporal death to his Creator, lives on, his soul surviving, and when he has been glorified, the soul, having returned into his glorified body, will dwell there, so that body, soul, and spirit may be gathered together as one, and may be able to demonstrate their heavenly glorification, which will never be able to be separated for all eternity, etc.
      Wherefore man, by reason of his soul, is known as a fixed creature, since (although outwardly considered he dies) he is destined to live eternally. For the death of man is merely a glorification, so that he may thus be freed from the sins to which he is subject, through certain degrees ordained by God, and be transported to a better place, which does not happen to brutes. Therefore they are considered as non-fixed creatures: For after their demise they will be able to enjoy no resurrection, since they lack a rational soul, for which the unique and true Mediator, the Son of God, suffered and shed His blood.
      A spirit can indeed dwell in a certain body, but it does not therefore follow that it will be fixed, although the body may agree with the spirit, and the spirit by no means quarrels with the body. For both are destitute of that strong element which binds and strengthens body and spirit, and protects and defends against all dangers, namely, the most precious, noble, and fixed soul. For where the soul is entirely lacking, there no hope of redemption remains. For a thing without a soul is imperfect, and this is one of the greatest secrets, which it behooves the wise and those dedicated to inquiry to know. And my conscience has not allowed this to pass in silence, but to reveal it to those who love the foundation of all wisdom. Hence be most diligently attentive to my discourse, that the spirits lurking in metals are unequal, one more volatile or more fixed than another: just as also...

And although out of love I would reveal something more to you, nevertheless the Creator has forbidden it: wherefore it would be improper for me to speak more clearly about these things, lest the gift of the Most High come into abuse, and I become the cause of many sins being committed, so that I might arouse divine wrath against myself, and cast me with others into eternal punishments.
But if, my friend, even that is not clear enough to understand, then I will lead you into my practice, how I, with God's help, perfected that stone of the ancients; which you should consider well, and diligently and repeatedly examine my twelve keys: and proceed thus, as I teach and fundamentally instruct you here in a figurative manner:
Take some part of the best and finest gold, and separate it by those means which nature has granted to men who love the art, from each other, just as an anatomist divides a human cadaver, and through it examines the interior parts of the human body: and make from your gold that which it was before: Then you will find the seed, the beginning, the middle, and the end: From which our gold and its wife were made, namely, from a penetrating subtle spirit and a pure, chaste, and immaculate soul; as well as astral salt and balsam: which after their conjunction are nothing else than a mercurial liquor: And that very water was led to its own God Mercury into the school, who examined that water, and when he found it legitimate and without deceit, he entered into friendship with it, and joined it to himself in marriage: and thus from both an incombustible oil was made: For Mercury became so proud that he scarcely recognized himself: He cast off his eagle wings, and he himself the tail

Meanwhile, while the lictor performs his duty, a beautiful woman, shining with whiteness, arrived in a long silver-colored garment, interwoven with many waters, who, when she was recognized, was found to be Luna, the wife of Sol. She fell prostrate on her face, and with many tears and groans, pleadingly prayed for her husband Sol to be released from prison, into which he had been treacherously thrust by the deceit and power of Mercury, and where he was still detained by the command of the other Planets. But Vulcan utterly refused; for it had been forbidden to him. But persevering in his purpose, he diligently oversaw the execution of the sentence that had been passed, until at last Lady Venus arrived in a most red garment, interwoven with green, with a most beautiful face, with most eloquent and delightful speech and most charming gesture, carrying most fragrant flowers in her hand, which would wonderfully refresh and delight human eyes with their appearance and variety of colors. She interceded with Judge Vulcan in the Chaldean language for the release, and reminded him that redemption would come through the female sex. But his ears were closed.

   Meanwhile, while these two were thus conversing, the sky opened itself, and from there a powerful animal came forth with many thousands of young, driving away and expelling the lictor. It opened its jaws wide and devoured most precious Venus, its helper, at the same time exclaiming with a clear voice: "I was born of women, and women copiously propagated my seed, and thereby enriched the earth. Her soul is bound to mine, and therefore I will feed and nourish myself with her blood." And when the animal had clearly said these things, it withdrew into a certain chamber and locked the door behind itself. But all the young followed in order, and needed far more food than before; and they drank of the former incombustible oil; and they digested food and drink most easily, and many more young were produced than before, and this happened so many times until they themselves had filled the whole world.

What is above, make below; and what is visible, [make] invisible; palpable, [make] impalpable; and cause it again that from the below, the above may become, from the invisible, the visible, from the impalpable, the palpable: This is the whole part, utterly perfect, without any defect or diminution: but in which death and life, destruction and resurrection dwell, is a round sphere, by which the Goddess of Fortune drives her chariot, and imparts the gift of wisdom to the men of God: but by its own name, according to temporal understanding, it is called 'all in all': above the eternal, that highest Arbiter and Judge exists.

God, for His grace and wisdom, which He mercifully imparted to me for a long time, is to be praised through all ages, Amen.

And so he vanished before their eyes:

This discourse finished, each one betook himself to his own place, whence they had come, thinking and laboring day and night about these things, according as each's intellectual capacity allowed, etc.

And just as a physician purges and purifies the inner parts of the body by means of his medicines, and expels all impurities from it: So too ought our bodies to be purified and purged of all their impurity, so that perfection may operate in our generation. Our Masters require a pure, unblemished body, which has not been corrupted by any stain or mixture of foreign matter. For the addition of foreign matter is the leprosy of our metals.
Let the king's diadem be of pure gold, and let a chaste bride be joined to him in marriage.

Therefore, if you wish to operate through our bodies, take the grey, most ravenous wolf, who by reason of his name is subject to warlike Mars, but by origin of birth is the son of old Saturn, who is found in the valleys and mountains of the world, consumed by most fierce hunger, and cast to him the body of the king, so that he may have nourishment from it, and when he has devoured the king, make a great fire, into which throw the wolf to be utterly consumed, then the King will be freed again. And when this has been done three times, then the Lion will have overcome the wolf, nor will it find anything further to consume in it. And thus our body is suitable for the beginning of our work.

And know that this is the only right and legitimate way to purify our bodies. For the Lion purifies itself with the blood of the wolf, and the tincture of its blood wonderfully rejoices in the tincture of the Lion: inasmuch as the blood of both of them is joined together by a certain affinity of kinship. And when the Lion is satisfied, its spirit has become stronger than before, and its eyes radiate with great splendor, like the Sun. And its inner essence is very powerful and useful for all things for which it is required. And when it has been thus prepared, the sons of men, afflicted by most grievous falling sicknesses and other ailments, give thanks to it. Those ten leprous men pursue it and desire to drink of the blood of its soul, and all who are afflicted by evil rejoice utterly in its spirit.

A maiden to be given in marriage is first splendidly adorned with a variety of most precious garments, so that she may please her groom, and by the sight of herself may thoroughly arouse the fire of love in him. But when the bride is to be joined to her husband in the carnal rite, all diversity of garments is removed, nor does the bride retain anything, except that which was granted to her by the Creator at birth.

In the same way, when our groom Apollo is about to celebrate nuptials with his bride Diana, first, various garments are also prepared for them, and their heads and bodies are thoroughly washed with waters, which waters you ought to learn about through various methods of distillation, since they are very unequal, some great, some small, according as their necessity requires, just as I spoke concerning various kinds of drinks. And know that, when the humidity of the earth ascends and mist is raised, it freezes in the upper part, and falls downwards by its own weight, by which means the humidity taken from the earth is restored; and this refreshes, nourishes, and sustains the earth, so that leaves and grasses may spring forth from it. Therefore, some preparations of your waters ought to be repeated more often by distilling, so that what has been drawn from the earth, you may very often return to it and again draw it away, just as the Euripus of the sea often leaves the land and again covers it, until it reaches a certain goal.

When thus in this way the King's Palace has been prepared and adorned with various manual crafts, and the glassy sea has completed its course, and has filled the palace with good things, then the King will be able to safely enter and place his seat therein.

But, my friend, note this first of all, that the groom with his bride be joined naked with naked; and therefore all things prepared for the adornment of garments and the beauty of the face ought to be removed again, so that naked they may possess the tomb, just as they were born naked, lest their seed be corrupted by foreign admixture.

For the conclusion of this discourse, I tell you in all truth, that the most precious water, with which the bath of the groom ought to be made, should be prudently prepared with great care from two combatants (understand, from two contrary matters), so that one adversary may drive out the other, and fit for battle.

When ash and sand are well matured and thoroughly baked by fire,

From stones, the craftsman also prepares lime by burning, so that it may be useful for

can be compared to the fiery spirit of lime, if it has been brought to its perfection.

Natural heat preserves the life of man: For if natural heat should

The vine in its final maturation has more need of the sun's rays and heat than in the beginning of spring. Although the sun performs its function well in autumn, the vine usually yields its sap better and stronger than if the solar rays were lacking due to a lack of heat.

In winter, the common people believe all things are dead, because cold has constricted the earth, so that nothing can grow from it. But as soon as spring appears, so that the cold is diminished by the sun's ascent, all things are recalled to life, trees and plants grow, and creeping creatures, which had fled the cold winter, creep forth from the caves and hollows of the earth. All plants emit a new fragrance from themselves, and their outstanding work is indicated by the beautiful, lovely, and varied colors of flowers. And thus summer progresses by its operation, so that from such blossoms it bears fruits of every kind, for which you rightly ought to give thanks to the Creator, who has set a limit to such an arrangement through nature. Thus year after year works, until the world by its Architect

But if we rightly look after our soul, then we too shall finally become sons and heirs of God, to accomplish that which is now impossible for us; but this cannot happen, unless all water is dried up, and heaven and earth with all men are judged by fire.

[An alchemical woodcut illustration depicting a symbolic scene. In the foreground, two figures emerge from open graves. In the background, a skeleton with a bow and arrow stands near a figure rising from another grave. Various symbols are present, including a cross, a circle with rays, and architectural elements.]

All flesh, whether human or of animals, can produce no augmentation or propagation of itself, unless it occurs by a principle.

--- Page 424 ---
410           *Fr. Basil Valentine*

principle of putrefaction; also the seed of the field and everything that is subject to and
appropriate for vegetables, cannot be augmented except by putrefaction: Moreover,
many small animals and worms are endowed with life, so that from mere
putrefaction they obtain a vivifying power and operation,
which, among all miracles, ought deservedly to be recognized
as a miracle; but nature has granted this very thing, since such a vivifying aug-
mentation and inspiration of life is for the most part found in the earth, and is excited by
other elements through a spiritual seed in that manner.

This is to be demonstrated by examples; the farmer's wife knows it very well;
For she can raise no hen for the household unless it happens
by the putrefaction of the egg, from which the chick is generated.

If bread falls into honey, ants are born in it, which is also a sin-
gular miracle of nature above others. The farmer also observes,
that from putrid flesh maggots arise in humans, horses, and the bodies
of other animals, just as also in nuts,
apples, pears, and such things, spiders, worms, and whatever else there may be,
and who can enumerate the various genera and species of worms that
proceed from putrefaction alone?

In herbs, the same is to be seen, that diverse kinds of herbs, such as net-
tles and many such things, arise in those places where such a herb never
grew, or its seed fell: only from putrefaction; the cause
of this is that the earth in those places is deposited and, as it were, im-
pregnated for these fruits, which flowed into it from above by sidereal property:
so that it spiritually produced seed in it; which seed in the earth putre-
fied itself, and through the operation and aid of the elements, generated corpo-
real matter, according to the species of nature: Thus, the stars together
with the Elements can excite some new sperm that never
existed before: and afterwards it can be augmented through subsequent putrefaction:
However, it is not granted to man alone to excite new
sperm: For the operation of the elements and the essence of the stars
is not in his power to form: Thus, various kinds
of herbs grow at least from putrefaction, but because the farmer considers these things
customary, he no longer reflects on them, nor can he imagine the cause of this knowledge for himself.

...can imagine, among the common people it holds the place of custom: But you, to whom it is fitting to know more than any common person, by perceiving broader discourses and opinions, learn the causes down to their foundations, through which and from what the vivification of resuscitation and generation arises from such putrefaction: not by knowing it as a custom, but as an investigator of nature: since, in sum, all life originates and is caused by putrefaction:

Each element by itself has its own corruption and, in turn, generation: For let the one desirous of this art be made more certain of this, and from an abundant foundation know, that in each element the other three lie hidden: For air has fire, water, and earth within itself, which might seem incredible, though it is the very truth. So also fire contains air, water, and earth within itself, otherwise it would generate nothing. And water is a participant of earth, air, and fire, otherwise nothing could follow in generation, not considering that each Element is separate, since they are nevertheless mixed: All this is found through distillation in the separation of Elements.

And so that I may show you this by legitimate proof, lest you ignorantly say that what I have brought forth are mere words and by no means true, I declare to you, to whom the investigation of nature's separation is fitting and the division of Elements is proposed to be known, that in the distillation of earth, first air passes most easily of all, after which, by a certain continuation, the Element of water precedes: Fire lies hidden in the air, because both are of a spiritual essence, and they wonderfully love each other, Earth remains at the bottom, in which is the salt of preciousness.

In the distillation of water, air and fire first proceed, after which water and the body of earth remain at the bottom. The element of fire, if it is reduced to an invisible substance through the extraction of fire, water, and earth, each can be drawn out separately: similarly, air dwells in the other three Elements: For none of them can be without air: Earth is nothing, nor can it produce anything without air, fire does not burn, nor has it life without air, Water can generate no fruit without air: Furthermore, neither can air consume anything nor dry out humidity, unless

unless it happens by natural heat: Since therefore fervor and heat are found in the air, the Element of fire will certainly be in the air: For everything that is hot and dry is assigned to the fiery substance, wherefore one Element cannot lack another, but a commixture of the four Elements is always found in the generation of all things: and he who asserts the contrary, in no way understands the secrets of nature, nor has he investigated their properties:
   For you ought to know, if anything is to be born through putrefaction, it must happen in this way: Earth, through hidden and enclosed humidity, is reduced to a certain corruption or destruction, which is the beginning of putrefaction: for without humidity, as the Element of water, no true putrefaction can occur: if now a certain generation is to follow from putrefaction, through the warm property, as the Element of fire, it is necessary that it be kindled and brought forth:
For without natural heat, no birth can occur: but if the generated thing is to assume vital breath and motion, this cannot happen without air: for if air did not cooperate in this, and exert its function, then the first compound and substance, from which generation would proceed, would suffocate and perish within itself, due to the lack of air: Therefore it is clearly found, and fundamentally demonstrated, that nothing perfectly generated can be deprived of the ministry of the four Elements, and that one Element always shows its operation and life in another, and thus manifests it through putrefaction: For without it, nothing is brought to light at this time or in the future: and that this is true, namely, that for any living and perfect generation and resuscitation all four Elements are necessary, know this, that when Adam, the first man, was formed from a clod of earth by the supreme Creator, he did not yet exhibit any perceptible movement of life, until God himself breathed a spirit into him: then the clod of earth was endowed with vital power; In the earth was salt, that is, the body: the inspired air was Mercury, the Spirit; through this inspiration the air gave him genuine and temperate heat, which was sulfur, that is, fire, Then Adam moved and manifested himself with such motion, that a vital soul had been infused into him. For fire cannot exist without air, and conversely no air without fire:

**IX. THE KEY.**

[An alchemical woodcut illustration depicting a winged figure, possibly Saturn or Mercury, holding a caduceus and standing over a smaller figure. Below them is a globe and a heart-shaped object, with various symbolic elements surrounding them.]

Saturn, called the highest of the celestial planets, is of the vilest authority in our magistery; nevertheless, he is the principal key of the entire art, yet placed in the lowest degree, and held in the least esteem in our art, although he has also elevated himself by swift flight to the highest summit above all luminaries, nevertheless, by the restoration of his wings, he must be reduced to the lowest of all illumination and promoted through corruption into amelioration, so that black may be changed into white, and white into red, and through the course of the colors of the whole world, the other planets may also pass, up to the superabundant proper color of the triumphant King: And thus I say, even if Saturn appears the vilest before the whole world, nevertheless, he has such power and efficacy in himself that, if his precious essence, which is an immeasurable insensible frigidity, by its ingress, a fiery metallic body is reduced, its current vivacity can be taken away from it, and it can be reduced to such a tractable body as Saturn himself is, but of far greater constancy: which transmu-

permutation from Mercury, sulfur, and salt obtains its origin, beginning, and end. This will seem difficult for many to understand, as it is, but since the matter is vile, it is necessary that the intellect be acute and profound, so that unequal statuses may remain in the world for distinguishing masters from servants.
   From Saturn multiple colors arise: which are produced through preparation and art, such as black, ash-gray, white, yellow, and red, and besides these, the colors that arise from mixtures. Thus also the matter of all the wise will pass through various colors, before that great stone is exalted to a certain goal of perfection: For as often as a new gate of admission is opened to the Fire, so often a new form and kind of vestment is granted as a reward, until the poor man himself acquires riches, and no longer needs what is given by another's loan:
   When generous Venus possesses her kingdom, and, according to the custom of the Royal court, duly distributes offices, she appears with magnificent splendor, and Music presents to her a beautiful banner, of red color, on which Charity, most beautiful in green garments, is painted, and Saturn is appointed master of her court, who, when he performs his office, Astronomy presents to him a black banner, on which Faith is seen depicted in yellow and red attire.
   Jupiter, with his scepter, performs the duty of Marshal, and Rhetoric carries for him a banner of ash-gray color, on which Hope, most adorned with splendid colors, is depicted.

   Sol (the Sun) is the vicar of the kingdom, and Grammar presents to him a yellow banner, on which Justice is depicted in golden attire: which vicar, although he may have more power in his kingdom, yet Queen Venus has blinded and conquered him with her most superabundant splendor.

All tree fruits, if they are plucked before maturation, are useless and premature, nor can one conveniently use them: so unless the potter sufficiently burns and bakes his works by fire, they are unsuitable for use, because they are not sufficiently matured by fire.

Thus also concerning our Elixir it must be observed and diligently considered, so that the just time is given to it, nor anything be detracted from its goodness before that time, lest it be accused in the name of falsehood, and be esteemed as unworthy: For if the flowers are plucked, it easily becomes known that no fruit can grow from them: Therefore haste is not suitable for the mastery: For he who hastens too much, rarely achieves anything good in this art, but by hastening more is corrupted than perfected.

Therefore let the seeker of truth not allow himself to be led astray by excessive desire, to take out or pluck anything before its time, lest the apple fall from his hand, and nothing but the stalk remain in his hand: For in truth, if our stone is not sufficiently matured, it will not be able to produce anything mature.

In the bath, the matter is dissolved and united through putrefaction: In the ashes, it produces flowers: through sand, all superfluous humidities are dried out: But the living flame of fire brings forth exact maturation with fixity: not that the Bath of Mary, horse dung, ashes, or sand are successively necessary or to be used, but that the degrees and regimen of fire are perfected by that method: For the stone is made in an empty furnace, of triple fortification, firmly locked, enclosed, cooked with continuous fire, until all mists and vapors vanish, and the garment of honors appears with greatest splendor, and it remains in one place, of the lowest heaven, and is stopped in its course, and when the arms of the King can no longer be raised upwards, the dominion of the world is occupied: For the King has become of eternal fixity, no danger will harm him in the future: Since he has become unconquerable. When the medicine and stone of all the Sages has been made from the true virgin's milk and perfectly prepared, take one part of it, and three parts of the best and purest gold, fused and purified by Antimony, and reduce it into the thinnest possible lamellae; put these together into a crucible, in which metals are accustomed to be liquefied; first give a slow fire for twelve hours, then let it stand in liquefaction for three days and nights continuously; then the purified gold and the stone have become a pure medicine, of the most subtle, spiritual, and penetrating property: For without the ferment of gold, the stone cannot operate or exert its power of tinging: For it is too subtle and penetrable, but if it is fermented and conjoined with its like ferment, then the prepared Tincture has gained the power to operate on other things: Then take one part of the prepared ferment for a thousand parts of liquefied metal if you wish to tinge; then know by the highest truth and faith, that only that will be transmuted into good and fixed gold: For one body apprehends another, although it may not be similar to itself, nevertheless, by the force and power joined to it, it is compelled to assimilate to it, since like draws its origin from like.

A SHORT AND CLEAR APPENDIX AND RE-
PETITION OR ITERATION OF BROTHER BASIL VALENTINE, OF THE BENEDICTINE ORDER,
IN HIS BOOK CONCERNING THE GREAT STONE OF THE ANCIENTS.

I, Basil Valentine, Brother of the Benedictine Order, have already written a certain
small book, and, like the ancients, philosophically revealed how the most ancient
treasure should be acquired, by which true sages have prolonged their lives to a
greater age.
   And although, as my conscience must attest before the Most High in heaven, to
whom all hidden secrets are manifest, I have written nothing false, but have
expounded the truth itself, so that the intelligent would need no further light,
(For my theory, prescribed to them, which has been confirmed and approved by the
practice of the twelve keys, would be more than enough) nevertheless, the disquiet
of sleepless nights has driven me, through various thoughts, to undertake to
demonstrate my aforementioned little book by a shorter path, and by this means,
as it were, to purify the kindled light, so that any lover of sought-after wisdom
may have more splendor and clarity to fulfill their desire: And although many will
think that it has been opened too clearly, and that I have therefore taken upon
myself the burdens of many sins, let everyone nevertheless know that for those who
are stiff-necked, it will be quite difficult to find what they seek: but for the
elect, clear and easy: Therefore, my follower of truth, listen to my prayer, and
then you will find the true path to the art.
   However, I have written nothing further, except what I myself would wish to
attest after my death and the resurrection of my flesh.
   You will perceive the shorter path faithfully and simply from the following
narration: For my words are founded in simplicity and without any verbal
embellishments.
   I have made mention and indicated that all things are made from three essences
                                                                                                    made

--- Page 441 ---
Practica, concerning the Philosopher's Stone. 427

are made and composed, namely from Mercury, sulfur, and salt, and that is true, which I have taught.
Moreover, know that the stone is made from one, two, three, four, and five: From five, that is, the fifth essence of its substance: From four, by which are understood the four Elements: From three, these are the three principles of things: From two, for there is a twofold Mercurial substance: From one: that is the first Being of all things, which from the word of the first creation, came into being, flowed forth.
Many, however, could become hesitant in mind from all these discourses, in order to obtain a foundational understanding and perception: and therefore first I will speak very briefly about Mercury, second about sulfur, third about salt: For these are the essences of our stone's matter.
First, know that no common quicksilver is useful, but our quicksilver is made from the best metal through the spagyric art, pure, subtle, clear, shining, like a small spring, translucent, like crystal, without any impurity: From this, make a combustible water or oil: For Mercury was originally water, as all Sages agree with this opinion and doctrine of mine.
In this oil of Mercury, dissolve the proper Mercury, from which the water itself was made, and precipitate the same Mercury with its own oil, then a twofold Mercurial substance is obtained: know, however, that your gold must first be dissolved in a certain singular water, expressed by my second key, after its purification by the first key, and reduced to a subtle calx, as is found in the fourth key, and then such a calx should be sublimated by the spirit of salt and precipitated again, and by reverberation reduced to a subtle powder; then its proper sulfur will be able to enter its substance more easily, and become friendly with it: For they wonderfully love each other: And thus you have two substances in one, and it is called the Mercury of the Sages, and it is at least a single substance, that is, the first ferment.

                        *I will also give my opinion.*
                            *Concerning the Salt of the Philosophers.*

   Salt makes fixed and volatile, according as it is ordered and prepared
into its state. For the spirit from salt of tartar, if extracted by itself
without addition, through dissolution and putrefaction makes all metals
volatile, and dissolves them into true living or running Mercury:
as my practical doctrines hold.
   Salt of tartar by itself fixes most firmly, especially if the heat of
quicklime is incorporated into it: For both of these obtain a singular
degree of fixing.
   Thus also the vegetable salt of wine both fixes and makes volatile
according to different preparation, as its use demands, which is certainly
a secret of nature, and a miracle of the Philosophical art.
   If a man drinks wine for some time, and a clear salt is made from his
urine, that is volatile, and makes other fixed things volatile, and with it through
                                                                                                 alembic-

--- Page 443 ---
*Practica, de Lapide Sapient.* 429

...and with itself through the alembic elevates: but it does not fix. And although a man has drunk nothing but wine, from whose urine that salt has been made, nevertheless it has a different property than salt of tartar or from the dregs of wine: For a certain transmutation has occurred in the human body, so that from a vegetable (substance), that is, from the spirit of wine, an animal spirit of salt has been made; just as horses from oats, hay, and the like, with the strengthening of their powers, undergo a change, grow fat in body, and produce flesh therefrom: Likewise, the bee makes honey from the most precious of flowers and herbs.

So also is it to be understood concerning other things: more clearly, the cause consists solely in putrefaction, whence such separation and transmutation derives its origin.

The common spirit of salt, which is extracted in a peculiar way according to my last declaration, makes gold and silver volatile, dissolves them, and elevates them with itself into the alembic, if a small quantity of the spirit of the dragon is added to it, just as the eagle also achieves with the spirit of the dragon, which dwells in rocky places; but when something is melted with salt, before its spirit is separated from its body, it fixes much more than it provides volatility.

Moreover, I say this, if the common spirit of salt is united with the spirit of wine, and distilled together a third time, it becomes sweet and loses its acrimony. This prepared spirit does not dissolve gold corporally, but if it is poured into prepared gold calx, it extracts its highest color and redness: which, if rightly done, reduces white and pure moon (silver) to such a color as that of the body from which it was previously extracted. The original body can also be endowed again with its color through the love of alluring Venus, since it arose from its origin and state, as well as blood, concerning which there is no longer room for dispute.

Note, however, that the spirit of salt also destroys the moon (silver) and reduces it to a spiritual essence, according to my instruction: whence potable moon (silver) can afterwards be prepared: which spirit of the moon is appropriated to the spirit of the sun, like male and female, through the copulation and conjunction of the spirit of Mercury or its oil.

The spirit lies hidden in Mercury; you should seek color in sulfur, and coagula-
tion in salt. Then you have three things which will be able to generate something perfect again.
That is, the spirit in gold ferments with its own oil; sulfur is found abundantly
in the property of precious Venus, which ignites the fixed blood, born from it; the spirit from
Philosophical salt gives victory over hardness, although the spirit of tartar
and the spirit of urine together with true vinegar can do much. For the spirit
of vinegar is cold, and the spirit of quicklime is intensely hot, and therefore they are held
and found as adverse natures. Now I have not spoken according to the
usual philosophical custom; but it will not be fitting for me to tell anyone further
how the doors are locked within.

This I faithfully say as a farewell: Seek your matter in a
metallic substance. Make Mercury from it, which you ferment with
Mercury; a certain sulfur, which you ferment with its own sul-
fur, and with salt reduce to order. Distill together, combine all
according to their weights; then one thing will come forth, which also arose
from one before. Coagulate and fix that very thing by continuous heat;
then augment and ferment it yet a third time according to the doctrine of my
two last keys; then you will have and find the end and
limit of your desire. The twelfth key absolutely delivers the use of the Tincture
without a parable through a certain process.

*Thanks be to God.*

For a final appendix, I am compelled to tell you that from black Satur-
n and by the benefit of Jupiter, a spirit can also be extracted, which afterwards
is reduced into a truly sweet oil, as its noblest part. Which medicine will be able
to most firmly strip the common running Mercury of its vivacity in a particular way
and amend it, as is also taught in my book.

*Addition.*

Since you have now obtained the matter in this way, care for nothing else after the fire, how you observe its regulation; for in this lies the sum of the matter and the end of the work: For our fire is common fire and our furnace is a common furnace: And although those who were before me left it written that our fire is not common, yet in truth I tell you that they concealed all secrets according to their custom: Since the matter is vile, and the work is trifling, which is only aided and made manifest by the regulation of the fire.
The fire of a lamp with spirit of wine is useless. Moreover, an incredible expense is incurred thereby: Horse dung is a waste, nor can the matter be perfected by means of perfect degrees of fire.
Many and various furnaces are not suitable: For in our triple furnace, only proportional degrees of fire are observed; Therefore, let not the talkative Sophist lead you into error with many furnaces: since our furnace is vile, our fire is vile, and our matter is vile, and the glass is likened to the circumference of the earth: You do not need further instruction concerning the fire, its regulation, and the furnace. For he who has the matter, will find a furnace for himself, he who has flour, will find a furnace for himself, he who has flour, can also find a baker's oven, lest he be too anxious about the baking of bread.
It is not necessary to write special books about this matter, provided that you observe the regulation of heat, by which you may know how to distinguish between cold and hot; if you achieve this, you have completed the work, and brought the art to its end, for which the Creator of all nature is to be praised forever, AMEN.

EPIGRAM BY M. M. ON NORTON'S ALCHEMICAL TREATISE.

As the Nile, with its overflowing current, submerges the neighboring lands
   And pours forth waters sent forth everywhere:
And carries fruitful mud with rich moisture,
   From which afterwards there will be good hope of a coming harvest,
So also Norton spreads himself out with a wide scope,
   While he revealed the noble work of Nature.
He extends himself in immense scope, so that he may fertilize
   The alchemical fields, and bless the practitioners.
If you are fortunate, beneath such a current you will catch a fish,
   With which your stomach may be satisfied.
But if not, he will instruct your mind with precious doctrine,
   So that you may be certain to have your wish.
The riches of Hermes are not shown in one book;
   Perhaps this one gives what that one, deceitful by art, denies.

PREFACE I. OF THE AUTHOR HIMSELF.

This book shows knowledge to clerics,
This book increases ignorance for laymen,
A book of honor, helping through abundance,
And a book for the poor, driving away destitution,
It is a book of trust and and truth,
Counsel for kings, doctrine for prelates,
And a useful book for blessed men,
Who desire to live without sins,
A secret book, a book of God's Gift,
A path for chosen men of good hope,
Strong for those constant in firm faith,
And for those believing the words of my mouth.
The false also seek Alchemy, as do the upright,
The false without number, but these are cast out,
And by desires (alas) so many are infected,
That among a thousand thousands scarcely three are chosen.
Many are called to this knowledge,
Nobles and paupers, ignorant, learned,
Who are unwilling to endure labors nor time,
Therefore they will not succeed, because they are ungrateful.
This book teaches the sons of the art sufficiently,
To whom God has given to perceive these things freely,

--- Page 450 ---
436.
Believe these four prophetic verses,
The fountain of divine piety gives all things freely.
This noble science is given only to those,
Who love justice with a blessed mind,
But it is denied to the deceitful and to robbers,
On account of sins, welcome gifts are delayed.
Often this matter would have adorned the Kings of England
If their hope in the Lord had been firm,
But he who will receive honors through this matter,
Will change ancient customs into better ones.
And when he comes, he will reform the kingdom,
And with virtues and morals he will give an example
Eternal to kings; then the people will rejoice,
And loving each other, will give praises to God.
O King, about to do these things, pray to God the King,
And implore his help for this matter,
Then a beautiful, welcome hour will come upon the just king, to his shining mind,
An hour which will not be hoped for.

*Chapter One.*

**T**he truly wonderful Magistery and Arch-Magistery is the Tincture of sacred Alchemy, a wonderful science of secret Philosophy, a singular gift and grace of almighty God, which was never discovered by man through the labor of hands, but only by revelation and the teaching of others. Never was this sold or bought for a price by anyone who sought it: But it is given by God's grace only to a worthy man. It is perfected with great expense, long labor, and time. It helps someone in times of need, removes vain glory, hope, and fear, takes away ambition, violence, and excess, mitigates adversities, lest they oppress anyone. Whoever has perfect knowledge of it is content with moderation, fleeing extremes. Some disdain to call this art sacred and in this way propose, saying that accursed ones acquire this science for themselves, to whom God wishes to bestow nothing good: For their voluntary and false infidelity does not allow them to possess that which is a cause of good. Moreover, it accomplishes no other thing except at least gold or silver for money, cups, or rings, which have been proven and found by the wise to be the least virtuous things of all upon the earth: Hence, men of that ilk conclude

And they deny this science to be sacred as to its effect.
	To these things we respond and declare, as we know;
That this science was never handed down to anyone,
Unless to one most thoroughly tested in every respect for a long time,
Whether he is worthy to receive this grace,
By reason of its truth, power, and absolute understanding,
From which, if anything is lacking to him, he will never have it.
	Thus no one could attain this art,
Unless someone has been sent by God, by whom he might be instructed:
For the thing is so honorable and rare,
That it must necessarily be handed down to another by word of mouth,
So that it is necessary, even if the will is most ready,
To receive it under the most sacred and highest oath,
That, as we refuse great dignities and fame,
In the same way he himself should wish to refuse the same,
And that he will never be so bold,
As to presume to reveal this secret to his own son,
	For proximity of blood or affinity
Is not to be received to this dignity,

	All the character and virtues, as well as the ability

But when Daulton rose from the place, he looked around with a sad face, and went away, oppressed by distresses, nor did he desire to live for another year. This injury happened to him, as I have narrated, through men not fearing hell.

Harbard died not long after, and Delvis was beheaded in Tewkesbury. In this way, great trouble, as you see, accompanies this art at every step. Here the king himself is frustrated in his intention, because Harbard was insolent and violent, since he proudly oppressed a man so noble, and led him captive as if he were a sorcerer, when however with gentleness, patience, and grace much solace would have resulted from it, not only to the king, as you understand, but also to the entire Commonwealth of this kingdom.

But it is not to be wondered at that grace does not come, for sins reign everywhere in this country. Behold, here perfect grace was at hand, for removing taxes and tributes from the people,

Tonsilus had labored in fire

Brian was another with Howlton in the western part
Always busy, exercising the practice,

Because they knew neither the matter nor the root of the art,

They suffered much expense, damage & distress

*Chapter Five.*

When Brizeus altered the coinage,
It was to the detriment of very many, to the joy of many,
And just as that change seemed to various people
A new and very rare thing,
So at that time something marvelous occurred,
Which pertained to this science,
When three masters of this art
Were lying in one bed near Leadenhall,
Who possessed the perfect white and red Elixir.
It is wonderful for three such men to lie in one bed,
And for this period of ten days,
Indeed, they are scarcely found among a million men.
One of them was from the Duchy of Lorraine, as I was told,
The second from the middle of England,
Under the cross near the border of three Counties.
The third was born the youngest in age:
Who, from his birth chart, was judged by the learned
To adorn the English land.
One could travel through the whole world,
And not find three such masters.
Two of them were to depart, but the younger was to remain,
Destined to do much good in this region someday,
But the sins of princes would delay
That good which he himself was to perform.
The senior master prophesied concerning him

Regarding the aforesaid four primary qualities,
Heat and cold are active qualities:
Humidity and dryness, however, are passive:
For these are always acted upon by those,
As stones when they become lime and water ice,
From which you will be able to judge very easily,
Nothing is generated except by heat or cold,
Nevertheless, the passive qualities have some activity,
As we see daily in mechanical works,
In the baking of bread and brewing of beer and other crafts
Humidity and dryness operate.
Aristotle in his Physics, and many others
Say, speculation proceeds from actions,
They report that practice is the root and beginning
Of speculation and all knowledge.
For the properties of all things
Were perceived through their operations:
As through the colors of urines we dare
To pronounce concerning heat or cold,
Through these four primary qualities
We investigate colors in the course of time;
Concerning which we cannot be certain
Except in a very pure substance.
You will gain much doctrine from this,
If you know how colors are generated daily,
Color is the extremity of every clear body,
A clear, well-defined substance here is the matter,
If heat dominates in dry matter,
A white color will most certainly be present there,
As it appears to the eye from burnt bones,

**Chapter Six.**

REgarding the matter of concordances,
You will consider that there should be no variation
Between those things which ought to agree,
For from variation discord could arise,
Whereby your labor would be spent in vain,
Whoever is about to begin our work,

The first rule is that he observe,
That his mind should agree with the work,
Which ought to predominate above all things,
Otherwise it will frustrate all your labors,
The second rule is necessary for understanding
The distinction between this art and its practitioners,
The third will serve your Intention,
When the work agrees with the instruments,
The fourth concordance ought to be well sought out,

# THE TESTAMENT

### *Benedictine Order.*

[Large decorative woodcut initial A]This is the perfection and truth of Alchemy, clear by reason, omitting all the explained terms of that art itself, which has been no small impediment to all professors of this discipline. And I, as a diligent follower of this art and faculty, was retarded in a wonderful way by things explained obscurely to me in many and various books, which I read and practiced according to their instructions for the space of thirty years, to my great expense and the detriment of my labor. And the more I read, the more I erred, until by divine providence I betook myself to Italy, where it pleased God, the best and greatest, to destine me for the fellowship of a man no less endowed with dignity than with every kind of erudition, named Raymond, in whose fellowship I long remained, and thus [found] favor in the sight of this good

--- Page 550 ---
536          *Cremer, Abbot of Westminster.*

On this condition only, that the king in his own person should wage war against the Turks, enemies of God, and spend (his efforts) for the house of the Lord, and by no means in pride or in waging war against Christians: but (alas!) this promise was made void and violated by the king, then that pious man, afflicted in the spirits and innermost parts of his heart, fled from here across the sea in a lamentable and miserable manner, which burns my heart intensely: and I earnestly beg to be with him daily in body, for the integrity of his daily life, appearance, and morals would easily lead obstinate sinners to repentance.

I (most blessed Raymond) will pour out prayers for you to God, the best and greatest, and likewise my brothers.

All wisdom is from God, and with Him it always ends, and it is before eternity. Whoever loves wisdom, let him seek it from Him, and ask it from Him, because He will give abundance and will not reject. For sometimes the height and depth of all knowledge and the treasure of wisdom is given to men by God, because from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things, and without His will nothing can be done. On the first day of my discourse, I invoke His help, who is the fount and origin of all good things, that He, through His kindness, may deign to increase my knowledge through truth, that through the grace of the Holy Spirit He may wish to manifest the light of my doctrine (which lay hidden in darkness), and lead those who err into the path of truth, which He may deign to grant, who sits on high, who disposes and rules all things for ever and ever. Amen.

LIVING WATER, SO CALLED, WHICH GIVES LIFE TO THE WHOLE WORK OF OUR ART.

Take three ounces of good tartaric acid from claret wine, strong and pure; and to these,
five ounces of Petroleum, two ounces of live sulfur, two ounces of yellow Arsenic, three
ounces of Rabusenus, two ounces of willow charcoal; mix and distill all these in
a Neptune's bath, in a glass vessel, whose neck must be well sealed:
The receiver will be one cubit high, well sealed, so that the spirit or
fume does not escape; and when you see it distilling with a pale color, then
take no more; remove the upper part of the still until it cools down:
which is completed in four days: Avoid its odor,
for it is dangerous: This water is to be preserved in a strong and thick glass vessel,
diligently sealed, and to be used as assigned in the following [pages].

THE SECOND WATER IS TO BE DISTILLED

*Chapter Two.*

Take the water of an undefiled youth after his first sleep for three or four nights or longer, so that three sextarii are produced, and thus pour it each night into a stone cup sealed on all sides, and then take the dregs from it, then from the purest and thinnest part of the same take a measure of one sextarius: two urns of very strong wine vinegar; two ℥ of quicklime, half an ounce of living water, as we made mention in the first chapter, and pour into an earthen pot, and place over it an alembic or still well sealed with clay, and let it stand for one day and one night before you build a fire under it, beware lest you affect it with too much heat, and thus distilling for five or six days, and as many nights, without interruption, so that it drips drop by drop into your glass receiver, which must be carefully sealed and luted with clayey material lest the spirit or smoke of the same escape; and when the liquid distills or flows down, blue or pale, no more is to be drawn from it.

*Chapter Three.*

Chapter Five.
Take eight pounds of the purest and softest lead, two pounds of pure
tin, and melt that in a well-covered earthenware pot (as written before),
and then place it on a wood fire, and blow on it with a gentle draft
for three hours, then remove the scum of the metal dross, until it is pure
and clear, then throw in a quarter part of one ounce of true powder
of red stone, purely crushed, and likewise diligently stir it with an iron
rod, until the metals are reddish, then cover the pot and let it stand for seventy-

and when it is liquid and not fixed, you will be able to change it into whatever form you wish,
thus you have the completion of the whole work clearly placed before your eyes:

METHOD OF MAKING LUTE.
Make your lute so that you may keep your receiver sealed,
and stop up your glass vessel, and the upper part of the same, for the
works of the forty days, as follows: make it with bitumen or quicklime,
mastic, and egg white, diligently ground, with a small amount of
Armenian bole.
Diligently ensure that your petroleum is splendid, pure, and
yellow; if it is not so, it is imperfect.
Also ensure that your Rabusenum is red and white,
according to the color of Vermilion.
To my dearest brothers in this monastic life and profession,
Alexander, Richard, to whom I give command, that they observe these rules
(written down in the name of the most blessed Trinity), and guard them
with the utmost diligence and care;
Firstly, I command that this divine work be revealed to no one
greedy for human things or contaminated by the most wicked deed, nor to any
other whatsoever, except to the Abbot and Prior who shall succeed in this
dwelling hereafter; and this not even before the keys of our treasury are
committed to their custody, and then you shall take an oath from them
on the most holy Gospels, that they shall not reveal this mystery to any
powerful man or most noble man, nor to any inferior
brothers of this house.
Furthermore, I command that none of you shall perform this work in this
our house, unless it should fall into some poverty or ruin, which indeed
seems impossible to you and me, because I have left so great a treasure
(which is not unknown to you); and therefore I give you a command,
that you, who are placed in the highest degree of dignity in this house,
namely the Abbot, Prior, and the most senior elders, that one of you
shall renew this work of mine, and the practice by rewriting it
whenever the number of sixty years is completed; For that will preserve this
work of mine so that it can be understood as correctly as possible: And since
the method of writing letters by characters varies, a complete rewriting
is the safest way of preserving our work, so that it may be left whole and
inviolate to our successors.

# PREFACE.

To all genuine Inquirers into the CHYMICAL art, namely the Sons of Hermes, the Author prays for health and blessing from God.

When I considered with myself, Candid Reader, that many adulterated Books, and false (as they call them) Recipes of Alchemists, compiled by the fraud and avarice of Impostors, in which not even a spark of truth shines forth, are circulated among the inquirers into natural and and occult arts; by which very many have been deceived, and are still being deceived: I thought I could do nothing more useful than if I shared the Talent entrusted to me by the Father of lights with the sons and heirs of knowledge. So that posterity might also observe that not only in previous centuries, but also in this our own, that singular Philosophical blessing of God had not been denied to certain men. It seemed not advisable to publish my name for certain reasons, while I do not seek praise for myself, but strive to benefit the lovers of Philosophy. Therefore, to benefit, I leave the vain desire for glory to those who prefer TO SEEM than TO BE. What I write here in undoubted attestation of Philosophical truth, comprehended in a few words, has been drawn forth from manual experience granted to me by the Most High: so that those who in this most praised science have laid the first and real foundations,

Zzz 2                                                                 hac

--- Page 562 ---
548           PRÆFATIO.
*by this exhortation, may not abandon the practice of most beautiful things:*
*and thus may be safe from the wicked crowd of Smoke-sellers, for whom it is sweet*
*to deceive. They are not dreams, as the ignorant common people say,*
*nor empty inventions of idle men, as the foolish and*
*unwise, who laugh at the art. It is the very Philosophical Truth;*
*which, as a lover of truth, in aid and confirmation of Chemical truth, undeservedly*
*proclaimed, I neither ought nor could I hide or wrap in silence.*
*Although in these malignant times (where virtue and vice are equated) because of the age's*
*unworthiness and men's ingratitude and infidelity*

*public. I could adduce witnesses of this Chemical truth,*
*namely, most authoritative authors, according to the unanimous*

Furthermore, I offer these present Treatises, written from my experience, to the sons of science: so that while they are engaged with every thought and movement of their mind in investigating the operations in the eyes of Nature, they may thence perceive and know the truth of things, and Nature itself: in which thing alone consists the perfection of the whole most holy Philosophical Art, provided they proceed by the Royal Way, which Nature prescribes in all operations. FIRST TREATISE
On
N A T U R E,
What it is, and what kind of Investigators it should have.

[Large decorative initial M] Many wise and very learned men, many centuries ago, indeed (as Hermes testifies) before the flood, wrote many things about making the Philosopher's Stone; and they left us so many writings that unless Nature daily worked credible things for us, hardly anyone would now believe NATURE to be real: because in previous centuries there were not so many inventors of things; Nor did our ancestors consider anything else besides Nature itself, and Nature's potential. And although they remained only in the simple path of Nature, yet they discovered things which we, now engaged in so many things, could scarcely imagine with our intellects. This happens because to us, Nature and the generation of things in the world now seem commonplace and simple. And therefore our intellects we direct not towards known things, but towards such things as cannot or can scarcely be done: wherefore it is easier for us to devise subtle things, things which the Philosophers themselves would not know how to imagine, than to arrive at the true course of Nature and the meaning of the Philosophers. And thus the nature of men is constituted, that it neglects what it knows, always seeks other things; much more so human intellects, to which Nature is subject. For example; you see any artisan, when he has already reached the highest perfection of his craft, he seeks other things, or abuses it, or plainly gives up. So also generous Nature always acts even into the very Iliad,
hoc

--- Page 568 ---
454	*New Chemical Light.*
this is, the ultimate limit, after which it ceases. For a certain permission was instilled in Nature from the beginning, so that through its entire course it could come to better things, and have complete rest, towards which it strives with every effort, and rejoices in its end, not otherwise than an old Ant, for whom Nature creates wings in old age. So indeed our intellects have progressed so far, especially in the Philosophical Art, or the practice of the stone, that we have now almost reached the very Iliad (climax). For the Art of Chemistry now discovers such subtleties, that scarcely greater ones can be found; and to that extent it differs from the Art of the ancient Philosophers, as a Clockmaker from a simple Blacksmith: And although both handle Iron, nevertheless neither would know the labors of the other, even though both are Masters in their art. If Hermes himself, the father of Philosophers, were to revive, and Geber of subtle genius, with the most profound RAYMOND LULLY, they would be considered not as Philosophers, but rather as disciples by our Chemists: They would not know so many distillations used today, so many circulations, so many calcinations, and so many other innumerable works of Artists, which men of this century have found and devised from their writings. Only one thing is lacking for us, that we know what they themselves did, namely the Philosopher's Stone or the Physical Tincture. While we seek that, we find other things: and if human procreation were not so common, and nature held its right in it, we would now almost certainly go astray. But, to return to the purpose, I promised in this first Treatise to explain Nature; lest vain imagination deflect us from the simple true path. Therefore I say NATURE is One: true, simple, entire in its being, which GOD made before the ages, and enclosed a spirit within it: know however that the Terminus (end/limit) of Nature is GOD, who is also the beginning of Nature; since no beginning is ended except in that in which it begins. I said it is only one, through which God makes all things: not that God would not know how to operate without it, (since He Himself made Nature, and is omnipotent;) but thus it pleased Him, and He did it. All things proceed from that one Nature; nor is there anything in the world outside of Nature: And although sometimes failures occur; this is not a fault of nature, but either of the artist or of the place. This Nature is divided

*Novum Lumen Chemicum* 555

is divided into four places, in which it operates all these things which appear and are in shadow, since things are rather in shadow than that they truly appear. It is changed into male and female, and resembles Mercury, because it joins itself to various places; and according to the places of the earth, it produces good or bad things; although there are no bad places on Earth, as it seems to us. Qualities, however, are only four, and these are inherent in all things, nor do they agree; always one exceeds the other. Nature, however, is not visible, although it acts visibly; for it is a volatile spirit, which performs its office in bodies: it has its place and seat in the Divine will. To us in this place, it profits nothing else, unless that we know its places, which are more suitable or nearer to it; that is, that we know how to join thing to thing, according to Nature, lest wood be mixed with man, or an Ox or animal with metal; but that each thing acts on its like: and then also Nature will perform its office. The place of Nature is no other than, as said above, in the will of God.

INVESTIGATORS of Nature ought to be such as Nature itself is: truthful, simple, patient, constant, etc., and what is greatest, pious, fearing God, not harming their neighbor. Afterwards they should diligently consider whether their purpose agrees with Nature; whether it is possible they learn from apparent examples, from which things, namely, what is made, how, and in what vessel Nature operates. For if you simply wish to do something, as Nature itself does, follow Nature: but if you attempt something more excellent than Nature, observe in what, and by what it is improved, and let it always be done in its like. For example, if you wish to promote metal (which is our intention) further in virtue than Nature has made it, it is necessary to take Metallic Nature, and this in male and female, otherwise you will accomplish nothing: For if you intend to create Metal from herbs, you will labor in vain; just as you will not produce wood from a dog or a beast.

TREATISE TWO,
*On the Operation of Nature in our purpose*
*& in Seed.*

I HAVE already said that Nature is true, unique, everywhere apparent,
continuous, which is known from the things produced, namely woods,
herbs, &c. I have also said that the scrutineer of Nature must be truthful,
simple, patient, constant, applying his mind to at least one thing, &c.
Now we must begin concerning the act of Nature. Just as Nature
is in the will of God, and God created it, or imposed it upon all imagination:
so Nature made for itself a seed, that is, its will in the Elements. Indeed, it
is one, and yet it produces diverse things; but it operates nothing without
seed: whatever the seed wills, Nature operates, for it is like an instrument
of some Artist. Therefore, the seed of each thing is better
and more useful to the Artist than Nature itself: For from Nature without
seed you will accomplish as much as a goldsmith without fire, gold or silver,
or a farmer without grain and seed. Having the seed, Nature
will be ready, whether for evil or for good. It operates in
the seed as GOD in the free will of man: and this is a great
miracle, that Nature obeys the seed, not compelled, but of its own
accord; just as God also grants all that Man wills, not compelled,
but from His own will: Therefore He gave man free will,
whether for evil or for good. Therefore, seed is the Elixir of each
thing, or the fifth essence, or the most perfect decoction and digestion
of a thing, or the Balsam of sulfur, which is the same as the radical
moisture in Metals. Indeed, a great discourse could be instituted here
concerning this seed, but we tend only to our purpose in the Chemical
Art. The four elements generate seed, by the will of GOD and
the imagination of Nature: For just as the seed of a man has
its center, or vessel of its seed, in the kidneys; so the four elements
                                                                                              by motion

--- Page 571 ---
*Novum Lumen Chemicum* 557

by unceasing motion (each according to its quality) they project sperm into the center of the earth, where it is digested, and by motion it is emitted outwards. But the center of the earth is a certain empty place where nothing can rest: into the Excenter (so to speak), or the margin and circumference of the center, the four Elements project their qualities. Just as a man emits his seed into the womb of a woman; in which nothing of the seed remains, but after the womb has received its due portion, it casts the rest out: similarly it happens in the center of the earth that the Magnetic force of some part of a place attracts to itself a thing suitable for itself for bringing forth something; the rest is cast out as stones and other excrements. For all things have their origin from that source, nor is anything born in the whole world except through this source. For example; Let there be on some flat table a small vessel of water, which is placed in the middle of the table, and around it let various things be placed, and various colors, also salt, etc., each separately: then let water be poured into the middle; you will see that water flow here and there, and while one stream reaches a red color, it will become red from it, if it reaches salt, it will borrow the taste of salt, and so for the rest. For water does not change places, but the diversity of places changes the water. In a similar way from the center of the earth, the seed or sperm projected by the four elements into the center passes to various places, and according to the Nature of the place, the thing takes on its nature: if it reaches a pure place of earth and water, a pure thing is made. The seed and sperm of all things is unique, and yet it generates various things, as appears from the following example. The seed of a man is a noble seed, and at least it is created for the generation of man; nevertheless, if a man abuses it, which is in his free will, an abortion is born: For if, against the most serious inhibitions of God, a man were to enter a cow, or another beast, the beast would easily conceive the man's seed, because Nature is but one; and then not a Man would be born, but a beast and an abortion; since the seed did not find a place suitable for itself. By such inhuman and detestable commixture of men with beasts, various beasts similar to humans would be produced. For so it happens, if sperm enters the center, that which ought to be born from it is born; but

But now we must explain how the Elements generate sperm, and it happens in this way. # TREATISE THREE
### *Concerning the True Matter of Metals.*

The primary matter of Metals is twofold, but one without the other does not create metal. The first and principal is the moisture of the air mixed with heat; this the Philosophers named Mercury, which is governed by the rays of the Sun and Moon in the philosophical sea: The second is the dry heat of the earth, which they called sulfur. But because all true Philosophers have especially concealed this, we will explain it a little more clearly; especially the weight, which being unknown, all things are destroyed. Hence it happens that many produce abortions from a good thing: for there are those who take the whole body as matter or seed or sperm, others a fragment, and all these deviate from the right path. For example; if someone were to take a man's foot and a woman's hand, and wished to [produce] from

--- Page 573 ---
*New Chemical Light.* 559

from this mixture to create a human, it would not be possible. For there is in every body a center and a place, or a point of seed or sperm, and always the 8200th part, even in a grain of wheat itself; and this cannot be otherwise: For not the whole grain or body is turned into seed, but only some necessary spark is in the body, which is guarded by its body from all excessive heat and cold, etc. If you have ears and senses, pay attention here and you will be safe, not only from those who are ignorant of the place of the sperm, and strive to reduce the whole grain into seed; but also from all those who engage in vain solutions of metals, and wish to dissolve metals entirely, and afterwards from their mutual mixture, create a new metal. But these, if they considered the process of Nature, would see that the matter stands far otherwise: For no metal is so pure that it does not have its impurities, one having fewer or more than another. But you, friendly Reader, will first observe the point of Nature, as said above, and you have enough: but take this caution for yourself, that you do not seek that point in common metals, in which it is not. For these metals, especially common gold, are dead; but ours are living, having spirit, which must be taken entirely: for know that the life of metals is fire, while they are still in their mines, and death is also fire, namely that of fusion. But the primary matter of metals is a certain humidity mixed with warm air; and it is in the form of a fatty water, adhering to every pure or impure thing; yet more abundantly in one place than in another, which happens because the earth is more open and porous in one place, having an attractive force, than in another. It sometimes comes forth by itself into light, clad in some garment, especially in places where it does not have to adhere to anything; it is known thus, because every thing is composed of three principles: But in the matter of metals, there is only one without conjunction, except for the garment or its shadow; namely sulfur, etc.
