TREATISE FOUR.

*How metals are generated in the bowels*
*of the earth.*

Metals are produced in this way: after the four Elements have projected their virtues into the center of the earth, the Archeus, by distilling, sublimates them with the heat of perpetual motion to the surface of the earth: For the earth is porous, and the wind, dripping through the pores of the earth, is resolved into water, from which all things are born. Let the sons of doctrine therefore know that the seed of metals is not different from the seed of all things, namely, a humid vapor: therefore Artists seek in vain the reduction of metals to the prima materia, which is only vapor. The Philosophers did not understand such a prima materia, but only a second materia, as Bernard Trevisan most excellently argues, although not so clearly, because he speaks of the four Elements. Nevertheless, he wished to say that, and spoke only with the sons. But I, in order to reveal the Theory more clearly, wished to warn everyone here to be cautious, that so many solutions, so many circulations, so many calcinations and reiterations should cease; for it is sought in vain in a hard thing when it is soft everywhere by itself: Let not the first, but only the second materia be sought, such, namely, as cannot be changed into another form as soon as it is conceived. But if you ask how metal is reduced to such a materia, I follow in that the intention of the Philosophers: This alone I wish above all else, that the sons of art understand the meaning of the writings, not the syllables, and where Nature ends, namely in metallic bodies perfected before our eyes, there art must begin. But to return to the subject (since our intention here is not about the stone alone,) let us now speak of the materia of metals. A little earlier I said that all things are born from liquid air or vapor,
                                                                                                        which

which the Elements, with perpetual motion, distill into the bowels of the earth; after
the Archeus of Nature has received this, it sublimes it through pores and, with its own
sagacity, distributes it to each place (as we have related in the preceding [parts]),
thus, by the variety of places, various things also arise and are born.
Some are of the opinion that Saturn has one seed, and gold also

only one seed, the same is found in Saturn as in gold,

**TREATISE FIVE**

*On the generation of all kinds of stones.*

**T**he matter of stone is the same as that of other things; and they are born in this way according to the purity of the places. When the four Elements distill their vapor into the center of the earth, and the Archeus of Nature expels and sublimes it; this [vapor], while it passes through the places and pores of the earth, draws with it all the impurity of the earth up to the surface, which the air afterwards freezes (for what pure air creates, crude air freezes, because air has ingress into air and they join each other, for nature rejoices in Nature:) and thus rocks and stony mountains are formed, according to large and small pores. And the larger the pores of the earth, the better the place is purified: for while greater heat and a greater quantity of water pass through such an opening, the more quickly the earth is purified; and thus afterwards metals are more conveniently born in such places. As experience itself testifies, that gold is sought and found nowhere else but in mountains, which cannot happen in a plain, except rarely: for most often such places are humid, not with vapor, but with Elemental water, which draws that vapor to itself, and they embrace each other so that they are not easily separated; afterwards the Sun of heaven, digesting it, makes a rich clay, which they use for seals. But in places where there is coarse sand, and the vapor does not have fatness or sulfur with it, it creates herbs and grass in the meadows. There are also other precious stones, such as Diamond, Ruby, Emerald, and other gems: all are generated in this way.
                                                                                                   Quan-

--- Page 577 ---
*New Chemical Light* 563

When the vapor of Nature is sublimated by itself, without the addition of the fatness of sulfur, and comes to the place of pure salt water, Diamonds are formed; and this in the coldest places, to which that fatness cannot arrive, because the fatness would not permit these things. For it must be known that the spirit of water is very easily sublimated by gentle heat; but oil or fatness is only raised by great heat, and into warm places: for even if it proceeds from the center, it is congealed by slight cold, and thus remains; but the vapor ascends to the proper places, and is congealed in pure water into granular stones. But how colors are made in gems; it must be known that this happens by reason of sulfur in this manner: if the fatness of sulfur is congealed, by that perpetual motion afterwards the spirit of water, by passing through, digests and purifies it by the power of salt, until it is colored with a digested red or white color, which color, tending towards better things with that spirit, because it has been subtilized by so many repeated distillations, is elevated: the spirit afterwards has the power of entering imperfect things, and thus introduces the color, which is afterwards joined to that water then partly congealed, and thus fills its pores, and is fixed with it by an inseparable fixation. For all water is congealed by heat if it is without spirit, it is congealed by cold if it has spirit; but he who knows how to congeal water with heat, and to join the spirit with it, will certainly find a thing a thousand times more precious than gold and everything. Let him therefore cause the spirit to be separated from the water, so that it may putrefy, and a grain may appear; afterwards, the dregs having been rejected, let him bring back the spirit from above into the water, and cause them to join together: For that conjunction will generate a branch dissimilar in form to its parents.

TREATISE SIX.
*On the Second Matter, & the putrefaction*
*of things.*

We have spoken of the first matter of things, and how things are born from Nature without seed, that is, how Nature from the Elemen-

...elements receives matter from which it generates seed: But now we will institute a discourse concerning seed, and things generated from seed.
Every thing having seed multiplies in it, but it does not happen without the aid of Nature: for seed is nothing other than air congealed in some body, or a humid vapor; and unless this is resolved by warm vapor, it is of no use. Let the investigators of the art therefore know what seed is, lest they seek a thing which is not: and let them know that it is threefold, which is produced from the four elements. The first is MINERAL, of which there is discourse in this place; the second VEGETABLE; the third ANIMAL. MINERAL seed is known by Philosophers: VEGETABLE is common and vulgar, as we see in fruits: ANIMAL is known from imagination. Vegetable shows us how nature creates it from the four Elements. For it must be known that winter is the cause of putrefaction; inasmuch as it congeals the vital spirits in trees: and when these are resolved by the heat of the Sun (in which is the magnetic power attractive of all humidity), then the heat of nature, excited by motion, drives a subtle vapor of water to the circumference, which opens the pores of the tree, and causes drops to distill, always separating the pure from the impure. However, sometimes the pure precedes the impure; the pure stands and congeals into flowers, the impure goes into leaves, the gross and thick into bark: the bark of trees remains fixed, leaves fall by cold or heat, when its pores are obstructed: flowers congeal in such a color as the heat itself is, and bring forth fruit and seed (just as an apple in which there is sperm, from which a tree is born; but in that sperm there is seed or grain intrinsically, from which a tree is also born without sperm; for multiplication occurs not in sperm, but in seed.) Thus we visually see Nature create seed from the four elements, lest we should be occupied in this in vain; for that which is created does not need a creator. Let it suffice to have admonished the reader with this example; but I return to the proposed Mineral [seed]. Nature creates Mineral or Metal seed in the bowels of the earth: therefore, such seed is not believed to exist in the nature of things, because it is invisible. But it is not surprising'

Every single thing is multiplied in male and female, as I mentioned in the treatise on dual matter: The division of sex creates or produces nothing, but its proper conjunction brings forth a new form: Therefore, seeds or sperms, not bodies, are to be taken: Take therefore a living male and a living female; join these together so that they may conceive sperm among themselves for procreating the fruit of their Nature. Let no mortal also believe that he can make the first matter: The first matter of man is earth, and no man can create a man from it, only God knows this; but from the second matter, which is already created, if it has been placed in the proper place, that, of which it is the seed of the form, will easily be generated by Nature working. The artisan here does nothing but know how to separate the subtle from the dense, and place it in the proper vessel. For this must be considered, as a thing is begun, so it is finished: from one two are made, from two one, and no further. God is one; from this one God the son is begotten: The one gave two, the two gave one Holy Spirit proceeding from both: thus the world was made, and thus will be its end. Consider the first four points most exactly: in them you have the Father, the Father and the Son, lastly the Holy Spirit. You have four Elements: you have four luminaries, two Celestial, two Central: Nothing more is, was, or will be, than is evident in this figure; if I were to record all the mysteries to be drawn from here, a great volume would arise: I return to the purpose, and I tell you the truth, my son, one is not created from one, because this is proper to God alone: it is sufficient that you can create one useful thing for yourself from two. Know therefore that multiplicative sperm is the second matter, and not the first: For the first matter of things is not seen, it is hidden in nature, or in the Elements: but the second sometimes appears to the sons of doctrine.

TREATISE SEVENTH.

On the virtue of the Second matter.

But so that you may more easily comprehend what this second matter is, I will describe to you the virtues by which you will recognize it. And first, know that Nature is divided into three Kingdoms: the Mineral, Vegetable, & Animal. Two of these Kingdoms can stand by themselves, even if the other two did not exist. The Mineral can subsist by itself, even if no human being were in the world, nor tree, or words. The Vegetable likewise, even if no metal, nor animal existed, can stand by itself: these two are created from one through one. The third, however, has life from the two aforementioned, without which it could not exist, and is nobler and more excellent than the two aforesaid, just as it is also the last among them, and dominates them: because virtue always ends in the third, and multiplies in the second.

Do you see in the vegetable Kingdom? The first matter is the Herb or Tree, which you do not know how to create; Nature alone does this. In this kingdom, the second matter is the seed which you see: in this, the Herb or Tree multiplies. In the Animal Kingdom, the first matter is the Beast or Man, whom you do not know how to create: but you know the second matter, sperm, in which it multiplies. In the mineral Kingdom, you do not know how to create metal, and if you boast, you are vain and a liar; Nature made this: and although you might have the first matter according to the Philosophers, that central salt, yet without gold it would be impossible for you to multiply it: but only the sons of doctrine know the vegetative seed of metals.

In vegetables, the seed appears externally; the Renes of its digestion is warm air. In animals, the seed appears internally & externally; the Renes of its digestion are the kidneys of man. In minerals, water is the seed in the center of their heart and life: the Renes of its digestion is fire.

--- Page 582 ---
468 *A New Chemical Light.*

The receptacle of the vegetable seed is the earth: The receptacle of the animal seed is the womb of the female: The receptacle of water, the mineral seed, is the air. And these are the receptacles of seeds, which are congelations of bodies: that is digestion which is solution: that is putrefaction which is destruction. But the virtue of each seed is to join itself to each thing in its own Kingdom, because it is subtle, and nothing else than air, which is congealed by richness in water: it is known thus, because it does not naturally mix itself with anything outside its own Kingdom: it is not dissolved but congealed, because it does not need solution, but congelation. It is therefore necessary that the pores of bodies be opened, so that the sperm may be emitted, in the center of which lies the seed, which is air: that, when it comes into the proper womb, is congealed and congeals what it finds pure, or impure mixed with pure. As long as the seed is in the body, the body lives; when it is entirely consumed, the body dies, but all bodies are weakened after the emission of the seed. Experience also testifies that men who indulge too much in Venus become weaker, just as trees bearing too much fruit afterwards become sterile. The seed therefore, as has already been repeated many times, is an invisible thing, but sperm is visible, and is almost a living soul; it is not found in dead things: It is drawn out in two ways, gently and with violence. But, because here at least the discourse is about its virtue, I say that nothing is born without seed; all things are made by the virtue of the seed: and let the sons of art know that the seed is sought in vain in cut-down trees, which is found only in green things.

TREATISE EIGHT.

*How nature operates through art in the Seed.*

Every seed by itself is of no moment, if it is not placed, either by art, or by Nature, into its proper matrix. And although seed by itself may be nobler than every creature, nevertheless its matrix is life, which causes the sperm or grain to putrefy, and brings about the congelation of a pure point; moreover, with the heat of its body, it nourishes that and makes it grow; and this happens in all the aforementioned three kingdoms of nature, and occurs naturally, through months, years, and seasons. But that art is sagacious which can shorten something in the mineral and vegetable kingdoms, but not in the animal: in the mineral kingdom alone it perfects that which nature cannot, because the crude air with its violence has filled the pores of every body, not in the viscera, but on the surface of the earth, as I said before in the preceding chapters. But so that this may be understood more easily, I still wanted to add that the Elements contend among themselves, casting their seed into the center of the earth, as if into kidneys: but the center through motion emits that into the matrix: but matrices are innumerable; as many places, so many matrices, one purer than another, and thus almost to infinity. Know therefore that a pure matrix will give a pure offspring in its like: For example, in animals there are matrices of humans, cows, horses, dogs, etc. so in the mineral and vegetable kingdoms there are metals, stones, salts: for salts in these two kingdoms are to be considered, and their places, according to more or less.

NINTH TREATISE.

*Concerning the Mixing of Metals, or concerning the eliciting*
*of the Metallic seed.*

We have spoken of Nature, of Art, of the body, and of sperm and
seed: now let us descend to practice, namely how metals
should be mixed, and what their correspondence among themselves is.
Know therefore that a woman does not differ from a man; from the same seed and in a
single matrix both are born; nothing was lacking except digestion, and just as
a matrix is purer in blood and salt: so the Moon from the same seed with
the Sun, and the same matrix: but the matrix had more of water than of
digested blood, according to the time of the celestial Moon. But so that
you may more easily imagine how metals unite, so that they emit
and receive seed, look at the heavens and the spheres of the planets: you see
that Saturn is the highest, to whom Jupiter succeeds, to him Mars, then
the Sun, whom Venus follows, her Mercury, in the last place the Moon is
placed. Consider now that the virtues of the planets do not ascend,
but descend: experience itself has shown this, that from Venus there is not
made Mars, but from Mars is made Venus, as being one sphere lower: so
also Jupiter is easily transmuted into Mercury, because Jupiter is se-
cond from the Firmament, and Mercury second from the earth: Saturn
first from heaven, Luna first from earth: The Sun mixes itself with all, but never
is it improved by inferiors. Let it not escape your notice, moreover, that there is a great
correspondence between Saturn and the Moon, in the middle of which
the Sun is placed: just as between Jupiter and Mercury, in the middle of which
the Sun also stands: In precisely the same way between Mars and Ve-
nus, which two also have the Sun as an intermediary. Chemists have known
how to change iron into copper or Venus without the Sun: they have also known
how to make Mercury from Jupiter: there are also some who from Saturn make
(make/produce).

--- Page 585 ---
**New Chemical Light.** 571

...the Moon; but if they knew how to manage nature through these changes of the Sun, they would certainly find a thing more precious than any treasure. Therefore, I say that one must not be ignorant of which metals are to be joined together, and whose nature corresponds to nature. Therefore, there is one metal given which has the power of consuming others; it is, namely, almost like their water, and almost a mother: only one thing, the radical moisture, namely of the Sun and Moon, resists it, and is improved by it: but, to reveal it, it is called Chalybs (Steel). If gold copulates with it eleven times, it emits its seed, and is weakened almost to death: Chalybs conceives, and generates a son brighter than the father: afterwards, when the seed of the already born (son) is placed into its matrix, it purges it, and makes it a thousand times more suitable for bearing the best fruits. There is also another Chalybs which is similar to this one, created by nature itself, which knows how to extract from the sun's rays (with wonderful power and virtue) that which so many men have sought, and is the beginning of our work.

**TREATISE X.**

*On the Supernatural Generation of the Son of the Sun.*

**WE** have treated of things which Nature creates, and which GOD created; so that seekers of the art might more easily understand the possibility of nature. But, lest I delay any longer: I approach the method and art of making the Philosopher's Stone. The Philosopher's Stone or tincture is nothing other than Gold digested to the highest degree: for common Gold is like a herb without seed; when it matures, it produces seed; thus gold, when it matures, gives seed or tincture. But someone will ask why gold or another metal does not produce seed: the reason given is such, because it cannot be mature; due to the crudity of the air, it does not have sufficient heat: and it happens in some places that pure gold is found
                                        Cccc 2                                        which

--- Page 586 ---
572 *A New Chemical Light.*

which nature wanted to perfect, but was hindered by crude air. For
example, we see that orange trees in Poland grow like other trees; In Italy and elsewhere, where their native soil is, they give and bear fruit, because they have sufficient heat; but in these colder places, very little, for where they ought to mature, they cease, because they are oppressed by cold; and so their fruits are never had by Nature in these places: but if nature is sometimes helped gently and with skill, then art now perfects what nature could not have. Exactly the same happens in metals: Gold can give fruit and seed, in which it multiplies itself, by the industry of a sagacious artisan, who knows how to promote nature; but if he wishes to attempt it without nature, he will err. For not only in this art, but also in everything, we can do nothing but help Nature; and this by no other means than fire or heat. But since this cannot be done, inasmuch as spirits do not appear in a congealed metallic body, it is necessary that the body first be dissolved, and its pores opened, so that nature can operate. What kind of solution that ought to be, here I would like the reader to be advised, that there are two kinds of solution, although there are many other solutions, but useless; only one is truly natural, the second is violent, under which all others are comprehended. The natural one is such that the pores of the body are opened in our water, so that the digested seed may be emitted, and placed in its matrix: Our water, however, is a celestial water, not wetting the hands, not of the common sort but almost like rain: The body is gold which gives the seed: Our Moon is (not common silver) which receives the seed of gold. It is then governed by our continuous fire, for seven months, and sometimes ten, until our water consumes three, and leaves one; and this in double. Afterwards it is nourished by the milk of the earth, or by its fat which is born in the udders of the earth, and is governed or preserved from putrefaction by the salt of Nature. And thus is generated that infant of the second generation.
Now let us proceed from theory to practice.

TREATISE XI.

*On the Practice & preparation of the stone or tincture*
*by art.*

THROUGH so many chapters has the discourse on things by examples been scattered, so that the practice, which must be done by imitating nature, may be more easily understood in this manner.
Take: Of our earth through XI degrees, XI grains; of our gold, not common, I grain; of our Moon, not common, II grains. But be warned of this: do not take the gold and silver of the common folk, for these are dead; take ours, which are living. Afterwards, place them in our fire, and from this will come a dry liquor; first, the earth will resolve into water, which is called the Mercury of the Philosophers, and another water will resolve those bodies of the Sun and Moon, and consume them so that nothing remains but a tenth part with one part, and this will be the radical metallic humidity.
Afterwards, take: water of saltpeter from our earth, in which there is a rivulet and a living wave if you dig a pit to your knee; therefore, take water from it, but take clear water. To this, add that radical humidity, and apply the fire of putrefaction and generation, not such as you used in the first operation. Govern all with great skill, until colors appear like the tail of a Peacock; govern by digesting, and do not be weary, until the colors cease, and one green color appears throughout, and so for the rest. And when you see brown ashes at the bottom, and the water almost red, open the vessel, moisten a feather, anoint some iron; if it tinctures, have ready the water, of which there will be talk afterwards, and pour in as much of that water as crude air entered. Cook again with the former fire until it tinctures again. My experience has reached this far; I can do no more, I have found no more. That water, indeed, must be the menstruum of the world, from the sphere of the Moon, so many times rectified that it can calcine the Sun. Here I wished to reveal everything to you,

it is, which by its perpetual motion drives heat or rays upwards to the earth's surface. This intrinsic heat is much more effective than this elemental fire, but it is tempered by earthly water, which day by day penetrates the pores of the earth and cools it: just as the celestial Sun and its heat are tempered by the air which day by day flies around the globe: and unless this were so, by such heat all things would be consumed, nor would anything be born.

For just as that invisible fire or central heat would consume all things if water did not intervene, so the Sun's heat would destroy all things without intervening air. But how these Elements act among themselves, I will say briefly. In the center of the earth is a central Sun, which by its motion or that of its firmament gives great heat, which extends itself even to the earth's surface. That heat causes air in this manner: The matrix of air is water, which gives birth to sons of its own nature, but dissimilar, and much more subtle, for where the entrance of water is denied, air enters. When therefore that central heat, which is perpetual, acts, it causes water to distill and be heated, and so that water by the force of heat is turned into air, and in this way it erupts to the surface of the earth, because it does not allow itself to be enclosed: where afterwards, having cooled, it resolves into water.

In opposite places meanwhile it also happens that not only air, but also water exits, just as it appears when black clouds are violently lifted into the air: Of which thing, let this be a domestic example for you. Make water boil in a pot, you will see with a slow fire slow vapors, and winds: With a more vehement fire, thicker mists will appear. In exactly the same way the central heat operates, it raises subtle water into air, what is thick from salt or fat it distributes to the earth, from which various things are born, the remainder becomes rocks and stones.

Someone might object, if the matter were so, then it ought to happen continuously, when nevertheless often no wind is felt. I reply, if water is not violently poured into a distilling vessel, no wind is made, for a little water excites little wind: you see that thunder is not always made, even if there is rain and wind, but only when by the force of air turbid water is carried to the sphere of fire, for fire does not tolerate water. You have an example before your eyes, when you pour cold water into a hot furnace, from which thunders

576               *A New Chemical Light.*

thunders are produced. But why water does not uniformly enter into those places and cavities, the reason is that there are many such vessels and places; sometimes one cavity drives, with winds, water from itself for some days and months, until again a repercussion of water occurs: as we see in the sea, whose waves are sometimes agitated for many miles, before they meet a repercussion, so that they may return, but to our matter. I say that fire or heat is the cause of the movement of air, and the life of all things: and the earth is the nurse, or receptacle, of all these. But if there were no water which cools our earth and air, then the earth would dry out, because of these two reasons, namely because of the central movement and the heat of the celestial sun: nevertheless this happens in some places, when the pores of the earth are obstructed, so that moisture cannot penetrate, then through the correspondence of the celestial and central sun (because they have a magnetic force between them) the earth is ignited by the Sun: and so also sometimes the heavy orbit of the world will fall. Therefore, let such an operation be in our earth: that central heat can change water into air, so that it may emerge into the plane of the world, and scatter the residue, as I said, through the pores of the earth, and then, conversely, air will be turned into water much more subtle than the first: and this will happen thus, if you give our old man gold and silver to swallow, so that he may consume them, and finally he, about to die, is also burned, his ashes are scattered into water, boil it until it is enough, and you have a medicine for curing leprosy. At least observe this, lest you take cold for hot, or hot for cold, mix natures with natures, if there is anything that is contrary to nature (since one is necessary for you) separate it, so that nature may be similar to nature, do this with fire, not by hand, and know that if you do not follow nature, all things are in vain: and here I have told you by holy God what a father owes to a son: he who has ears, let him hear, and he who has senses, let him pay attention.

**TREATISE XII.**

*Concerning the Stone, and its virtue.*

IN the preceding [sections], sufficient has been said concerning the production of natural things, concerning the Elements, and concerning the first matter and second matter, concerning bodies and seeds, concerning their use and virtue: I have also written down the practice of making the Philosophers' Stone: but concerning its virtue, as much as nature has granted me, and experience has revealed, I will now disclose. But, so that first, I may still briefly and in few words summarize the argument of all these treatises, so that the God-fearing reader may grasp my mind and my meaning, this is how the matter stands. If anyone doubts concerning the truth of the art, let him read the copious writings of the most ancient Philosophers, verified by reason and Experience, to whom, as worthy of faith, faith in their art must not be denied: but he who does not give faith to them, then we know that one should not dispute against him who denies the principles: For the deaf and mute cannot speak. For what prerogative would all things in this world have over metals? Why should we unjustly exclude these alone, by denying them a seed, from the universal blessing of multiplication of the supreme Creator, which the sacred scriptures affirm to have been implanted and imparted to all created things immediately from the creation of the world: but if they have a seed, who is so foolish as not to believe that they can be multiplied in their own seed? In its nature, the art of Chemistry is true, nature is also true, but rarely is the artist true: One nature, one art, but many artists. But that nature creates things from the elements, it generates them by the will of God from the first matter, which God alone knows: nature creates things and multiplies them from the second matter, which the Philosophers know. Nothing happens in the world without the will of God and nature. For each element is in its own sphere, but one cannot exist without the other, one lives from the other, and yet when joined, they do not agree; but water is more worthy than all elements, because it is the mother of all things: the spirit of fire floats upon this. I wanted to signify to you as a Father to a son. Do not wonder that I have written so many Treatises; it was not done for my sake, since I do not need books, but so that I might warn many who labor in vain things not to incur expenses in vain. Indeed, all things could have been comprehended in very few lines, nay, words; but through reasons and examples, I wanted to lead you to the knowledge of nature; so that above all you might know what you ought to seek, whether the first or second matter: You would also have nature revealed, and its light and shadow. Do not be moved if sometimes contradictions occur to you in my Treatises, in the customary manner of Philosophers; you have need of them if you understand, a rose is not found without thorns. Consider diligently what I said above, namely how the four elements distill into the radical humid center of the earth, and how the central earthly sun by its motion produces and sublimates that [humid radical] to the surface of the earth. I also said that the celestial sun has a correspondence with the central sun: for the celestial sun and moon have a peculiar power and virtue of distilling through their rays into the earth: for heat is easily joined to heat, salt to salt. And just as the central sun has its sea, and a perceptible crude water; so the celestial sun also has its sea and a subtle and imperceptible water: On the surface of the earth, rays are joined to rays, and produce flowers, and all things. Therefore, when rain occurs, it receives from the air that vital force, and joins it with the saltpeter of the earth, (because the saltpeter of the earth is like calcined Tartar, drawing air to itself by its dryness; which air is resolved into water within it: Such a power of attraction does that saltpeter of the earth have, which was also air, and is joined to the fatness of the earth) and the more copiously the solar rays strike then, the greater the quantity of saltpeter becomes, and consequently a greater abundance of grain grows, and this happens from day to day. So much I wanted to hint to the ignorant concerning the correspondence of things among themselves, and the efficacy of the sun and moon and stars; for the knowing do not need this instruction. Our subject is before the eyes of the whole world and is not known. O our heaven! O our water! and our Mercury! O our saltpeter dwelling in the sea of the world! O our vegetable! O our fixed and volatile sulfur! O our dead head, or dregs-

My intention was not, for reasons mentioned in the preface, to publish this book; nevertheless, the desire to earn the favor of liberal and philosophical minds overcame me; so that to those who know me I might show a good spirit; at the same time, to those who understand the art, I might make it clear that I am their equal and companion, and that I seek their acquaintance.

I do not doubt that many men of good conscience and will secretly possess that gift of God; let these, warned by my example, and made more cautious and provident by my dangers, keep the silence commended by Harpocrates: for whenever I wished to reveal myself to great men, it always resulted either in loss or danger to me.

With this writing, I reveal myself to the adept sons of Hermes, and I instruct the ignorant and erring, and lead them back to the true path. Let the heirs of knowledge believe that they will never have a better path to follow than that which is demonstrated to them here; for I have said everything openly: at least the extraction of our Sal Ammoniac or Philosophical Mercury from our Pontic water, and its mere use, I have not so openly revealed, because I did not have further license to speak from the master of nature; and this alone God must reveal, who knows the hearts and minds of men, whom if you diligently pray to, through repeated reading of this book, He will be able to open your understanding.

TO THE SONS OF TRUTH.
PREFACE TO THE *Philosophical Enigma.*

Now to you, sons of science, from the wellspring of the universal fount I have revealed
all things, so that nothing more remains. For in my preceding
Treatises I have sufficiently explained nature by examples: I have manifested
theory & practice as far as was permissible. But lest anyone complain of Laconicism,
that I have omitted something, I will still describe the whole art to you enigmatically,
so that you may see how far I have progressed by God's guidance.
There are infinite books treating of this art, scarcely in any
will you find the truth revealed to you to this extent: which I wished to accomplish
for this reason, because I conversed with many who thought they understood the writings
of the philosophers well; but I found that they explained the same writings
far more subtly than nature, which is simple, required:
indeed, all my truthful sayings seemed to those always wise in high matters
too base & incredible. Sometimes it happened
that I insinuated the art to some word for word, but they could by no means
grasp it, not believing that there is water in our sea,
and yet they wanted to appear as Philosophers. Therefore, since my words
spoken orally they could not understand, I do not fear (as other Philosophers
feared) that anyone could so easily conceive [it]. It is a Gift, I say, of God.
It is indeed true, if in the study of Chemistry a subtle
                                                                                                   genius

--- Page 598 ---
584          *A New Chemical Light.*
sharpness of intellect, and if the matter were such that it could be seen by the eyes of the common people; I deemed their intellects sufficiently apt for investigating such things. But I tell you to be simple, and not too clever, until you have found the secret. Once you possess it, prudence will necessarily follow, and then the facility for writing infinite books will not be granted to you. This will be far easier for him who is at the center and sees the thing, than for him who walks on the circumference and has nothing but hearsay.

You have the secondary matter of all things most clearly described. But I commend this caution to you: if you wish to attain this secret, know that first God must be prayed to, and then your neighbor must be loved. Finally, do not imagine things so subtle for yourselves, about which nature knows nothing. Instead, remain, I say, remain in the simple path of nature; for in simplicity you will more quickly grasp the thing, and then you will be able to see it in its subtlety. In reading my writings, do not always cling to the syllables, but rather, in reading, always consider nature and its possibilities.

But before you gird yourselves for the work, diligently imagine what is sought, and what is the scope and end of your intention; for it is much better to learn first with the brain and imagination than with manual labor and expenses. And I tell you this: it is necessary to seek something hidden, from which (in a wondrous way) such a humidity is produced that dissolves gold without violence or noise, indeed, as gently and naturally as ice melts by the warmth of hot water. If you have found this, you have the thing; for gold is produced by nature from water. And although all metals and all things have their origin from it, yet nothing is so akin to it as gold; for impurity adheres to other things, but to gold, none. Therefore, it is like a mother to it. And so, I finally conclude: if you do not wish to be cautious with these my writings and admonitions, will you hold me, who desires to serve you well, excused? I have acted faithfully as far as was permitted, as befits a man of good conscience. If you ask who I am, I am a Cosmopolitan. If you know me, and desire to be good and honest men, you will be silent. If you do not know me, do not inquire about me, for to no mortal, as long as...

*New Chemical Light.* 585

as long as I live, more will be revealed by me than has been done in this public writing. Believe me, if I were not a man of such status and condition as I am, nothing would be more pleasant to me than a solitary life, or to lie hidden with Diogenes under a barrel: for I see that all things that exist are vanity, that fraud and avarice have prevailed where all things are for sale, and that iniquity has overcome virtue: I see better things of a future life before my eyes, in these I rejoice. Now I no longer wonder, as I did before, why Philosophers, having obtained such a medicine, did not care to shorten their days; because for every Philosopher, the life to come is before their eyes just as your own face appears to you in a mirror. And if God grants you the desired end, afterwards you will believe me, and you will not reveal yourself to the world.

# P A R A B L E
### OR
### A PHILOSOPHICAL ENIGMA,
### *added by way of a conclusion and an appendix.*

IT happened once, when for so many years of my life I sailed from the Arctic Pole to the Antarctic Pole, that by a singular nod of God I was cast ashore on the coast of a certain great sea: and although I had the approaches and properties of that sea of the world very well known and understood, nevertheless I was ignorant whether that little fish Echeneis was also generated in those regions, which so many men of great and small condition have hitherto sought so diligently. While, however, on the shore I behold Melosynae swimming here and there with Nymphs, weary also from previous labors, and burdened by various thoughts, I am overcome by sleep from the murmur of the waters: and while I sweetly fall asleep, a wonderful vision appears to me in my dreams. I see from our sea the venerable old man Neptune, with his trident, emerging, who, after a friendly greeting, leads me to a most pleasant Island. This most beautiful Island towards the South-

--- Page 600 ---
586 *A New Chemical Light.*

The island was situated, and most abundantly supplied with all things pertaining to human necessity and to his very own delights: Virgil's Elysian Fields could scarcely be compared with it. The entire shore of the island was everywhere encircled with green myrtles, cypresses, and rosemary. Green meadows covered with variegated flowers, a most pleasant sight, smelled most sweetly. Hills were adorned in a wondrous way with vineyards, olive trees, and cedars, groves filled with orange and lemon trees. Public roads, planted on both sides with laurel and pomegranate trees, interwoven with singular artistry, provided the most pleasant shade for travelers. To say it in a few words, whatever exists in the whole world seemed to be there. While walking, the aforesaid Neptune showed me, hidden under a certain rock, the two mines of that island, Gold and Steel. Not far from there I was led to a meadow, in which a peculiar Garden was planted with various and most worthy of sight trees. Among several trees, however, he showed me seven Trees marked with names; and among these I observed two principal ones more prominent than the others, one of which bore fruit like the brightest and most shining Sun, and its leaves were like Gold: The other, however, produced fruits whiter than the whitest lilies, and its leaves were like fine Silver: These Trees were called by Neptune, one the Solar Tree, and the other the Lunar Tree. And although everything on this island was at one's beck and call, yet one thing was lacking: Water was not to be had except with great

D I A L O G U E
OF MERCURY, THE ALCHEMIST
AND NATURE.

AT that time the Chemists gathered and held a council, how they
should make and prepare the PHILOSOPHER'S STONE, and so they
decided that each one should state his opinion by vote. And that
gathering took place during the day in a certain meadow, on a certain
clear day. And many agreed that Mercury was its first matter, others
Sulphur, others other things. But concerning Mercury, their opinion
was strongest, especially from the sayings of the Philosophers, because
they hold it to be the true first matter, and also the first matter of
Metals: for the Philosophers exclaim: OUR MERCURY &c. And when
they thus contended among themselves with various arguments, (for
each of them awaited the conclusion with desire and joy) meanwhile a
very great storm arose with gales, rain clouds, and an unheard-of wind,
which dispersed that gathering into various provinces, each one
separately without a conclusion. Each of them, however, impressed
upon himself what the end of that disputation ought to be. Therefore
each one began his labors as before, one in this, another in another
matter, seeking the PHILOSOPHER'S STONE, and this continues up to
now without ceasing. But one of them, mindful of the disputation,
that it must necessarily be sought in Mercury

--- Page 605 ---
*New Chemical Light.* 591

...should be the Philosopher's Stone, he said to himself: Even if no conclusion has been reached, nevertheless I will work with Mercury, and I will make the conclusion when the blessed stone is made; for he was a man who always used to speak as Alchemists do. Therefore, he began to read the Books of the Philosophers, and he came across the Book of Alan, which treats of Mercury, and thus that Alchemist became a Philosopher, but without a conclusion. And having taken Mercury, he began to work; he placed it in a glass, and applied fire. Mercury, as it usually does, evaporated. The wretched Alchemist, not knowing nature, beat his wife, saying: no one could have come here except you, you took my Mercury from the glass. The wife, weeping, excused herself, and said quietly to her husband: You make shit out of these things. The Alchemist took Mercury again, and again placed it in a vessel, and guarded it lest his wife take it. But Mercury, in its own way, evaporated again. The Alchemist, remembering that the primary matter of the Philosopher's Stone must be volatile, rejoiced greatly, entirely persuading himself that he could no longer be deceived, having this material. He now began to treat Mercury boldly; he later learned to sublimate it, to calcine it in wondrous ways, now with salts, now with sulfur, now with metals, now with minerals, now with blood, now with hair, now with strong waters, now with herbs, urine, vinegar, but he could find nothing for his purpose; he left nothing untouched in the world with which he had not treated the good Mercury. And since he could achieve absolutely nothing, he came across this saying, *that which is found in dung*. He began to treat Mercury with various dungs, both together and separately; and when he was thus tired and full of thoughts, he fell asleep. And in his dreams, a vision appeared to him: an old man came to him who greeted him and said: Friend, why are you sad? He replied, I would gladly like to make the Philosopher's Stone. Then he (the old man said), Friend, from what do you wish to make the Philosopher's Stone? *Alchemist.* From Mercury, Sir. *Old Man.* But from what kind of Mercury? *Alchemist.* There is only one Mercury. *Old Man.* It is true that there is one Mercury, but varied in various places; one part purer than another. *Alchemist.* O Sir, I know how to purify it very well with vinegar and salt, niter and vitriol,
                                                                                             Old Man.

592          *The New Chemical Light.*

*Old Man.* I tell you, this purification is not true, nor is Mercury thus true: for wise men have another Mercury, and another purification of it, and thus he vanished. Awakened from sleep, the Alchemist pondered what that vision might be, he pondered what that Mercury of the Philosophers ought to be: he could think of nothing else than this his common Mercury. But nevertheless he desired that he might have spoken longer with that old man: nevertheless he worked assiduously, now even in the dung of animals, and of children, afterwards he began to work even in his own dung. And every day he went to the place where he saw the vision, so that he might speak to that old man again: sometimes he feigned sleep, he lay with closed eyes, waiting for the old man. But since he would not come, he thought that he (the old man) was afraid, and did not believe that he (the alchemist) was sleeping, therefore he swore, saying: My Lord Old Man, do not be afraid, certainly I am sleeping; look at my eyes if you do not believe: And that wretched Alchemist, after so many labors and the consumption of his goods, now even fell into delirium, always thinking about that old man.

And from that very strong imagination a phantom appeared to him through sleep, in the form of that old man, and said to him: Do not despair, friend; your Mercury is good, and your Matter, but if it does not want to obey you, conjure it, lest it be volatile; Yet even serpents are accustomed to be conjured, why not Mercury too? And thus the old man wished to depart. But the Alchemist asked him, saying: Lord, wait, and the wretched man was awakened by the cry, yet not without great consolation.

Afterwards he took a vessel full of Mercury, and began to conjure it in wondrous ways, just as the dream had taught him. And he remembered the words of the old man, that he had said thus: *Serpents are conjured, and Mercury is depicted with serpents*, he thought, certainly it must be conjured like a serpent. And having taken the vessel with Mercury, he began to say: *Ux ux, ostas &c.* And where the name of a serpent ought to have been, he put Mercury, saying. PREFACE.

Since it is not permitted for me, kind Reader, to write more openly than other ancient Philosophers have written, perhaps you will not be content with my writings; especially since you have so many other books of Philosophers at hand. But believe me, I also have no need to write books, because from them I seek neither profit nor vain ostentation; therefore, I do not wish to reveal who I am. Those things which I have already delivered to the public for your benefit seemed to me more than sufficient; the rest I intended to relegate to *Harmonia*, where I have copiously set forth matters concerning natural things. Nevertheless, at the urging of friends, I had to write this treatise on Sulphur, in which I do not know if it is necessary to add anything to the former things. Indeed, neither will this satisfy, if the writings of so many Philosophers do not satisfy you; and especially if the daily operation of nature is not sufficient as an example for you, no examples will help. For if you were to consider with mature judgment how nature operates, you would not need so many volumes of Philosophers, because in my judgment it is better to learn from Nature herself, the teacher, than from disciples. Enough has been said in the preface of the book of XII Treatises, and also in the first treatise: there you have why in this art so many and such great books are found that they now hinder enquirers more than they help; and so it seems to be because the writings of the Philosophers- Gg gg

If in any science it helps or harms greatly if one word is missing or superfluous, that is especially true in this one. Indeed there are many who interpret him, as well as other Authors; but I see the explanation is more difficult than the text. My advice is that you remain with the text, and whatever you read, apply everything to the possibility of nature; and first inquire what nature is. Indeed all write that the thing is vile, easy, common: and indeed it is true, but it should have been added, "To the knowledgeable." The knowledgeable person recognizes it even among dung, and the ignorant person does not believe it to be there even in gold. I do not wish to praise my writings, he will judge who applies them to the possibility and course of nature: and if from my writings, counsels, and examples, he cannot recognize the operation of nature, and its vital spirits constricting the air, as well as the subject of the prime matter, he will scarcely understand it from Raymond Lull: for it is difficult to believe that Spirits have such great power in the belly of the wind. ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH.

EARTH is an Element quite worthy in its quality and dignity: In this Element the other three, and especially Fire, rest. It is a most excellent Element for concealing and manifesting those things which have been entrusted to it: it is gross and porous, heavy in respect of its smallness, but light in respect of its nature: it is also the Center of the World, as well as of the other Elements: Through its Center passes the Axis of the World of both Poles: It is porous, as we have said, like a sponge which brings forth nothing from itself; But whatever the other three distill into it and cast forth, it receives all things, preserves what is to be preserved, manifests what is to be manifested. Nothing, as we have said, does it bring forth from itself, but it is the receptacle of others, and it is in which every product remains, and through the motive heat in it, it putrefies, and through the same (heat), the pure being separated from the impure, it is multiplied: what is heavy is hidden in it, and heat drives what is light to its surface. It is the nurse and matrix of every seed and mixture: indeed it can do nothing else than to protect the seed and the compound until maturity. It is cold, dry, tempered by water;

   Now to the topic of the courses of waters, and the ebb and flow

Pole has a magnetic power of attracting: but the Antarctic Pole
has a magnetic power of expelling, which nature shows us an example
in the magnet. Therefore the Arctic pole draws waters, through the axis,
which, when they have entered, again burst forth through the axis of the Antarctic Pole:
and because the air does not permit inequality, they are forced again to the Arctic
Pole, their center, to return and thus continuously observe their course.
In this course from the Arctic Pole to the Antarctic Pole through
the middle or axis of the world, they are diffused through the pores of the earth, and thus, according
to greater or lesser extent, springs arise; and afterwards they grow into rivers,
converging, and again return to where they emerged from;
and this happens incessantly by universal motion. Some, as we

There are also in some places larger and wider pores and passages through which salty water erupts, whence afterwards salt mines and springs are found, as at Halle in Germany; in some places also they are constricted by heat and salt is left in the sands, while the water sweats into other pores, as in Wieliczka and Bochnia in Poland. Through these burning places, the running water, according to its proximity and remoteness, becomes more or less warm, and thus erupts onto the surface of the earth, and retains the taste of sulphur, just as every broth from its boiling of meat. In the same way it happens when water, passing through mineral places, whether coppery or aluminous, acquires their taste. Such, then, is the distiller, the creator of all things, in whose hand this distillery is, after whose example all distillations were invented by Philosophers, which the Most High and merciful God himself, without doubt, inspired in humans; who will be able, when it shall be his holy will, either to extinguish the central fire or to abandon the vessel, and it will be the end of all things.              ON THE ELEMENT OF AIR.

[Large initial A] IR is an integral element, most worthy in its quality, out-
wardly light and invisible, but inwardly heavy, visible, and fixed. It
is hot and humid, tempered by fire, it is more worthy than earth and water.
It is indeed volatile, but it is fixed, and when fixed it renders every body
penetrable. From its purest substance were created the vital
Spirits of animals, the less pure part was elevated into air's own Sphere,
but the remainder, its grosser part, remained in water,
which circulates with water, just as fire with earth, because they are friends.

**CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF FIRE.**

**F**IRE is the purest element and the most worthy of all, full of adhering unctuous corrosiveness, penetrating, digesting, corroding, most adhering, outwardly visible, but inwardly invisible; it is most fixed, hot and dry, and tempered by earth. Its purest substance and essence of all was first elevated with the Throne of Divine Majesty in creation, when the waters of the heavens were established, as we said in the Element of Water: from its less pure substance, Angels were created: from its less pure [substance] mixed with the purest air, the luminaries and stars were created: the still less pure [substance] was erected into a Sphere to enclose and uplift the heavens: but the impure and unctuous [substance] was left and enclosed in the center of the earth by the most wise supreme Creator, to continue the operation of motion, which we call Gehenna. All these fires are indeed divided, but they have a natural sympathy with each other. This

--- Page 629 ---
This element is the most tranquil of all and like a chariot, when
it is drawn, it runs; when it is not drawn, it stands quietly. It is also present in all
things imperceptibly. In it are vital principles and intellect,

the rational soul, by which alone man differs from other animals, and to God
is assimilated. This soul is that purest elemental fire, into the spiri-

What kind of trembling when the whole host of the heavenly army moves around Him? But someone will ask how we know these things, since heavenly things are hidden from human intellect. To these we reply that these things are manifest to all philosophers; indeed, incomprehensible wisdom itself has inspired them that all things are created after the example of nature, and that from those arcana, nature derives its power and operates, and that nothing happens on earth except after the example of the heavenly monarchy, which is understood from the various offices of angels. So also nothing is born or generated except naturally. All human inventions, indeed, even arts, which either exist or will exist, arise only from the foundations of nature. The Most High Creator willed to manifest all natural things to man; therefore He also showed us the heavenly things made naturally, from which His absolute and incomprehensible power and wisdom might be better known; all of which philosophers are able to see as in a mirror in the light of nature. Therefore, they greatly valued this science, not out of a desire for gold or silver, but for the knowledge not only of all Natural things but also of the Creator's power itself, and they wished to speak about these things as sparingly as possible and only figuratively, lest divine mysteries, by which nature is elucidated, be revealed to the unworthy. Which you, if you know how to know yourself and are not stiff-necked, can easily understand; you who were created after the likeness of the greater world, indeed, after the image of God Himself. You have in your body the anatomy of the whole world; you have as a firmament the fifth essence of the four Elements, extracted from the Chaos of seeds into the matrix, and further constricted into the skin; you have the purest blood in place of fire, in which the seat of the soul (in place of a King) is located by the vital spirit; you have the heart in place of earth, where the central fire continuously operates and sustains this machine of the Microcosm in its being; You have the mouth as the Arctic pole; you have the belly as the Antarctic, and all members correspond to the celestial bodies: concerning which we will at some point leave more extensively in our Harmony in the Chapter on Astronomy, where we wrote how Astronomy is an easy art, na-

It governs the mind, but the mind governs the body: when the soul conceives something, the mind knows everything, and all members understand the mind and obey the mind, and eagerly await to fulfill its will. For the body knows nothing; whatever strength or movement is in the body, the mind does these things; the body is merely to the mind as the instruments of some artisan. But the soul, by which man differs from other animals, operates in the body, but has a greater operation outside the body; because it absolutely dominates outside the body, and by this it differs from animals which have only mind and not the soul of divinity. So also God and the creator of things, our Lord and God, operates in this world those things which pertain to the necessities of the world, and in these things is included in the world; whence God is to be believed to be everywhere. But that immense wisdom of His is excluded outside the body of the world, by which He operates outside it and imagines other things much higher than the body of the world can conceive, and these are outside nature, the secrets of God alone. Just as there is an example in the soul, which outside the body imagines many most profound things, and by these things is assimilated to God who operates outside His world, outside nature; although even these things are still like a lit candle compared to midday light: because the soul imagines but does not execute except in the mind, but God brings all things into being at the same moment He imagines them; just as the soul imagines being in Rome or elsewhere, whatever happens, in the blink of an eye, but only in the mind; but God does such things essentially, who is omnipotent. Therefore God is not enclosed in the world except as the soul of the body.

...its own separate absolute power; so also the soul of whatever body it is, has absolute and separate power to do other things than the body can conceive; therefore it has the greatest power over the body if it wishes, otherwise our Philosophy would be in vain. From these things therefore learn to know God, and you will know how the Creator differs from created things. You yourself will be able to conceive greater things, since you now have an open door from us. But lest this treatise grow too large for us, let us proceed to the matter at hand.

We said above that Fire is the most quiescent Element, and that it is excited by motion, which excitation wise men have known. A Philosopher must know all generation and its corruption; to whom not only the Creation of heaven is manifest, but also the composition and commixture of all things: but although they know all things, they cannot do all things. Indeed, we know the composition of man in all qualities, yet we cannot infuse the soul; because this mystery belongs to God alone; and by infinite mysteries of this kind, He surpasses all things. Since these things are outside nature, they are not yet in the disposition of nature: nature does not operate until matter is presented to it: The first matter from the Creator, the second from the Philosopher. But in the operation of Philosophers, nature has to excite the fire which is secretly enclosed by the Creator in the center of every thing: such excitation of fire occurs by the will of nature, sometimes by the will of a sagacious artisan disposing nature. For naturally all impurities and pollutions of things are purged by fire: Every compound is dissolved by fire: just as water washes and purges all imperfect things that are not fixed; so fire purges all fixed things, and they are perfected by fire: Just as water joins everything dissolved; so fire separates everything joined, and what is of its nature and property it purges and augments excellently, not indeed in quantity but in virtue. This Element acts in wondrous ways secretly upon other Elements and upon all things: for just as the soul is from that purest [thing], so the vegetable [life] is from the Elemental which is governed by nature. This Element acts in the Center of every thing in this way: nature gives motion, motion excites air, air excites fire, and fire separates, purges, digests, colors, and causes every seed to mature, matu-

--- Page 633 ---
*On Sulphur.* 619

and expels the mature [substance] through sperm into places and matrices, places pure or impure, hot, more or less, dry or humid; and according to the disposition of the matrix, or place, various things are produced on earth, just as also in the booklet XII. Treatises on matrices mention was made that there are as many matrices as places.

Thus the creator of all things, the Most High God, constituted and ordained all things so that one is contrary to another, and yet that the death of one is the life of another: that one produces, another consumes, and something else from this, and something nobler is naturally produced: and by these means the equality of the Elements, and thus of the composite, is preserved.

The separation of all things, especially living ones, is natural death: therefore it is natural for man to die; because since man is composed of four Elements, he is subject to separation, since every composite is naturally separated. But this separation of human Composition ought only to have happened on the Day of Judgment: for in paradise man was immortal. Which all Theologians, and Sacred Scripture itself attest; yet no Philosopher has hitherto shown a sufficient reason for immortality; which it is fitting for the holy inquisitor of this science to know, so that he can see how all these things happen naturally, and can be understood most easily.

It is true and most true that every composite of this world is subject to corruption and can be separated; which separation in the animal kingdom is called death: but since man also is composed and created from four Elements, how could he be immortal? To believe this happens naturally is difficult, indeed it has hitherto been considered something supernatural, yet God inspired good philosophers many centuries ago that this is natural, which you are to receive from us in this way.

Paradise was and is such a place created by the supreme Creator of things from true Elements, not elementalized but purest, tempered, brought to a perfect state of balance; and all things whatsoever in Paradise are created from the same Elements and are incorruptible; there also man was created, constituted from the same incorruptible Elements in a just equality of balance, so that he could in no way be corrupted, therefore he was consecrated to immortality: because God undoubtedly created this paradise solely for men, concerning which we Iiii 2 and where

But when afterwards, by the sin of disobedience, he transgressed the command of the Most High Creator, man was expelled to the beasts in this corruptible, elemental world, which God had created only for beasts. For him, since he could not live without nourishment, it was necessary to take nourishment from the corrupt, elemental elements. Afterwards, those who were already begotten in corrupt elements from corrupt seed and not in Paradise were still closer to corruption and death, because seed produced from corrupt nourishment cannot be durable; and the longer [the time passes] from the expulsion from Paradise, the closer men approach corruption: hence also a shorter life, and it will come to pass that even procreation will cease due to the shortening of life. There are nevertheless some places where they have a more benign air and more propitious stars; there natures do not corrupt so quickly, because men also live more naturally. But our people, rashly, by gluttony and a disordered life, hasten to corruption: experience teaches this, that those born from the seed of infirm parents do not last. But if man had remained in Paradise, in a place suitable to that nature, where the incorrupt elements are all virgin, he would have been immortal forever: for it is certain that when pure elements are joined in equality of qualities, this subject is incorruptible, and such ought to be the Philosopher's Stone: it was assimilated by ancient Philosophers to such human creation, but modern Philosophers, understanding all things literally, to this world's ge...

It was inspired that the composition of such elements exists in gold, because in animals it is impossible, since they must sustain life from corrupted elements; nor is it in vegetables, because an inequality of Elements is found in them. And since all created things are inclined to multiplication, the Philosophers proposed to test this possibility of nature in this mineral kingdom; which having been found, they saw innumerable other secrets of nature to be inherent, about which they left very little, as if about divine secrets. Thus, therefore, you have how corrupted elements fall in the subject and are separated, when one overcomes another; and because then putrefaction occurs through the first separation, and through putrefaction the separation of the pure from the impure, if then there is a new conjunction by the power of fire, it acquires a form much nobler than the first. For in its first state, corruption was from a gross admixture which is not purified and improved except through putrefaction; and this cannot happen unless the forces of the four elements which are in every compound are conjoined. For when a compound must fall, it falls through the element of water; and while they thus lie confused, the fire which is potentially in any of the others, as in earth, in air, they come together, and with united hand, they afterwards conquer the water, which they digest and cook, and finally congeal; and in such a way nature helps nature. For if the hidden central fire, which was captured by life, conquers, it acts upon that which is closer and purer to itself, just as it itself is most pure, and is conjoined with it: thus it conquers the contrary, and separates the pure from the impure, and a new form is generated, and if it is still aided, it is much more excellent than the former. Sometimes, by the ingenuity of a sagacious artisan, immortal things are made, especially in the mineral kingdom. Thus all things are made by fire alone, and by the rule of fire, and are brought into being, if you have understood me.

Here, therefore, the origin of the Elements, and their natures and operations are described as briefly as possible, which suffices for our purpose in this place. For otherwise, if each Element were described as it is, a large volume would arise, not necessary for our purpose. All these things, as we have said, we refer to the Harmony, where, God willing, if life remains to us, we will leave more copiously concerning natural things.

These four Elements having been described, let us descend to the three principles of things: and how those are produced from the four Elements, thus learn. After Nature received from the Most High Creator of all things the privilege of a feudal grant over this Monarchy of the world, she began to distribute places and provinces to each according to dignity; and first of all, she constituted the four Elements to be the princes of the world; and so that the will of the Most High might be fulfilled (in whose will

For even if the soul is taken from the noblest place, yet it cannot arrive where it tends except through the spirit, which is the place and dwelling of the soul; which, if you wish to lead back to its proper place, it is necessary that it be washed from every sin, and that the place also be purified, so that in it the soul may be glorified, and no longer separated. Now therefore you have the origin of the three Principles, from which it is your task, imitating nature, to produce the Mercury of the Philosophers and their first matter, and to lead these principles of things, especially metals, to your purpose: since without these principles it is impossible for you to accomplish anything by art, seeing that nature itself does nothing without them, nor produces anything. These three are in all things, and without them there is nothing in the world, nor naturally will there be. But since we have written above that the ancient Philosophers named only two principles, lest the inquirer err, it must be known that although they described Sulphur and Mercury, yet without Salt they could by no means approach this work, since that is the key and principle of this sacred science: that is what opens the gates of justice, that is what has the keys to the infernal prisons, where bound Sulphur lies, as these things will sometimes be given more broadly in the third treatise of principles, concerning Salt. they are deprived of life: but those who invaded our goods lost their own goods, some even kingdoms: Moreover, we know that many infamous ones who detracted from our honor have perished: such great protection we have always had from the Creator of all things, who immediately received us from our mother's womb under the shadow of His wings, and infused the spirit of understanding of natural things, to whom be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages. We have received such great benefits from the Most High God our Creator, that it is impossible to comprehend them not only with a pen but also with the mind: God has scarcely ever bestowed greater, indeed, at least such, things upon any mortal. Would that we had so much spirit, so much intellect, and eloquence, and understanding, that we could render due thanks to Him; for we know we have not deserved such things: this one thing we believe to be true, that in Him alone we have always hoped, we hope, and we shall hope. For we know that there is no one among mortals who can help us, except this sole God and our Creator; because it is vain to trust in princes, since they are men (as the Psalm says). All these have the Spirit of life from God, which being taken away, all things are dust; but to hope in the Lord God, from whom, as from a fount of goodness, all good things most abundantly flow, is safe and secure. Therefore, whoever you are who wish to approach this Holy Science, place first your complete hope in God your Creator, and weary Him with prayers, and firmly believe that you will not be forsaken by Him: for if God recognizes your pure heart and your complete hope placed in Him, He will easily provide a means, through this or another way, He will help you to obtain your wish. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Pray, but nevertheless also work: God indeed gives understanding, but you must know how to use it: for just as good understanding and good opportunity are gifts of God, so it is a punishment for sin when a good opportunity is neglected. But to return to our purpose, we say that quicksilver is the first matter of this work, and truly nothing else; whatever is added to it originates from it. We have said sometimes that all things in the world are made and generated from three Principles; but we purify some things from accidents, and having purified them, we join them again; adding what needs to be added, supplying what is lacking—

we fill, and imitating nature, we concoct it to the end of highest perfection, which nature could not perfect because of an accident, and has now finished where art ought to begin. Therefore, if you wish to imitate nature, imitate it in those things in which it operates. Nor let it move you that our writings seem contrary to each other in some places; for it is necessary lest the art be betrayed: But you choose those things which agree with nature; take the roses, leave the thorns. If you intend to make metal, let metal be your foundation, because nothing is generated from a dog but a dog, from metal but metal: for know for certain, if you do not take from metal the radical moisture most excellently separated, you will never make anything; Without a grain of wheat, you cultivate the earth in vain: one thing, one art, one operation. If therefore you wish to produce metal, you will ferment with metal; but if a tree, let the seed of the tree be your ferment. As we have said, the operation is one, outside of which there is no other that is true. Therefore all err who say that any particular thing outside this one way and natural matter is true; for a branch is not had except from the trunk of a tree: It is impossible and foolish to wish to produce a branch before the tree; it is easier to make the Stone itself than any particular, even the simplest, that would be useful and would persist in examination with the natural. There are nevertheless many who boast that they can make fixed moon, but they would do better to fix lead or tin, since in my judgment it is the same labor; because these do not resist the test of fire as long as they are in their own nature; but moon in its nature is sufficiently fixed, and has no need of Sophistic fixation. But since there are as many opinions as heads, we leave to each his own opinion: whoever does not wish to follow our counsel and imitate nature, let him remain in his error. Indeed, particulars can be well made, having a tree, whose shoots can be grafted onto various trees: just as, having one water, various kinds of meats can be boiled in it, and according to the diversity of the meats, the broth will have flavor, but this from the same foundation. We conclude therefore that there is but one nature, both in metals and in other things, but a diverse operation of it, also one universal matter accord-

following Hermes. Thus from this one thing all things are born. Many,

that it is most false that that extracted soul can tinge some other metal in a Sophistic manner,
and that all who boast about this are deceivers:

ABOUT SULPHUR.

[Large initial letter I]
AMONG the three Principles, the Philosophers deservedly placed Sulphur in the first place,
as the most worthy Principle, in whose preparation the whole science lies hidden.
For sulphur is threefold, and to be chosen among others:
                                                                                                Sul-

--- Page 646 ---
632                                     *On Sulphur.*

Sulphur tinging or coloring: Sulphur congealing Mercury:
The third is essential maturing. Indeed, we ought to have treated this
seriously, but because we have published one of the principles through a Dialogue,
we are thus compelled to conclude the others, lest we seem to inflict injury upon any of them.
Sulphur is more mature than the other Principles, and Mercury does not coagulate
except by sulphur: therefore, our entire operation in this art is nothing other than
knowing how to extract sulphur from metals, by which our quicksilver is
congealed into gold and silver in the bowels of the earth: which
sulphur, indeed, in this Work, is held in the place of the male, and therefore considered more worthy,
while Mercury is in the place of the female. From the compound and
action of these two, the Mercury of the Philosophers is generated.
      We have described in the Dialogue of Mercury with the Alchemist that gathering
of Alchemists where they consulted from what material and
how the Philosopher's Stone should be made. It is also written
how, by the misfortune of a storm or a Conclusion, they were dispersed almost throughout the entire
World. For a strong storm and a very great wind arose which scattered them
here and there, and so blew through the heads of some that to this very day
they cannot recollect themselves, whence various kinds of flies are generated in their brains. Now,
among them were men of various nations and conditions, among whom
was also this Alchemist, about whom we have begun to speak in this Treatise:
he was otherwise a good man, but without a Conclusion, from the number of those
who propose to find the Philosopher's Stone by chance:
and he was a companion of that Philosopher who contended with Mercury. This one,
however, said, "If it had happened to me to speak with Mercury, I would have
extracted it from him in a few words: that other fool," he said, "did not know how to
proceed with him. Indeed, Mercury never pleased me, nor
do I believe there is anything good in it; but Sulphur is approved by me,
because in those Assemblies we disputed about it most excellently: if
that storm had not disturbed us, we would have concluded that it was the prime matter:
since in my head there are not usually trivial things, my head
is full of profound imaginations." And so, confirmed, he resolved
to work on sulphur. Therefore, he began to
