It happened one time, when he was walking almost in an ecstasy of contemplation, he came to a very green grove, most abundant in all things, in which there were mines of all minerals and metals, and all kinds of animals and birds, and an abundance of all trees, herbs, and fruits: there were also various aqueducts there: because in those places water was not available, except that which was drawn through various instruments and channels; and this by various artisans from various places: the principal one was that, clearer than the others, which was drawn from the rays of the Moon; and this was procured only for the Nymph of that grove. There also grazed bulls and rams, and and there were two young shepherds, whom the Alchemist asked: "Whose," he said, "is this forest?" to whom they replied: "It is the grove and garden of our nymph Venus." The Alchemist walked here and there: the place indeed pleased him, but he nevertheless always thought about his sulphur; and so, weary from walking, the poor man sat down by the side of a channel, under a certain tree, and began to lament most miserably, deploring the time and expenses spent in vain on his work (he was not otherwise of a deceitful disposition, but harmful to himself) and said. "What is this? Everyone says the thing is common, cheap, easy, and I am a learned man, and I cannot devise this wretched stone." And so, lamenting, he began to curse sulphur, because he had spent so many expenses, so many labors on it in vain: and sulphur was also in that grove, but unknown to the Alchemist. Meanwhile, while he was thus lamenting, he heard a voice as if of an old man: "Friend, why do you curse sulphur?" The Alchemist looked around everywhere, and seeing no one, was terrified. *Alchem.* Master, is he old?

*Voice*: Friend, his mother has only one such son; his other brothers are bad associates; he has a sister whom he loves, and by whom he is loved in return, for to her he is like a mother.
*Alchem.* Master, is he uniform everywhere?
*Voice*: As to his nature, he is uniform, but in prisons he is changed: his heart, however, is always pure, but his garments are stained.
*Alchem.* Master, was he ever free?
*Voice*: Most certainly he was, especially in those times when there were wise men with whom a great friendship existed between him and his mother.
*Alchem.* And who were these?
*Voice*: They were innumerable: There was Hermes who was one with his mother: after him there were many Kings and Princes, as well as many other wise men, such as in these centuries Aristotle, Avicenna, etc., who freed him: for these knew how to dissolve his bonds.
*Alchem.* Master, what did he give them for his liberation?
*Voice*: He gave them three Kingdoms: for when someone dissolves and frees him, then he conquers his custodians, who now govern in his Kingdom, and hands them over bound as subjects to him who frees him, and gives their Kingdoms into possession: but what is greater, in his Kingdom there is a mirror in which the whole World is seen. Whoever looks into this mirror can see and learn three parts of the wisdom of the whole World in it, and thus will become most wise in these three Kingdoms; such as Aristotle and Avicenna were and many others who, like the other predecessors, saw in this mirror how the World was created: from it they learned the influences of celestial virtues on lower things, and how Nature through the weight

fire composes things; then also the movement of the Sun and Moon, but especially that universal movement by which its mother is governed: from that they learned the degrees of heat, cold, humidity, and dryness, and the virtues of herbs and all things; from which they became the best Physicians. And certainly, unless a Physician is such that he knows why this herb is such and such, why it is hot in this degree, why dry, why humid, not from the books of Galen or Avicenna, but from the fount of Nature, from which even they had these things, he cannot be a fundamental Physician. All these things they diligently considered, and left their writings to their successors, so that men might be enticed to higher studies, and learn to liberate Sulphur, and dissolve its bonds: but men of this age now hold their writings as the final foundation, and seek no further; and it suffices for them that they know how to say, "Thus Aristotle, thus Galen wrote."
*Alchemist.* And what do you say, my Lord, can an herb be known without a Herbal?
*Voice.* Those ancient Philosophers wrote down their remedies from the very fount of Nature itself.
*Alchemist.* How, my Lord?
*Voice.* Know that all things on earth and above the earth are generated and produced from three Principles: sometimes from two, to which nevertheless a third adheres: whoever therefore knows the three Principles, and their weight as Nature combines them, will easily be able to understand from the decoction the degree of fire in the subject, whether it is well, badly, or moderately digested, and that according to more or less: for all plants are known by those who know the three Principles.
*Alchemist.* And how is this?
*Voice.* By sight, by taste, and by smell; in these three senses are also contained the three Principles of things, and the degrees of their decoction.
*Alchemist.* Lord, they say that Sulphur is Medicine.
*Voice.* Indeed, he himself is the Physician, and those who liberate him from his prisons, to them, out of gratitude, he gives his blood as Medicine.
*Alchemist.* Lord, having the universal Medicine, how long can a man preserve himself from death?
*Voice.* Until the term of death; however, this Medicine must be taken cautiously; for many wise men have perished by this Medicine before their appointed time.

And so Saturn departed. But a heavy sleep invaded the weary Alchemist, and such a vision appeared to him. He saw in that grove a spring full of water, around which Salt and Sulphur were walking, arguing with each other, until finally they began to fight; and salt inflicted an incurable wound upon sulphur, from which wound, instead of blood, water, like the whitest milk, flowed out, and grew into a great river. Then from that grove returned Diana, a most beautiful virgin, who began to wash herself in that river: whom, as a certain Prince, a very strong man (and greater than his servants), passing by, saw, he began to admire her beauty, and that she was of a nature similar to his own, and he was captivated by her love: which when she saw, she in turn burned with love for him; wherefore, as if falling into a swoon, she began to sink: seeing this, that Prince commanded his servants to help her: but all feared to approach the river; to whom that Prince said: Why (he said) do you not help the virgin Diana? To whom they replied, Lord, the river is indeed small, as if dried up, but most dangerous: Once, without your knowledge, we wanted to swim across this, and we barely escaped the danger of eternal death; we also know that others of our ancestors perished here. Then that Prince, having laid aside his thick cloak, just as he was armed, leaped into the river to bring aid to the most beautiful Diana, and extended his hand to her; who, wishing to save herself, also pulled the Prince himself to her, and both were submerged. So he took two quicksilvers of different substance, but of one root, which Saturn washed with his urine, and called them sulphurs of sulphurs, and mixed the fixed with the volatile; having made the composition, he placed it in a suitable vessel, and lest the sulphur escape, he placed a guardian beneath it, and so afterwards he placed it in a bath of very slow fire, as the matter required, and he did everything excellently. So they made the Philosopher's Stone, because from the proper material, only the proper work results. The alchemist, greatly rejoicing, took the stone with the glass, marveling as he considered its color, which was like burnt blood, and from excessive joy he began to dance, in which dance the glass slipped from his hands to the ground and was broken; and so Saturn vanished. The alchemist also, awakened from his dream, found nothing in his hands except those little candles he had made from sulphur: but the stone flew away, and flies to this day, whence it is called volatile: and so that wretched alchemist learned nothing else from that vision than how to make sulphur candles: who afterwards, having abandoned the stone, began to be a Physician; by seeking the Philosopher's Stone, he acquired a kidney stone. Finally, he lived his life as such alchemists usually do, for the most part they become Physicians or perfumers, which will happen to all who, without foundation, from hearsay or casually received recipes, approach the art through dialectic.
   Some afterwards, when it does not succeed for them, say: "We are wise men, we hear the grass grow; if the art were true, we would have possessed it before others": and so, clothed in shame lest they be considered unworthy (as they are, indeed, and stiff-necked), they rail against the art. This science hates such people, and always shows them the beginning at the end. But we concede that this art is nothing to the unworthy, but to lovers of virtue, and true seekers, and sons of doctrine, we highly commend it, and we affirm it to be true, and altogether most true. Which we have sometimes proven in reality before men worthy of that spectacle, men of high and low condition: (However, this Medicine was not made by our hands, but we received such things from a friend,

most true, however) for investigating which we have sufficiently informed the investigators; if our writings do not please them, let them read lighter works of other Authors, yet with this caution that whatever they read they should always compare to the possibility of nature, nor attempt anything against nature. Nor should they believe, even if it were written in the books of Philosophers, that fire does not burn, because this is against nature: but if it is written that fire has the power of drying and heating, this, since it happens naturally, must be believed; for nature always agrees with sound intellect, and in nature nothing is difficult, and all truth is simple. Then also let them learn to recognize which things in nature are closer to each other, which we believe can be done more easily through our writings than through others, since we think we have written enough until someone else comes who will write down the entire recipe as one makes cheese from milk, which is not permitted to us.

But lest we turn everything to the foolish, we will also say something to you who have already passed through these troubles. Have you seen that region where the man led his wife to himself, whose nuptials were celebrated in the house of nature? Have you understood how the common people saw this sulfur with you? If therefore you wish that old women practice your Philosophy, show them the whitening of these sulfurs; Say to the common people: come and see, for now the water is divided and the sulfur has come out; it will return white, and will congeal the waters. Therefore burn sulfur with incombustible sulfur, and wash, whiten, redden, until sulfur becomes Mercury, and Mercury becomes sulfur, which afterwards you will adorn with the soul of gold. For if you do not sublimate sulfur from sulfur, and mercury from mercury, you have not yet found the water which is created and distilled as the fifth essence from sulfur and mercury; he who does not descend will not ascend. Whatever is notable in this art is lost by many in the preparation. For our mercury is sharpened by sulfur, otherwise it would not be useful. A prince without people is miserable: so is the Alchemist without sulfur and mercury. If you have understood me, I have spoken.

The Alchemist, having returned home afterwards, lamented the lost stone, and grieved greatly that he had not asked Saturn what kind of Salt this was, since so many different kinds of salts are found; the rest he told his wife. CON-

--- Page 657 ---
De Sulphure.                                                                 643

CONCLUSIO.

EVERY investigator of this art ought first to examine with mature judgment the creation, operation, and virtues of the four elements, along with their actions: for if he ignores their origin and nature, he will not arrive at the knowledge of the principles, nor will he know the true matter of the stone, much less will he attain a good end; because every end is determined by its beginning: He who knows well what he begins will know well what he will finish. For the origin of the elements is chaos, from which God, the creator of things, created and separated the elements, which belongs to God alone: From the elements, however, nature produces the principles of things, and this, by the will of God alone, is nature's work: From the principles afterwards nature produces minerals and all things: from which also the artisan, by imitating nature, can do many wonderful things. Because nature, from these principles which are Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, produces minerals and metals and all kinds of things; and does not simply produce metal from the elements, but through principles which are a medium between the elements and metals: Therefore if nature does not do this, much less can art

--- Page 658 ---
644.                                  *On Sulphur.*
Regarding salt, since here we are treating the virtue and origin, not the practice, of sulphur.
    Nevertheless, we have not written this treatise to refute ancient philosophers, but rather to confirm their writings and to complete some things which they omitted; since philosophers too are men, they cannot do all things so perfectly, nor can one person sufficiently [deal with] all things. Miracles also led some astray from the straight path of nature, as we read happened to Albertus Magnus, a most sagacious man and philosopher, who wrote that in his time golden grains were found between the teeth of a dead person in a tomb. He could not find a certain reason for this miracle, but he attributed this to a mineral force in man, and upon this opinion, the saying of Morienus was confirmed for him: "*and this matter, O King, is extracted by you*." But this is erroneous, for Morienus also intended these things to be understood philosophically. For mineral virtue is located in its own kingdom, just as animal [virtue is located] in its own kingdom, as we distinguished these kingdoms in the little book of XII Treatises and divided them into three kingdoms; because each of these stands and multiplies within itself without external ingress. It is indeed true that in the animal kingdom there is Mercury as matter and sulphur as virtue, but animal, not mineral. If the force of animal sulphur were not in man, it would not congeal blood (Mercury) into flesh and bones; so also if there were not the force of vegetable sulphur in the vegetable kingdom, it would not congeal water or vegetable Mercury into herbs and trees. So too it must be understood in the mineral kingdom. Indeed, these three Mercuries do not differ in virtue, nor do those three sulphurs, because every sulphur has the natural power to coagulate its own Mercury; and every Mercury has the power to be coagulated by its own sulphur, but not by an extraneous one. But why gold was found or generated between the teeth of the deceased, this is the reason: that in the life of the deceased, Mercury was introduced into that infirm body by some physician, either by unction, or by turbith, or by another method, as is custom and use, and the nature of Mercury is to ascend to the mouth's opening and to be evacuated through the wounds of the mouth with phlegm. If therefore the sick person died during such a treatment,

--- Page 659 ---
*On Sulphur.* 645

(he) died, that Mercury, having no exit, remained in the mouth within the teeth, and that corpse became a natural vessel for Mercury. Thus, enclosed for a long time, it was coagulated into gold by its own sulphur, by the natural heat of putrefaction, purified by the corrosive phlegm of the human body. But if mineral Mercury had not been introduced there, gold would never have been produced. And this is a very true example that nature in the bowels of the earth produces gold and silver, and other metals, from Mercury alone, according to the disposition of the place or matrix. Because Mercury has within itself its own sulphur, by which it is coagulated into gold, unless it is hindered by an accident, or does not have the required heat, or does not have an enclosed place. Therefore, the power of animal sulphur does not coagulate Mercury into gold, but into flesh; for if such a power were in man, this would happen in all bodies, which is not the case. Many such miracles and accidents occur which, not well considered by writers, introduce errors to readers: a good inquirer, however, ought to apply everything to the possibility of nature: if they do not agree with nature, they are to be omitted.

It is sufficient for the diligent student to have received here the origin of the Principles, since with an unknown beginning, the end is always doubtful; concerning which we, in this treatise, have addressed the inquirer not enigmatically, but in the clearest language we could and were permitted: through which, if God illuminates someone's mind, he will know what a successor owes to his predecessors, since this knowledge is always acquired through such talents: which (knowledge), after such a clear demonstration, we place in the bosom of God Most High, our creator and Lord, and we commend ourselves, together with good readers, to His grace and immense mercy. To Him be praise and glory through infinite ages of ages.

**THE AUTHOR'S PREFACE.**

[Large initial A]s an Adept, I, Anonymous Philaletha, a Philosopher of arcane chemical and physical medicine, in the year of the Redeemed world one thousand six hundred forty-five, and in the twenty-third year of my age, have decided to write this little treatise, so that I might pay the debt to the Sons of Art and extend a hand to those entangled in the Labyrinth of Error, and so that it may appear to the Adepts that I am their equal and brother, and that those deceived by the trifles of Sophists may see and embrace the light by which they may safely return. Furthermore, I predict that not a few will be enlightened by these labors of mine. These are not Fables, but real Experiments, which I have seen, done, and known, as the Adept will easily gather from these lines. Therefore, as I write these things for the good of my neighbor, let it suffice that I have professed that no one writing in this art has ever written so lucidly, and that I, while writing, have often laid down my pen, for I would rather have hidden the truth under the mask of envy; but God compelled me, whom I could not resist, who alone knows hearts, to whom alone be glory forever. From this I undoubtedly conclude that many will be blessed by this secret in this last age of the world. Because I have written faithfully, and I have left no doubt for the diligent beginner that is not perfectly satisfied. I also know that many possess this Secret together with me, and I am persuaded that there are many more, whose acquaintance, so to speak, I shall soon obtain anew every day. May the holy will of God do what pleases Him; I confess myself unworthy, through whom such things are accomplished: Nevertheless, in these matters I adore the holy will of God, to whom all created things are bound to submit, for whom alone He created them, and protects them once created.

CHAPTER I.

On the Necessity of Sophic Mercury for the Work of the Elixir.

Whoever desires to possess this golden Fleece, let him know that our aurific powder, which we call our stone, is gold merely digested to the highest degree of purity and subtle fixity, to which it can be brought by Nature and sagacious artifice; which gold, thus Essentified, called our gold (no longer that of the common folk), is the culmination of Nature's and Art's perfection. I could cite all Philosophers concerning this matter; but I do not need witnesses, because I myself am an adept, and I write more lucidly than anyone before. Let him believe who wishes, let him disapprove who can, let him carp who pleases, he will certainly carry away this reward: profound ignorance. Subtle minds, I confess, dream chimeras; but on the simple path of Nature, the diligent one will find the truth. Therefore, let the true purification of gold be the one sole principle. Our gold, however, is twofold, which we seek for our work, namely, mature, fixed yellow Laton, whose heart or center is pure fire, wherefore it defends its body in Fire, in which it receives depuration, so that nothing yields to its tyranny, or suffers from it; This, in our Work, plays the part of the male, wherefore it is joined to our cruder white gold, the female sperm, in which it emits its sperm, and finally, both unite in an indissoluble bond, thus our Hermaphrodite, potent in both sexes, is made. Therefore, the corporeal gold is dead before it is joined with its spouse, with whom the coagulating Sulphur, which is in the gold, is inverted outside its natural course. Thus the Height is hidden and the Depth is manifested. Thus the fixed becomes volatile for a time, so that it may afterwards possess a nobler state by inheritance, in which it obtains a pre-eminent fixity. It is clear, therefore, that the whole Secret consists in Mercury, concerning which the Philosopher says: In Mercury, he says, is whatever the Sages seek,

--- Page 666 ---
Ad occlus. Regis Palatium. 653

The matter. Concerning this, GEBER says: "Praised be the Most High, who created our Mercury and gave it a nature surpassing all things. For certainly, unless this were, let alchemists boast as much as they wish, but the alchemical work would be in vain. It is clear therefore, that this Mercury is not common, but Sophic, because all common Mercury is male, that is, corporeal, specific, and dead; but ours is spiritual, a living and life-giving female. Therefore, pay attention to what I am about to say about Mercury, because, as the Philosopher says, 'our Mercury is the Salt of the Sages, without which whoever works is like an archer who shoots without a bowstring, and yet [this Salt] is nowhere to be found on earth.' The Son, however, is formed by us, not by creating but by extracting from those things in which it is, with nature cooperating, in a wondrous manner through sagacious art."

CHAPTER II.

Concerning the Constituent Principles of Sophic Mercury.

The intention of some working in this art is this, that they purify Mercury in various ways: for some sublimate it with added salts, some from various dregs, others vivify it only by itself; thus they suppose the Mercury of the Philosophers is made by repeated operations, and they err, because they do not work in nature, which alone is perfected in its own Nature. Let them know therefore, that our water is composed of many things, yet it is one thing made from diverse Substances concreted of one Essence. Indeed, in our Water is required firstly Fire, secondly the liquor of vegetable Saturn, thirdly the bond of Mercury. The Fire is of mineral Sulphur, and yet it is not properly mineral, much less metallic; but intermediate between ore and metal, partaking of neither, Chaos or Spirit, because our fiery Dragon, which conquers all things, is nevertheless penetrated by the odor of vegetable Saturn, whose Blood concretes with the juice of Saturn into one marvelous body, and yet it is not a body, because it is entirely volatile, nor a spirit, because in fire it resembles molten metal. It is therefore truly Chaos, which relates to all metals as a mother.

For from it I know how to extract all things, even the Sun and Moon without a Transmuting Elixir, which he who has likewise seen, can attest. This Chaos is called our Arsenic, our air, our Moon, our Magnet, our Steel, yet in different regards, because our matter undergoes various states, before the Royal Diadem is extracted from our harlot's menstruum. Learn therefore, who are Cadmus's companions, and who is the Serpent that devoured them, what is the hollow oak, to which Cadmus transfixed the Serpent. C H A P T E R III.

*Concerning the Steel of the Sages.*

The Wise Magi handed down much about their Steel to posterity, nor did they attribute slight importance to it, wherefore among the common alchemists there is no slight contention, what exactly is to be understood by the name of Steel. Various people have given various interpretations of this. The Author of the New Light wrote candidly about this, yet obscurely. I, so that I might conceal nothing from the Inquisitors of the Art out of envy, will describe it sincerely. Our Steel is the true Key of our Work, without which the fire of the lamp cannot be lit by any art: It is the ore of gold, a spirit exceedingly pure above all others, it is an infernal fire, secret, in its kind supremely volatile, a miracle of the world, a system of superior virtues in inferior ones, wherefore the Almighty marked it with a notable sign, whose nativity is announced through the East in the Horizon of its philosophical Hemisphere. The Wise Magi saw in that Age, and were astonished, and immediately recognized the most serene King born in the world. You, when you have beheld its Stars, follow even to the cradle, there you will see a beautiful infant,

C H A P T E R IV.
*Of the Magnet of the Sages.*

Just as Steel is drawn to the Magnet, and the Magnet spontaneously turns itself to the Steel, so also the Magnet of the Sages draws their Steel. Therefore, just as I taught that Steel is the Ore of gold, likewise our Magnet is the true Ore of our Steel. Furthermore, I make known that our Magnet has a hidden center abundant in Salt, which Salt is the menstruum in the Sphere of the Moon, which knows how to calcine gold. This center turns itself with an archetypal appetite towards the Pole, in which the virtue of Steel is exalted to a higher degree. In the Pole is the Heart of Mercury, which is the true Fire, in which is the rest of its Lord; sailing through this great sea, let it reach both Indies, let it direct its course by the aspect of the Northern Star, which our Magnet will make appear to you. The wise man will rejoice, but the fool considers these things of little importance, nor will he learn wisdom, even though he may have seen the central Pole turned outwards, marked with the notable sign of the Almighty. So stiff-necked are they, that even if they have seen signs and wonders, they will not lay aside their sophistries nor enter the right path.

C H A P T E R V.
*The Chaos of the Philosophers.*

Let the Son of the Philosophers hear the Sages unanimously concluding that this Work is to be assimilated to the Creation of the Universe. In the beginning, therefore, GOD created Heaven and Earth, and the Earth was void and empty, and the Spirit of GOD moved upon the face of the waters, and GOD said: Let there be Light, and there was Light. These words will be enough for the Son of the Art. For Heaven and Earth must be joined upon the bed of friendship. Thus

Earth is a heavy body, the Matrix of minerals, which it secretly preserves within itself, although it brings forth trees and animals into the light. Heaven is that in which the great Luminaries with the Stars revolve, and sends its powers through the air to the lower regions, but in the beginning all things confused together made Chaos. Behold, I have sacredly revealed the truth: for Our Chaos is like a Mineral Earth, in respect of its coagulation, and yet a volatile air, within which is the Heaven of the Philosophers in its Center, which Center is truly Astral, irradiating the Earth even to its surface with its radiance. And what Magus is so prudent as to gather from these things that a new King is born, excelling all, the Redeemer of his brethren from Original sin, whom it is necessary to die, and to be lifted up on high so that he may give his flesh and blood for the life of the world? Good God, how wonderful are these Thy Works? This has been done by Thee and a miracle appears in our eyes. I give thanks to Thee, Father of the Lord of heaven and earth, because Thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones.

These are they, concerning which the Author of the New Light [says]; which exist, but do not appear, until it pleases the Artist. Therefore, just as Air distinguishes between Waters, so too does our air [distinguish] all extracentral

CAPUT VIII.

*Of the labor and weariness of the first Preparation.*

Some ignorant Chemists dream that the entire work from beginning to end is pure recreation full of delight, but they place labor outside the bounds of this art: yet let them safely enjoy their opinion. In the Work, which they have so easily fashioned for themselves, they will indeed reap an empty harvest from their idle operation. We know, for example, that after divine Blessing, and a good root, labor, industry, and diligence hold the first place; Nor indeed will the labor of the family (which is rather to be considered a game, or recreation of the mind) grant what we so greatly desire, according to our wishes; nay, as Hermes says, one must not spare the soul and labor. Otherwise, what the wise man predicted in parables will be verified, namely that the desire of the slothful will kill him; Nor is it surprising if so many men dealing with Alchemy are reduced to poverty, for they flee labor, and do not endure expenses. But we, who know these things and have labored, have found for certain that no labor is more tedious than our first preparation. Therefore Morienus seriously exhorts the King concerning this matter, saying: Most of the Wise Men

**CHAPTER X.**
**Concerning Sulphur, which is in the Sophic Mercury.**

Above all things, this is wonderful, that in our Mercury not only actual, but also active Sulphur is present; And yet it retains all the proportions and form of Mercury. Wherefore it is necessary to introduce a form to it through our preparation, which form is metallic Sulphur, which Sulphur is fire, which putrefies the compounded Sun. This sulphureous Fire is a spiritual seed, which our virgin (nevertheless remaining undefiled) has contracted, because incorrupt Virginity can admit spiritual love, according to the Author of the Hermetic Arcanum, and Experience itself. By reason of this Sulphur it is Hermaphroditic, because the same Mercury includes both an active and a passive principle at the same time, conspicuous through the same degree of digestion. Indeed, when joined with the Sun, it softens, liquefies, and dissolves it, with heat tempered to the requirement of the compound. By the same Fire it coagulates itself, and in its Coagulation it gives the Sun, and that according to the pleasure of the Operation. This will perhaps seem incredible to you, but it is true, namely that homogeneous, pure and clean Mercury, pregnant with internal Sulphur through our artifice, by applying only suitable heat, coagulates itself, in the manner of a flower of milk, with a subtle earth, as it were, floating above the waters. But when joined with the Sun, not only is it not coagulated, but the compound will be seen to be softer daily, until, with the bodies almost dissolved, the spirits begin to coagulate, in a very black color, in a very foul odor. It is therefore clear, that this spiritual metallic Sulphur is truly the prime mover, which turns the wheel, and turns the axle in a circle. This Sulphur is truly volatile Gold, not yet sufficiently digested, but sufficiently pure, wherefore by mere digestion it passes into the Sun. But, if it is joined to the Sun already

CHAPTER XI.
*Concerning the Discovery of the Perfect Magistery.*

**T**he Sages of old, as many as attained this *Art* without the aid of books, were led to achieve it in this manner by the will of GOD. For I cannot persuade myself that it came to anyone by immediate revelation, unless perhaps *Solomon* had it, which I would prefer to leave to the *Judge* rather than determine myself. And yet, even if he had it, what prevents him from having arrived at it through investigation, since he requested *Wisdom* alone, which GOD had given him in such a way that with it he also possessed riches and peace? Because he explored the nature of plants and trees from the *Cedar* in *Lebanon* down to the *hyssop* and *wall-rue*, who in his right mind would deny that he likewise understood the natures of minerals, the knowledge of which is no less pleasant?

But to the point. We say that it is probably to be believed that the first adepts who mastered this Magistery, among whom was *Hermes*, and who lacked an abundance of books, sought primarily not a more-than-perfection, but only a simple exaltation of imperfect metals to a royal state, and since they perceived that all metallic things were of *Mercurial* Origin, and that *Mercury* in weight and homogeneity was most similar to the most perfect metal, gold, they were therefore prepared to digest it to the maturity of *Gold*, but they could not achieve this with any *Fire*. Therefore, they considered among themselves that, besides external heat, an internal fire was at least required to fulfill their desires. So they sought this in many things. First, they distilled extremely hot *Waters* from lesser minerals, and with the same, corroded *Mercury*.

--- Page 676 ---
**To the King's closed Palace.** 663

only agents would be in the manner of fire, though differently: And these menstrua, as they called them, did not remain with the dissolved body:
Confirmed by the same reasoning, they rejected all salts, except for one Salt, which is the first Being of Salts, which dissolves any metal, and by the same operation coagulates Mercury; but this only by a violent way. Therefore, an Agent of this kind, with its full weight and powers, is again separated from the substances. Therefore, the wise Men finally recognized that in Mercury, watery crudities and earthy dregs obstruct its digestion, which, being radically fixed, can only be exterminated by the inversion of the entire composite. They knew, I say, that Mercury, if it could shed these, would immediately become fixed. For it indeed has fermentative Sulphur within itself, of which even the smallest grain would be capable of coagulating the entire Mercurial body, provided that the dregs and crudities could be removed. Therefore, they attempted this with various purifications, but in vain; inasmuch as the aforesaid demands both mortification and regeneration, for which an Agent is necessary. And finally they knew that Mercury in the bowels of the Earth was destined to become a metal, for which purpose it maintained a daily motion, as long as the suitability of the place and other external conditions remained well-disposed; but if these were corrupted by chance, this immature offspring spontaneously rushed forth. Thus, that which is seen as somewhat deprived of motion and life, an immediate return from privation to habit is impossible. Passive, for example, is in Mercury what ought to have been Active; so that it is necessary to introduce another life, of the same nature, into it, in the introduction of which it awakens the latent life of Mercury. Thus life receives life; Then finally it is fundamentally changed, and dregs or impurities are spontaneously rejected from the center, as we have written sufficiently in previous chapters. This life is in metallic Sulphur alone: The Magi sought it in Venus, and similar substances, but in vain. Finally they took the offspring of Saturn into their hands, and proved it to be the Stylange of gold. Therefore, what had the power to separate dregs from mature Gold, they trusted would do the same in Mercury, by an argument drawn from the greater to the lesser. But this too retained its impurities, as shown by experiment...

--- Page 677 ---
664		*Open Entrance*

...proved, and remembered the well-worn proverb: Be clean yourself, who wish to cleanse another. Therefore, attempting to purify this, they thoroughly discovered it to be impossible, because it contained no metallic Sulphur in itself, although it abounded in the purest Salt of nature. What therefore they noted as a small and only passive Sulphur in Mercury, they found no actual, but only potential Sulphur in this Offspring of Saturn. Therefore, it entered into a pact with burning Arsenical Sulphur, and without this, foolishly, it cannot subsist in a coagulated form, and yet it is so stupid that it prefers to dwell with this enemy, by whom it is most tightly imprisoned, and to commit prostitution, rather than renounce this, and appear in mercurial form.

Therefore, seeking active Sulphur further, the Magi finally sought and found it most deeply abolished in the House of Aries. This, however, was most eagerly received by the Offspring of Saturn, which, being a most pure and tender metallic matter, and most akin to the first metallic Being, deprived of all actual Sulphur, yet in potential for receiving Sulphur. Therefore, like a Magnet, it draws this to itself, and absorbs and hides it in its belly, and the Omnipotent, to supremely adorn this Work, imprints His Royal Seal upon it.

Then immediately the Magi rejoiced, when they saw Sulphur not only found, but also prepared. Finally, they proceeded to purify Mercury by this, but the outcome did not respond, because the arsenical malignity was still mixed with this Sulphur absorbed in the offspring of Saturn, which, although it was now small, compared to the abundance it had in its mineral nature, nevertheless prohibited all entry. Therefore, by the Doves of Diana, they tried to temper this aerial malignity, and the outcome responded to their wishes.

Then they mixed life with life, and moistened by the dry liquid, and sharpened the passive by the active, and vivified the dead by the living. Thus the sky was clouded for a time, which after heavy rains again became clear. Here Mercurius emerged Hermaphroditic. Therefore, they placed this into the fire, and coagulated it in no very long time, and in its coagulation they found the purest Sun and Moon.

Finally, returning to themselves, they thought that Mer-

This purified Mercury, not yet coagulated, was not yet a metal, but made volatile, so that it would leave no residue at the bottom in its distillation. Therefore, they named it immature Sun and their living Moon. They also considered that since the true First Being of Gold still existed as volatile, why should it not be a field in which the sown Sun would be increased in virtue. Therefore, they placed the Sun in the same, and what easily accomplished admiration, the volatile was made fixed in the same, the hard soft, the coagulated dissolved, nature itself being astonished. Therefore, they espoused these two to each other, enclosed them in glass, placed them at the fire, and governed the work according to the exigency of nature, for a long time. Thus the dead was vivified, and the living died, the body putrefied, and the glorious spirit resurrected, and the soul was finally exalted into the Fifth Essence, the highest Medicine for animals, metals, and vegetables.

Cᴀᴘᴜᴛ XII.
*Of the Method of making the perfect Magistery*
*in General.*

IMmortals, we ought to give thanks to God, because He has shown us these secrets of Nature, which He has hidden from the eyes of many. Therefore, what has been freely given to us by that great Giver, we will freely and faithfully reveal to other diligent students. Know therefore that the greatest Secret of our Operation is nothing else than the Cohobation of Natures, one upon another, until the most digested Virtue is extracted from the digested through the crude. For this, first, an exact comparison and preparation, and adaptation of the things entering the work is required. Secondly, a good disposition of external things; Thirdly, for things thus prepared, good governance is required; Fourthly, foreknowledge of what appears in the Work is desired, lest one proceed blindly; Fifthly, patience, lest the work be rushed, or governed precipitously. Concerning all these things, we will speak in order, as brother to brother.

They say, for example, that common Gold is dead, but their own is living; similarly, a grain of wheat is dead, that is, the germinating activity in it, being suppressed, succumbs, and thus it would remain eternal, if only it is kept in dry ambient air: but let it be cast into the earth, and it soon receives fermentative life, it swells, softens, and germinates. The matter stands thus with our Gold: it is dead, that is, its vivifying power is sealed under a corporeal rind, in the likeness of a grain, although differently, inasmuch as a great difference exists between a vegetable grain and metallic gold. But just as a grain remains perpetually unchanged in dry air, is destroyed by fire, and is reducible in our sole water, and then our grain is alive, just as wheat sown in the field, its name changed, is the farmer's seed, which, as long as it remained in the granary, was grain, suitable as much for bread-making and other uses as for sowing. Similarly, Gold, as long as it is seen in the form of a ring or vessel, or coin, is common; in the former way it is called dead, because it would remain unchanged until the end of the world; in the latter way it is called living, because it is thus in potential, which potential can be brought into actuality within a few days; gold then will no longer be gold, but the Chaos of the Sages. Therefore, the Philosophers rightly say that Philosophical Gold differs from common Gold, which difference consists in its composition. For just as a man is called dead who has already received the sentence of death, so Gold is called living when it is mixed with such a composition and subjected to such a fire, in which it will necessarily soon receive germinative life, indeed, within a few days it will demonstrate the actions of incipient life. Wherefore the same Sages, who say their Gold is living, command you, investigator of the Art, to revive the dead; if you know this, and have prepared the agent, and have rightly mixed your gold, it will not slowly become living: In which vivification your living menstruum will die. Therefore the Magi command to vivify the dead and to mortify the living, and yet they call their Water living at the first threshold, and they say that the death of one principle has one and the same period with the life of another. CHAPTER XIV.

Concerning the general requirements for this work and accidental circumstances.

We have separated the Hermetic Art from all vulgar errors, and having conquered sophistries and the curious dreams of the deluded...

We have demonstrated the former to be perfect and marketable by nature; we have shown the latter to be manufactured by art. We have added reasons so clear and perspicuous that unless you wished to be blind to the Sun, you could not but perceive them. We have professed, and again we profess, that we have brought forth these things not from faith which we give to the writings of others; we have seen and known what we faithfully declare, we have made, seen, and hold the great Elixir Stone. Therefore, having obtained animated Mercury and gold, there remains the accidental purification, both of Mercury and of Gold, afterwards the espousal, thirdly the rectification.

CHAPTER XV.
Concerning the accidental purification of Mercury and gold.

[Large initial A] Perfect Gold is found in the bowels of the Earth, whence it is sometimes found in small pieces and sand. If you can have this pure, it is pure enough; but if not, purify it either with Antimony, or by cupellation, or by boiling with aqua fortis, the gold having been granulated first. Afterwards, melt it by fusion fire, and file it, and it is prepared. Mercury, however, needs an internal and essential purification, which is the gradual addition of true Sulphur, according to the number of eagles, then it is radically purified. But moreover, it demands an accidental cleansing to wash away external impurities ejected from the center. This labor is not absolutely necessary,

--- Page 688 ---
*At the closed Royal Palace.* 675

labor, however, it accelerates the work, and therefore it is suitable. Therefore take
your Mercury, which you prepared by the appropriate number of eagles, and
sublime it three times from common salt and Mars' dross, grinding it at the same time with vinegar
and a little sal ammoniac, until the Mercury disappears, then dry
and distill through a glass Retort with the fire gradually increased, until
all the Mercury has ascended. Repeat this four times, afterwards
boil the Mercury in spirit of vinegar for an hour in a cucurbit, or a glass with a wide bottom
and narrow neck, stirring vigorously at times. Then decant the vinegar,
and wash away the acidity with spring water, poured on repeatedly. Then dry
the Mercury and you will marvel at its brilliance. You could wash with urine or vinegar
and salt and spare the sublimation, then at least distill four times, after
you have completed all the eagles without addition, washing the
steel Retort each time with ash and water, finally boil in distilled vinegar
for half a day, stirring vigorously at times and pour out the blackish vinegar,
and pour in new, finally wash with hot water, and you can
free the spirit of vinegar from blackness by redistilling it and have it of the same virtue.
All this is for removing external impurity, which
does not adhere in the center, and yet is a little more stubborn on the surface,
which you will perceive thus; Amalgamate Mercury with the purest Gold,
let the amalgam be made on the cleanest paper, and you will see that the amalgam
has stained the paper with dark blackness; You will counter this dross by the
aforesaid distillation and boiling and agitation, which preparation
greatly promotes the work by accelerating it.

These things having been duly performed, you will take one part of purified and laminated, or

(which is not so good) or boxwood, but glass or stone is preferable.
I am accustomed to using a white coral one. Grind, I say, vigorously,
until it becomes impalpable, grind with as much diligence as painters are
accustomed to comminuting their colors, then observe the consistency, if it is
pliable like butter not too warm, much less cold, yet in such a way that the tilted
amalgam does not allow the Mercury to run off, like subcutaneous dropsical
water, the consistency is good; if not, add as much water as is sufficient
to make such a consistency. The law of the mixture is this: that it be most
readily pliable and very soft, and yet capable of being formed into
round little lumps like butter, which, although it yields to the lightest touch
of a finger, can nevertheless be formed into balls by a washing woman.
Observe the example given, as most exact, because like butter, even if it is
tilted, it does not pour out anything more liquid than the whole mass;
likewise our mixture. For the intrinsic nature of Mercury, this sign will be
given, either in a double or triple proportion of Mercury to the body, or even
in a triple of the body to a quadruple of the spirit, or double to triple.
And according to the difference of Mercury, the amalgam will be softer
or rougher; always remember, however, that it should coalesce into little lumps,
and those separated lumps should solidify in such a way that no livelier
Mercury appears at the bottom than at the top. Note, for indeed, that
if the amalgam is allowed to rest, it spontaneously hardens. Therefore,
the consistency is to be judged while stirring, and if it is then pliable like
butter, and allows lumps to be formed, and its lumps placed on clean paper
solidify without trouble in such a way that the bottom is not more liquid
than the top, the proportion is good. This done, take spirit of vinegar,
and dissolve in it a third part of Sal ammoniac, and place the Mercury
and Sun (Gold) previously amalgamated, into this liquid, place it in a
long-necked glass vessel, and allow it to boil for a quarter of an hour,
with strong ebullition, then remove the mixture from the glass, set aside
the liquid, heat the mortar, and grind, as above, strongly and diligently,
then with hot water, wash away all blackness. Place it again into the
former liquid, and boil again in the same glass vessel, grind again vigorously
and wash. Repeat this, until you can wipe no color from the amalgam
with any effort,

--- Page 690 ---
Ad occlus. Regis Palatium. 677

Thus, the amalgam will then become clear, like the purest and most polished silver,
with astonishing whiteness. Still observe the temperature and be careful
that it is precise according to the given rules; if not, make it correct, and pro-
ceed as above. This work is laborious, yet you will see the labor compen-
sated by the signs appearing in the work. Finally, boil it in pure
water, decanting and repeating until all saltiness and acrimony have
vanished; then, with the water poured out, dry the amalgam, which will happen quickly.
But so that you may be very secure (because too much water will ruin the work, breaking the vessel,
however large, with its vapor), stir it on clean paper with the tip
of a knife, from place to place, until it is dried perfectly; then proceed,
as I will teach.

CHAPTER XVII.
Concerning the Proportion, Form, Material, and Closure of Vessels.

You shall have an oval or round glass, so large that it may hold
one ounce of distilled water in its sphere at the very least, nor indeed
less, if you can; but procure it as carefully as you can around that measure.
Let the glass have a neck one palm in height; let the glass be very
clear, thick, the thicker the better, provided you can distinguish the
actions in the concave part of the glass. Let it not be thicker in one place than in another.
Let the material adapted to this glass be one and a half ounces of Gold with one ounce of
Mercury; and if you add triple Mercury [in proportion to the gold], the whole compound
will still be within two ounces. And this proportion is exquisite. Furthermore, unless
the glass is thick, it will not be able to endure in the fire, because the winds (gases) which are
formed in the vessel by our Embryo will break the vessel. Let the glass be
sealed at the top, with the caution that there be neither a fissure, much less a hole,
otherwise the work would perish. Thus you will see that the work in its material
principles does not exceed the price of three gold coins. Indeed, in the making of the water,
the cost of one pound scarcely exceeds two crowns. Instruments, I con-
fess, are several, yet those are by no means expensive, and if you have my
distilling instrument, you will easily be excused from fragile glasses.
There are however some who dream that the price of perhaps one imperial coin will serve the whole
work, to whom it is permitted to respond that they will never experience the work...

--- Page 691 ---
678                                     *Introitus Apertus*

...proven this work by experiment. For other things are necessary in the work, which require expenses. But these will insist, from among the Philosophers, that everything bought at a great price is found to be false in our work. To whom I would answer, and what is our Work? Namely, to make the Stone? That indeed is the final goal: But, the work is to find the humidity in which gold melts like ice in warm water; to find this is our Work; in this many toil, some to gain the Mercury of the Sun, others the Mercury of the Moon; but in vain. For in this work, everything that is sold at a high price is false. Amen I say, that of this Water, the material principle can be bought for the price of one florin, as much as is sufficient to animate two whole pounds of Mercury, so that it may become the true Mercury of the Sages. Meanwhile, glass vessels, coals, earthen vessels, a furnace, and iron vessels and instruments cannot be acquired for nothing. Therefore, let the base garrulities of the Sophists be impudently silenced.

--- Page 692 ---
Ad occluf. Regis Palatium. 679

while: Know that our Mercury gives gold from itself; which if you do not know, what is the subject of our secrets, it is necessary that you sell it for common Gold; And it is true Gold in every test, and therefore it is salable, that is, it can be sold to anyone without scruple. Our Gold, therefore, is commonly salable, but not commonly to be bought, because for it to be ours, our art is needed.

You can find our Gold in common Gold and Silver. I myself have sought and found it in these. But the work is by no means easy. The Stone itself is to be made with less difficulty than you will find the proximate matter of the Stone by buying common gold. Therefore, our gold is the proximate matter of our Stone, common gold is near, other metals are remote, and those things which are not metallic are most remote, or rather, alien.

Because our Gold is Chaos, whose soul has not been put to flight by fire. Common gold is that whose soul, so that it might be safe from the fiery tyranny of Vulcan, has retreated into a closed citadel. But if you seek our Gold in anything in the middle, between the perfect and the imperfect, seek and you will find it; if not, loosen the bars of common gold, which is called the first preparation, by which the enchantment of its body is dissolved, without which the work of the husband cannot be perfected.

If you have entered the former path, you are bound to proceed with the most benign fire; but if the latter, then you must implore the aid of scorching Vulcan. Such a fire, for example, must be applied, as we supply in multiplication, while the Elixir of the corporeal Sun and Moon of the common people is applied as a ferment for perfecting. This will certainly be a Labyrinth, unless you know how to extricate yourself.

In any progress, however, you will need equal and continuous heat, whether you have worked with common Gold or with our own. Know both, that our Gold will give you the Work perfected two or three months sooner than common Gold, and the Elixir in its first perfection will be of a thousandfold virtue, which in the other work will scarcely be of a hundredfold.

Moreover, if you have perfected the Work with our Gold, you must feed it, imbibe it, ferment it, etc., by which its power will grow immensely; but in the other Work, you must illuminate and incerate it; as is abundantly taught in the Great Rosary.

Furthermore, if you have worked with our Gold, you can calcine, putrefy, and whiten, with the help of a benign intrinsic fire along with a dewy warmth, administered externally. If you have worked with common Gold, by sublimating and boiling

--- Page 693 ---
680                                  *The Open Entrance*

...by boiling the materials must be prepared, so that afterwards you may be able to unite them with Virgin's Milk. However much progress you may have made, you will nevertheless be able to achieve nothing at all without fire. Therefore, not without reason did the truthful Hermes establish fire, nearest to the Sun and Moon, as the governor of the work. However, I would wish this to be understood of our truly secret furnace, which the common eye never saw. There is also another furnace, which we call common, which will be built either of bricks, or of potter's clay, or of iron and brass plates well armored with clay. This furnace we call Athanor, whose form, more pleasing to me, is a Tower with a nest. Therefore, let it be a Tower about three feet high, nine digits wide, or a common span; after the sole or fundamental layer, let there be a small door for clearing out ashes, of three or four digits, everywhere with an adapted stone, above which a grate is immediately placed; a little above the grate let there be two openings, about two digits, through which heat is sent into the vessel placed within the Athanor. Moreover, let the Tower be exactly closed off from cracks; from above, coals are to be put in, which, once lit, then others are to be thrown in, and then finally the Mouth is to be exactly sealed. With such a furnace, you can complete the work according to your heart's desire. Moreover, if you are curious, you can find another and yet another way of administering the proper fire. Therefore, let the Athanor be made in this manner, so that in it, after the material has been placed, without removing the glass, you can apply any degree of heat, as desired, from a feverish heat up to the fire of minor reverberation, and in its most intense degree it may last by itself for at least ten or twelve hours. Then the Gate of the Work is open to you. But when you have obtained the Stone, you can more usefully construct a portable furnace, because the Stone, once made, is multiplied in less time and with a more benign fire of Nature.

                                  CHAPTER XIX.
          *On the Progress of the Work during the first forty days.*

Our Mercury and our Sun being prepared, enclose them in our vessel and govern with our fire, and within forty days you will see the entire material converted into shadow, that is, into atoms, without any mover or
motion

--- Page 694 ---
Ad occluſ. Regis Palatium. 681

visible motion, or any detectable heat, except that it grows warm.
But if the Mystery of Our Sun and Our Mercury has hitherto escaped you,
take your hand from the Work, for nothing but loss awaits you; But if
you do not yet know the mystery of our Sun in its full extent, but
you have attained knowledge of our Mercury, then take one part of the common Sun
well purified, and three parts of our most luminous Mercury,
join them as said above, and place them on the fire, giving heat, in which it may boil
and sweat, and its sweat may circulate, and this day and night for ninety
days and nights, and you will see this Mercury have separated all the Elements of the
common Sun, and again joined them, boil afterwards for another
fifty days, and you will see the common Sun converted by our Mercury
into our Sun, which is a Medicine of the first order. This Sulphur is therefore
now ours, but it does not yet tinge. — And believe me, many Philosophers
have worked by this way, and they have attained the truth, and it is a very
tedious way, and it is for the Magnates of the earth, because having obtained this Sulphur
do not believe that you have the Stone, and its true matter, which
you can seek and find in an imperfect thing within a week. This is
our way, easy and rare, and God has reserved this for the poor and
despised, and for his humble Saints. Concerning this matter, I have now decided to say many words,
although at the beginning of this book I had decided to bury it in deep
silence. This is one great Sophism of all Adepts, some speak
of the common Gold and Silver, and they speak truly, and others deny
the same, and they speak truly. I, moved by charity, will now extend
my hand, and now I call upon all Adepts, and I accuse all of them
of envy. I too had decided to tread the same path of envy,
unless God diverted us contrary to our plan, to whom be eternal sanctification!
I say therefore, that both ways are true, because there is only one way in the End;
but not in the Beginning. Because the whole is in our Mercury and our Sun.
Our Mercury is our way, and without it nothing will be done. Our Sun
also is not the common Gold, and yet it is in it. And if you have worked
in our Mercury with the common Gold, with due regimen, from those
one hundred and fifty days you will have our Gold, because our Sun is from our Mercury.
Therefore if Au

Therefore if common Gold shall have been disintegrated into its Elements by our Mercury, and again conjoined, the whole mixture, by the benefit of fire, will be our Gold, which Gold, if then repeatedly decocted by Mercury, will certainly give all the signs described by the Philosophers with such fire as they themselves wrote of. But now if you apply the regimen of the stone to the decoction of common Sun, however pure, with our Mercury, you are certainly on the path of error: And this is that great Labyrinth in which almost all beginners are stuck, because Philosophers in their books write of both ways, which in truth are nothing but one way, except that one is more direct than the other. Therefore those who write of common Sun, as we do in this little treatise, as also Artephius, Flamel, Ripley and many others, are not otherwise to be understood than that the philosophical Sun is made from common Sun and our Mercury, which then by repeated liquefaction will give fixed, incombustible Sulphur and quicksilver, and tinging in every test. Likewise and by this mode of understanding, our stone is in every metal and mineral, because, for example, common Sun can be extracted from them, from which our proximate Sun can be sought. In all, for example, common metals is our Sun; but in Gold and Silver it is contained more proximately. Therefore, says Flamel, some labored in Jupiter, others in Saturn, but I, he says, labored in the Sun and found it. There is however one thing in the metallic Kingdom, of wondrous Origin, in which our Sun is more proximate than in common Sun and Moon, if you seek it in the hour of its nativity, which liquefies in our Mercury, just as ice in warm water, and yet is in some way assimilated to Gold. You will not find this immediately in common Sun, but from that, through our Mercury, by digesting for one hundred and fifty days, you will find this true and same matter, which is our Gold, sought by a longer way, nor yet as potent as that which nature has left ready at hand, and yet by rotating the wheel a third time, you will find the same in both, with this difference however, in the former, in seven months, in the latter, in the space of a year and a half. I know both ways, I praise however the easier way; but I have described the more difficult one, lest I draw the anathema of all Sages upon my head. ...[the difficulty lies in] reading the books of more candid men, because all of them vary in their method to a man. And when they speak of one Work, they teach the method of another, in which net I was entangled for a long time, before I could free my feet from the snare. Therefore I make known, that the heat in our Work is of the most benign nature, if only you rightly understand our work. But if you work with the common Sun, that work is not properly our work, and yet it will lead directly to our work, in its determined time; in that [case], however, you need a strong decoction and a proportionate fire, and afterwards you will proceed with a most benign fire, in our turretted Athanor, which is to be highly praised by me. Wherefore, if you have worked with the common Sun, take care to diligently prepare the nuptials of Venus, then place it on its bed, and with due fire you will see the Emblem of the Great Work, namely black, the peacock's tail, white, citrine, and red. Then repeat this Work with Mercury, which is called Virgin's Milk, applying the fire of the dew bath, and at most that of sand tempered with ashes: And then you will see not only black, but blacker than black, and all blackness, thus also white and completed red, and this by the nod of God in a gentle breeze, who addressed Elijah with a silent voice. Therefore, if you know the art, extract our Sun from our Mercury, then from one thing you will perfect the Work, which, believe me, is more perfect than all mundane perfection, according to the Philosopher: "If from Mercury alone," he says, "you can perfect the work, you will certainly be the seeker of a most precious work." In this Work there are no superfluities; but the whole, by the living GOD, is converted into purity, because the action occurs in one thing alone. But if you have begun the process in the Work of the common Sun, then action and passion occur in two things, of which only the middle substance of both is taken, the dregs being rejected. If you deeply meditate on these things, which I have briefly concluded, you have the key to resolving all apparent contradictions among the Philosophers. Wherefore Ripley teaches to turn the wheel a third time in the chapter on Calcination, where he expressly speaks of the common Sun, and is thus to be understood. In the doctrine of his proportions, he is very obscure, because those three proportions serve three works. One work is most secret, and purely natural, and is done in our Mercury with our Sun, to which work is to be ascribed...

CHAPTER XX.
*Of the Coming of Blackness in the Work of the Sun & Moon.*

[Large initial S] IF you have worked in the Sun and Moon, so that you seek our Sulphur in them, consider, if you have observed your matter swollen like a paste, boiling like water, or rather like liquid pitch; Because our Sun, and our Mercury, have an emblematic type in the Work of the common Sun

Rejoice then, because for certain you will soon see the whole as black as coal, and all the parts of your compound will be reduced to atoms. For this operation is nothing else than the resolution of the fixed into the non-fixed, so that both together afterwards may produce one matter, partly spiritual, and partly corporeal. Therefore the Philosopher says: Take a Corascene Dog, and an Armenian Bitch, join them together, and they will bear you a son of the color of the sky. Because these natures will be turned by a short decoction into a broth like sea foam, or a thicker mist, which will be tinged with a livid color. And I swear to you in good faith that I have concealed nothing except the regimen; but this, if you are prudent, you will most easily gather from my words. Once the regimen is known, seize the stone demonstrated above, and govern as you know, and these notable things follow: First, as soon as the stone has felt its fire, Sulphur and Mercury will flow together over the fire like wax, and the Sulphur will be burned, and it will change colors from day to day, and Mercury will be incombustible, except that it will be tinged for a time by the colors of the Sulphur; but it will not be corrupted, and therefore it will thoroughly wash Latona from all her impurities. Repeat the heaven over the earth so many times, until the earth has conceived the celestial nature. O holy nature! who alone do what is utterly impossible for every man. Therefore when in your glass you have seen the natures mixed together like coagulated and burned blood, let it be certain that the female has suffered the embrace of the male. Therefore, from the first desiccation of your matter, seventeen days having passed, the two natures will be converted into a fattened broth, which will simultaneously revolve like a thicker mist, or sea foam, as has been said, whose color will be very dark. Then firmly hold the conceived royal offspring, because from then on you will see green, yellow, black, and blue vapors in the fire and at the sides of the vessel. These are the winds which are frequent in forming our Embryo, which must be carefully retained, lest they escape and the Work be annihilated. Also beware of the smell,

Then watch over the work, because within perhaps two weeks from that time you will see the whole earth dry, and remarkably black. CHAPTER XXI.

*Concerning the Combustion of the Flowers and its Caution.*

**I**t is no slight error, and yet one easily committed, the combustion of the flowers, before the tender natures are well extracted from their depth. This error is especially to be guarded against after the third week. For in the beginning there is such an abundance of moisture, that if you govern the work with a stronger fire than is proper, the fragile vessel will not bear the quantity of vapors, but will immediately burst: unless perhaps your vessel is too large. And then indeed the moisture will be so scattered that it will no longer return to its body, at least not enough to revive it. But when the Earth has begun to retain part of its water, then indeed, with the vapors diminishing, the fire can be intensified beyond measure without any harm to the vessel, but the work will thereby be corrupted, and will give the color of a wild poppy, and the whole compound will finally become a dry powder, uselessly reddened. You will judge by this sign that the fire was stronger than it should have been, specifically, one that was inimical to true conjunction. For you must know that our Work requires a true mutation of natures, which cannot happen,

except in the form of water: For there is no union of bodies, but at least a bruis-

among themselves will be able to unite well. Therefore, a homogeneous metallic

prolong the work, or even finally destroy it.

CHAPTER XXIV.
*Concerning the first Regimen of the Work, which is that of Mercury.*

AND truly first we will speak concerning the regimen of Mercury, which is a secret never expressed by all the Sages. They, for example, began from the second work, or the Regimen of Saturn, and revealed no light to the novice before the principal sign of blackness. On this point, that good man Count Bernard of Trevis kept silent, who in his parable teaches that when the King comes to the Fountain, having left all strangers behind, he enters the bath alone, clothed in a golden robe, which he takes off and hands to Saturn, from whom he receives a black silken robe. But he does not teach in what space of time that golden robe is taken off, and therefore he is silent about an entire regimen of perhaps forty, or sometimes even fifty days, during which time the miserable novices, without a guide, undertake uncertain experiments; From the advent of blackness to the end of the work, new appearing signs daily sufficiently refresh the artisan, but here, without a guide or sign or direction, to wander for fifty days, I confess is tedious. I say therefore that the entire interval of time from the first ignition up to the blackness is the regimen of Mercury; of Sophic Mercury, I say, because he alone operates throughout that entire time, remaining dead for a period of time suitable to his own nature, and no one before me has revealed this. Therefore, with the materials joined, which are the Sun and our Mercury, do not believe with the common run of Alchemists that the setting of the Sun happens quickly. Certainly not. We have waited much and long before patience was made between water and fire, and the envious understood this under a brief saying, when they named their matter in the first Work Rebis, that is, a thing made from two things, according to the Poet:
*The Rebis is a thing joined of two, yet one,*
*It is dissolved so that the first may be either Sol, or the seeds of Luna.*

--- Page 703 ---
690               *An Open Introduction*

Therefore know for certain that although our Mercury devours the Sun, it is not, however, in the way that the Chemical Philosophaſters think. For even if you join the Sun with our Mercury, you will recover it safe and sound and possessed of its original virtue after a year's waiting, unless you have cooked it in a suitable degree of fire; he who asserts the contrary is not a Philosopher. Those who are on the path of error think that it is such a light matter to dissolve bodies, that they suppose gold immersed in Sophic Mercury is devoured in the blink of an eye, misunderstanding that passage of Count Bernard of Trevis, concerning his golden book irretrievably immersed in a fountain. But how difficult it is to dissolve bodies, those who have toiled in Dissolution can attest. I myself, who have often been taught these things by ocular testimony, attest that it is very ingenious to regulate the fire after the material is prepared, so that it may properly dissolve bodies without burning the tinctures. Therefore attend to my Doctrine: take the body which I have demonstrated, and place it in the Water of our sea, and continuously cook it with the proper fire, so that dew and mists may ascend, and drops may fall day and night without intermission. And know that in this circulation it ascends in its pristine nature, and the lower body is left in its pristine nature, until after a long time the body begins to retain some water, and thus each participates in the degrees of the other. But because not all the water ascends by sublimation, but part of it remains below with the body at the bottom of the vessel, therefore with vigilant assiduity the body subsiding in the water is boiled and sifted, and through its midst the falling drops perforate the remaining mass, and by continuous circulation the water, made more subtle, finally gently and sweetly extracts the soul of the Sun: Thus, by means of the soul, the spirit is reconciled with the body, and a Union of both occurs in a black color, and this at most in fifty days, and this operation is called *The Regime of Mercury*, because Mercury circulates upwards, and in it the body of the Sun is boiled downwards, and the body is passive in this work, until the appearance of colors, which sparingly appear around the twentieth day in good and continuous ebullition, which colors thereafter are increased and multiplied, and varied until completion in blackness.

CHAPTER XXVI.
*Concerning the Regime of Jupiter.*

Black Saturn is succeeded by Jupiter, who is of a different color. For after
the due putrefaction and conception made at the bottom of the vessel,
God willing, you will again see changing colors and circulating sublimation.
This Regime is not long-lasting, nor does it last beyond three weeks.
At this time all imaginable colors will appear, of which no certain
explanation can be given. Showers will multiply daily during these days,
and finally after all these most beautiful sights, the Whiteness will show
itself at the sides of the vessel like streaks or hairs. Then rejoice,
because you have successfully completed the regime of Jupiter. Let the
greatest caution be observed in this regime, lest the raven's chicks, after
they have left their nest, return to it. Likewise, do not so immoderately
drain the water, lest the subsiding earth be deprived of it, and be left
dry and useless at the bottom. Thirdly, do not so intemperately water
your earth, that you completely suffocate it. Against all these errors,
a good regime of external heat will provide a remedy.

CHAPTER XXIX.
*Concerning the Regimen of Mars.*

[P] The Regimen of Venus having been completed, whose color was principally greenish and a little reddish with a dark purple color, sometimes livid, during which time the philosophical tree blossomed with its discolored branches, with leaves and branches; The regimen of Mars succeeds, which principally demonstrates a certain yellowness, diluted as it were with a yellowish brown tint, and most gloriously exhibits the transitory colors of the Iris and the Peacock. Here is a drier state of the compound, in which the matter seems to imitate various masks of forms. A hyacinthine color with a very slight orange will frequently appear in these days. Here the sealed mother rises in the womb of her infant and is purified, so that on account of such purity, in which the compound is established, putrefaction may be banished from here. But indeed, dark colors play as a base throughout this regimen, and intermediate colors become most pleasing to behold. Now know that our Virgin earth undergoes its final cultivation, so that in it the fruit of the Sun may be sown and ripened, therefore continue a good heat, and you will certainly see around the thirtieth day of this regimen, a citrine color appear, which within two weeks from its first appearance, will imbue almost everything with a citrine color.

CHAPTER XXX.
On the Regime of the Sun.

NOW you are approaching the end of your work, and you have almost completed your task; now all things appear like pure gold, and the Virgin's milk, with which you imbue this matter, becomes very yellow. Now give immortal thanks to GOD, the Giver of all good things, who has brought the work thus far; humbly pray to Him that He may henceforth so guide your counsel, lest perhaps, striving to rush the already perfect work, you utterly destroy it. Consider now that you have waited for almost seven months, and it will not be wise to annihilate the whole in a single hour. Therefore, be very cautious, and all the more so, the closer you are to perfection. But if you proceed cautiously, these notable things will occur to you: First, you will observe a certain yellow sweat in the body, and then yellow vapors, as the body settles, tinged with violet, and sometimes with dark purple. After twelve or fourteen days of waiting in this regime of the Sun, you will observe the matter for the most part moist, and although heavy, yet entirely carried away in the belly of the wind. Finally, around the twenty-sixth day of this regime, it will begin to dry out, and then it will liquefy and congeal, and will liquefy again a hundred times a day, until it begins to granulate, and will appear as if entirely discontinuous with grains, and will coalesce again, and will assume infinite forms from day to day, and this will last for about two weeks. Lastly, indeed, by GOD's command, a Light will radiate upon your matter, which you can scarcely imagine; then quickly expect the end, which you will see after three days, because the matter will granulate like atoms of the Sun, and the color will be so intensely red, that due to its eminent redness it will blacken like very pure coagulated blood, although you may not believe that anything like this can be achieved for this Elixir by art. For it is a wondrous creature, having no equal in all of universal nature, much less one exactly like it.

                                  CHAPTER XXXI.
                             *The Fermentation of the Stone.*

Remember now that you have obtained the incombustible red Sulphur,
which could by no means be further advanced by any fire by itself, and be
especially cautious about what I forgot in the preceding chapter, lest in the
regimen of the citrine Sun, before the advent of the supernatural son, clothed in a
truly Tyrian color, lest, I say, you vitrify your matter by undue ignition,
because thus it would thereafter be insoluble, and consequently would not congeal into the most
beautiful, most rubicund atoms. Be cautious, therefore,
lest you deprive yourself of so great a treasure. And yet do not believe that you have
found the end of your labors here, but rather proceed further, so that from this
Sulphur, by repeated circulation of the wheel, you may obtain the Elixir.
Therefore, take three parts of the most purified Sun, and one part of this fiery
Sulphur (you could take four parts of the Sun and a fifth part of the Sulphur, but the
aforesaid proportion is better) melt the Sun in a clean crucible, and into the molten
[Sun] cast your Sulphur, but cautiously, lest it be lost by the smoke of the coals. Make them
flow together, then pour into a receiver, and you will have a pulverizable mass
of the most beautiful, most rubicund color, yet scarcely transparent.
Take one part of this finely ground mass, two parts of your Sophic Mercury,
mix them very well and enclose in glass, and govern as before, and in two
months you will see all the aforesaid regimens pass in their order; this is
the true fermentation, which you may repeat if you wish.
