I know that many Authors take fermentation in this work for an internal
invisible Agent, which they call ferment, by whose
virtue fugitive and subtle spirits spontaneously thicken without the
imposition of hands, and they call our aforesaid way of fermentation
'feeding with bread and milk'; thus Ripley. But I, not accustomed
to citing others, nor to swearing by their words, in a matter equally known to me as to them,
                                                                                              own

*At the closed King's Palace.*                                  697

(in a matter equally known to me and to them, to observe my own freedom.) There is therefore another Operation, by which the stone is increased in weight more than in virtue; that is, take your perfect sulphur, whether white or red, and add to three parts of sulphur a fourth part of Water, and after a little blackness of six or seven days' decoction, your recently added water will thicken like your Sulphur. Then add a fourth, not with respect to the whole Compound, which has already coagulated one fourth part; but with respect to the Sulphur before the first imbibition. Which having been dried, add with respect to the three parts of Sulphur first weighed before the first imbibition, and in this proportion imbibe and congeal three times. Finally, place five parts of water in the seventh imbibition, namely with respect to the Sulphur first taken. This having been added, seal your vessel, and with a similar previous fire, make the whole compound pass through all the aforesaid regimens, which will be done at most in one month. Then you have the true stone of the third order, of which one part falls upon ten thousand, and will perfectly tinge.

CHAPTER XXXIII.
*Multiplication of the Stone.*

[Large initial A] For this no other labor is required, except that the perfect Stone be taken, and one part of it be joined with three parts, or at most four, of Mercury of the first work, and be governed by a suitable fire for seven days, in a very strictly closed vessel, and all the regimens will pass with the greatest pleasantness, and you will have the whole enriched a thousandfold in virtue, compared to the stone before its multiplication. And if you try this again, you will run through all the regimens in three days, and the medicine will be exalted a thousandfold in tinging power. And if you still wish to repeat, you will lead the work through all the regimens and colors within a natural day, and the same will happen in a single hour, if you try again, nor will you ever finally be able to find the full virtue of your Stone; so great will it be, that it surpasses the capacity of the intellect, if only you persevere in this work. Remember now to give immortal thanks to GOD, because you now possess the whole treasure of nature.

CHAPTER XXXIV.
*Concerning the method of projection.*

Take your perfect Stone, as has been said, white or red, and according to the quality of the medicine, take four parts of either luminary. Melt them in a clean Crucible, then add your stone according to the type of luminary melted, white or red, and pour the mixture into a cone; it will be a pulverizable mass. Take one part of this mixture and ten parts of well-washed Mercury. Heat the Mercury until it begins to crackle, then throw in your mixture, which will penetrate in the blink of an eye. Melt it then with increased fire, and the whole will be a medicine of the inferior order. Then take one part of this, and project it upon any metal, melted and purified, as much, namely, as your stone wishes to tinge, and you will have gold or silver so pure that nature will not give anything purer. It is better, however, to project gradually, until the Tincture ceases, for thus it will be extended more widely, because when so little is projected upon so much, unless the projection is made in Mercury, a notable loss of the medicine occurs, due to the dross that adheres to impure metals. Therefore, the better the metals are purified before projection, the better the operation succeeds in the fire.

CHAPTER XXXV.
*Concerning the manifold Use of this Art.*

Whoever has once perfectly elaborated this art according to God's blessing, I do not know what he could desire in this whole world, except that, safe from all evil fraud and deceit, he may continually serve his God. But it will be vain, indeed the vainest of all, to pant for popular applause and pomp; indeed, such things are not dear to those who are skilled in this art, but rather they scorn and despise them. Therefore, he who is blessed by God with this talent, for him such a field of pleasure lies open:
Firstly, if he were to live a thousand years, and daily feed a thousand thousands of men, he would not be in want, because he is able to multiply the Stone according to his wish, both in weight and in virtue. So that all imperfect things which are in

--- Page 712 ---
*To the closed Royal Palace.* 699

...in the world, comparable metals, he could, if he had this in his wishes, tinge all into true gold or silver.

Secondly, he will be able to make precious stones and gems with this art, such as none in the nature of things could be acquired without this art.

Thirdly and finally, he has a universal medicine for all diseases, so that at least one truly Adept may be able to cure all the sick in the entire world.

Therefore, to the eternal, immortal, and sole omnipotent King, let us give praises for these His gifts forever.

Whoever therefore enjoys this talent, I warn him to use it for the Honor of GOD and the utility of his neighbor, lest he be found ungrateful towards GOD his Creditor, who blessed him with such a great talent, and be condemned as guilty on the last day.

**[Main Text]**

**S**ince I had already spent the greater part of my life in the studies of humane
letters and liberal arts, and in conversations with all the more
learned men, who seemed to know something beyond the common crowd,
so that I seemed to myself to have acquired something of a firmer judgment partly
by assiduous reading, partly by the very experience of things, I began
to consider more acutely the various actions of men, most of which looked
either to pomp and the desire of dominating others and being preferred in
honors, or to promoting gluttony and bodily luxury, or other such
enormous vices, and that most people, by hook or by crook, were preoccupied
almost solely with accumulating riches, with all regard for conscience, zeal for piety or
virtue set aside; Whence for a long time, wavering and uncertain,
I hesitated whether I should subscribe to the *Democritean* laugh or the *Heraclitean*
lament for the same reason, or indeed, with the *Ecclesiastes*, declare,
*All is vanity of vanities*. But having weighed each thing carefully, at last returning
to myself, after the acknowledgment of God, the Best and Greatest, drawn from the
*Fountains of Israel or the Holy Scriptures*, I found nothing better, earlier, or
more ancient than the investigation of hidden things existing in nature, and most useful
to man, instituted in whatever way, whether at home through books left by others,
with prior meditation and subsequent manual experience, or abroad by
turning over that great code of the *World*; From none of these methods of seeking
knowledge did I abstain, but indulging now in one, now in another, the
more I drank, the more, like *Tantalus*, I thirsted: But among other things,
I had heard that there was a certain bird, at least unique in the whole world, called the PHOENIX,
whose bodily remains, that is, feathers or flesh, were considered the
*most excellent Medicine of all Medicines*, inasmuch as it would be a remedy for
ANGER & GRIEF, or NEPENTHES, about which it is read in the writings
of the ancients, that *Helen*, abducted by *Paris the Trojan*, offered it to
*Telemachus*, by which he forgot all past labors, cares, and sorrows.

Therefore, having departed from my native land on the very day of the Vernal Equinox, with the Moon and Sun positioned in the sign of Aries near the Dragon's Head, as astronomers call it, I first resolved to travel through EUROPE, so that I might ascertain something certain: whether the Phoenix bird itself was there, or whether its fame was to be observed somewhere else. Now, EUROPE is a stable land, as it were the base and foundation of the entire inhabited world, for the following reasons: The Earth, as can be seen on the terrestrial globe, is far surpassed by waters on its surface, although it sustains water and is itself sustained by no other element, except by itself or by the powerful hand of the Divine. Hence Europe is far smaller than the other parts of the earth, but in strength, peoples, fortitude, and spirit it far surpasses them. There are those who say that the chain of mutable elements observes this series: that one handful of earth yields ten handfuls of water, a hundred of air, and a thousand of fire. If these things are true, they easily indicate the excellence, compactness, gravity, and stability of Earth, above the other elements. In the same way, *Europe* (I say this with due respect to the other parts of the world) is the strongest of all, most vigorous in arms, and more ready to resist. Indeed, since offspring follow their mother in character, hence *Europeans* have always been warriors, dominators and subjugators of other nations, themselves unconquered by others. To demonstrate this by experience, let us look at the four greatest empires of the world, which are mentioned in the sacred prophecies of Daniel the Prophet. Asia obtained the first monarchy, being fortunate from its initial state, and also the second, but it scarcely extended any dominion into *Europe*, except perhaps a very little. But *Europe*, through that Macedonian youth, Alexander the Great, subjugated an immense space for itself, even to the Indies, in other parts. So also, with *Julius Caesar* as Roman Emperor, it was mistress of Asia and Africa for a large part.

They say that Asia is named from Asius, son of Manaeus Lydus, just as Europe [is named] from Europa, daughter of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, carried off by Jove and taken to Crete, and America indeed from Amerigo Vespucci, its discoverer, and Africa (which the Greeks called Libya) from Afer, one of the descendants of Abraham by Keturah, who is said to have led an army into Libya and settled there: Whatever the reason for the names, this has nothing to do with the matter at hand: Asia, however, is the third continent of the world, or an aerial land and of a more temperate nature than the other parts: For just as Europe is troubled by cold in some regions, so Africa is troubled by heat, but Asia is not subject to extreme cold or heat, whence it best represents to us the element of air, which is hot and humid, tempering cold with heat and dryness with humidity: For regions situated in the sea, even if they are quite hot, nevertheless their heat is mitigated by the humidity of the waters, and if they are cold, their cold is mitigated by the same. For if we consider well the nature of hot and humid air and investigate its genealogy from its causes, we will find igneous heat to be its father, and watery humidity its mother, of which parents Air, as if a son, retains the more active qualities, namely heat and humidity simultaneously. Hence it is a mediator between the aforementioned contrary elements, and, as if joined to both by kinship, it renders them friendly and unites them in every mixture of bodies. In this way, Asia, a most powerful part of the terrestrial globe, connects Africa and Europe with a certain intermediate bond, that is, the most gracious and subtle element (air), mediating between fire and earth: Otherwise, there would be no coherence between the two, nor could one perform its natural virtues in mixture without the other. Fire indeed willingly adheres to earth as tinder and a hearth, but take away the air, from which it breathes, and it will soon disappear. Therefore, it is considered Asia's prerogative to be in the middle of the terrestrial globe, to experience the temperateness of the air, and to provide us with aerial fruits, such as dates, balsam, spices of all kinds, and gold itself. The sources of the Nile are not known, but its mouths are.

The Nile is the father of Mercury.

Mercury will show the Phoenix, where it is to be sought.

The seven mouths of the Nile

A miracle not far from Memphis, Egypt, occurring annually, in the elevation of bones from the earth. An example of the Resurrection of bodies.

the people of that little region hardly found what to answer: The more learned among them said, "Egypt, *as Hermes testifies*, reflects heaven to us, and [Marginal note: Egypt is an image of heaven, as Hermes testifies.] its seven mouths of the Nile are so many planets, among which the Canopic is the highest, and is subject to the younger son of heaven. Astonished by this answer, after much time and error committed, I realized that I had to go to another place, more familiar to Mercury.

Therefore, I did not hesitate to proceed straight to the second, called Bolbitic. [Marginal note: 2. Bolbitic mouth of the Nile.] But when I had inquired of some people I met there, whether they had seen Mercury, the son of the Nile, whom I was to meet there, and they had answered that they knew nothing of the Mercury of that place, I did not wish to proceed further, lest I waste both time and expense in vain.

Therefore, having been informed about two mouths of the Nile, I ran with hasty foot to the third. [Marginal note: 3. Sebennytic mouth of the Nile.] Near this is the city of *Sebennytos*, from which it is called *Sebennytic*, inhabited by not very numerous residents, whose customs I found so barbaric and rigid that I considered them alien to all humanity; I did not wish to linger there any longer, nor inquire further about *Mercury*'s abode. "For how," I said, "*Mercury*, the author of all more humane literature and doctrine, could remain among such savage peoples? For either they would make him fierce and barbaric, and like themselves, or he would make them mild and humane by a longer stay and proximity." Therefore, leaving the town after I had departed, I asked a certain farmer of that place, "Does *Mercury* not have a hall here?" He replied, "He does indeed have a very fortified hall here, but he never inhabits it."

Therefore, I proceeded to the fourth *Mouth*, called *Pelusiac*, the most famous of all, [Marginal note: 4. Pelusiac mouth of the Nile.] because of the city of the same name adjacent to it, whose founder, as is rumored, was Peleus, the father of Achilles. This divides Asia and Arabia from Egypt, and was once most abundant in riches. Concerning it, after

which I had approached, and whose endowments and conditions I had perceived, I did not doubt: that I would find a Mercurial seat there: For, he said, just as *Troy* could not be besieged without *Peleus' son* or *Achilles*, so neither can *Mercury* be obtained without *Pelusium*: This is the noblest emporium of *Egypt*, which abounds especially in *Arabian* gold: When I approached it, I asked where *Mercury* resided: But one of the inhabitants replied that Mercury is not always present in this place, although he is a most welcome guest when he is present: Bearing with difficulty so many journeys undertaken here in vain, I did not wish to settle down before I had visited the remaining mouths, not despairing that I would finally meet the desired Mercury in person in the following ones.

[Marginal note: 5. Tenitic mouth of the Nile.]
The fifth in order was the Tenitic mouth, whose name, although it may have been more obscure, I nevertheless wished to visit it, lest I seem to have given any cause for avoiding it: but I brought back just as much from there as from the previous ones, namely absolutely nothing, except that I learned that Mercury, whom I was seeking, by no means resided there: O unhappy me, I said, must I pursue him so, who is either nowhere, or flees from me pursuing him, like that beautiful Alexis from Corydon? Would it not have been better to have proceeded from the later to the earlier, imitating a crab? Does that fleeting and winged-hatted youth, foreseeing my gaze, disdain me, and therefore takes flight before I approach? But he will not finally escape, nor can he be hidden for long, wherever he may be: Two mouths of the Nile remain for me out of all of them, which, with God's favor, I will also survey, and then I will bid farewell to all of Egypt.

[Marginal note: 6. Phannitic mouth of the Nile.]
Therefore, I set out for the sixth *mouth of the Nile*, the *Phannitic*, which I believed was due to *Mercury* by reason of the heavens, led by firm hope in my mind that now at last there would be an end to so many labors: But that confidence also failed, as so often before. For I received the answer from the inhabitants of that place that Mercury had indeed resided here, but had long since changed his abode and migrated elsewhere: often an inquiry about him was made here by many, but he was never found at home.

[Marginal note: 7. Mendesium mouth of the Nile.]
From here I undertook the last journey to the *Mendesium* mouth, and when I arrived there, I inquired about *Mercury*, who was not found here either: Indeed, very many replied that they did not know *Mercury*.

**On the Secrets of Alchemy.** 737

And so, having explored the seven *mouths of the Nile* in order, since I had not found him whom I sought, I judged myself to have been deceived by the *Sibyl*, who had at least thrown me into these labyrinths, so that she might lead astray a mind nourished by false hope, perhaps from envy or a preconceived hatred towards strangers. But when I reviewed each thing that had happened on the journey, I conjectured that I had perhaps been most badly misled by the deceptive responses of the inhabitants of whatever places, for the reason that by a certain innate ferocity they disdained and hated all foreigners: And therefore, I carefully considered what had been answered by them concerning the first, second, and third, and other mouths, from which very many things occurred that rather increased the doubt conceived before, than removed it: Whereupon, retracing my steps backwards [Marginal note: *Mercury found where.*] from the last towards the first, I returned, and finally, before I reached the first, I found *Mercury* in one of the mouths, where the inhabitants had previously seemed to deny his presence: [Marginal note: *Many things learned from Mercury.*] Approaching him, after many conversations held together, I learned from him things I had been ignorant of; He especially showed me the *Phoenix* [Marginal note: *Where the Phoenix lies hidden.*], where it ought to be met, and most clearly told me that it lay hidden in a place I had not even thought of before, but when I arrived there, to my misfortune [Marginal note: *Phoenix finally not found.*], it had gone out, (perhaps then appointed *Arbiter* between the *Owl* and other birds pursuing it, concerning which battle we have spoken elsewhere) but was to return after a few days, or a few weeks: But since it would not be advisable for me to wait so long in foreign lands, especially because the return of the *Phoenix* would be very uncertain, I decided to prepare my journey home as soon as possible; deeming it sufficient for the time being to have known *Mercury* [Marginal note: *The Phoenix, father of the sought-after Medicine.*], where he resided, and also the *Phoenix*, the father and efficient cause of the sought-after *Medicine*, to whom I thoroughly resolved to return at the first opportune occasion. So, having boarded a ship from the *Pelusiac* mouth, I again set course for *Europe*, having sailed across so many islands and kingdoms all around, until I set foot on *German* soil, from where I had first departed: [Marginal note: *Return to Germany.*] But lest I seem ungrateful towards anyone from whom I received any benefit bestowed upon me on this journey, I will first render due honors and praises to the *Sibyl*, then to *Mercury*, and finally to the *Phoenix* and the *Medicine* itself, with epigrams dedicated to each.

EPIGRAM
IN HONOR OF THE ERYTHRÆAN SIBYL,
Called Herophyle.

[Marginal note: Herophyle, called the Erythræan Sibyl, celebrated in song.]
To you, great Priestess, moved by God (not by a demon),
From within, the just grace of the Charites returns:
They do not turn their backs to you, but their grateful faces,
And promise their generous gifts with their hand:
Because you sent me, born by the Nile, on a straight
Path, which might show me the Phoenix bird,
You, a prophetess full of sacred inspiration, gave oracles,
(About) God, who would come with a human mouth, while you sing:
Who, bringing the just judgments of the highest
Omnipotent Arbiter of the whole world, will be.
He was dear to your heart, although you are an Ethnic Virgin,
And are said to have known nothing of God.
Your Erythræan caves are not capacious enough for Christ,
As your hope, and you yourself will be placed in heaven.

PRAISE OF PHOENICIAN, OR
HERMETIC, MEDICINE.

[Marginal note:] *Praise of Phoenician Medicine.*

*IF mountains are heaped up with various riches and gold,*
   *What good are they to a man who will soon be dead?*
*Unless someone more divine provides him aid,*
   *By which welcome health may return through a propitious Deity.*
*Therefore, nothing in the whole world can be more precious*
   *Than Medicine, which by its art alleviates the evil of men.*
*Let riches and wealth yield, let gold also yield to this,*
   *To whom the mind is not the same, is not a man, but a beast.*

C H A P T E R I.

*On the Law of the Art, its Cultivators, and the True Method*
*of Seeking the Secret.*

[Large decorative initial Q] uandoquidem all men of every kind and fortune propose to themselves some goal for the hours they spend in investigating things, so that indeed they may attain proficiency in the art in which they are engaged, and they strain all their efforts to aim for its summit.

Yet this fortune blesses very few, for although many aspire to Architecture, very few are found to be Archimedes. Very many, however much they devote themselves to Medicine, are not many Paracelsi, few are endowed with the genius of Helmont; indeed, if they can even attain mediocrity in their art, they will not think they have wasted their oil or labor. Hence it happens that no one thinks he has studied in vain, although not every Geometer is equal to Archimedes, or every Poet to Homer, or every Rhetor to Cicero. For indeed, even rhetors of a lower sort can be useful to the Republic [for the Talent granted to them]. They can, I say, any men, even if less skilled in the art in which they have been engaged, be considered useful in that Republic [where they live].

However many devote themselves to the Metamorphosis of Metals, they seem to aspire to a most useful thing, not uselessly at least, and even foolishly. The peak, for example, of this art is the Artifice itself; he who has attained it, has acquired the summit, but he who has not arrived here, will report nothing profitable. For nothing but loss, both of money and of time, comes from a half-learned science of Alchemy. Moreover, and to ridicule

--- Page 757 ---
744                                    CHAP. I.
...and to the ridicule of the Myso-chemists, he will expose himself to shame and disgrace. Yet the object of the Art is so noble that it promises infinite riches to the possessor, and moreover, most perfect health. Hence it happens that there is scarcely any unlearned person who, after having heard even the slightest bit about the art, does not immediately apply himself to its investigation and straightway assumes the name of Chemist. Soon, as soon as he has conceived some hope from the reading of some recipes, he immediately claims the Title of Philosopher. But lest he seem to cultivate a foolish Philosophy, each one, according to the felicity of his own genius, devises subtleties, and according to the abundance of his money, constructs furnaces, procures glass vessels for himself, and undertakes the work with wondrous solemnity. Thus he boils (digests) until at last late parsimony is at the bottom, and very little, if any, equipment remains. But lest he be accused of insane rashness in the meantime, he knows how to discourse about the Metallic First Matter, the rotation of the Elements, the marriage of Gabritius with Bega, and that in an idiom generally unknown; he will cite Philosophers and explain them at will, and he will console himself not a little with the hope of future fortune. Meanwhile, however, he endures labors, even to the point of consumption, in this Philosophy, both of strength and of money, until that Metamorphosis which he sought in Metals, he has miserably experienced in himself.

When the cunning Myso-chemists observed this, and saw that the same outcome awaited many, they immediately laugh at the art as fabulous and hold it in derision. But those who deceived themselves by their own rashness strive to entice others into the same path of loss, and with their own fabrications and fictitious recipes, they defile paper, so that they may appear to have gained at least some skill along with the loss of money. The world is seen to be so filled with these Sophistications that scarcely any novice student of the Art is not led astray by them, and no despiser of science who cannot seize ample occasion from them for scoffing. Thus both the Art itself and its sincere Cultivators suffer indignantly on account of the wickedness of certain scoundrels, who, although they are stupider than wood in the Art, nevertheless write as if they were truly adepts, and freely promulgate their impostures, to such an extent that the first un-

--- Page 758 ---
*De Metall. Metamorph.* 745

an inextricable Labyrinth it is for the chemical Novice to discern true and false among books; from which deceptive Sophists construct an edifice no less specious than true Artists, indeed for the most part they promise greater things. Concerning these, Bernard of Treviso [a man not inexperienced in this kind of imposture] thus writes: *“Unless [he says] you avoid these as a plague, you will never taste anything good in this art.”* Therefore, I have described this treatise, so that I might more fully instruct the blind in this science, lest wandering through byways, they miserably stray. And first indeed I have decided to vindicate the Art from slanders. Then it seemed good to subjoin the qualifications of those who apply themselves to this; but finally I will describe the method of inquiry. These things having been premised by way of a prologue, I will afterwards gird myself to elucidate the art itself.

For it is not the case that, because very many deceptive Sophists are found treating Alchemy, it should therefore be accused of either falsity or ineptitude. Indeed, the possibility of things must be weighed, by which, if the truth of the art can be disproven, it should fall; but if not, to disparage it is to be judged not only foolish, but also unworthy of a Philosopher. For example, the wickedness of men who rashly treat the art does nothing to destroy it. For example, the Light of nature is clearer than that it should be obscured by those who dwell in darkness. Therefore, I will instruct the Son of Doctrine, lest they be led astray by errors; and to them it will appear more evident than the Sun, that the transmutation of Metals is real, possible, and true, from a state of imperfection to a perfect one, and that through the cooperation of Nature and Art. Indeed, no material or essential difference is observed between perfect and imperfect Metals, but only an accidental one, which consists in a disproportion of maturity. This [alone], greater or lesser, diversifies Metals by their species, except that certain superfluous supervening impurities appear distinct among metals, which dregs indeed have no correspondence with the Matter, but, entirely substituted into it by way of infiltration, having not been purged due to a defect of digestion, remained mixed with the undigested pure [substance]. Hence the distinction of metallic forms. But if ever, through the complete perfection of digestion, these superfluous things have been rejected, then no longer

Which in Art would be impossible, unless Nature supplied the possibility of this through the correspondence of Matter.

Furthermore, other arguments are not lacking to prove this same thing. And first indeed, this is no small thing, that all Metals can be reduced into flowing Mercury, as also Minerals, which consist of Metallic principles. Moreover, these Metallic Mercuries can thus be transmuted, that Saturnine becomes Martial [its own powers meanwhile neglected] by the decoction of only the Martial essence in the same through sagacious Artifice: furthermore, the same Martial [Mercury] will become Venereous by the ferment of Venus; the same also Lunar, Jovial, or even Solar, by the ferment of these, no alteration meanwhile being made either in flux or in color, except that one Mercury becomes purer and more refined than another. As for the former, we shall posit and profess it to be nothing other than Gold digested to the highest degree [to which it can be brought by Nature and Art], which then will be seen not simply as Gold, but a thousand times more perfect than any common Gold. Therefore, the tincture does not lack the power to transmute; but the corporeality of the tinging agent obstructs the transmutation. But if this corporeal, earthy thing were to become Spiritual and fiery, its nature being changed, then indeed it would enter radically, and what it had done externally to the sight, it would perform the same alteratively internally, and even much more, inasmuch as fire is of a much subtler property and essence than earth. If, therefore, there is a seed of gold in gold, it follows that this [seed] resides in water [which is the dwelling place of spirit], for seed is a certain spiritual medium for the conservation of the species. Hence the possibility of gold's dissolution, although to discover an agent capable of performing this requires the work of a highly sagacious Philosopher, blessed by God with no mediocre talent. Furthermore, if gold is dissolved to extract its seed, does not Reason persuade that this must be done only into water of its own homogeneous kind? Once this dissolution is done, its body has shed its form, namely the terrestrial form of gold, and has put on another aqueous golden form. Moreover, every motion is from something to something, and the perfect end of every generative motion is in the same species, whence motion is progress, which will occur through various homogeneous changes of the moved thing. Therefore, since "goldness" is the starting point, the same will be the end point, and the intermediate progressions will occur in metallic homogeneity, by the necessity of the Law of Nature; which being observed, the effect is driven to its end by the necessity of the end, provided that the operations have not been interrupted by contrary actions. Therefore, we place the return of the dissolved gold, of the same dissolved gold, to "goldness" beyond controversy, and conclude it proven. Briefly, however, I will touch upon the rest in order.

All common philosophers have handed down that four Elements are given, originally composing all things, from which all things are resolved, and from whose diverse combination diverse things proceed. To this unfortunate opinion, almost all Chemical Philosophers have subscribed. I cannot conjecture another cause for this than that, without mature deliberation, [intent on their own matter] and hastening, they described these first foundations of things. Which opinion of theirs, not daring to disapprove, I will otherwise treat philosophically according to the truth of the matter, for the sake of their honor and respect. FROM the aforesaid source, as has been said, Sol (Gold) was born, and his sister Luna (Silver): when indeed through digestion this matter was brought to perfection. Perfection moreover is twofold, either inchoate, or complete, that is, in part & in whole. Complete perfection is the highest goal, towards which Nature spontaneously aims, namely, that with all crudity boiled away and all dregs purged, the pure Metallic nature, coagulated without any impurity, may triumph. Here our Sol has its origin, and with its radiance and splendor illuminates the earth. Inchoate perfection, however [so to speak], is not perfection properly so called, and yet in respect to that which is formally imperfect, it deservedly may be called perfection not improperly. For formal imperfection is to be judged when the crudity which adhered to the pure [substance] in generation [by accident] is not so boiled away, much less is the heterogeneous superfluity purged, but rather is left mixed with the pure [substance] in coagulation in such a quantity that it predominates over it and finally overcomes it: thus it happens to all metals [except Sol & Luna] which are easily corrupted by all corrupting Elements, and likewise consumed by fire. But when crudity is thus overcome, and the dreggy superfluity is so purged before coagulation, that the pure [substance] thus has predominance over the impure, so that it is freed from the corruptive tyranny of the latter, this is to be considered the first degree of perfection. Total purgation of dregs, and rejection of impurity, is the colophon or highest perfection of metallic operations. And yet these crudities and dregs, originally, were not of the same imposition or nature as the metallic Mercury (☿), indeed they were separable, whose separation before coagulation is the perfection of the Metal. But if they were not purged before their congelation, this [congelation] nevertheless by no means united them to the pure [substance], indeed they are still separable, although not by nature without the aid of another, but by Art administering to nature. Hence the basis and Origin of the Transmutatory Art, and this is the true foundation of Alchemy. Our secret Elixir effects all this; moreover, it also has the property that it actually communicates both color and fixity to the imperfect, inasmuch as it itself becomes supremely exuberant in both color and fixity.

C A P U T IV.

*Concerning the Seed of Gold: Also, whether other Metals*
*have Seed, a determined question.*

For the conservation, propagation, and also the production of each species, seed was established by the Great Creator for all things. And seed is the perfection of each thing, and that which has no seed must by right be judged imperfect. Therefore, it is not to be doubted that metallic seed exists. For these things (metals) either all were created in the first six days, which now are and have been in the world, or at least they grew and solidified daily. Both reason and experience deny the former; therefore, if the latter, then certainly no one will be able to deny that metallic seed exists. But if it exists, the Metal certainly does not lose it in coagulation. Coagulation, indeed, is the effect of perfection [or rather, of maturation, which leads directly to perfection, if the external conditions have been legitimately disposed.] Moreover, the sign of perfection is its seed, which is thus matured; therefore, it is not probable that the seed is lost through coagulation, but rather that it is rendered nobler. It is clear that metallic seed is present in Metals through this seed. Therefore, it can be asked whether all metals have seed within themselves, and I would answer by stating: All have one and the same seed, but

**CHAPTER V.**

*On the virtue of the Golden Seed, and in what it is most immediately*
*contained.*

**B**ut so that we may be able to achieve this secret, by which we might bring imperfect things to perfection by projection upon them, first, it must be noted that which we said about this secret of ours, namely, that it is Gold exalted to the highest degree of perfection, to which it could be brought by nature and art. It must also be observed that in Gold, Nature has reached the limit of its operations, nor will it further advance it of its own accord. And yet its seed must be further matured with sagacious skill. This, however, lies hidden more deeply, nor does it easily appear to sight, as the seed of plants and animals can otherwise be presented to the eyes. Nevertheless, it can be extracted by sagacious artifice, and be exalted to such an extent above its own virtue [in which nature rested], that it may surpass it a thousandfold. I could relate many things about this seed, which are rather to be kept silent: but especially to be noted is the difference between this metallic and vegetable or animal seed. For this (vegetable or animal seed), on account of the dissimilarity of the parts bearing the seed, is distinguished when cut from the whole body. But that metallic (seed) is not so, but since the smallest particle of

The place in which the seed resides is proximately water, for properly and exactly speaking, the smallest part of metal is the seed, and that (part) is invisible: but because this invisible (part) is universally diffused throughout all water of its kind, and inhabits it, and exerts its powers within it, and nothing else is manifested to the eyes than water, although reason suggests that an internal agent [which is properly the seed] is present: therefore we promiscuously call all water seed, just as we call the whole grain seed, although the germinating life is nothing but a certain smallest particle of the grain. But it is enclosed within the body of Gold, under very dense coverings, which are manifestly quite contrary to that hidden thing we seek. Therefore, this water must be drawn out by a subtle artifice, but it does not enter spontaneously; Therefore, this must be accomplished by something else, which indeed must be of the same nature as that which we seek to draw out. For everything similar generates its like, that is, every agent exercising a generative action upon something transforms that upon which it acts into its own nature [as closely as possible]. Next, this water must be akin to the body to be dissolved, and therefore pure, clean, and most exquisitely cleansed and purified from all impurity.

That is crude, this subtle; that dead, this living and life-giving; and all other conditions, in a word, are required in this [water] which we seek in that [Gold] after dissolution, but are absent in the coagulated dead body. Therefore, it is concluded that Mercury (☿) alone is the true key of the Alchemical art, which is truly that dry water so often described by the Philosophers, flowing, volatile, and yet not wetting the hand that touches it, nor anything else that is not of the unity of its own matter; nor is this all, but it is moreover endowed with the virtues described above.           C H A P T E R VIII.
Concerning the Genealogy, Origin, Nativity, and Diagnostic Signs Preceding and Accompanying the Philosophical Mercury.

Certain boastful and arrogant Sophists, after they have learned from the reading of books that common Mercury is most alien to this art, and likewise reading that Philosophers call this by various names, immediately led by blind opinion, confidently entrust themselves to the art, and are not ashamed to affirm themselves masters of this science: while meanwhile they are more stupid than wood itself. When it has shed its own form, it may put on its true Philosophical form.
To recount such labors would be tedious; therefore, since the truth is the index of itself and of falsehood, and the straight is also the index of itself and of the crooked, I pass on to the matter itself.
I have taught above that all Metals are of the same Material principle, namely Mercury (☿). It follows therefore, that Mercury (☿) is truly a metallic thing, and therefore [although common] it nevertheless originally obtains a homogeneous Matter with all metals. If therefore Philosophical Mercury is to be a homogeneous metallic Water, it follows that materially and fundamentally it is not distinguished from other Mercury, except insofar as one is purer than the other, and hotter, and yet both are dry mineral water. Let the sons of Doctrine therefore know that the matter of common Mercury ought and can enter into the matter of Philosophical Mercury, although not the entire substance which is seen in the latter. For ingenious Chemists should know for certain that no other Mercury exists, from which all Metals [are formed], than the common one [with respect, of course, to its origin], which, generated within the veins of the earth, as long as it remained safe from crude air in a place apt and accommodated for generation, was entirely destined to procreate metal, and retained its own motion and excitation within itself, so that it might be excited to perfect generation. But if by some chance the aptitude of the place is violated or corrupted, this matter immediately, as if struck by the Hammer of Death, completely loses all motion, nor can it be further promoted, just as an egg [upon which a Hen has sat for some time] when cooled, is thereafter rendered unfit for producing a fetus, for example, life or the internal altering heat having vanished due to the external failing, and thus what previously tended daily towards perfection, now impeded by chance, becomes an abortion, with no hope left of future spontaneous motion. This is the reason that when some have attempted to digest Mercury (☿) above ground with artificially devised heat, they have brought back a ridiculous reward for their work. Therefore, the form is removed, or rather impeded in its approach, which [as said above] is a particle of ineffable light, which is readily present, illuminating its dwelling, provided that all things from outside have been aptly disposed, and thus leaves its impression in things, which, received by things, produces a ferment, which is the true author of all transmutation.

# A SHORT HANDBOOK

# THE CELESTIAL RUBY.
### *Concerning the Philosopher's Stone, and its Secret.*

The Philosopher's Stone is a certain Celestial, Spiritual, penetrative, fixed substance, perfecting all Metals into true Gold & Silver [according to the quality of the Medicine], exposed to every test, and that by imitating Nature and its operations, as closely as possible.
The Art of Chemistry is concerned with this substance, which treats and teaches the method and way of perfecting it: but it is not done by diverse things, but by one single thing only, to which nothing is to be added, nothing diminished, but only the superfluous things are to be removed.
But as far as the right of this art is concerned, experience in this matter would be best for convincing men: if, when it is proven that true Gold is made by this art, then indeed there will be no doubt at all about the right as well as the utility of the Art. But that imperfect Metals are transmutable in this way, is clear, because all were destined to one perfection, but some remained imperfect due to a defect of digestion. Therefore, if they could be properly cooked, they too would be perfected, since there is nothing in the matter that prevents this from happening, for indeed all Metals originated from one source, namely, the crude, cold, and humid Mercury (☿), in which there was no difference between Sol & Saturn.

--- Page 789 ---
776                                 *Brevis Manuductio*

difference; however, what Nature afterwards worked in this matter, namely by decocting it more or less, this alone created the diversity. Therefore, all other Metals can be perfected into Gold by the work, namely, of our divine and most perfect Magistery, which, when projected upon imperfect Metals, is able to perfect them by decocting them to such an extent, as it itself possesses more than the due perfection [which is required in Gold]. Here therefore one may observe of what great virtue, and of what spiritual Nature is this our Divine Stone, which by mere projection can perfect that above ground in one hour, which Nature would by no means have perfected by subterranean operations. How much therefore Nature can achieve when aided by Art, from this it will be clear to perceive.

For indeed our Stone, as it was perfected by Nature without the aid of art, was only of unary virtue: but the virtue which is acquired through art, with Nature cooperating and assisting, in each regimen is tenfold, that is, in a certain way infinite; for indeed it cannot be computed: for first, by dissolving it, and again coagulating and decocting it, one part of the Medicine falls upon 1000 parts of imperfect Metal, penetrating and perfectly tinging: but if by repeated dissolution and coagulation, you attempt to further advance this medicine, now behold, it extends to infinity: for your ingenuity will sooner fail in computing than the Elixir's virtue in penetrating and tinging: not that such a tiny amount of thus multiplied Elixir immediately tinges the whole by its corporal touch, but by its virtue and influx it permeates the whole: for indeed the smallest particle of the imperfect body is touched and tinged immediately by the medicine. However, the matter stands thus: each tinged part acts upon the contiguous part like leaven; thus the Elixir tinges that which it next touches with a tincture a little weaker than that with which it itself was endowed and imbued; this in turn ferments what is next to it by communicating the tincture, and this continues so long, until at last the entire mass is brought to the perfection of true Gold. But this happens in a short space of time, on account of the spirituality of our agent; which, since it is a true Metallic fire, no differently than that Elemental fire, imperceptibly penetrates and heats even the hardest bodies, even those par-

Thus it has often been observed that dough is leavened by ferment, even that outer part which the physical part of the ferment never reaches by touching; it is done no differently in this work. Observe therefore how natural our process is in this work: for we do not profess to create Gold or Silver [as some false accusers object], but only from those things in which these exist by Nature, we say by our art, namely from metals which are of the same matter as Gold and Silver, but of unequal digestion, and on account of this remain imperfect; these we digest by the projection of our arcanum upon them and in this way perfect them, since for perfecting them nothing else is required except this simple decoction of their crudity, which our medicine can abundantly provide.

Hearken therefore, sons of doctrine! Attend to me, because I will most certainly make known to you the whole arcanum of that Stone, which is not a Stone, and is in every man, and at any time you will find it in its place. If you have this, you possess the most precious thing in the whole world. Indeed, it is divine, and therefore not to be communicated to all. But to you, sons of Doctrine, I will manifest the whole matter, nor will I conceal anything necessary for this Magistery. But you, be present with attentive minds, and perceive my words, and store them deep in your heart.

You have heard before of the possibility of Transmutation, namely that a thing destined for perfection, but left imperfect due to a defect of decoction, can, by the application of an agent of the same essence and Nature as the perfect thing for which this imperfect thing was destined, but of greater perfection, be perfected and matured to the extent that the agent is more than perfect in exuberant maturity and virtue. Such, moreover, is our Stone in relation to any other imperfect metals; whence we place it beyond controversy that these can be transmuted into Gold and Silver by means of it.

Observe therefore, lovers of Wisdom, what and of what kind should

...ought to be that which can accomplish this: that which is called the Stone by Philosophers. But it is in every human being, and in every thing, and to be found in its own place at any time of the year.
	Note the words, mark the mysteries: because it will most certainly consist of the Elements; than which nothing is more universal: and these not bare, but compounded and analyzed, that is, each Element presenting itself to be recognized by its own quality; therefore in every thing, that is, Element, is our Stone: for if any of them is destroyed, the goldenness perishes. But what that is, it will be yours to pay attention to, and not to introduce anything heterogeneous into this work; but to leave that to others, who seek our Stone in such things, but they will always labor in vain, as long as they are ignorant of what that unique true principle of ours is.
	But I make that known to you; Remember, therefore, that from a Lion, a Lion, from a human, a human is generated, but to expect these to be generated from others would be absurd and a mockery; likewise from combustibles, combustibles, from eternals, eternals are produced. Do you believe that you can gather grapes from thistles, or roses from thorns? It will be just as absurd if anyone tries to fabricate our Stone from Animals, Herbs, or suchlike, as if the principle of making gold should be sought elsewhere than in Gold: therefore, our Stone is not to be sought from such things, which ought to reflect the natural properties of true Gold, which are not in things of that kind.

of that kind, nor to be sought from them, unless we wish to create seeds, which is the prerogative of no man, but of God alone, and if anyone were to promise to do this, he would be false and a liar. Therefore, no credence whatsoever should be given to him who professes that he will produce the seeds of Metals from Herbs and such things. For although he may wonderfully impress the more ignorant with the title of a skilled Philosopher and artisan, yet while he does not know how to use what is created, it is much less probable that he can create seeds himself.

Therefore, whoever is to be a son of the art, let him learn and acknowledge that our Stone, the transformer of Metals into a perfect form, is most intimately enclosed and contained within the most perfect Metals: and therefore let him be admonished to learn its production from these, and not from others.

Now therefore, unless I am mistaken, you have heard clearly enough from where the material of this so secret stone is to be sought. And if you have paid good attention, it will not happen that you err in this matter. Now let us say something about its name, for how it is in every place and man has been explained. Now I will teach how and why it is called a stone, and not a stone; finally, I will outline how it is to be found. For the Philosopher says that it is a stone, and not a stone: which some, and almost always the common people, understand wrongly; for they interpret it literally as being something, the true nature of which they ignore, yet resembling the form of a stone, tinging anything, even by mere touch, into proven Gold; whether it be wooden or stony, which they consider to be most false [and rightly so]: and therefore judge it impossible for any art [except the Diabolical]: wherefore, upon hearing even the name of a Chemist, he immediately recoils and abhors, nor does he consider him otherwise than impious and a foolish squanderer of his goods, incited to this by this false and confused understanding of our most secret stone: therefore, the more ignorant men superstitiously believe that such men should be punished by Civil Law: but under the name of ignorant men, not Fff ff 2 those

### CONCERNING CALCINATION.

And Calcination is the first purification of the Stone, the drying out of humidity, by the force of natural heat, excited by the external heat of water, whereby the compound is turned into a calx or powder of black color, yet unctuous and retaining its radical humidity. Therefore, when we speak of our operations, do not believe that we perfect them in one or two days, nor that we see colors or signs in the first hour; not so, but we waited much and long, until patience was established between contrary qualities, wherefore that Trevisan, a man learned and good in this art, teaches in his practice that he remained in prison, that is, in doubt and suspension of mind, for forty days, but afterwards returned and saw clouds and mists. Moreover, if you cast even a grain into good earth, you would not inspect the earth every hour by moving it aside, to see whether and how much it has begun to grow; if you were to do this, you would not expect even pleasant vegetation, much less fruit from it. So foolish and senseless are those who, as soon as they have joined the dissolvent with the dissolved, immediately seek some signs of the operations, nor can they satisfy themselves without either moving or opening, or adding something, or taking something away: or at least increasing the fire to accelerate the work, and thus in this way they hinder the work of nature, and consequently do not attain the desired ends. Wherefore, attend to my teaching: as soon as you have prepared the matter, that is, mature, yellow Sulphur, with its crude, whitish Sulphur, and have duly espoused them, enclose it in the vessel and allow it to stand without disturbance; if you proceed correctly, within twenty-four hours at the latest, you will see your compound swelling, and perhaps emitting some bubbles, by reason of the heat of your pontic water striving to excite heat in the enclosed matter; but you will perceive a variation of colors slowly [as it will at least seem to you] at the first threshold, because then the gatekeeper necessarily undergoes many labors, because whatever is done, he alone then does it, because the bath is not yet prepared, that is, the heat of the Natural King is not yet excited. But when the bath is heated, our steward will suffer only a few labors, and the operations will be very easily distinguishable. Wherefore, let the sons of this art know for certain that the first color which appears—

nor is there a moment in which it neither ascends nor descends, for nothing
rests except in its end, but blackness is not the end of our Stone, therefore
it does not rest in it either.

Therefore, you who seek this, consider the example given to you, and you will have the answer.
Obj: But after the first excitation of the matter, the tincture exits every hour and moment, and the color of the exiting tincture is the blackest blackness; therefore, after the first excitation of the matter, the blackest blackness will appear within an hour.
But it is answered that the blackest blackness is of the tincture *after* it has exited, not *while* it is exiting; or if so, nevertheless, a truly imperceptible blackness exits imperceptibly, and although the blackest (tincture) having exited into much white, will not manifest the blackest blackness in the whole compound, but a whitish color, if only the subject of whiteness is not subtle and well-purified, just as this white now is. But also the tincture in its first exit is not completely black, but obtains this through putrefaction, which is not a mere exit of the tincture, but has arisen from that repugnance and resistance which exists between the exited tincture and the extracting water, that is, between Sulphur and Mercury. Concerning this, hear Morienus saying: *“Our operation is nothing other than the extraction of water from its earth, nor that alone, but also the remission of water upon the earth, until the earth putrefies.”* The tincture, therefore, is not entirely black by itself, but very white; but it exits with a sign of blackness, because the more the tincture, which is the soul, exits, the more the earth, which is the body, is deprived of its soul, and thus putrefies and blackens.
For how long, therefore, must one wait before it perfectly blackens? In this matter, pay attention to what Flamellus says: *“The color which you must first see is blackness, and not just any, but the darkest, and that within a space of forty days;”* Ripley says the same: *“Allow the mixed and equalized natures to lie together for six weeks, for conception, which time you await with a slow fire;”* The colors, when they die, will show it, for at that time they will boil like liquid pitch, and putrefy. And Bernard says in his parable: *“The King, taking off his splendid garments, hands over the silken ones to Saturn, clothed in black, which he retains for forty days,”* but understand all this concerning blackness at its peak: which is clear from the above repeated words of Flamellus, but a more remiss blackness

      But do intermediate colors appear in the progression from white to black, just as in the progression from black to white? For it seems that they do, because there is no transition from one extreme to another except through intermediates: And we respond that they do appear, though indeed confusedly, and some will appear in some work in the progression to the highest blackness, which perhaps will not appear in another, inasmuch as they are nothing but accidental colors: but not entirely the same between the first whiteness and blackness, as those between this [blackness] and the ultimate whiteness; because the nature of the matter is not the same; in the former it was coarse and more earthy, to be burned and purified; in this work, however, the matter is more spiritual and purer, therefore, in a pure or purified subject, in the progression from the extreme of blackness to the extreme of whiteness, the intermediate colors will be much brighter and more admirable than those which appeared in the earthy subject. But in both progressions they will appear; in the former transition between the extremes, darker, and fewer, and uglier; in the latter, more numerous, brighter, and more splendid, as the Philosopher testifies, after the highest blackness, before whiteness, at the hour of the greatest conjunction, marvelous things will appear: for as many colors as can be conceived in the whole world, then they will be visible: and Ripley says, in our work, colors will appear than which none more beautiful have ever appeared, likewise, before perfect blackness, intermediate colors will show themselves, as the Philosopher testifies, who, describing the colors of the Dragons, says they are black, yellow, and azure, and these intermediate colors, he says, denote that your preparations are not yet perfectly putrefied, in a word, during the dying process, various darker colors will be seen, but rare and few, and this before the black night completely obscures the Horizon.

	But in what order will these aforesaid colors appear? This certainly

	And the Dissolution of our Stone is a reduction to its primal matter,
a manifestation of the moist, and an extraction of the Natures from
their depth, which is accomplished by leading it into a mineral water.
	This operation is not of light work or moment, for how difficult it is,
those who have toiled at it can attest.

Why do we not therefore command mature and fixed Sulphur to be mixed with crude and volatile Mercury, so that we may assert that Sulphur in one is different from that in the other, and Mercury is different? by its nature it is cold and humid; nevertheless, if it (water) is mixed with any vegetable in decoction, it takes on and assumes other qualities of the thing, namely, of that which is mixed: whose power and spirit or life, which resides in the water, comes out into the water through decoction, and the water reciprocally receives its nature; however, the thick and corporeal earthy part of the decocted substance is not that spirit which changes the watery qualities, but is separable from the liquid after decoction. Therefore, metallic and mineral species are to be decocted subordinately and alternately in it, and it is their water, into which the mineral spirits are emitted through decoction; and they alter it, no differently than vegetables decocted in their simple water. However, a twofold difference is to be noted between the aforesaid decoctions: first, that water with vegetables is not fixed in coagulation, as Mercury is with metals, wherefore these compositions are stronger than those. Second, that in the decoction of vegetables or animals, water, being a diaphanous liquid, not only receives new power and qualities, but also a different color from that which it had. But it is not so with Mercury. For its nature is altered, but not its color nor its flowing form: but the color of the dissolved metal lies hidden beneath the form of liquid quicksilver, and does not appear by its own power. Therefore, first Mercury acts by dissolving into the Metal, then the Metal acts by coagulating into Mercury; and just as in dissolution the form and color of the Metal lay hidden beneath the form and color of Mercury, so also in coagulation the form and color of Mercury are hidden beneath the color and form of the Metal. Thus, neither do the qualities of the Metal in dissolution prevent the flow of Mercury, nor do the qualities of Mercury in coagulation impede the fixity of the metal. Do you not observe here a certain wonderful concordance between Mercury and Metals? For they love each other as mother and son, sister

would not be perfected except in a long time, and with very many expenses,
which it would be foolish to incur in forming simple Gold. There is therefore
a unique Sulphur in the world, which nature has perfected, which is most
familiar to Mercury. This therefore is radically mixed with that, and by this
Mercury is decocted, and Mercury, because of the repugnance of qualities,
putrefies it, and thus through

...it rises again through regeneration, not Gold, such as is found in mines, but spiritual, penetrative, and tinging, to such an extent that it easily enters any imperfect metals when it is projected upon them, which it digests in a very short time to the authentic proportion of Gold, and having rejected the dregs, restores to perfect health. You see therefore that Mercury is in no way to be disproportioned from its nature which it has, but to be matured, and that not by itself without any addition, and yet without any extraneous addition, but through a radical union of the pure body with it through the smallest particles, which occurs by our secret conjunction.

See however that you are not deceived, for this conjunction is not made by manual operation, but only naturally, man not only not helping, but also not well understanding its cause, wherefore this work is called Divine. Fools know how to mix the body of Gold with Mercury, and then they call it animated Gold, but they find nothing in it. For even if these two were to remain together for a thousand years, afterwards nevertheless one would separate from the other in its own nature. Wherefore it was not an alterative conjunction, but only a confusion of two things with each other. But in our operation, the spirit of the Sun infuses itself into the spirit of Mercury, so that afterwards one never separates from the other, just as water mixed with water does not. In this operation therefore lies the greatest, indeed the whole secret of the art. Attend therefore, son of Doctrine, and carefully see that you do not err here. The body of the Sun therefore will never be joined with Mercury intimately, unless by means of the Moon, or an imperfect body and fire. And this Moon is the juice of the water of life, which lies hidden in Mercury, which is sharpened with fire, and is a spirit entering the body, and altering it and compelling it to retain its soul. Now therefore you see what kind of Mercury we have spoken of thus far, not common but pluvial, which, properly speaking, is not Mercury, but Mercurial water: For the Mercury of the common people is water, but it lacks spirit and igneous power for burning: supply if you can what is lacking with the greatest artifice, then it will no longer be the Mercury of the common people, but similar to ours. But if you cannot do this, abandon that Mercury, because nothing from it except

But let us return to the conjunction, which, believe me, is the whole secret of the art: for earth is not inseparably united with water, but water strongly adheres to water: hence it follows that this praiseworthy conjunction is celebrated only after dissolution: therefore, attend to the solution, and nature will conjoin, and this dissolution occurs in Mercury through the aid of the included Luna and fire. For Luna penetrates, and whitens, and fire mortifies, and grinds, but water includes both these virtues, according to the saying of the Philosopher; *The fire which I will show you is water: and another [saying]. Unless bodies have been subtilized by fire and water, nothing is done in the magistery.* O our blessed Mercury, who frees us from so many labors which the Sophists suffer! For they perform many operations with their own hands, and accomplish nothing, because they are ignorant of the true course of nature. But we do nothing, but commit all things to be done to Mercury, who proceeds by a better method according to his natural instinct than any man can devise: for he is bound by the necessity of his end, wherefore he never deviates from the right path, if he is not hindered.

   There are, however, some Sophistic workers, who commit accepted Gold and ☿ Mercury, they enclose these in a phial, and place them over fire, expecting something excellent therefrom; but since they inject rich and good seed into sterile earth, it happens that they are deceived, for they find no harvest which they expect, because, as was said above, and will be said more widely below; Gold is not the matter of our stone in its whole essence, much less Mercury: wherefore a mere mixing of these cannot generate our stone, but Gold behaves in the work as the male for the work of generation, whose seed lies hidden in the innermost kidneys: but if it has once emitted [it], and this is received in the proper matrix, and conjoined with passive female sperm, with due heat

Thus neither can man, as man, be called the Father, nor the material of the embryo; but he has within himself such material, from which, through the conjunction of dissimilar spermatic material of the same kind, by an apt disposition, an infant is formed. I believe the same way should be understood concerning Gold. Gold is certainly the most perfect of all Metals, and the father of our stone, yet it is not its material: but the sperm which is in Gold, which it emits, if only it is treated by art, this indeed will be the very masculine material of our stone, and it is nothing other than the most digested virtue of Gold, which is extracted from it by sagacious art, and then it is called our living Gold, and not the common [Gold], which is dead: so too in the procreation of man, the man can be called dead [with respect to the act of generation] until he has poured out the due material, which he has within himself, into an apt place; it happens not dissimilarly in our art.

Therefore our Gold is not the Gold of the common people: for they differ just as the father differs from his [which he has] sperm: the former is useful and living for our work; but the latter is dead and useless, until it is vivified, that is, it emits its sperm [which is the active virtue of our stone]. So therefore proceed with the utmost caution, take this body, which I have demonstrated, and gently extract the seed from it, then indeed [and not before] this Gold [which was previously dead, idle, and useless], made living, active, and suitable for our work by this art, will suffice for you as the first material of our stone, namely the masculine, and thus this is no longer called Gold by us, but bronze, magnesia, lead, dung, nor can it properly even be called Gold; for Gold is a body, but this is chaos, that is, spirit, nor will it return by any art to its pristine form of Gold, because the body has been converted into spirit. We have said that to these must be added a furnace, a vessel, and a threefold fire: note well what and about what things I speak here; for the furnace is of clay or brick, the vessel is of glass, and the fire is elemental, about which we will speak later in the last section of this little treatise concerning our disposition: but here we speak about things essentially and substantially pertaining to the work. For indeed, that brick furnace is not usually called our furnace by us, nor the elemental fire our fire, nor the glass vessel our vessel: for these are common to the common people and to Sophists with us, and in the curiosity of these external things they often, or even always, surpass us; but we call those things ours which they neither have nor can have. Verily I say, that our fire, our furnace, our vessel are secrets, and are met with only by Philosophers, since they even enter into the very essence of our work. Hence a certain Philosopher, writing about this fire, says, "Behold, the fire which I will show you is water"; Likewise another testifies thus about the vessel: "The vessel of the Philosophers is their water." Another likewise writes that the intention of all Philosophers is this: that all operations should be done with their humid fire, in a secret furnace and a hidden vessel, which testimonies clearly enough demonstrate another fire, vessel, and furnace, than those which are commonly known. with its glorified, fiery, external, more-than-perfect (form), with all the colors of the World, like a shining carbuncle, or a transparent, compact, and heavy crystal, a Salamander spitting out waters and, by its benefit, washing away leprous metals in Fire [as I myself have seen]. What's more? They will see the ABYSS of Spagyric Art, where for so long in the Mineral Kingdom this Royal Art has lain and been hidden, as if in the safest bosom of all, for many years now. I pass over the fact that those praised genuine sons of this Art will also examine not only such a river Numicius, in which long ago, by VENUS's command, AENEAS, washed and absolved from his Mortality, was immediately transformed into an immortal God: But also the Lydian river Pactolus, entirely transformed into Gold, as soon as Midas Mygdonius had washed himself in it. Moreover, those bright rivals of this Art will also see there in a long line partly DIANA's naked Bath and NARCISSUS's fountain, and Scylla walking in the sea without clothes because of the very hot rays of the sun; partly also the blood of Pyramus and Thisbe collected by themselves, by whose help ripe mulberries are dyed red; partly also ADONIS's blood, transformed by the descending Goddess Venus into the rose of Anemone; partly also AJAX's blood, from which the most beautiful Hyacinth flower was born; partly also the blood of the Giants struck by Jove's lightning; partly also ALTHEA's shed tears, when she herself laid aside her golden garments, having taken them off; partly also drops from MEDEA's boiled water, from which grasses immediately grew forth from the earth; partly also MEDEA's Potion, cooked from various herbs collected continuously for three days during the full moon, for the healing of Jason's old father; partly also ASCLEPIUS's Medicine; partly also the Leaves, by whose taste GLACUS's whole nature is changed into Neptune; partly also JASON's pressed juice, by whose benefit he himself received the GOLDEN FLEECE in the land of Colchis, after he had nobly fought for it, armed and not without danger to his life, in the Field of Mars; partly also the garden of the Hesperides, where golden Apples can be plucked from the trees; partly also HIPPOMENES

partly also HIPPOMENES with ATALANTA running competitively for the prize, and being slowed down by the same three golden apples given by Venus, and equally overcoming her; partly also Aurora (carrying off) Cephalus; partly also Romulus transformed into a God by Jupiter; partly also the Soul of Julius Caesar transfigured into a Comet by the Goddess Venus and placed among the stars; partly also Juno's serpent Python born after Deucalion's flood from the putrid earth heated by the sun's rays; partly the FIRE by which MEDEA lit seven candles; partly also the MOON inflamed by Phaeton's conflagration; partly also a dried OLIVE shoot growing green again with berries; indeed, a new and tender OLIVE tree; partly also Arcadia, in which Jupiter used to walk; partly also PLUTO'S dwelling, at whose entrance the three-headed Cerberus kept watch; partly also that MOUNTAIN, where HERCULES burned all his limbs received from his mother upon wood, and indeed the parts from his Father remained fixed and incombustible in the fire, and nothing of his life was lost, but he himself was finally transformed into a God. Furthermore, those true, genuine sons of the Philosophers will finally enter into the TEMPLE of the transformed rustic House, whose Roof had been fashioned from pure Gold. Certainly I cannot but once more exclaim with the Adepts: O happy, and thrice happy, is that Artist who obtains from the most merciful blessing of the most high JEHOVAH the Art of making and preparing that quasi-divine SALT, by whose efficacious operation the Metallic or Mineral Body is corrupted, destroyed, dies: yet its Soul is meanwhile revived for the glorious Resurrection of the Philosophical Body. Moreover, most happy is the son of that man who obtains and procures this Art of Arts for the glory of God by his prayers. Indeed it is certain that this Mystery is known in no other way unless it is drawn and imbibed from God, the fount of founts. Therefore, let any serious Lover of this inestimable Art believe that this alone is given to him as his chief task, that in all his work he implore and solicit the nourishing grace of the Holy Spirit with perpetual vows and prayers of living faith. For God's

and whose alone is the solemn custom to communicate his Gifts from his Goods candidly and liberally to no one except to candid and liberal minds, whether Mediately or Immediately. For by this holy path of Practical Piety all seekers of arduous Arts find, if ever in their work they religiously exercise themselves Theosophically through solitary Colloquies with JEHOVAH with a pure heart and mouth. For Heavenly SOPHIA indeed seeks our friendship, by showing and offering to us her most abundant streams of gracious goodness and benevolence, and these never to be exhausted. But happy is he to whom by some Adept of this Arcanum the Royal Way shall be shown, by which he may follow it. Indeed I seem to myself to foresee that by this little Preface I have not satisfied all Readers equally, just as if I presume to teach them an Art unknown to myself, concerning a good part of whom, however, I hope for better things. For it was my purpose to narrate to you only a certain History. Therefore drink, my Friends, from the following Dialogue or gushing Colloquy benevolently offered to you by me, until you have quenched and satisfied all the thirst of your thirsty minds. For I would not doubt that this study of divine Wisdom will have been sweeter to you than any Nectar and Ambrosia. I will communicate nothing else, I have nothing in common, except that saying of Julius Caesar Scaliger, that the end of the wise is the Communication of Wisdom, according to that of Gregory of Nyssa: *He who is good by nature, the same also and entirely communicates his goods willingly with others. For it is characteristic of good men to benefit others.*

Lo, and immediately all the Quicksilver, with some noise, stopped flowing, and congealed, settling down like yellow wax; after its fusion, with the bellows blowing, eight ounces of purest Gold were found, lacking eleven grains; And so one grain of that powder had transmuted into the best Gold 19186 times its own weight in quicksilver. *The Golden Calf.* 831

Read a true Extract from a Letter written by Mr. Dr. KUFFLER.
*Kuffler:* First, in my laboratory, I found Aqua Fortis. Secondly, again in the laboratory of *Charles de Roy*, I poured that Aqua Fortis over the calx of the Sun, that is, Gold prepared in the common way, and after a third cohobation, it sublimated with itself the Tincture of Gold in the neck of the Retort, which I mixed with silver precipitated in the common way, and I saw that one ounce of the sublimated Tincture of Gold, in a crucible with ordinary flux, transmuted, from two ounces of precipitated silver, one and a half ounces into the best gold; truly, the remaining third part of the silver was white and fixed gold, and the other two parts were the best silver, fixed in every fire test. This is my experience, but afterwards we were never able to find such Aqua Fortis: And I, HELVETIUS, saw this Gold without tincture, White.
